- **Why air, rather than water, with the same mechanism?** Nothing in the theory forces the choice. He may have liked air because it is invisible, everywhere, and linked to life.
- **Condensation needs space to pack into.** Later, Parmenides and Melissus would ask whether "thinner" means "partly empty", and whether emptiness, nothing, can exist. The Milesians never faced that question; the next generation could not avoid it.

**The Milesian achievement, in one line.** Three men in one city, in about sixty years, invented the habit of saying **what the world is made of, how it works, and why, and of correcting each other's answers**.
Xenophanes: the critique of the Homeric:
A wandering poet who turned the new critical habit on religion, and then on knowledge itself.

**Who.** Xenophanes of Colophon in Ionia, **about 570 to about 475 BC**. He left home young, probably when the Persians took the city in the 540s, and in his own words had spent sixty-seven years wandering the Greek world, by then aged ninety-two. He wrote in verse, performing at dinners. He is not a natural philosopher first; he is a critic.

**The attack on anthropomorphism.** *Anthropomorphism* is picturing gods in human shape. All quotations here are from Burnet's translation (1908), using Diels's numbering:

> "Homer and Hesiod have ascribed to the gods all things that are a shame and a disgrace among mortals, stealings and adulteries and deceivings of one another." (fragment 11)

> "The Ethiopians make their gods black and snub-nosed; the Thracians say theirs have blue eyes and red hair." (fragment 16)

> "Yes, and if oxen and horses or lions had hands, and could paint with their hands, and produce works of art as men do, horses would paint the forms of the gods like horses, and oxen like oxen" (fragment 15)

**The argument, set out:**
1. Each people pictures its gods in its own likeness.
2. These pictures contradict each other, and each matches its makers too neatly to be evidence of anything but its makers.
3. So the pictures tell us about the believers, not about the gods.
4. And a being worthy of the name god could not do what Homer's gods do.

**His positive view.** "One god, the greatest among gods and men, neither in form like unto mortals nor in thought" (fragment 23). This god "sees all over, thinks all over, and hears all over" and "without toil he swayeth all things by the thought of his mind" (fragments 24–25), never moving from place to place. Whether "greatest among gods" means strict monotheism or one supreme god among lesser ones is **a genuine dispute**. (How such arguments bear on later theology is taken up in the Theology curriculum.)

**Nature.** He explained the rainbow as a coloured cloud, and Hippolytus reports that he cited **fossil shells inland and impressions of fish in rock at Syracuse** as evidence that land was once under the sea: an argument from evidence to the deep past.

**The limits of knowledge.** His most influential lines:

> "There never was nor will be a man who has certain knowledge about the gods and about all the things I speak of. Even if he should chance to say the complete truth, yet he himself knows not that it is so. But all may have their fancy." (fragment 34)

Here he separates **true belief from knowledge**: you can be right by chance and still not know. That distinction drives Plato's *Theaetetus* and most of epistemology since (*epistemology* is the study of knowledge). Yet he was no despairing sceptic: "by seeking they find in time what is better" (fragment 18). **Inquiry makes progress even without certainty.**

**The objection.** His argument shows that our pictures of god are projections; **it does not show there is no god behind them**, nor that his own "one god" is not a projection too. He seems aware of this: his own views are offered as "fancies something like the truth" (fragment 35).
Pythagoras and the Pythagoreans: number,:
The most famous name in this stage, and the hardest to pin down.

**Who.** Pythagoras was born on **Samos, about 570 BC**, and moved around **530 BC to Croton** in southern Italy, where he founded a community with its own rules of life. It gained political power, and a violent reaction later drove him to Metapontum, where he died about **495 BC** (all dates approximate). **He wrote nothing.** Within a generation he was a legend: a golden thigh, appearing in two cities at once.

**The problem of evidence.** Later Pythagoreans credited the founder with everything, and the Neoplatonist biographies of the third and fourth centuries AD (Porphyry, Iamblichus) are full of wonders. The earliest witnesses are few: Xenophanes, Heraclitus, Herodotus. Since Walter Burkert's study (1962), many scholars think **Pythagoras was mainly a religious teacher about the soul**, and that the mathematics belongs largely to later followers. Others give him more. **This is a genuine dispute.**

**What is well attested: the soul.** Pythagoras taught ***metempsychosis***, **the transmigration of the soul**: it survives death and is reborn in other bodies, human and animal. Xenophanes mocked it. In Burnet's rendering (1908), Pythagoras saw a dog being ill-treated: "'Stop!' he said, 'don't hit it! It is the soul of a friend! I knew it when I heard its voice.'" From this came a way of life: purifications, silence, and rules called *akousmata* ("things heard"), such as abstaining from beans. Heraclitus called him a man of much learning and no understanding.

**What his school developed: number.** The core discovery is musical. **The concords of Greek music correspond to simple whole-number ratios** of string lengths:

| Interval | Ratio |
| --- | --- |
| octave | 2 : 1 |
| fifth | 3 : 2 |
| fourth | 4 : 3 |

All use only 1, 2, 3, 4, which sum to 10, the sacred ***tetractys*** (a triangle of ten dots). If something as qualitative as harmony is secretly number, perhaps everything is. Aristotle reports that the Pythagoreans held that **things are numbers**, or are made in imitation of numbers.

**Philolaus of Croton** (about 470 to about 385 BC), the first Pythagorean whose writings partly survive, put it more carefully: the world is made of **limiters and unlimiteds**, fitted together by **harmony**, and only what has number can be known. He also moved the earth from the centre: it circles a central fire.

**The theorem.** The rule about right-angled triangles was known in Babylon more than a thousand years earlier, and the proof in Euclid is not Pythagorean. **Its credit to Pythagoras is late and doubtful.** Legend also says a Pythagorean, Hippasus, discovered that the diagonal of a square cannot be measured as a ratio of whole numbers (it is *incommensurable*), and drowned for revealing it. The discovery is real; the story is not reliable.

**Why it matters.** Two ideas enter philosophy here and never leave: **that the structure of reality is mathematical**, and **that the soul is distinct from the body and its true good lies in purification**. Plato takes up both.

**The objection.** Saying that things are numbers confuses the structure of a thing with the thing itself. Aristotle pressed it: numbers have no weight, yet bodies do.
Heraclitus: the Logos, flux and the unit:
The dark sayer of Ephesus, who wrote in riddles on purpose.

**Who.** Heraclitus of Ephesus, a noble of the Ionian city, **flourished about 500 BC**. He wrote one book in short, oracular sayings; about 130 survive. Ancient readers called him "the Obscure". He despised the crowd and most other thinkers. All quotations here are from Burnet's translation (1908), with Burnet's (Bywater's) number and the DK number.

**The Logos.** *Logos* means word, account, reason, proportion. For Heraclitus it is **the rational order that runs through all things**, which his own words express but which is not his property:

> "It is wise to hearken, not to me, but to my Word, and to confess that all things are one." (1; DK B50)

Most people, he complains, live as if asleep, never grasping it, though it is common to everyone.

**The unity of opposites.** His central thesis: **opposites are bound together**, depend on each other, or are the same thing seen from two sides.

| Kind | Saying |
| --- | --- |
| **Relative to the observer** | "The sea is the purest and the impurest water. Fish can drink it, and it is good for them; to men it is undrinkable and destructive." (52; B61) |
| **One road, two directions** | "The way up and the way down is one and the same." (69; B60) |
| **Held in tension** | "It is an attunement of opposite tensions, like that of the bow and the lyre." (45; B51) |

**Strife is creative.** "War is the father of all and the king of all" (44; B53). The world exists because opposites pull against each other; peace without tension would be death. **Stability is a balance of contrary forces**, as a strung bow seems still only because both ends pull.

**Fire.** "This world, which is the same for all, no one of gods or men has made; but it was ever, is now, and ever shall be an ever-living Fire, with measures kindling, and measures going out" (20; B30). Fire is the stuff that is always changing yet keeps a constant measure: a model, perhaps, rather than a Milesian "stuff".

**The river.** "You cannot step twice into the same rivers; for fresh waters are ever flowing in upon you" (41; B91, B12). Plato read Heraclitus as teaching that **everything is always changing** (flux). **Whether that is right is a major scholarly dispute.** One reading (G. S. Kirk, 1954) says the point is the reverse: the river stays the same river *because* its waters change, so **identity is kept through change**, not destroyed by it. Others (Daniel Graham, among them) defend a version of the flux reading.

**The argument, as a defender might put it:**
1. Every thing we observe is maintained by the opposed processes that compose it.
2. What is maintained by opposed processes is a unity of opposites.
3. So everything is a unity of opposites, governed by one measured order, the Logos.

**The objections.**
- **Aristotle accused him of denying the law of non-contradiction** (that a thing cannot both be and not be so, in the same respect). The reply: Heraclitus' opposites usually differ in respect ("good for fish, bad for men"), so there is no contradiction.
- **The riddling style** makes him impossible to refute and easy to misuse. That may be the point: "Nature loves to hide" (10; B123).

**His ethics** fits one line: "Man's character is his fate" (121; B119).
Parmenides: the way of truth and the imp:
The most important argument in this stage, and perhaps the most influential in the history of metaphysics (the study of what there is and what it is like).

**Who.** Parmenides of Elea, a Greek city in southern Italy. **Born perhaps about 515 BC**, if Plato's report is right that he visited Athens at about 65 when Socrates was very young (about 450 BC). An older ancient date would put his birth about 540. He wrote a **poem in hexameters** (the metre of Homer), of which about 160 lines survive, mostly through Simplicius.

**The poem's shape.** A young man rides a chariot through the gates of Night and Day to a goddess, who promises to teach him two things: the **Way of Truth**, and the **opinions of mortals** in which "is no true belief at all". The framing is religious; the content is pure argument. **This is the first sustained deductive argument in Western philosophy.**

**The two ways.** The goddess says there are only two routes of inquiry: that **it is**, and cannot not be; or that **it is not**, and must not be. The second is closed, because "thou canst not know what is not ... nor utter it" (Burnet's translation, 1908). A third route, the mortals' way, treats being and not-being as "the same and not the same", and so wanders "two-faced".

**The core argument, set out as its defenders reconstruct it:**
1. Whatever can be thought or spoken of must be (you cannot think of nothing; thinking is always *of something*).
2. So what is not cannot be thought or spoken of.
3. Coming to be would mean coming from what is not. Passing away would mean going into what is not. Change would mean something becoming what it is not.
4. Each of these requires thinking of what is not.
5. **So there is no coming to be, no passing away, no change, no motion.**

**What follows about what is (fragment 8).** It is **ungenerated and imperishable**; **whole and one**, since nothing else could divide it; **continuous**, with no more of it here and less there; **motionless**; **complete**, "like the mass of a rounded sphere". The world of many changing things the senses show us is, strictly, unreal.

**Why it mattered.** **Every later Presocratic is an answer to Parmenides.** Empedocles, Anaxagoras and the atomists all accept that nothing comes from nothing, and try to rescue change as the rearrangement of things that never come to be or perish. Plato's unchanging Forms are in part his heir.

**The objections.**
- **Premise 1 is the weak point.** It seems to confuse "it is not" in the sense of *does not exist* with "it is not" in the sense of *is not F* (not red, not here). To say "the cup is not hot" is not to speak of a nothing. Plato in the *Sophist* (about 360 BC) attacked exactly this, arguing that **not-being, understood as difference, can be thought**.
- **Thinking of the non-existent seems possible**: we think of unicorns. The reply: then a unicorn is something thought; Parmenides' "what is not" is absolute nothing.
- **Is the conclusion self-refuting?** His argument is a sequence of steps; the goddess and the youth move. If nothing changes, where did the argument go?

**A broad agreement**: the argument as stated does not succeed. **A genuine dispute**: what exactly it argues. The next two lessons read the text, then the rival interpretations.
Reading: Parmenides on the two ways and:
A close reading of Parmenides' key lines, in John Burnet's translation (*Early Greek Philosophy*, second edition, 1908, Project Gutenberg). Burnet's numbers follow Diels; his "4, 5" is DK B2 with B3, and his 8 is DK B8. Italics in the original are kept as *It is*.

**The two ways (fragments 4, 5):**

> "Come now, I will tell thee—and do thou hearken to my saying and carry it away—the only two ways of search that can be thought of. The first, namely, that *It is*, and that it is impossible for it not to be, is the way of belief, for truth is its companion. The other, namely, that *It is not*, and that it must needs not be,—that, I tell thee, is a path that none can learn of at all. For thou canst not know what is not—that is impossible—nor utter it; for it is the same thing that can be thought and that can be."

| Phrase | What to notice |
| --- | --- |
| **"ways of search"** | the subject is *inquiry*: which routes can a thinker take at all |
| **"*It is*"** | **no subject is given.** What is "it"? Whatever we inquire into? Being itself? The missing subject is the root of every dispute about the poem |
| **"impossible for it not to be"** | not just "it is" but "it must be": the claim is about **necessity** |
| **"none can learn of at all"** | the second way is closed not as false but as **unlearnable**, empty |
| **"the same thing that can be thought and that can be"** | the premise doing all the work: **thinkability and being go together** |

**The first sign (fragment 8, lines 1–10):**

> "One path only is left for us to speak of, namely, that *It is*. In it are very many tokens that what is is uncreated and indestructible; for it is complete, immovable, and without end. Nor was it ever, nor will it be; for now *it is*, all at once, a continuous one. For what kind of origin for it wilt thou look for? In what way and from what source could it have drawn its increase? I shall not let thee say nor think that it came from what is not; for it can neither be thought nor uttered that anything is not. And, if it came from nothing, what need could have made it arise later rather than sooner?"

Read step by step:
1. **"tokens"** (signposts): what follows is a list of properties, each to be proved.
2. **"Nor was it ever, nor will it be; for now *it is*"**: no past or future, only a present. Some read this as the first idea of a **timeless eternity**; others as only unending duration. A genuine dispute.
3. **"from what source"**: coming to be needs a source. Not from what is (it already is); not from what is not (unthinkable). So there is no coming to be.
4. **"later rather than sooner"**: if it came from nothing, nothing could explain why then and not before. This is **Anaximander's sufficient-reason pattern**, now turned against all becoming.

**The verdict (lines 15–16):** "Our judgment thereon depends on this: "*Is it* or *is it not*?"" The whole of cosmology is reduced to a single either/or, and the either/or is decided by logic, not by looking.

**What the reading teaches.** Watch how **one premise**, that what is not cannot be thought, generates every property in turn: no birth, no death, no division, no motion. If you accept it, the conclusions are hard to escape. That is why every later thinker in this stage attacks or reinterprets that one premise, or accepts it and bargains over its consequences.
Interpreting Parmenides: strict monism a:
What did Parmenides actually claim? Scholars have argued for over a century, and the answer changes what his successors were reacting to.

**The traditional reading: strict monism.** *Monism* is the view that there is only one thing. On this reading, Parmenides holds that **exactly one thing exists**, a single, changeless, undivided whole, and that the plural, changing world is an illusion. This is how Plato and Aristotle mostly took him, and how G. E. L. Owen read the argument in an influential paper of 1960. Its strength: it explains why Zeno defends him by attacking plurality, and why Melissus says outright that what is is "one".

**The predicational reading.** Associated with Alexander Mourelatos (1970) and Patricia Curd (1998). The "it is" of the poem is the "is" of **predication**: "X is F" (the *predicate* is what is said of a subject). Parmenides is setting a standard for **what a genuine, fundamental thing must be**: whatever it is, it must be that wholly, unchangingly, with nothing of "is not" mixed in. Such things could in principle be many. Its strength: it makes the later pluralists (Empedocles, Anaxagoras, the atomists) **followers who obey his rules** with many such things, rather than rebels who simply ignore him.

**The modal reading.** John Palmer (2009): the poem is about **what must be**, the way of necessary being, as opposed to what is and is not by turns. Parmenides describes necessary being without denying that the ordinary world exists in its own lesser way.

**Comparing them:**

| Reading | "It is" means | The many changing things |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Strict monism** | there exists (one thing only) | do not exist |
| **Predicational** | is, wholly and stably, what it is | are not fundamental things |
| **Modal** | is, and necessarily is | exist, but contingently |

**The problem of the Way of Opinion.** After the Way of Truth, the goddess gives a full cosmology, built on two forms, light and night, which she calls "the deceptive ordering of my words" (Burnet, 1908). Why would Parmenides write a long account of a world he has just proved unreal? The proposals:
1. **A warning example**: the best false account, so you will not be fooled by worse ones.
2. **A second-best**: what can be said of appearances, which we must live among.
3. **A dialectical exercise**: the views of others, set out to be refuted.

None is agreed. Note that his cosmology included real discoveries: he is reported to have said **the moon shines by light from the sun**.

**What everyone agrees on.** Whatever "it is" meant, Parmenides left two demands that no Greek after him could ignore:
- **Nothing comes from nothing**, and nothing passes into nothing.
- **Reason can overrule the senses**: an argument may show that what we see is not how things are.

**Why the dispute matters.** If he was a strict monist, later thinkers simply rejected him, at the price of ignoring a valid-seeming argument. If he set standards for real being, they accepted his rules and **looked for a way to have many such beings and still explain change**. That second story is how this stage's remaining natural philosophers make most sense.
Zeno of Elea: the paradoxes against plur:
Parmenides' pupil defended the master not by repeating his argument but by showing that the opposite view is worse.

**Who.** Zeno of Elea, **born about 490 BC**. Plato's *Parmenides* has him visit Athens at about forty with Parmenides. He wrote one book of arguments; a late source says there were forty. Aristotle called him the inventor of **dialectic**, arguing from an opponent's own premises.

**The method: *reductio ad absurdum*.** "Reduction to absurdity": **assume what your opponent believes, and derive a contradiction from it.** Then the assumption must be false. Plato has Zeno explain his purpose: his book answers those who mocked Parmenides, showing that **their hypothesis, that there are many things, leads to consequences even more absurd** than Parmenides' one.

**The paradox of size (DK B1–B2, from Simplicius).** Suppose there are many things.
1. Each of the many must be one thing, a unit.
2. A true unit has no parts, so it has no size (anything with size could be divided).
3. A thing with no size, added to another, makes it no bigger. So the many, made of sizeless units, are **so small as to be nothing**.
4. But if each thing does have size, it has parts, each with size, each with parts, without end. So each thing contains **infinitely many parts of some size**, and is **infinitely large**.
5. So if there are many, they are both nothing in size and infinite in size. Absurd.

**The paradox of number (DK B3).**
1. If there are many, they are just as many as they are: a definite, **limited** number.
2. But between any two things there must be another (else they would not be two, but touching, one), and between those, others.
3. So they are **unlimited** in number.
4. Both limited and unlimited: absurd.

**The paradox of place**, reported by Aristotle: if everything that is is *in* a place, the place too is something, so it is in a place, and so on without end.

**The objections and replies.**
- **The size paradox fails at step 4**, on the modern view. Dividing a line forever yields infinitely many parts, but **their sizes shrink**, and infinitely many shrinking sizes can add up to a finite total (as 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 ... = 1). The deeper reply, made precise only in the nineteenth century with Cantor's set theory, is that a line is made of points of zero size, but **uncountably many** of them, and size is not got by adding up points one by one.
- **The number paradox** plays on the idea that "between any two there is a third". That is true of points on a line, false of, say, people in a room. So it refutes plurality only for continuous things.
- **Aristotle's reply** distinguished a **potential** infinity (a line *can* be divided without end) from an **actual** one (a line *is* made of infinitely many actual parts). Zeno, he said, assumes the second; only the first is true.

**The verdict.** **There is broad agreement that, given modern mathematics, these paradoxes do not prove that plurality is impossible.** There is less agreement about whether mathematics fully answers the physical and metaphysical questions behind them, which is why they are still taught.
Zeno's paradoxes of motion: the dichotom:
Four arguments, preserved by Aristotle in *Physics* VI.9, that motion is impossible. They are the most famous puzzles in ancient philosophy.

**1. The dichotomy (the race course).** *Dichotomy* means "cutting in two". As Burnet (1908) sets out Aristotle's report:

> "You cannot traverse an infinite number of points in a finite time. You must traverse the half of any given distance before you traverse the whole, and the half of that again before you can traverse it."

So to run any distance you must complete **infinitely many tasks**, and you cannot complete infinitely many tasks. So you cannot start, let alone finish.

**2. Achilles and the tortoise.** In Burnet's words:

> "Achilles will never overtake the tortoise. He must first reach the place from which the tortoise started. By that time the tortoise will have got some way ahead."

Every time he reaches where it was, it has moved on. **The fastest can never catch the slowest.**

**3. The arrow.** At any instant, a flying arrow occupies a space exactly its own size. Something that occupies a space just its own size, at an instant, is at rest there. Time is made of instants. **So the arrow is at rest at every instant, and never moves.**

**4. The stadium (moving rows).** Three rows of equal blocks: one still, two moving past it in opposite directions at the same speed. A block in a moving row passes two blocks of the other moving row in the time it passes one block of the still row. If the smallest units of time and space are indivisible, then **half the time equals the whole**. Aristotle thought this a simple mistake about relative speed. **Many modern scholars think its target is the assumption that space and time come in indivisible minimal units**, against which it has real force.

**The standard modern reply to the first two.** **An infinite series can have a finite sum.** If Achilles runs ten times as fast and gives a 10-metre start, the catch-up distances are 10 + 1 + 0.1 + 0.01 ... metres, which sum to exactly 11 1/9 metres, run in a finite time. The calculus of limits (made rigorous by Cauchy and Weierstrass in the nineteenth century) proves this.

**But is the sum enough?** Defenders of Zeno's point reply: **knowing that the sum is finite does not explain how infinitely many acts can be completed one after another.** This led to debate about "supertasks", an infinite series of tasks done in finite time. James Thomson's lamp (1954), switched on and off infinitely often within a minute, asks: is it on or off at the end? There is no agreed answer.

**The standard modern reply to the arrow.** Bertrand Russell's **"at-at" theory** (1903): motion simply *is* being at different places at different instants. There is no extra "moving" state at an instant. An arrow at rest and a moving arrow are alike at any single instant, and differ only in where they are at *other* instants. Critics say this leaves out velocity, which seems a real property of the arrow *now*.

**Aristotle's reply.** Time is not made of instants, nor a line of points; both are continuous and only **potentially** divisible. You cross infinitely many *potential* halves without performing infinitely many *actual* tasks.

**The verdict.** **Broad agreement**: motion is not impossible, and the paradoxes rely on assumptions (that infinitely many tasks cannot be done, that time is made of instants with no further facts) that can be denied. **Open**: which denial is right, and whether physics' continuous space and time is the true picture.
Melissus of Samos: Eleatic monism in pro:
The last of the Eleatics was an admiral, and he made Parmenides' conclusions plainer, and in one respect different.

**Who.** Melissus of Samos, **flourished about 441 BC**. Plutarch reports that he commanded the Samian fleet that **defeated an Athenian squadron during the Samian revolt of 441–440 BC**. He was not from Elea, but is grouped with the *Eleatics* (Parmenides' followers) because he defended the same conclusions. He wrote in clear prose, and about ten fragments survive through Simplicius. Quotations are from Burnet (1908).

**The argument, in his own order:**
1. "What was was ever, and ever shall be. For, if it had come into being, it needs must have been nothing before it came into being. Now, if it were nothing, in no wise could anything have arisen out of nothing." (fragment 1)
2. What has no beginning and no end in time is **without limit**.
3. It is unlimited in size as well. "If it were not one, it would be bounded by something else" (fragment 5). So **it is one**.
4. It is alike throughout, and cannot change: "if it changed by so much as a single hair in ten thousand years, it would all perish in the whole of time" (fragment 7).
5. **There is no void.** "Nor is anything empty. For what is empty is nothing. What is nothing cannot be." (fragment 7)
6. **So there is no motion**: "it has nowhere to betake itself to, but is full." (fragment 7)

**Where he differs from Parmenides.** Parmenides' being had a limit, like a sphere. Melissus says it is **infinite** in extent. He also states explicitly that it is **one**, and that it feels no pain or grief: things the poem left vague.

**Two big contributions.**
- **The void becomes the issue.** Melissus makes explicit that motion needs empty space to move into, and that empty space would be "nothing". **The atomists will accept the first premise and deny the second**: they will say the void exists.
- **The challenge to pluralism (fragment 8).** "If there were a many, these would have to be of the same kind as I say that the one is." That is: if you want many real things, each must be ungenerated, unchanging, and full. **Leucippus and Democritus took this as a recipe**: their atoms are exactly Melissus' "one", multiplied.

**The objections.**
- **Aristotle thought him crude.** Step 2 slides from "no beginning in time" to "no limit in space", a fallacy of equivocation (using "limit" in two senses), and Aristotle also charged him with arguing that because what has come into being has a beginning, what has not come into being has none, which does not follow.
- **The argument against change** assumes that any change means something coming from nothing. Aristotle's later reply: change is a subject gaining or losing a form, so nothing comes from absolute nothing.
- **Against the senses**, Melissus argued that our senses contradict themselves (we see hard iron worn away by a finger), so cannot be trusted. Critics reply that showing the senses *sometimes* mislead does not show they *always* do.

**The verdict.** He is generally ranked below Parmenides in depth but above him in clarity, and **his statement of the Eleatic case is the form that the atomists answered**.
Empedocles: the four roots, Love and Str:
A Sicilian poet, healer and self-proclaimed god who found a way to keep the world of change without breaking Parmenides' rules.

**Who.** Empedocles of Acragas (modern Agrigento, Sicily), **about 495 to about 435 BC**. He was active in his city's politics, reputedly refused a crown, and claimed miraculous powers. Legend says he leapt into the crater of Etna to prove himself divine. He wrote in hexameters: a poem *On Nature* and *Purifications* (some scholars think these were one poem). In 1999 a papyrus at Strasbourg, published by Alain Martin and Oliver Primavesi, added new lines. Quotations here are from Burnet (1908), using Diels's numbers.

**Accepting Parmenides.** Empedocles agrees that nothing comes from nothing:

> "Fools!—for they have no far-reaching thoughts—who deem that what before was not comes into being, or that aught can perish and be utterly destroyed." (fragments 11–12)

**The rescue: mixture.** What we call birth and death are only mixing and separating of things that always exist: "There is no coming into being of aught that perishes, nor any end for it in baneful death; but only mingling and change of what has been mingled" (fragment 8).

**The four roots.** He names four eternal, unchanging stuffs, giving them divine names: "Hear first the four roots of all things: shining Zeus, life-bringing Hera, Aidoneus, and Nestis" (fragment 6). Which god is which element is disputed in antiquity and now, but the roots are **fire, air, earth and water**. **This is the origin of the four elements**, which Aristotle adopted and which dominated Western science until the seventeenth century.

**The two forces.** Mixture needs a cause. Empedocles names two: **Love** (*Philotēs*), which unites unlike things, and **Strife** (*Neikos*), which separates them. **For the first time, the stuff of the world and the causes of its motion are kept apart.**

**The cosmic cycle.** "I shall tell thee a twofold tale. At one time it grew to be one only out of many; at another, it divided up to be many instead of one" (fragment 17). Under Love, all comes together into a perfect **Sphere**; under Strife, all separates into four masses; our world lies between. The cycle repeats forever. Its exact stages are **much disputed**, and the Strasbourg papyrus reopened the question.

**Living things.** He described a stage in which separate limbs wandered and joined at random, producing monsters; only combinations that fitted survived. Aristotle (*Physics* II.8) took this as the view that order arises by chance, and rejected it. **Calling it a theory of natural selection is an overstatement**, but it is the first known idea that fit forms might be what survives out of random combination.

**An experiment.** He used the *clepsydra*, a vessel with holes in its base, to show that **air is a body**: with the top closed, water cannot enter, because air fills the space (fragment 100).

**The soul.** In the *Purifications*, he teaches transmigration, like the Pythagoreans, and says he has himself been a boy, a girl, a bush, a bird and a fish.

**The objections.**
- **Why four, and why these?** The number seems chosen, not argued for.
- **Love and Strife are pictures, not mechanisms.** They name the fact that things join and part, without saying how.
- **Does mixture save Parmenides' rules?** A strict Eleatic answers no: rearrangement is still motion, and motion still needs a place that was empty. Empedocles denies there is any void, so the objection bites.
Anaxagoras: everything in everything, an:
The man who brought philosophy to Athens, and was tried there for saying the sun is a stone.

**Who.** Anaxagoras of Clazomenae in Ionia, **about 500 to about 428 BC**. He settled in Athens and lived there for many years (the dates are disputed), a friend of Pericles, Athens' leading statesman. He was **prosecuted for impiety** for saying the sun was a fiery stone, and withdrew to Lampsacus, where he died. Quotations are from Burnet (1908), Diels's numbers.

**Science.** He explained **eclipses correctly**: the moon shines with light from the sun, and is eclipsed by the earth's shadow. The fall of a large meteorite at Aegospotami in 467 BC was linked by ancient writers to his view that the heavenly bodies are hot stones.

**The starting point.** He accepts Parmenides: nothing comes into being or perishes. "Coming to be" is only mixing and separating. But unlike Empedocles he will not stop at four roots. The question is pointed:

> "How can hair come from what is not hair, or flesh from what is not flesh?" (fragment 10)

We eat bread, and it becomes hair and flesh. If nothing comes from nothing, **hair and flesh must already be in the bread**.

**The theory: everything in everything.** In the beginning "All things were together infinite both in number and in smallness" (fragment 1). And still, now: "In everything there is a portion of everything except Nous" (fragment 11). Gold is not pure gold; it is a mixture in which gold predominates. **There are no elements, only predominance.** There is also no smallest piece: matter can be divided without end, and every piece still holds a portion of everything.

**Mind (Nous).** What set the mixture moving and sorting? Anaxagoras' answer is *Nous*, **mind** or intellect:

> "Nous is infinite and self-ruled, and is mixed with nothing, but is alone, itself by itself." (fragment 12)

It is "the thinnest of all things and the purest", "has all knowledge about everything and the greatest strength", and began a **rotation** that separated the dense from the rare, the hot from the cold, and spreads further still. **For the first time, a mind is named as the cause of the cosmos**, and set apart from the matter it orders.

**Socrates' disappointment.** In Plato's *Phaedo* (97b–99c), Socrates says that as a young man he was thrilled to read that Mind orders all things, expecting to learn **why each thing is arranged for the best**. Instead, Anaxagoras explained everything by air, water and whirling. **Mind starts the machine and then does nothing.** This complaint launches the search for purposive explanation in Plato and Aristotle.

**The objections.**
- **The theory seems to explain too much.** If everything is in everything, one can always say any change was the predominant ingredient emerging. Critics ask what could ever count against it.
- **Aristotle** objected that infinitely many infinitely mixed ingredients cannot be known, and so explain nothing.
- **Is Nous material?** It is "thinnest" and "purest", which sounds like a very fine stuff. Scholars dispute whether Anaxagoras reached the idea of a fully immaterial mind or only of a special, unmixed kind of matter.
Leucippus and Democritus: atoms and the:
The most successful answer to Parmenides, and the ancestor of modern physics, in a very loose sense.

**Who.** **Leucippus**, flourished about 440 BC, from Miletus or Abdera (sources disagree); so little is known that Epicurus later claimed he never existed. **Democritus of Abdera** in Thrace, **about 460 to about 370 BC**, his pupil, wrote an enormous range of books on physics, ethics, mathematics and music. Hundreds of short sayings survive, mostly ethical, and some are of doubtful authenticity. **Their physical theories cannot be fully separated**, so they are treated together.

**Accepting the Eleatic rules.** Real being cannot come to be or perish, change in itself, or be divided without end (Zeno showed the trouble that brings). Melissus said: if there were many, each would have to be like the one. **The atomists said: then let there be many such ones.**

**The theory.**
- **Atoms.** *Atomos* means **uncuttable**. Infinitely many tiny, solid bodies, each ungenerated, indestructible, unchanging and full, with no empty space inside. They are too small to see.
- **The void.** Empty space. Here is the bold move: **"what is not" exists.** Aristotle reports their slogan that what is not is no less real than what is. The void is nothing, but it is real, and it is what allows the atoms to move.
- **Motion.** Atoms move eternally through the void, collide, rebound and **entangle** by their shapes (hooks, barbs, hollows), forming the things we see. Worlds form and dissolve without end.
- **Necessity, not purpose.** The single surviving sentence of Leucippus, in Burnet's translation (1908): "Naught happens for nothing," ... "but everything from a ground and of necessity."

**How atoms differ.** Aristotle (*Metaphysics* I.4) gives their three ways, with letters as examples:

| Difference | Example |
| --- | --- |
| **shape** | A differs from N |
| **arrangement** | AN differs from NA |
| **position** | Z differs from N (the same letter turned on its side) |

**Just as a few letters make every word, a few kinds of difference make every thing.**

**The argument, as an atomist might put it:**
1. Real being is unchanging and ungenerated (Parmenides).
2. Yet we observe motion and change.
3. Motion requires empty space; so the void exists, and what is real is many, separated by void.
4. Infinite division would dissolve bodies into nothing (Zeno); so division stops at uncuttable bodies.
5. So the world is atoms moving in void, and all change is their rearrangement.

**The objections.**
- **Aristotle**: a void is unintelligible (how can nothing be a place?), and an indivisible body with size seems self-contradictory, since anything extended has a left and a right half.
- **Where do colour, taste and warmth come from**, if atoms have only shape, size and position? The atomists bit this bullet, as the next lesson shows.
- **Necessity with no purpose** leaves no room for Socrates' question of why things are arranged for the best. Plato and Aristotle rejected atomism largely for this reason; Epicurus revived it (Stage 5).

**The verdict.** Ancient atomism was a speculative theory with no experimental test, and its atoms are not modern atoms. **But its central idea, that the visible world is explained by the arrangement of small, invisible, law-governed parts, has proved the most fruitful idea in this stage.**
Democritus on knowledge and the cheerful:
If only atoms and void are real, what becomes of what we see and feel, and how should we live?

**The senses.** Democritus drew the consequence of his physics plainly. The sceptic Sextus Empiricus (about AD 200) and the physician Galen (second century AD) preserve his most famous saying, here **paraphrased**: by convention there is sweet, by convention bitter, by convention hot and cold, by convention colour; in reality there are atoms and void (DK B9, B125). "By convention" (*nomō*) means **by human usage, not in the nature of things**.

**What this means.** Qualities such as colour and taste are **effects of atoms on our sense organs**, not properties of atoms. Sweet is how smooth, round atoms affect the tongue; bitter, how sharp, hooked ones do. This is the first statement of the distinction later called **primary and secondary qualities** (by John Locke, 1690): shape and size belong to things themselves; colour and taste exist only in perceivers. It will return in Stage 9.

**Two kinds of knowledge.** Democritus distinguished (DK B11, here paraphrased) a **"genuine"** kind of knowledge, reached by reasoning, from a **"bastard"** (illegitimate) kind given by sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch. When the senses can go no finer, reason takes over.

**The sceptical worry.** Galen preserves a reply Democritus gave to himself (DK B125, paraphrased): the senses say to the mind, "wretched mind, you take your evidence from us, and yet you would overthrow us? Our overthrow is your fall." **The theory that the senses mislead was itself built from what the senses report.** If they cannot be trusted, neither can the theory. Democritus saw the problem; he did not solve it. Whether he was a sceptic or only cautious is **disputed**.

**The ethics: cheerfulness.** Most surviving sayings are ethical, and they make him the first Greek to leave a substantial body of moral advice. The goal is ***euthymia***, **cheerfulness** or contentment: a calm, well-balanced state of soul. It comes from:
- **moderation**: neither too much nor too little pleasure;
- **measuring yourself against those worse off**, not those better;
- **doing your own business**, and not taking on more than you can bear;
- **acting rightly from shame before yourself**, not only before others.

**Does it follow from the physics?** One can link them: a soul made of fine atoms is disturbed by violent motions, so strong passions literally shake it. But **many scholars think the ethics stands largely on its own**, as practical wisdom.

**Objections.**
- **If everything happens of necessity, is there any point in advice?** The question returns with Epicurus, who added a random swerve of atoms partly to answer it.
- **If colours are only convention, so perhaps are values.** Democritus himself did not say so, but the link between his "by convention" and the Sophists' debate over law and nature is direct.
The Sophists: teachers of virtue for a f:
In the second half of the fifth century, philosophy turned from the heavens to the city. The men who led the turn were called Sophists, and Plato made their name an insult.

**The word.** *Sophistēs* first meant simply **a wise man, an expert**. By the late fifth century it meant **a travelling professional teacher who charged fees**. Plato's hostility made "sophist" mean a trickster with words, and "sophistry" clever, dishonest argument. Keep the two senses apart.

**Why they appeared.** In democratic Athens, a citizen had to speak in the assembly and defend himself in court, with no lawyers. **Success depended on persuasion.** Wealthy families would pay to have their sons taught to speak, argue and manage affairs. The Sophists offered to teach ***aretē***, **excellence** or **virtue**: the skill of living and managing well, in public and private.

**The main figures.**

| Sophist | Dates (about) | Known for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Protagoras** of Abdera | 490–420 BC | "man is the measure"; two arguments on every question |
| **Gorgias** of Leontini | 483–376 BC | rhetoric; *On What Is Not* |
| **Prodicus** of Ceos | 465–after 399 BC | the correct use of words |
| **Hippias** of Elis | late fifth century | universal knowledge; nature against law |
| **Thrasymachus** of Chalcedon | late fifth century | in Plato, justice is the advantage of the stronger |
| **Antiphon** | late fifth century | *On Truth*; law against nature |

**Prodicus.** He taught ***orthoepeia***, "correctness of words": **careful distinctions between near-synonyms**, such as "enjoying" and "taking pleasure". Plato's *Protagoras* teases him for it, yet it is an early form of the philosophy of language. He also proposed that **people first deified whatever was useful to them**, such as bread and wine and rivers: an early natural account of religion. And he wrote the parable of **the Choice of Heracles**, preserved by Xenophon (*Memorabilia* II.1): young Heracles at a crossroads meets two women, Vice offering an easy path and Virtue a hard one, and chooses Virtue.

**What they shared.**
- **A focus on human affairs**: ethics, politics, language, education.
- **Relativism in some form**: different peoples have different customs, and the Greeks had seen enough of the world to know it.
- **Argument on both sides**: a trained speaker can argue for and against any thesis.
- **Scepticism about the natural philosophers**, whose rival theories of the cosmos contradicted each other.

**The case against them (Plato's).** They took money, so their teaching served whoever paid. They taught people to win arguments, not to find the truth. Their relativism dissolved the basis of morality. Socrates, by contrast, took no fees and sought definitions.

**The case for them.** Since George Grote's *History of Greece* (1846–56), many historians have argued that **Plato's portrait is a caricature**. The Sophists were the first to study language, rhetoric, the origins of society and the nature of law; they were the Greek enlightenment's educators. G. B. Kerferd's *The Sophistic Movement* (1981) made this case influentially. Even Socrates was mistaken for one by his fellow citizens, as Aristophanes' comedy *Clouds* (423 BC) shows.

**What is agreed.** They were not a school with a doctrine but a profession with common methods. **Most of what they wrote is lost**, and much of what survives comes through their enemy Plato, so judgement must be cautious.
Protagoras: man the measure, and the god:
The first and most respected Sophist, and the first clear relativist in Western philosophy.

**Who.** Protagoras of Abdera, **about 490 to about 420 BC**. He taught for some forty years and visited Athens several times. According to a report in Diogenes Laertius, Pericles asked him to write laws for the new colony of Thurii (founded 444/3 BC). Plato's dialogue *Protagoras* treats him with real respect.

**The measure doctrine.** It opened his book, called *Truth*. Plato quotes it in the *Theaetetus* (152a), in Benjamin Jowett's translation (first published 1871):

> "Man, he says, is the measure of all things, of the existence of things that are, and of the non-existence of things that are not"

Socrates glosses it: things are to you such as they appear to you, and to me as they appear to me. His example: the same wind blows; one of us feels cold, the other does not. **Is the wind cold?** Protagoras: it is cold *for* the one who feels it cold, and not for the other. **There is no further fact about the wind in itself.**

**Readings of "man".** It is **disputed** whether "man" means:
1. **each individual** (what seems to me is true for me): individual relativism, Plato's reading;
2. **each community** (what a city believes just is just, for it): cultural relativism;
3. **humanity**, as opposed to the gods: we can know only as humans can.

**The self-refutation objection.** Plato's *Theaetetus* (171a–c) presses it, and it is the objection most often called decisive:
1. Protagoras says every belief is true for whoever holds it.
2. Many people believe Protagoras' doctrine is false.
3. So, by his own doctrine, it is true (for them) that his doctrine is false.
4. So he must grant that his own view is false for most people, and cannot claim it is true *simpliciter* (without qualification).

**Replies.** A defender can say "true for them" is all Protagoras ever claimed, so step 4 is no defeat, only a restatement. The rejoinder: then the doctrine gives us **no reason to accept it**, since it is no more true than its denial. **There is broad agreement that a global relativism about truth faces this problem; whether a careful relativist can escape it is still argued.**

**The gods.** Another book began with words reported by Diogenes Laertius, here **paraphrased**: about the gods I cannot know whether they exist or not, or what they are like; many things prevent knowing, the obscurity of the subject and the shortness of human life. This is **agnosticism** (from the Greek for "not knowing"): not denial, but suspension of judgement. Late reports say his books were burned in Athens; the story is doubted.

**Two arguments on every question.** He held that there are two opposed arguments (*logoi*) on every matter, and claimed to teach how to **make the weaker argument the stronger** (the phrase is reported by Aristotle). Critics heard: make the worse cause win. Defenders hear a skill: finding the case that has been underrated.

**Virtue can be taught.** In Plato's *Protagoras* (320c–328d), he tells a myth: Zeus sent Hermes to give all humans reverence and justice. In Jowett's translation, the god answers Hermes: "'To all,' said Zeus; 'I should like them all to have a share; for cities cannot exist, if a few only share in the virtues, as in the arts." The moral: **every citizen has a share of political virtue**, which is why democracy lets everyone speak on justice, and teachers like Protagoras can improve it. It is one of the first arguments for democracy.
Gorgias: On What Is Not and the power of:
The Sicilian master of rhetoric, who wrote a parody of Eleatic metaphysics, or perhaps the real thing.

**Who.** Gorgias of Leontini in Sicily, **about 483 to about 376 BC**; he is said to have lived well past a hundred. In **427 BC** he came to Athens as an ambassador asking for help against Syracuse, and dazzled the Assembly with his style: rhyming clauses, balanced antitheses, poetic words in prose. Plato named a dialogue after him.

**On What Is Not, or On Nature.** The book is lost; two summaries survive, one in Sextus Empiricus (*Against the Logicians*), one in a short treatise falsely attributed to Aristotle. It argues three theses, each a fall-back for the last:

1. **Nothing exists.**
2. **Even if something exists, it cannot be known.**
3. **Even if it can be known, it cannot be communicated to another.**

**The arguments, in outline (paraphrased from Sextus).**
- **For 1.** If something exists, it is either what is, or what is not, or both. What is not cannot exist. What is cannot exist either: it would have to be either generated or eternal, and Gorgias uses Eleatic-style arguments against each. Both together is impossible. So nothing exists.
- **For 2.** What we think is not the same as what is: we can think of a chariot racing on the sea, and that does not make it so. So thinking of something does not show that it exists, and existence cannot be grasped by thought.
- **For 3.** We communicate by words, but words are not the things they name; colours are seen and sounds heard, and a word cannot carry the colour. So what is known cannot be passed on.

**What was he doing? A genuine dispute.**
- **A parody**: he turns the Eleatics' own methods against them, showing they can "prove" the exact opposite of Parmenides. On this reading the target is philosophy's pretension to prove things about being by argument alone.
- **A rhetorical showpiece**: a demonstration of how far skilled argument can go.
- **Serious philosophy**: a real sceptical case, and an early study of the gap between thought, language and reality.
Many scholars now hold that it can be both a display and philosophically serious.

**The *Encomium of Helen*.** An *encomium* is a speech of praise. This one survives whole. Gorgias defends Helen of Troy, blamed for causing the Trojan War. She went to Troy for one of four reasons: the will of the gods, force, persuasion by words, or love. In each case she is not to blame. The core is about speech: here **paraphrased**, he calls *logos* a great power that with the smallest body does the most divine work, acting on the soul **as drugs act on the body**. He ends by calling the speech his own plaything.

**Why it matters.** Gorgias puts on the table the question of rhetoric: **if speech can move souls regardless of truth, what makes persuasion legitimate?** Plato's *Gorgias* (probably the 380s BC) is a long answer, and Aristotle's *Rhetoric* another.

**The objection.** The three-thesis argument refutes itself in practice: Gorgias communicates, in words, an argument that nothing can be communicated in words. Defenders reply that this is exactly the joke.
Nomos and physis: is justice natural or:
The most important ethical debate of the fifth century, and one that has never closed.

**The two words.** ***Nomos***: law, custom, convention; what is so because people have made or agreed it. ***Physis***: nature; what is so of itself, whatever anyone thinks. Democritus applied the pair to colour and taste. The Sophists applied it to **justice, morality, and the gods**.

**The background.** Greeks who travelled saw customs vary wildly. Herodotus (writing about 430 BC) tells how the Persian king Darius asked some Greeks what they would take to eat their dead fathers, and some Indians, the Callatiae, what they would take to burn theirs: both were horrified. He concludes, with the poet Pindar, that **custom is king of all**. If customs differ so, are any of them by nature?

**Position 1: law is a tyrant over nature.** In Plato's *Protagoras* (337c–d), the Sophist Hippias says, in Jowett's translation (first published 1871): "by nature like is akin to like, whereas law is the tyrant of mankind, and often compels us to do many things which are against nature." **Antiphon**, in papyrus fragments of *On Truth* found at Oxyrhynchus in Egypt and published in 1915 and 1922, argues (here **paraphrased**) that the rules of law are agreed, while those of nature are necessary; so one should keep the laws when witnesses are present and follow nature when alone, since breaking a law harms you only if you are seen. (Whether this Antiphon is the same man as the Athenian orator Antiphon is **disputed**.)

**Position 2: nature's justice is the rule of the stronger.** Plato gives the strongest form to Callicles, in the *Gorgias* (483b–484a, Jowett's translation):

> "the makers of laws are the majority who are weak; and they make laws and distribute praises and censures with a view to themselves and to their own interests ... nature herself intimates that it is just for the better to have more than the worse, the more powerful than the weaker"

Set out:
1. Conventional justice was made by the weak majority, to protect themselves.
2. In nature, among animals and between cities, the strong rule and take more.
3. What nature shows is just, by nature.
4. So conventional justice is a fraud, and true justice is the strong taking more.

**Position 3: convention is what makes us human.** The Protagoras of Plato's dialogue, and the "Anonymous of Iamblichus" (an unnamed late fifth-century writer), argue the reverse: without law, humans would destroy one another; **nomos is not against our nature but what lets it flourish**. Plato's Glaucon, in *Republic* II, states a related view: justice is a **social contract**, a compromise between doing wrong freely and suffering it.

**The objections.**
- **Against Callicles**: step 3 assumes that whatever happens in nature is right, which is exactly what is in question. (Inferring what ought to be from what is was later criticised by Hume; see Stage 9.) Also, if the weak majority combine and win, by his own standard they *are* the stronger.
- **Against Antiphon**: if justice pays only when you are watched, why did nearly every culture make it a virtue? Plato's whole *Republic* is an attempt to show **justice is good for the just person even unseen**.
- **Against pure conventionalism**: if all morality is convention, the claim "our convention is better than slavery" says nothing. Defenders reply that conventions can still be compared by how well they serve human needs.

**Open.** Whether there is a natural law of justice, discoverable by reason, is debated to this day; the tradition of **natural law** starts here, in reaction.
Looking back: from the Milesians to the:
About a hundred and fifty years, from Thales' eclipse in 585 BC to the Sophists in Athens, in which the main questions of Western philosophy were first asked.

**What was invented.**
- **Natural explanation**: the world explained by its own stuff and laws, not by the choices of gods (the Milesians).
- **Argument as a public practice**: claims made with reasons, and corrected by rivals.
- **Deductive proof** from premises to necessary conclusions (Parmenides), and **reductio ad absurdum** (Zeno).
- **The critique of religion** by reason (Xenophanes), and the distinction between **true belief and knowledge**.
- **Mathematical structure as the key to nature** (the Pythagoreans).
- **The study of language, rhetoric and law** (the Sophists).

**The great sequence, in one table.**

| Problem | Answer |
| --- | --- |
| What is everything made of? | water; the boundless; air; fire |
| How can one stuff become many? | condensation and rarefaction (Anaximenes); balanced opposites (Heraclitus) |
| Can anything come to be at all? | **no**: what is not cannot be thought (Parmenides, Zeno, Melissus) |
| Then how is there change? | mixture of four roots (Empedocles); everything in everything (Anaxagoras); atoms in the void (Leucippus, Democritus) |
| Are our laws and gods by nature? | convention, nature, or the rule of the strong (the Sophists) |

**What was broadly settled.**
- **Nothing comes from nothing.** Every thinker after Parmenides accepted it; it remained a fixed point of physics until modern times.
- **The senses can be overruled by reason.** Parmenides' demand stuck, though how far reason may override them was left open.
- **Zeno's paradoxes do not prove motion impossible**, by broad modern agreement, though what exactly goes wrong was disputed for two thousand years.

**What was left open.**
1. **What is "being"?** Parmenides' "it is" was never agreed on. Plato's *Sophist* and Aristotle's distinction of the senses of "is" are attempts to answer him.
2. **Change.** The pluralists rescued it as rearrangement, at the price of saying nothing really changes, only moves. Aristotle will propose another way: change as a subject gaining a form it lacked.
3. **Explanation by purpose.** Anaxagoras named Mind and then explained by whirling. The atomists dropped purpose altogether. Is the world ordered *for* anything?
4. **The soul.** Pythagoras and Empedocles taught that it survives death; Democritus made it atoms. Which is right?
5. **Knowledge.** Xenophanes, Democritus and Protagoras all raised doubts. Can we know anything for certain, and how?
6. **Justice.** Is it natural, conventional, or the interest of the strong? Is it good for the one who has it?

**What the next stage picks up.** **Socrates** (469–399 BC) turned from nature to the questions of the Sophists, but rejected their answers and their fees: he asked what justice, courage and virtue *are*, and showed that those who claimed to know could not say. **Plato** (about 428–348 BC) then took up nearly every open question above: Parmenides' changeless being (the Forms), the Pythagorean soul, Heraclitean flux as the condition of the visible world, Anaxagoras' unfulfilled promise of a mind ordering all for the best, and Callicles and Thrasymachus as the opponents his *Gorgias* and *Republic* exist to answer.
Context: Athens in the age of Socrates a:
Socrates and Plato are Athenians, and their questions are Athens' questions. To read them you need the city they lived in.

**Socrates** was born in Athens about **470/469 BC** and executed there in **399 BC**. **Plato** was born about **428/427 BC** and died about **348/347 BC**. Between them they span the city's greatest century and its worst defeat.

**The rise.** Athens led the Greek defence against Persia (Marathon, **490 BC**; Salamis, **480 BC**). Afterwards it turned the alliance of Aegean cities into an empire, paid for a navy, and built the Parthenon. Under **Pericles** (died 429 BC) it became the cultural capital of Greece.

**The democracy.** Athens was a **direct democracy** for adult male citizens. Women, slaves and resident foreigners had no vote.

| Institution | How it worked |
| --- | --- |
| **The Assembly** | every citizen could attend, speak and vote on war, peace and law |
| **The Council of 500** | chosen **by lot**, set the Assembly's agenda |
| **The jury courts** | hundreds of citizens chosen by lot; no judges, no lawyers; a verdict by simple majority, the same day |

**So whoever could persuade a crowd held power.** That is why the **Sophists** of Stage 2, paid teachers of argument and public speaking, flourished here, and why Socrates and Plato kept asking whether persuasion has anything to do with truth.

**The fall.** The **Peloponnesian War** against Sparta ran from **431 to 404 BC**. A plague in **430 BC** killed perhaps a quarter of the city, Pericles among them. In **416 BC** Athens destroyed the neutral island of Melos; the historian Thucydides gives the Athenian envoys the claim that the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must. The expedition to Sicily (**415–413 BC**) ended in disaster. Athens surrendered in **404 BC**.

**The Thirty.** Sparta installed an oligarchy, the **Thirty Tyrants** (404–403 BC), who killed some 1,500 citizens. Among their leaders were **Critias**, a cousin of Plato's mother, and **Charmides**, Plato's uncle. Both had been companions of Socrates. Democracy was restored in **403 BC**, with an **amnesty** forbidding prosecutions for what had happened before.

**The questions this world pressed:**

1. **Is justice real, or a convention the strong impose or the weak invent?** The Greek pair is **nomos** (law, custom) against **physis** (nature).
2. **Can virtue be taught**, and if so, who has the right to teach it?
3. **Should the many rule, or those who know?** A city that votes on generals and executes its own commanders has to ask.
4. **What is the soul, and does it outlast the body?**

**This stage follows the answers.** First Socrates, who wrote nothing and asked these questions in the street; then Plato, who wrote them up as dialogues and built from them the first great system of Western philosophy.
The Socratic problem: Plato, Xenophon an:
Socrates wrote nothing. Everything we know of him comes from others, and they do not agree. Working out the real Socrates from their portraits is called **the Socratic problem**.

**The sources:**

| Source | Date | His Socrates |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Aristophanes**, *Clouds* | staged **423 BC**, in Socrates' lifetime; the surviving text is a partial revision | a comic charlatan who runs a "Thinkery", studies the heavens, denies the gods and teaches students to make the weaker argument the stronger |
| **Xenophon** (about 430–354 BC), *Memorabilia*, *Apology*, *Symposium*, *Oeconomicus* | written after 399 BC | a pious, practical moral adviser, giving sound advice on friendship, household and self-control |
| **Plato**, the dialogues | written after 399 BC, over some fifty years | a relentless questioner who claims to know nothing, refutes the confident, and in later works voices grand theories of the soul and reality |
| **Aristotle** (384–322 BC) | born after Socrates died; studied twenty years with Plato | a short, careful report: Socrates sought **universal definitions** in ethics and argued from examples, but **did not make the Forms separate**. Plato did |

**Each source has a slant.** Aristophanes was writing comedy and lumped Socrates in with the natural philosophers and Sophists. In Plato's *Apology* Socrates himself names the play as the source of the old prejudice against him. Xenophon was away in Asia on campaign in 399 BC and did not see the trial; he writes partly to defend Socrates' reputation. Plato was at the trial (the *Apology* names him in the court) but was a philosopher with his own ideas, who used Socrates as his chief speaker for decades.

**Also lost or fragmentary:** other companions wrote Socratic dialogues too, among them Antisthenes, Aeschines of Sphettus, Phaedo of Elis and Euclides of Megara. "Socratic conversations" were a recognised genre.

**The main solutions, and the dispute over them:**

1. **The developmentalist answer**, associated above all with **Gregory Vlastos** (1907–1991). Plato's **early** dialogues give a recognisably historical Socrates: he only asks, defines nothing, and argues about ethics. The **middle** dialogues put Plato's own metaphysics into his mouth. Aristotle's report supports the line.
2. **The sceptical answer.** We cannot get behind the literary portraits. Each author's Socrates should be studied as that author's creation.
3. **The Xenophontic answer.** Xenophon, being less of a philosopher, may be the more faithful reporter. Most scholars think his portrait too flat to explain why Socrates mattered so much, but it has defenders.

**Where the field stands.** There is **broad agreement** that Aristophanes is caricature and that Plato is the richest source. Whether Plato's early dialogues give the historical Socrates is **genuinely disputed**. In this stage, "Socrates" means the Socrates of Plato's earlier dialogues unless said otherwise, which is the standard working convention.
Plato's dialogues: early, middle and lat:
Plato is the first Western philosopher whose works survive complete. Everything he is known to have published has come down to us, and every one of them, except the letters and the *Apology*, is a **dialogue**: a conversation, usually led by Socrates, with Plato himself never speaking.

**The corpus.** An ancient edition arranged by **Thrasyllus** (1st century AD) has **36 works** in nine groups of four. A few of these are probably not by Plato, and the authenticity of the thirteen *Letters*, especially the long *Seventh Letter* about his adventures in Sicily, is disputed. Passages are cited by **Stephanus numbers** (e.g. *Republic* 514a), the page and section of a 1578 edition. Every modern translation prints them in the margin.

**His life in brief.** From a rich, well-connected family, Plato was a young companion of Socrates. After 399 BC he travelled. About **387 BC** he founded the **Academy**, a school in a grove outside Athens, where Aristotle studied for twenty years. He went to Syracuse in Sicily three times, the last two times hoping in vain to make the young tyrant Dionysius II a philosopher-ruler.

**The usual grouping.** The order is reconstructed partly by **stylometry**: counting habits of style (particles, word order, avoiding clashes of vowels) that change over a writer's life. The *Laws* is reported to have been unfinished at his death, and the late group shares its style.

| Group | Dialogues (a standard, not a certain, list) | Character |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Early** | *Apology, Crito, Euthyphro, Laches, Charmides, Lysis, Ion, Hippias Minor, Protagoras* | Socrates asks "What is courage, piety, ...?", refutes the answers, ends in **aporia** (puzzlement, no answer) |
| **Transitional** | *Gorgias, Meno, Euthydemus* | new themes enter: recollection, mathematics, the soul's fate |
| **Middle** | *Phaedo, Symposium, Republic, Phaedrus* | Socrates sets out positive doctrine: **the Forms**, the immortal soul, the ideal city |
| **Late** | *Parmenides, Theaetetus, Sophist, Statesman, Philebus, Timaeus, Critias, Laws* | self-criticism, technical method, cosmology, law; Socrates often silent or absent |

**The late group is secure; the line between early and middle is not.** There is broad agreement on which works are late. The division of the rest is a working hypothesis.

**Three disputes about reading Plato:**

1. **Developmentalism or unity?** Did Plato's views change, so the early dialogues are Socrates and the middle Plato? Or, as **Charles Kahn** argued, did Plato write the early dialogues already knowing where he was heading, introducing his ideas step by step?
2. **Mouthpiece or drama?** Is the main speaker simply Plato's voice, or is each dialogue a drama whose meaning lies in the whole, including the characters' failures?
3. **The unwritten doctrines.** Aristotle mentions Plato's views not found in the dialogues (on "the One" and "the Great and Small"). The *Phaedrus* criticises writing. Some scholars, notably the **Tübingen school**, hold that Plato's real philosophy was oral. Most do not.

**How this stage reads him.** Early dialogues first, then the middle dialogues and the *Republic*, then the late works, with the disputes flagged as they arise.
The elenchus: how Socrates refuted:
Socrates' method has a name: the **elenchus**, Greek for "refutation" or "cross-examination". It is the engine of the early dialogues, and learning to see its moves is learning to read them.

**It starts with a "What is F?" question.** What is courage? What is piety? What is beauty? Socrates does not want examples. He wants **a definition**: the one thing all brave acts share, by which they are brave.

**The standard shape**, as Vlastos laid it out:

1. The interlocutor asserts a thesis, **p**.
2. Socrates gets him to agree to further premises, **q** and **r**.
3. Socrates shows that **q and r together imply not-p**.
4. Socrates claims that **p has been shown false**.

**A worked example (the *Laches*).** Laches, a general, says courage is **endurance of the soul**. Socrates gets him to agree that courage is always **fine and good**, and that **foolish endurance**, holding on stubbornly where it does harm, is **bad and shameful**. Then foolish endurance would be courage, and courage would sometimes be shameful. Contradiction. So courage is not simply endurance. Laches tries "wise endurance", which fails in turn.

**The rules of the game:**

- **Say what you believe.** Socrates insists the interlocutor answer sincerely. The person, not just the thesis, is being tested.
- **Short answers.** Socrates resists long speeches, the Sophists' specialty.
- **Agreement is the only authority.** Every premise is one the interlocutor accepts.

**Socratic irony.** Socrates praises the wisdom of the people he is about to refute and claims to know nothing himself. Whether this is mockery, teaching technique or sincere modesty is disputed, and the answer may differ from dialogue to dialogue.

**Objection one: the problem of the elenchus.** The method shows only that **p, q and r cannot all be true**. It does not show which to drop. Why should Laches give up his definition rather than his agreement that courage is always fine?

- **Vlastos's reply:** Socrates assumes that anyone's beliefs include enough truths to refute any false thesis, so the elenchus, repeated, tests for **consistency with what we really believe**. Critics call this assumption unearned.
- **The modest reply:** the elenchus is a **purgative**. It clears away false confidence and leaves the person ready to inquire. Plato's own *Sophist* later describes it this way.

**Objection two: the "Socratic fallacy".** Peter **Geach** (1966) charged that Socrates assumes you cannot know anything about F, not even that this act is brave, until you can define F. But we plainly know examples before we have definitions; that is how we test definitions. Defenders reply that Socrates only claims we cannot know **disputed** cases, or that he uses examples freely in practice. The **priority of definition**, and whether Socrates really held it, remains **disputed**.

**Why it matters.** The elenchus is the ancestor of every seminar, cross-examination in court and counterexample in a philosophy paper.
Socratic ignorance and the oracle at Del:
Socrates' most famous claim is a claim not to know. Plato's *Apology* tells where it came from.

**The story** (*Apology* 20e–23c). Socrates' friend **Chaerephon** went to the oracle of Apollo at **Delphi** and asked whether anyone was wiser than Socrates. The priestess answered that **no one was**. Socrates, sure he was wise in nothing, set out to refute the god by finding someone wiser.

**The search:**

| Who he questioned | What he found |
| --- | --- |
| **Politicians** | thought themselves wise and were not |
| **Poets** | wrote fine things, but by inspiration, and could not explain them |
| **Craftsmen** | really knew their crafts, but then thought they knew the greatest matters too |

**His conclusion, in his words** (*Apology* 21d; translated by Benjamin Jowett, first published 1871; text from Project Gutenberg):

> "Well, although I do not suppose that either of us knows anything really beautiful and good, I am better off than he is,—for he knows nothing, and thinks that he knows; I neither know nor think that I know."

**So his wisdom is "human wisdom":** knowing **the limits of what he knows**. The god, he concludes, used him as an example: the wisest human is the one who, like Socrates, knows his wisdom is worth nothing. He took this as a **mission** to go on testing people, which made him poor and hated.

**A common misquotation.** "I know that I know nothing" is not in Plato. Socrates says he does not **think** he knows; the paradoxical slogan, which would be self-contradictory, is a later simplification.

**The puzzle.** Socrates also claims to know some things. In the same speech (*Apology* 29b, same translation):

> "I do know that injustice and disobedience to a better, whether God or man, is evil and dishonourable"

How can he disclaim knowledge and claim it?

**The main readings:**

1. **Two kinds of knowledge** (Vlastos). Socrates disclaims **certain, expert knowledge**, the kind that could define virtue and explain why. He claims **elenctic knowledge**: beliefs that have survived every test so far.
2. **Irony.** The disavowal is a teaching pose, inviting the other to think for himself. Hard to square with how seriously he takes the oracle.
3. **Knowledge of a few moral truths without a theory.** He knows certain particular things, as anyone might, but lacks the definitions that would make him **wise**.

The first reading is the most widely held; none is settled.

**Why it matters.** Socratic ignorance changed what a philosopher is: not the person with the answers, like the natural philosophers of Stage 2, but **the person who knows which answers he lacks**.
The trial of Socrates and the Apology:
In the spring of **399 BC** Socrates, about seventy, stood trial for his life before an Athenian jury. Plato's *Apology* is his version of the defence; *apologia* is Greek for a defence speech, not an apology.

**The charge**, as Plato and later sources give it, was **impiety** (*asebeia*), in three parts:

1. **not recognising the gods the city recognises;**
2. **introducing new divine beings** (*daimonia*);
3. **corrupting the young.**

**The accusers** were **Meletus**, a young poet who brought the case, **Anytus**, a leading democratic politician, and **Lycon**, an orator. The jury was some **500 citizens** chosen by lot.

**The *Apology* has three speeches:**

| Speech | What Socrates does |
| --- | --- |
| **The defence** | answers the **old accusers** (decades of gossip, Aristophanes' play) and the new; tells the oracle story; cross-examines **Meletus** and catches him contradicting himself (he says Socrates believes in no gods at all, yet charges him with introducing divine beings) |
| **The penalty** | convicted, he must propose a penalty against the prosecution's death. He first proposes **free meals in the town hall**, the honour of Olympic victors; then a **fine of 30 minae**, guaranteed by Plato and others |
| **After the sentence** | death. He tells the jurors death is either a **dreamless sleep** or a journey to talk with the great dead. Either is no evil |

**The divine sign.** Socrates says that since childhood a **voice** (his *daimonion*) has come to him, which **only ever holds him back**, never urges him on. It never opposed his defence that day, so he takes his death to be no harm.

**His reason for not going quietly** (*Apology* 38a; translated by Benjamin Jowett, first published 1871; text from Project Gutenberg):

> "daily to discourse about virtue, and of those other things about which you hear me examining myself and others, is the greatest good of man, and that the unexamined life is not worth living"

**The vote.** Socrates says that if thirty votes had gone the other way, he would have been acquitted, so the verdict was close, perhaps about **280 to 220**. A later source says more jurors voted for death than had voted for guilt. The execution was delayed for a month while a sacred ship was away at Delos.

**Why was he really tried? The disputed question:**

1. **Religion, as charged.** Athenians took impiety seriously, and Socrates' private divine sign looked like a new cult.
2. **Politics.** **Critias** of the Thirty and **Alcibiades**, who betrayed Athens to Sparta, had been his companions. The amnesty of 403 BC forbade prosecution for past political acts, so the charge, on this view, was a cover. Half a century later the orator Aeschines told a jury that Athens had executed Socrates for having educated Critias.
3. **The method itself.** He humiliated powerful men in public for decades.

Most historians think **all three played a part**. How much weight each bears is **disputed**.

**Why the speech matters.** It set the picture of the philosopher as a person who **follows argument even to death**, and of a democracy that killed its best critic. Both halves of that picture are still argued over.
The Crito: why Socrates would not escape:
Between sentence and death, Socrates' old friend **Crito** came to the prison before dawn with a plan. The guards were bribed and friends in Thessaly would take him in. Plato's short *Crito* is Socrates' answer: he will not go.

**Crito's case:** people will think his friends were too mean to save him; he is helping his enemies; he is abandoning his children; it is cowardly to die.

**Socrates' first move: ignore opinion.** One should listen not to the many but to the **one who knows**, as an athlete listens to his trainer, not the crowd. The question is only whether escaping is **just**. He restates a principle (*Crito* 48b; translated by Benjamin Jowett, first published 1871; text from Project Gutenberg):

> "not life, but a good life, is to be chiefly valued"

**The argument**, roughly as he sets it out:

1. **One must never do wrong**, not even in return for a wrong done to you. (This rejects the common Greek morality of helping friends and harming enemies.)
2. **To escape would be to harm the Laws** of Athens: if verdicts could be ignored by anyone who disliked them, the city could not survive.
3. **One must keep just agreements.**
