4. **Socrates has agreed to obey the Laws.** He lived seventy years in Athens when he was free to leave, raised his children there, and at his trial proposed exile only to refuse it.
5. **So he must not escape.**

**The Laws speak.** Socrates makes the point vivid by imagining the **Laws of Athens** confronting him. They say they are like **parents**: they made his parents' marriage possible and raised and educated him. A citizen may **persuade** them that they are wrong, or he must **obey** them. Socrates had the chance to persuade, at the trial, and failed.

**This is the first social-contract argument in Western philosophy:** obligation to the state grounded in **tacit agreement**, shown by staying.

**Objection one: the apparent contradiction with the *Apology*.** There Socrates said that if the court let him go on condition he stop philosophising, he would **disobey**. So he does not always obey.

- **Reply:** the *Crito* allows **persuade or obey**, and refusing an order to do wrong is different from **evading a punishment**. Socrates would disobey an order to stop doing what is right; he would not run from the penalty for disobeying. This reading, close to later civil disobedience (Martin Luther King cited Socrates), is widely held, though **scholars still dispute** whether the two texts fully cohere.

**Objection two: the "parent" analogy.** Children owe parents a lot, but not unlimited submission, and a citizen did not choose his city as one chooses a contract.

**Objection three: tacit consent.** Staying is a weak sign of agreement when leaving means losing home, language and family. **David Hume** pressed this against social-contract theory in the 1700s (Stage 9).

**Do the Laws speak for Socrates?** Some scholars hold that the speech of the Laws is **rhetoric aimed at Crito**, who cannot follow pure argument, and is not Socrates' own view. The more common reading takes it as his argument. This is **disputed**.
Euthyphro's dilemma: is the pious loved:
Outside the court where Socrates is to be charged, he meets **Euthyphro**, a religious expert prosecuting **his own father** for murder: a hired labourer had killed a slave, and the father tied him up and left him in a ditch, where he died before word came back from the authorities. Euthyphro is sure he is being pious. Socrates asks him what piety is.

**The definitions fail one by one:**

| Euthyphro says piety is | Socrates' objection |
| --- | --- |
| what I am doing now, prosecuting wrongdoers | an **example**, not a definition |
| **what is dear to the gods** | the gods quarrel; the same act would be pious and impious |
| **what all the gods love** | leads to the dilemma below |
| a part of justice: **care of the gods** | care improves its object; we cannot improve the gods |
| a kind of **service, a trade** of sacrifice for favours | comes back round to "what the gods love" |

The dialogue ends in **aporia**, Euthyphro hurrying off.

**The dilemma** (*Euthyphro* 10a; translated by Benjamin Jowett, first published 1871; text from Project Gutenberg):

> "whether the pious or holy is beloved by the gods because it is holy, or holy because it is beloved of the gods."

**Socrates' argument against the second horn**, set out:

1. Euthyphro agrees: the gods love the pious **because it is pious**.
2. But something is god-loved **because the gods love it**. Being loved is a state brought about by the loving.
3. If **pious** and **god-loved** were the same, then substituting in (1), the gods would love the god-loved because it is god-loved; and substituting in (2), the pious would be pious because the gods love it.
4. These conflict with what was agreed. So **being god-loved is a feature of the pious, not what piety is**.

**The modern dilemma.** Put with one God instead of many, and "good" instead of "pious", the question is: **does God command things because they are good, or are they good because God commands them?**

- **First horn:** if God commands them because they are good, goodness seems to be a standard **independent of God**, which God follows.
- **Second horn:** if they are good because commanded, goodness looks **arbitrary**: had God commanded cruelty, cruelty would be good. This view is **divine command theory**.

**The main replies:**

1. **Bite the second bullet** (some medieval voluntarists, e.g. in the line of Ockham, Stage 7): God's will is the source of goodness.
2. **A third option** (a line from Aquinas, Stage 7, to modern defenders such as Robert Adams): goodness is grounded in **God's nature**, not in an arbitrary command or an outside standard. God commands what is good because he is good. Critics ask whether this only moves the dilemma: is God's nature good because it is God's, or because it meets a standard?

**Where there is agreement.** Socrates' own argument is generally thought **valid** once its "because" is read carefully, though some find step 2 too quick. Whether the modern dilemma defeats divine command theory is **live**. The theology of how God and goodness relate belongs to the **Theology curriculum**; here it is enough to see the argument's shape.
Virtue as knowledge: no one does wrong w:
The most startling Socratic thesis is that **virtue is knowledge**, with its twin, **no one does wrong willingly**. Most people think wrongdoing is a failure of will. Socrates thinks it is a failure of understanding.

**Two terms.** **Virtue** (*aretē*) means excellence, what makes a thing good at being what it is: a knife's sharpness, a person's justice, courage, wisdom, moderation and piety. **Eudaimonia**, usually translated "happiness", means **living well, flourishing**: a whole life gone right, not a mood.

**The argument, as its best defender would put it** (built from the *Meno* 77b–78b and the *Euthydemus*):

1. **Everyone wants to be happy**, and wants what they do to be good for them.
2. **Nobody wants what they know to be bad for them.** If someone pursues a bad thing, it is because they think it good.
3. Health, wealth, strength and the rest **benefit only when used wisely**; used foolishly they harm.
4. So **wisdom is the one thing always good**, and what makes everything else good.
5. So **virtue, the condition of a soul that lives well, is wisdom or knowledge**.
6. So **all wrongdoing comes from ignorance**. No one does wrong willingly.

**What follows from it:**

- **The unity of the virtues.** If courage, justice and the rest are each knowledge of what is good, they are at bottom **one knowledge**. You cannot have one without all.
- **Virtue should be teachable**, as all knowledge is. Why, then, do good fathers have bad sons? The *Meno* worries at this (Lesson 12).
- **Punishment should be teaching.** The wrongdoer needs correction, not retaliation, and the *Gorgias* adds that he is **worse off unpunished**, and that **it is better to suffer wrong than to do it**.

**The *Gorgias* challenge.** Callicles, an aristocrat, replies with the case from nature: by **physis** the strong should take more, and "justice" is a **nomos** the weak invented to restrain them. Socrates argues that unlimited appetite is a leaking jar and that the self-controlled person is the happy one. Callicles is silenced, not convinced. Plato returns to the challenge in the *Republic* (Lessons 16–17).

**The strongest objection: it denies the obvious.** People often know what is best and do something else: the smoker, the procrastinator, the man who knows he should not shout. This is **akrasia**, weakness of will, and it is the subject of the next lesson.

**A second objection: knowing is not enough.** Knowing what courage requires does not give a person the nerve to do it. Courage seems to need trained feeling as well as understanding. **Aristotle** made this point (Stage 4), and Plato himself, later, builds feeling into virtue through his divided soul.

**The defender's reply:** the thesis concerns **real knowledge**, a firm grasp of the good that shapes desire itself, not a sentence one can recite. If that is what knowledge is, it is less obvious that one can have it and act against it.

**Where the field stands.** Few philosophers accept the thesis in its strict form, but it is regarded as a **serious position**, not a muddle, and the Stoics revived it (Stage 5).
Akrasia: the Protagoras and weakness of:
**Akrasia** (Greek: "lack of mastery") is acting against your own better judgement: knowing, or believing, that A is better, being able to do A, and doing B. It seems the most ordinary thing in the world. In the *Protagoras*, Socrates argues it is **impossible**.

**The common view** (*Protagoras* 352b–c): people often know what is best but are **overcome** by pleasure, pain, love or fear. In Jowett's translation (first published 1871; text from Project Gutenberg), the many think of knowledge **"just as if knowledge were a slave, and might be dragged about anyhow."**

**Socrates' argument**, as its best defender would set it out (352–358):

1. Grant, for the argument, that **the good is pleasure** and the bad is pain, judged over the whole of life. (Whether Socrates himself held this **hedonism** is **disputed**; he gets Protagoras and "the many" to accept it.)
2. Then "he knew X was bad but did it, overcome by pleasure" means "he knew X was **less pleasant** overall but did it, overcome by **pleasure**".
3. That is absurd: overcome by pleasure into choosing **less pleasure**.
4. What really happens: near pleasures **look bigger**, as near objects do. The person **misjudges** the sizes.
5. So the cure is **a measuring art**: knowledge that corrects for nearness.
6. So "being overcome by pleasure" is **ignorance**. Akrasia, as described, does not happen.

**The strongest objections:**

- **It rests on hedonism.** Drop premise 1 and the substitution in step 2 fails. Defenders reply that the argument works for any **single measure of value**: if all goods are comparable on one scale, choosing the smaller good knowingly looks irrational in the same way.
- **It contradicts experience.** **Aristotle** said the view "plainly contradicts the appearances" (*Nicomachean Ethics* VII, paraphrased here). His own account: the akratic person knows in a way, but like a drunk reciting verses, does not **use** the knowledge at the moment of acting (Stage 4).
- **Desire can be blind to judgement.** Someone can see clearly that the second drink is worse and want it anyway. Nothing is misjudged; the wanting simply wins.

**Plato's later answer.** In the *Republic* (Lesson 19) Plato divides the soul into **reason, spirit and appetite**, which can pull in different directions. Then akrasia is easy to explain: **appetite overpowers reason**. His example is **Leontius**, who wanted to look at the corpses of executed men, struggled, and then ran to look, cursing his own eyes. Most scholars read this as Plato **giving up** the Socratic denial of akrasia. Some argue the two views are more compatible than they look.

**The modern debate.** **Donald Davidson**'s "How is Weakness of the Will Possible?" (1970) revived the problem: if acting intentionally means acting on what you judge best, how can anyone act against it? He answered that the akratic judges "all things considered" but acts on a partial judgement. Others distinguish **akrasia** from **weakness of will** as resolution-breaking. The phenomenon is **broadly accepted** as real; how to describe it is **open**.

**Why it matters.** The question is whether reason rules us or only advises. The answer shapes ethics, law and the study of addiction.
Meno's paradox and the theory of recolle:
The *Meno* opens with a blunt question from a young Thessalian aristocrat: **can virtue be taught?** Socrates says he cannot answer, since he does not know what virtue is. Meno's attempts at definition fail, and Meno, stung, strikes back with a paradox.

**Meno's paradox** (*Meno* 80d; translated by Benjamin Jowett, first published 1871; text from Project Gutenberg):

> "And how will you enquire, Socrates, into that which you do not know? What will you put forth as the subject of enquiry? And if you find what you want, how will you ever know that this is the thing which you did not know?"

**Set out as a dilemma** (Socrates' restatement, 80e):

1. For anything, either you **know** it or you **do not**.
2. If you know it, you **cannot inquire** into it: there is nothing to find out.
3. If you do not know it, you **cannot inquire** into it: you do not know what to look for, or would not recognise it if you found it.
4. So **inquiry is impossible**.

**Socrates calls it "a tiresome dispute"**, but does not dismiss it. It is a real puzzle about learning: how can you aim at an answer you do not have?

**The answer: recollection** (*anamnesis*). Socrates says he has heard from priests and poets that:

- **the soul is immortal** and has been born many times;
- it has **seen all things**, in this world and the next, and **learned everything**;
- so what we call learning is really **recollecting** what the soul already knows.

**So the dilemma is false.** There is a third state between knowing and not knowing: **knowledge latent in the soul**, forgotten but recoverable. Inquiry is the work of recovering it. Socrates adds that, whatever the truth of the story, believing it makes us **better and braver inquirers** than believing inquiry is hopeless (86b–c).

**He then offers a demonstration**, the questioning of Meno's slave (next lesson).

**Objections and replies:**

1. **The paradox trades on a sharp "know/not know".** In ordinary inquiry we know something about the target: **a description** ("the cause of this disease") that we can fill in. Many modern readers think this dissolves the paradox without recollection. A defender replies that this partial knowledge itself needs explaining, which pushes the question back.
2. **Recollection only moves the problem.** How did the soul learn in the first place, in a former life? If by inquiry, the paradox returns. Plato's answer, developed in the *Phaedo* and *Phaedrus*, is that the soul **saw the Forms directly**, without inquiry.
3. **Is it meant literally?** The myth is introduced as something priests say. Some scholars read recollection as a **picture** of a priori knowledge (knowledge not drawn from experience). Others hold that Plato believed it, since the *Phaedo* uses it as a proof of immortality. This is **disputed**.

**Why it matters.** Recollection is the first theory of **innate knowledge**. The debate between nativists and empiricists, Descartes and Leibniz against Locke (Stages 8–9), and modern arguments about innate grammar, descend from this page.
The Meno: the slave boy and knowledge ve:
To show that learning is recollection, Socrates calls over one of Meno's household slaves, a boy who speaks Greek and has never studied geometry, and asks him a question (*Meno* 82b–85b).

**The problem: double a square.** Socrates draws a square with sides of **2 feet**, so its area is **4 square feet**. How long must the side be for a square of **8**?

**The three stages:**

| Stage | The boy's answer | What happens |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Confident error** | "double the side": **4 feet** | Socrates shows that square is **16**, four times the original |
| **Second error** | **3 feet**, between 2 and 4 | that gives **9**, still not 8 |
| **Aporia** | "I do not know" | Socrates: he is **better off now**, knowing he does not know, and ready to look |
| **Discovery** | by questions only, the boy sees the answer is **the square on the diagonal** of the original | four half-squares of 2 make 8 |

The answer, in modern terms, is a side of **√8**, which is not a whole number of feet. That is why it has to be **shown** as the diagonal.

**Socrates' conclusion.** He taught nothing, only asked. The boy's true answers came **from within him**. So he had them all along, from a time before this life. This is offered as evidence for recollection.

**Objections:**

1. **The questions are leading.** Many of Socrates' questions are put so that the expected answer is yes, and the boy says yes. Defenders reply that the boy must **see** each step for himself, and that he gives wrong answers when he does not see.
2. **It shows a priori knowledge, not past lives.** The boy can grasp geometrical truths by reasoning, not by being told. That is impressive, but it is evidence that we can **reason**, not that we have been reborn. This is the standard modern objection, and widely accepted.

**The second half: knowledge versus true belief.** The dialogue returns to whether virtue can be taught. If virtue is knowledge, it is teachable. But there seem to be **no teachers of virtue**: great Athenians failed to make their sons good. Anytus, the future accuser, joins the conversation and warns Socrates against speaking ill of Athenians.

**Socrates' solution:** good men may act from **true belief** (or "right opinion", *orthē doxa*), not knowledge. True belief guides action as well as knowledge does. So what is the difference? (*Meno* 97e–98a; translated by Benjamin Jowett, first published 1871; text from Project Gutenberg):

> "they are not of much value until they are fastened by the tie of the cause; and this fastening of them, friend Meno, is recollection, as you and I have agreed to call it."

**The image** is the statues of **Daedalus**, so lifelike they were said to run away unless tied down. True beliefs, too, **"run away"**: they can be argued out of you. **Knowledge is true belief tied down by an account of why** it is true.

**The ending.** Virtue in good statesmen, Socrates concludes, comes neither by nature nor teaching but by **divine dispensation**, like the inspiration of prophets, unless a statesman appears who can teach it. Many readers find this ironic; it is **disputed** how seriously it is meant.

**Why it matters.** "Knowledge is true belief plus something" is the start of the analysis of knowledge. The *Theaetetus* (Lesson 25) tries "true belief with an account", and the twentieth-century debate over Edmund Gettier's counterexamples (1963) is about the same formula.
The Phaedo: four arguments for the immor:
The *Phaedo* tells of Socrates' last day. **Phaedo**, who was there, narrates to friends far from Athens. In prison, the two Thebans **Simmias** and **Cebes** ask Socrates why he faces death so calmly. He answers that philosophy is preparation for death (*Phaedo* 64a; translated by Benjamin Jowett, first published 1871; text from Project Gutenberg): the true philosopher **"is always pursuing death and dying"**, since he tries to free his soul from the body's distractions. But then he must prove the soul survives.

**The four arguments:**

| Argument | The idea | The main weakness |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1. From opposites** (cyclical), 70c–72e | everything comes to be from its opposite: hotter from colder, waking from sleeping. So the living come from the dead, and the dead from the living | true of states of one thing (warm to cold), not obviously of **existence**. Shows at most a cycle, not that the soul keeps its identity |
| **2. From recollection**, 72e–77d | we judge sticks and stones as **"equal"** but deficiently so. So we have a concept of **Equality itself** that no seen thing gave us. We had it before birth, so the soul existed before birth | grants pre-existence, not survival after death (Simmias and Cebes say so at once). Assumes recollection |
| **3. From affinity**, 78b–84b | there are two kinds of thing: visible, changing, composite; invisible, unchanging, simple. The body is like the first, the soul like the second; so the soul, like them, is probably **indestructible** | only **likeness**, and Socrates admits it. Many invisible things perish |
| **4. The final argument**, 102a–107b | the soul is what **brings life** to a body. A thing that essentially brings a feature cannot admit its opposite: snow, which brings cold, cannot admit heat but retreats or perishes. The soul brings life, so cannot admit **death**. It is **deathless**, and so indestructible | "deathless" might mean "**cannot be a dead soul**", which is compatible with the soul **ceasing to exist**, as snow does. Plato needs a further step, that the deathless is indestructible, which he asserts |

**The two objections in the middle (85e–88b):**

- **Simmias: the soul as attunement** (*harmonia*). A lyre's tuning is invisible and fine, but it dies when the lyre is smashed. Perhaps the soul is the **attunement of the body**. Socrates replies: an attunement cannot exist before its instrument, which conflicts with recollection; it cannot oppose its own parts, but the soul **rules and opposes** the body; and it admits degrees, while souls are not more or less soul. This view is an ancestor of modern **functionalism** about the mind.
- **Cebes: the weaver.** A weaver wears out many cloaks and dies before the last. The soul may outlast many bodies and still **wear out**. This objection drives the final argument.

**Before answering, Socrates warns against "misology"**, hatred of argument: after being let down by bad arguments, people decide no argument is sound. The fault, he says, is in us.

**The death.** Socrates bathes, sees his family, drinks the poison, and walks until his legs grow heavy. His last words (118a, same translation): **"Crito, I owe a cock to Asclepius; will you remember to pay the debt?"** What he meant, a thanks-offering for the cure of life or for a friend's recovery, is **disputed**.

**Where the field stands.** There is **broad agreement** that **none of the four arguments succeeds** as a proof. The final argument is the most serious and the most debated. The Christian doctrine of the soul and resurrection, which differs from Plato's, belongs to the **Theology curriculum**.
Plato's theory of Forms:
In the middle dialogues a new doctrine appears, and it is the one most associated with Plato's name: **the Forms**.

**The terms.** The Greek is **eidos** or **idea**, "look" or "shape". Translated "Form" or "Idea" (capitalised, because they are not ideas in anyone's head). Plato speaks of **the Beautiful itself**, **the Equal itself**, **the Just itself**.

**The claim, in brief.** Besides the many beautiful things we see, there is **one Beauty itself**:

| Beautiful things | Beauty itself (the Form) |
| --- | --- |
| many | **one** |
| seen by the senses | grasped **by thought** |
| change, come and go | **eternal, unchanging** |
| beautiful in one respect, ugly in another | **purely and only beautiful** |
| beautiful **by "participating"** in the Form | beautiful **in itself** |
| objects of **opinion** | objects of **knowledge** |

**The arguments for Forms**, as reconstructed from the dialogues:

1. **One over many.** Wherever many things share a name (many beds, many just acts), there is one Form they share (*Republic* X, 596a).
2. **From opposites, or "compresence".** Any sensible thing that is equal is also, from another angle, unequal; any of the many beautiful things will also, in some respect, appear ugly. So what we grasp when we grasp **Equality** cannot be any of these things. It must be something that is **never unequal** (*Phaedo* 74; *Republic* V, 479).
3. **From knowledge.** Knowledge must be of what **is**, stably. The sensible world **changes**. So there must be unchanging objects for knowledge (*Republic* V, 476–480; the Heraclitus of Stage 2 is in the background).
4. **From definition.** Socrates' "What is F?" question needs an answer that is one, unchanging, and the same in every case. The Form is that answer, made into a thing.

**Four disputed points about the theory:**

1. **Separation.** Aristotle says Plato made the Forms **separate** (*chōris*) from things. Separate in what sense? Able to exist without instances, or in a different "place"? **Disputed.**
2. **Self-predication.** Plato sometimes writes as if **Beauty is itself beautiful**, the most beautiful thing. Taken literally, this leads to the Third Man regress (Lesson 26). Whether he meant it literally is **one of the great debates**.
3. **Which things have Forms?** In the *Parmenides* the young Socrates is sure of Forms of Justice and Beauty, unsure about man, fire and water, and embarrassed to grant **hair, mud and dirt**. Plato never gives a settled list.
4. **Participation.** What is it for a thing to "participate in" or "resemble" a Form? Plato tries images (copies, shares) and, in the *Parmenides*, finds problems with all of them.

**The main objection, from Aristotle onward:** the Forms **duplicate** the world without explaining it. Saying a thing is beautiful because it participates in Beauty adds a second thing but no explanation. Aristotle's own answer, that forms are **in** things (Stage 4), starts here.

**Why it matters.** This is the founding text of **the problem of universals**: whether properties like redness and justice exist apart from the things that have them. The medieval debate (Stage 7) and modern metaphysics still divide over **realism**, **conceptualism** and **nominalism** on this question.
The Symposium: love and the ladder of be:
A **symposium** was a Greek drinking party. Plato's *Symposium* is set at one held in **416 BC** to celebrate the poet **Agathon**'s first victory in the tragic competition. The guests agree to drink lightly and each give a speech in praise of **Eros**, the god of love and erotic desire.

**The speeches:**

| Speaker | His account of love |
| --- | --- |
| **Phaedrus** | the oldest god; lovers will die for each other and fight bravely before each other |
| **Pausanias** | two loves: a common one, of bodies; a heavenly one, of souls, which makes the beloved better |
| **Eryximachus**, a doctor | a cosmic force of balance in bodies, music and the seasons |
| **Aristophanes**, the comic poet | humans were once double, round creatures; Zeus split them in two. **Love is the longing for our other half** |
| **Agathon** | Love is the youngest, most beautiful and best of the gods |
| **Socrates** | reports what **Diotima**, a wise woman of Mantinea, taught him |

**Diotima's teaching.** First, against Agathon: love is **desire**, and we desire what we **lack**. So Love is not beautiful but **wants** beauty. It is a spirit between mortal and divine, as the philosopher is between ignorance and wisdom.

**Then the definition:** love is **desire for the good to be one's own forever**. Since mortals cannot have anything forever, love works by **"giving birth in beauty"**: children of the body, or, better, children of the soul, such as poems, laws and virtue. It is a reaching for **immortality**.

**The ladder of love** (210a–212a). Rightly guided, a lover climbs:

1. love of **one beautiful body**;
2. then of **all beautiful bodies**, seeing the beauty they share;
3. then of **beautiful souls**;
4. then of **beautiful practices and laws**;
5. then of **beautiful kinds of knowledge**;
6. and at last, suddenly, a vision of **Beauty itself**, eternal and unmixed.

**In Diotima's words** (211c; translated by Benjamin Jowett, first published 1871; text from Project Gutenberg):

> "using these as steps only, and from one going on to two, and from two to all fair forms, and from fair forms to fair practices, and from fair practices to fair notions, until from fair notions he arrives at the notion of absolute beauty"

**Then Alcibiades bursts in**, drunk, and gives a speech in praise of Socrates instead: ugly outside like a statue of Silenus, full of gods within; unmoved by cold, wine or Alcibiades' own attempt to seduce him. The ladder is told in theory; Alcibiades shows a man who seems to have climbed it, and a lover who could not follow.

**The strongest objection: love for persons is lost.** **Gregory Vlastos** (1973) argued that on Plato's account we love people only as **bearers of good qualities**, and so would trade them for anyone better. The particular, irreplaceable person drops out, and the climber leaves individuals behind as "steps only".

**Replies.** Some argue the ascent **includes** love of persons, since one loves their souls and shares the climb with them. Others note that Aristophanes' speech, which puts the individual at the centre, is answered by Diotima's point that we do not love our "other half" unless it is **good**. Others hold that Alcibiades' speech is Plato's own reminder of what the theory leaves out. **Disputed.**

**"Platonic love"** in the modern sense, love without sex, is a later idea. Plato's love starts with desire and redirects it, rather than denying it.
Republic I: Thrasymachus and justice as:
The *Republic*, Plato's longest work after the *Laws*, asks one question across ten books: **what is justice, and is the just person happier than the unjust?** It opens, in Book I, like an early dialogue.

**The setting.** Socrates goes down to the **Piraeus**, Athens' port, for a festival, and ends up at the house of **Cephalus**, an old, rich resident foreigner.

**Two failed definitions:**

1. **Cephalus:** justice is **telling the truth and paying back what you owe**. Socrates: if a friend lends you a weapon and then goes mad, you should not give it back. So that is not a definition.
2. **Polemarchus**, his son, quoting the poet Simonides: justice is **helping friends and harming enemies**. Socrates: harming someone makes them **worse**, and justice cannot make anyone worse, any more than heat can make something cold. So **the just person harms no one**.

**Then Thrasymachus**, a Sophist, breaks in like a wild beast (*Republic* 338c; translated by Benjamin Jowett, first published 1871; text from Project Gutenberg):

> "I proclaim that justice is nothing else than the interest of the stronger."

**His argument, at its strongest:**

1. In every city **the ruling group makes the laws** in its own interest: democracies democratic laws, tyrants tyrannical ones.
2. They **call** obedience to those laws "justice".
3. So justice is what benefits **the stronger**, the rulers.
4. More bluntly: justice is **another's good**. The just person is a fool who serves others; the perfectly unjust person, the tyrant, takes everything and is **happiest**.

**Socrates' replies:**

- **Rulers make mistakes.** If they pass a law against their own interest, obeying it is just but not to their advantage. Thrasymachus answers that a ruler, **strictly speaking**, does not err, as a doctor in so far as he is a doctor does not.
- **The craft argument.** Then take ruling strictly, as a **craft** (*technē*). Every craft serves **its object**: medicine the patient, not the doctor; shepherding the sheep. So ruling serves **the ruled**.
- **The function argument.** Everything has a **function** (*ergon*) and a virtue by which it performs it well: eyes see, by sight. The soul's function is **living**, and its virtue is justice (agreed earlier). So the just soul lives well, and **the just person is happy**.

**Where these arguments stand.** Most readers, and Plato himself, find them **unsatisfying**. Thrasymachus can say a shepherd fattens the sheep **for the slaughter**, which he does in the text. The function argument assumes what is in question, that justice is the soul's virtue. Socrates admits at the end that he has not even said **what justice is**.

**Interpretations of Thrasymachus.** Is he a **conventionalist** (justice is whatever the rulers' laws say), an **egoist** (only one's own advantage is worth having), or a **nihilist** about justice? Scholars dispute which, or whether he is consistent at all.

**Why the book does not end here.** Book I works as a **failed early dialogue**: refutation without an answer. The next nine books are Plato's attempt to do better.
Republic II: Glaucon's challenge and the:
At the start of Book II Plato's brothers, **Glaucon** and **Adeimantus**, refuse to accept Book I. They restate Thrasymachus' case **more strongly** than he did, without believing it, and ask Socrates to answer it properly.

**Three kinds of good** (357b–d):

| Kind | Example |
| --- | --- |
| good **for its own sake** only | harmless pleasures |
| good **for its own sake and for its results** | sight, health, knowledge |
| good **only for its results**, burdensome in itself | exercise, medical treatment, earning money |

**Most people put justice in the third class.** Socrates says it belongs in the second, the finest. Glaucon demands he prove it.

**Glaucon's theory of where justice comes from**, the first **social contract** theory of justice:

1. **By nature**, doing injustice is good and suffering it is bad, but suffering it is **worse** than doing it is good.
2. People who cannot do injustice without suffering it **agree** to neither do nor suffer it.
3. **Justice** is the name for that agreement: a **compromise** between the best (injustice without penalty) and the worst (being wronged without revenge).
4. So no one is just willingly; only from **weakness** and fear.

**The ring of Gyges** (359d–360d), to prove point 4. A shepherd in Lydia (the Greek manuscripts call him an ancestor of Gyges; Jowett's text simply calls him Gyges, ancestor of Croesus) finds a gold ring in a chasm opened by an earthquake. Turning its setting inward makes him **invisible**. He goes to the palace, seduces the queen, kills the king and takes the throne. **Glaucon's challenge:** give such a ring to a just man and an unjust man, and both would act the same. **No one would stay just if they could not be caught.**

**The two lives** (360e–362c). Now imagine the **perfectly unjust** person: clever, never caught, with a **reputation for justice**, rich, honoured. And the **perfectly just** person: with a **reputation for injustice**, poor, tortured and finally impaled. Show that the second is happier. Strip justice of every reward, and prove it is worth having in itself.

**Adeimantus adds:** even parents and poets praise justice only for its **rewards**, in this life or from the gods, who, the poets say, can be bought off with sacrifice. No one praises justice **itself**.

**Why this is the key to the whole *Republic*.** Socrates accepts the challenge as set. The rest of the book must show that **justice is good for the just person's soul**, whatever happens to them. That is a very strong claim, and the test of the book.

**The modern afterlife of the argument.** Glaucon's contract is ancestor to **Hobbes** (Stage 8) and to game-theoretic accounts of cooperation. The ring is the standard test case for **why be moral** when you could get away with it. Whether Socrates finally meets the challenge, or changes the subject, is **the central dispute about the *Republic***, taken up in Lessons 19 and 23.
The Republic's city and soul analogy:
To find justice in a person, Socrates proposes, look first at a **city**. Justice in a city will be like justice in a soul, but written in **larger letters**, easier to read (368d). Then compare.

**Building the city** (Book II):

1. **The first city.** People need food, shelter and clothes, and no one is self-sufficient. So they divide labour: farmers, builders, weavers, traders. **Each does one job**, the one he is suited to by nature. Socrates calls this the **true and healthy city**. Glaucon calls it **"a city of pigs"**: no couches, no sauces.
2. **The luxurious city.** Add luxuries, and the city needs more land. That means **war**, and war needs a professional army.
3. **The guardians.** The soldiers must be fierce to enemies and gentle to citizens, like good dogs. They need a careful **education** in music, poetry and gymnastics, with the poets **censored**, since stories of gods behaving badly corrupt the young.

**The three classes:**

| Class | Job | Virtue that is theirs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Rulers** (the complete guardians) | decide for the whole city | **wisdom** |
| **Auxiliaries** (soldiers) | defend, enforce the rulers' decisions | **courage**: holding to right belief about what to fear |
| **Producers** (farmers, craftsmen, traders) | make and exchange goods | (share in moderation) |

**Moderation** is the **agreement** of all three about who should rule. **Justice** is **each class doing its own work** and not meddling in another's (433a–b). Injustice is meddling: a cobbler trying to be a general, a soldier trying to rule.

**The "noble lie"** (414b–415d). To hold the classes together, citizens are to be told a myth: all are born from the earth, brothers, but the god mixed **gold** in rulers, **silver** in auxiliaries, and **iron and bronze** in producers. Children may move between classes if their metal differs from their parents'. The Greek *gennaion pseudos* is translated "noble lie" or "magnificent myth"; how sinister it is meant to be is **disputed**.

**The strongest objection to the analogy: is a soul like a city?** Plato needs the **same** structure in both. But a city's parts are **persons**, and a soul's parts are not. And why think the virtue of a whole city is the same thing as the virtue of a person? **Bernard Williams** argued (1973) that the analogy, pushed hard, makes the lowest class need to be ruled from outside, and so creates trouble for Plato's picture of a just city of just people.

**A reply:** Plato offers the city as a **heuristic**, a guide for where to look, and then argues independently for the parts of the soul (next lesson). The analogy suggests; the argument proves.

**The political objection.** The city rests on rigid classes, censorship and myth. **Karl Popper**'s *The Open Society and Its Enemies* (1945) called Plato a forerunner of **totalitarianism**. Defenders reply that the city is a **model of the soul** (Plato says as much at the end of Book IX), and that Plato is no more advocating it than a doctor advocates a diagram. Both readings have serious modern defenders.
The tripartite soul and Plato's definiti:
In Book IV Plato argues that the **soul** (*psychē*, the source of life, thought and desire) has **three parts**, matching the three classes of the city. This is the first systematic theory of mental conflict in Western thought.

**The principle of opposites** (436b): **the same thing cannot do or undergo opposites, in the same respect, in relation to the same thing, at the same time**. A spinning top is moving at its edge and still at its axis; different parts. So when a person is pulled two ways at once, there must be **two parts** pulling.

**The arguments for three parts:**

1. **Reason against appetite.** A man is thirsty, and at the same time **holds himself back** from drinking, because he judges it harmful. The drive to drink and the restraint are opposites at once. So there is an **appetitive** part (desire for food, drink, sex, money) and a **rational** part (that calculates what is best).
2. **Spirit against appetite.** **Leontius**, walking up from the Piraeus, saw corpses by the executioner. He wanted to look, and was disgusted with himself. At last he ran up to them and cursed his own eyes for gazing. The **anger** at his appetite is neither appetite nor mere calculation. So there is a third part, **spirit** (*thumos*): the seat of anger, pride, shame and the sense of honour.
3. **Spirit against reason.** Odysseus, home in disguise, is furious at the maids, and **strikes his breast**, telling his heart to endure. Reason **checks** anger. And children and animals have spirit long before reason. So spirit is not reason either.

**The parts and their virtues:**

| Part | Like, in the city | Virtue |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Reason** | rulers | **wisdom**: knowing what is good for the whole soul |
| **Spirit** | auxiliaries | **courage**: holding to reason's judgement through pleasure and fear |
| **Appetite** | producers | (agreement that reason rule) |

**Justice in the soul** is **each part doing its own work**, reason ruling with spirit as its ally, appetite obeying. Justice is not first a matter of outward acts. It is **inner order, a kind of health of the soul**; injustice is a kind of disease, civil war among the parts.

**This is Plato's answer to Glaucon.** Who would choose to have a **diseased** soul, even with Gyges' ring? So justice is good **in itself**.

**The strongest objection: "the fallacy in Plato's *Republic*"** (David Sachs, 1963). Glaucon asked about **ordinary justice**: not stealing, not breaking promises. Plato has proved something about **inner harmony**. He never shows that a person with an ordered soul will not steal or betray, or that ordinary justice requires inner harmony. If not, he has **changed the subject**.

**Replies.** A well-ordered person, ruled by reason, will lack the **motives** for ordinary injustice: greed, ambition and lust are what drive it (Plato says as much at 442e–443a). Others argue Plato's reason, which loves the good itself, would favour ordinary justice. Whether these replies close the gap is **one of the most discussed questions** about the work.

**A second objection: the homunculus problem.** If each part has its own wants and beliefs, each looks like **a little person inside**, and each would need parts in turn. Defenders read the parts as **kinds of motivation**, not agents.

**Why it matters.** The divided soul lies behind Aristotle's ethics, Christian accounts of the passions, and, at a distance, **Freud**'s ego, superego and id.
Philosopher-kings and the three waves:
Book V turns from justice to the question Socrates has been dodging: **could the ideal city exist?** He answers in three proposals, which he calls **waves**, each bigger and more likely to drown him in ridicule.

**The first wave: women guardians** (451c–457b). Women of the guardian class get **the same education** and the same jobs as men, including ruling and war. Nature differs between the sexes in the way that matters for **childbirth**, not for **guarding**. Plato adds that women are on average weaker. The proposal was radical for Athens, where citizen women had no political role. Whether Plato is a **proto-feminist** or simply eliminating the household as a rival loyalty is **disputed**.

**The second wave: no private family** for the guardians (457c–466d). Guardians hold **no private property**, and men and women are mated in arranged festivals, the lots secretly **rigged** so the best breed with the best. Children are raised in common; no one knows their own. Everyone calls all of one generation father and mother. The aim: **unity**, so the city feels pain and joy **as one**, with no family interest to divide it.

**The third and biggest wave: philosopher-kings** (473c–d; translated by Benjamin Jowett, first published 1871; text from Project Gutenberg):

> "Until philosophers are kings, or the kings and princes of this world have the spirit and power of philosophy, and political greatness and wisdom meet in one, and those commoner natures who pursue either to the exclusion of the other are compelled to stand aside, cities will never have rest from their evils"

**Why philosophers?** A **philosopher** (literally "lover of wisdom") is defined here as one who loves **knowledge of the Forms**, not just sights and sounds. Socrates argues:

1. **Knowledge** is set over **what is**; ignorance over what is not; **opinion** (*doxa*) over what is in between, the changing, many things.
2. Lovers of sights know only beautiful things, so have only **opinion**. The philosopher knows **Beauty itself**.
3. **Rulers must know** what is good for a city.
4. So **philosophers, and only they, should rule**.

**The ship of state** (Book VI, 488a–489a). Imagine a ship whose owner is large but deaf and short-sighted. The sailors quarrel for the helm, though none has learned navigation, and they call the true navigator, who studies the stars and winds, a **stargazer** and good for nothing. That, says Socrates, is how democracies treat philosophers.

**Objections:**

1. **Who decides who has knowledge?** Every would-be ruler claims it. Plato has no procedure for checking the rulers, which is **Popper's** chief complaint.
2. **Knowledge of the Forms is not practical wisdom.** Mathematics and dialectic do not teach how to run a harbour or a war. Plato replies that the guardians spend **fifteen years in practical service** before ruling (Book VII), but critics, starting with **Aristotle**, insist that practical wisdom is a different kind of knowledge (Stage 4).
3. **The family proposals destroy what they aim at.** Aristotle again (*Politics* II, paraphrased): **what is common to the greatest number gets the least care**, and a son shared by a thousand fathers is in effect no one's son.

**Plato tried it.** His visits to Syracuse to make Dionysius II a philosopher-ruler failed. The ideal stayed on paper, and, as Lesson 29 shows, the old Plato sketched a different city.
The sun and the divided line:
In Books VI and VII Socrates gives three linked images to explain what the philosopher-kings must learn: the **sun**, the **divided line** and the **cave**. The first two set up the third.

**The highest object of study is the Form of the Good.** Socrates says he cannot tell what it is, only offer an image of it, which Jowett's translation calls **"the child of the good"**.

**The sun** (507b–509b):

| In the visible world | In the intelligible world |
| --- | --- |
| **the sun** | **the Good** |
| light | truth |
| the eye | the mind |
| seeing | knowing |
| visible things | Forms |
| the sun **makes things visible** and causes them to **grow and exist** | the Good makes Forms **knowable** and gives them their **being** |

**The Good is beyond being** (*epekeina tēs ousias*, 509b; Jowett: it "far exceeds essence in dignity and power"): it is the source of the being of other things. Glaucon laughs. What this means is **one of the most disputed sentences in Plato**. Later **Neoplatonists**, Plotinus above all (Stage 5), built a metaphysics on it.

**The divided line** (509d–511e). Take a line and cut it into two unequal parts, then cut each part again in the same ratio. Four sections:

| Section | State of mind | Its objects |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 4 (top) | **understanding** (*noēsis*) | **Forms**, reached by dialectic, rising to the Good, using **no images** |
| 3 | **thought** (*dianoia*) | mathematical objects; reasoning **down from assumptions**, using diagrams |
| 2 | **belief** (*pistis*) | ordinary physical things: animals, plants, artefacts |
| 1 (bottom) | **imagining** (*eikasia*) | shadows, reflections, images |

**Sections 1–2 are opinion; 3–4 are knowledge.** Each section relates to the one above as **image to original**: reflections to things, things to mathematical objects, those to Forms.

**The key contrast is between 3 and 4.** The mathematician **assumes** his starting points (odd and even, the kinds of angles) and reasons down from them, using drawn figures to think about the square itself. The dialectician treats assumptions as **hypotheses in the literal sense, things put under, stepping-stones**, and climbs up to an **unhypothetical first principle**, the Good, then comes back down using Forms alone. Only that is full knowledge.

**Puzzles and disputes:**

1. **The ratio problem.** If the line is cut as instructed, sections 2 and 3 come out **equal** in length. Is that significant, or an accident of the geometry? Debated.
2. **Are mathematical objects separate things?** Aristotle reports Plato held there were "intermediates" between Forms and sensibles. Whether the line commits him to them is **disputed**.
3. **What is dialectic?** Plato never gives a worked example of the climb to the unhypothetical. Its nature is reconstructed, and contested.

**Why it matters.** The line is the first map of **kinds of knowledge**, and its contrast between proof from assumptions and knowledge of first principles shaped the idea of **foundations** in philosophy, from Aristotle to Descartes (Stage 8).
Reading: the allegory of the cave (Repub:
The most famous image in philosophy, read closely. It opens Book VII (514a–520a). The text is **Plato, *Republic*, translated by Benjamin Jowett** (first published 1871), quoted verbatim from the Project Gutenberg text. Socrates is speaking to Glaucon.

**1. The prisoners** (514a):

> "Behold! human beings living in a underground den, which has a mouth open towards the light and reaching all along the den; here they have been from their childhood, and have their legs and necks chained so that they cannot move, and can only see before them"

Behind them a fire burns; between fire and prisoners runs a low wall, **"like the screen which marionette players have in front of them"**, along which people carry statues and figures. The prisoners see only **shadows** of these on the wall in front of them.

**Glaucon: "they are strange prisoners." Socrates: "Like ourselves."** The whole story turns on that reply. The cave is not about some other people.

**2. What they take for real:**

> "To them, I said, the truth would be literally nothing but the shadows of the images."

Notice **"shadows of the images"**: the carried figures are themselves copies. The prisoners are **two steps** from reality, as the bottom of the divided line is from things.

**3. The release.** A prisoner is freed and **"compelled suddenly to stand up and turn his neck round"**. The light hurts. Told that the objects are more real than the shadows, he thinks **"the shadows which he formerly saw are truer"**. Then he is **"reluctantly dragged up a steep and rugged ascent"** into the daylight.

Three things to see: education is **painful**; it is first a **turning around**, not filling up; and it needs **force**, someone else's or one's own.

**4. The ascent, in order** (516a–b): shadows, then reflections in water, then the things themselves, then the moon and stars at night, and

> "Last of all he will be able to see the sun, and not mere reflections of him in the water, but he will see him in his own proper place"

**5. The return** (516e–517a). Back in the cave, his eyes full of darkness, he cannot compete in the shadow-guessing contests:

> "Men would say of him that up he went and down he came without his eyes; ... and if any one tried to loose another and lead him up to the light, let them only catch the offender, and they would put him to death."

**Every Athenian reader knew whom that meant.**

**6. Socrates' own key** (517b):

> "the prison-house is the world of sight, the light of the fire is the sun, and you will not misapprehend me if you interpret the journey upwards to be the ascent of the soul into the intellectual world"

**How the parts map, on the standard reading:**

| In the cave | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| shadows on the wall | images; opinion at its lowest |
| fire, carried figures | the visible world and its sun |
| the world outside | the intelligible world of **Forms** |
| the sun | **the Good** |
| the freed prisoner | the philosopher; his return, the duty to rule |

**Open questions.** Does each stage of the climb match a section of the divided line exactly? Plato hints so (517b); scholars dispute how closely. And the return: the philosophers are **compelled** to go back down and rule (519c–520c). Glaucon asks if that is unjust to them. Socrates replies that the law aims at the good of the whole city, and that they owe the city their education. Whether this fits the claim that justice is good **for** the just person is **a standing puzzle**.
The decline of constitutions and the hap:
Books VIII and IX tell how the ideal city would **decay**, step by step, and match each worse city with a worse kind of person. Then Plato returns to Glaucon's challenge and argues that the just life is the happiest.

**Why decay at all?** Everything that comes to be passes away. The rulers will eventually miscalculate the right times for breeding (Plato gives a deliberately obscure number for this, which scholars call **the nuptial number**). Worse children are born, and the classes mix.

**The five constitutions, and the matching souls:**

| City | Who rules | The matching person | What rules in his soul |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Aristocracy** (rule of the best) | philosophers | the philosopher | **reason** |
| **Timocracy** (rule of honour, like Sparta) | soldiers who love honour | the ambitious man | **spirit** |
| **Oligarchy** | the rich | the miser | **necessary appetites**, above all for money |
| **Democracy** | the people, by lot | the man of every passing desire | **all appetites as equals**, taking turns |
| **Tyranny** | one man | the tyrant | **lawless appetite**, ruled by a single master passion, **erotic desire** |

**The portrait of democracy** is the most quoted and the most hostile. Freedom becomes so total that no one obeys, teachers fear pupils, even the animals walk proudly in the streets. The democratic man drinks one day, diets the next, does philosophy, then politics, with **no order** among his desires. **Out of extreme freedom comes the tyrant**, who arrives as the people's champion.

**Then the argument that the just are happiest**, given three times in Book IX:

1. **The tyrant's soul is enslaved.** The tyrant, who seems freest, is ruled by his worst part, full of fear, friendless, always craving. Like his city, he is **the most miserable**.
2. **The judge from experience.** Each part of the soul has its own love: reason of wisdom, spirit of honour, appetite of gain. Only the **philosopher** has tasted all three pleasures, and only he judges by reason. He ranks wisdom's pleasure highest. So it is.
3. **True and false pleasure.** Most bodily pleasures are only **relief from pain**, which feels like pleasure by contrast, as a middle point looks high to one who has only been low. The pleasures of knowing are of what is **more real**, so they are **truer**. Socrates calculates, half in jest, that the king lives **729 times** more pleasantly than the tyrant.

**Objections:**

- **Argument 2 assumes its conclusion.** The philosopher judges by reason, but the honour-lover and the money-lover can say their own pleasures were never tasted fully by the philosopher. Why trust reason as judge, unless reason is already ranked highest?
- **Argument 3 needs Plato's metaphysics.** "More real pleasures" makes sense only if Forms are more real than things.
- **The tyrant is a caricature.** Glaucon's challenge was the **perfectly unjust man who is never caught and suffers no fear**. A miserable tyrant does not answer it.

**Reply:** Plato's point is about the **soul's condition**, not outward fortune. Disorder within is misery whatever the reputation. Whether this meets the challenge returns to the Sachs debate in Lesson 19.

**Why it matters.** The sequence of regimes is the ancestor of every **theory of political cycles**, from Polybius to the modern fear that democracy breeds demagogues.
Republic X: the quarrel with the poets a:
Book X ends the *Republic* with two things that seem odd after the cave: an attack on poetry, and a story of the afterlife.

**The banishment of the poets** (595a–608b). The guardians' education in Books II–III censored poetry. Now Plato goes further: **imitative** poetry, including Homer, is to be **excluded** from the city, apart from hymns to the gods and praise of good men.

**Two arguments:**

1. **Poetry is three removes from truth** (Jowett's introduction says "thrice removed"). Take a bed. There is the **Form** of bed, made by god; the **carpenter's** bed, a copy of the Form; and a **painter's** bed, a copy of the carpenter's, showing only how it looks from one side. The painter knows nothing about beds. So too the poet: he imitates generals, doctors and good men without knowing generalship, medicine or virtue. The Greek word is **mimēsis**, "imitation" or "representation".
2. **Poetry feeds the worst part of the soul.** Tragedy makes us weep and indulge grief we would be ashamed of in our own lives. It **waters the passions** when they should be dried up, and sets up a bad constitution in the soul.

Plato calls this, in Jowett's words, **"an ancient quarrel between philosophy and poetry"**, and invites anyone to defend poetry in prose: show that it is **useful** as well as delightful, and it may return.

**Objections.** **Aristotle**'s *Poetics* (Stage 4) answered: imitation is natural and a way of **learning**, and tragedy, far from feeding pity and fear, brings a **catharsis** (purging or clarifying) of them. And Plato is himself a **great literary artist**, whose dialogues are full of myths, images and characters. Scholars dispute whether Book X is a total ban or an attack on a particular use of poetry, the Homeric education of Athens. Plato's views on art are among the most debated in his work.

**A proof of immortality** (608c–611a). Each thing is destroyed by **its own evil**: the eye by disease, wood by rot. The soul's evil is **injustice**. But injustice does not kill the soul; wicked people live on and on. So nothing can destroy the soul. **Weakness, widely noted:** that vice does not kill quickly does not show nothing could ever destroy a soul.

**The myth of Er** (614b–621d). **Er**, a soldier killed in battle, revives on his funeral pyre on the twelfth day and tells what he saw. Souls are judged: the just go up to a thousand years of reward, the unjust down to a thousand years of punishment, tenfold for each wrong. The worst tyrants never come out. Then souls gather before the **Spindle of Necessity** and the three Fates, and **choose their next lives** from a set laid out before them. The herald proclaims (617e; Jowett):

> "Virtue is free, and as a man honours or dishonours her he will have more or less of her; the responsibility is with the chooser—God is justified."

The first soul, who had been virtuous by habit without philosophy, grabs the life of a tyrant and then finds he will eat his own children. **Odysseus**, last, chooses the quiet life of a private man. All cross **"the plain of Forgetfulness"** and drink from **"the river of Unmindfulness"** (Jowett), and are born.

**Why end on a myth?** The argument has shown justice is good **in itself**. Now Plato gives back the **rewards**, after death, that Glaucon asked him to take away. The myth also says what philosophy is for: learning to **choose a life well**. How literally Plato meant his myths, and whether he believed in reincarnation, are **disputed**.
The Theaetetus: three attempts to define:
The *Theaetetus* is set in 399 BC, just before Socrates' trial; it ends with him going off to answer Meletus' charge. He talks with **Theaetetus**, a brilliant young mathematician (about 415–369 BC) who later did fundamental work on irrational lengths, and his teacher **Theodorus**. The question: **what is knowledge** (*epistēmē*)?

**Socrates as midwife.** He says he is like his mother, a **midwife**: barren of wisdom himself, he helps others give birth to ideas and tests whether what is born is, in Jowett's words, **"a false idol or a noble and true birth"**. This is the most famous self-description of the elenchus.

**Definition 1: knowledge is perception** (151e–186e). Socrates links it to two earlier theories:

- **Protagoras**: "man is the measure of all things" (Stage 2). If the wind feels cold to me, it **is** cold for me. No one can be wrong.
- **Heraclitean flux**: everything is always changing; perceptions are brief meetings between changing senses and changing things.

**The refutations, in rising strength:**

1. **Self-refutation.** If whatever anyone believes is true for them, then those who believe Protagoras is **false** are right, for them. So Protagoras must grant his own view is false. (Whether this argument is fair to Protagoras is **disputed**.)
2. **The future.** A doctor knows better than the patient whether he **will** have a fever. Expertise is about what will be, and there man is not the measure.
3. **Total flux ruins language.** If everything changes in every way, even "seeing" does not stay seeing long enough to be named.
4. **The decisive argument** (184b–186e). We perceive **through** the senses, each with its own objects: colour by sight, sound by hearing. But the soul **itself**, not any sense, grasps what is **common**: that a colour and a sound both **exist**, are **different**, are **two**. Since knowledge needs truth, and truth needs **being**, which perception does not grasp, **knowledge is not perception**. This argument is widely regarded as **successful**.

**Definition 2: knowledge is true judgement** (187a–201c). A long puzzle follows about how **false** judgement is possible at all. Two models of the mind:

- **The wax tablet:** memory as impressions; error as fitting a perception to the wrong impression.
- **The aviary:** knowledge as birds in a cage; error as grabbing the wrong bird.

Both fail for errors in pure thought, such as 7 + 5 = 11. Then the counterexample that sinks definition 2: a **jury** persuaded by an orator may reach a **true** verdict about a robbery no juror saw. They have true judgement, but **not knowledge**.

**Definition 3: true judgement with an account** (*logos*; 201c–210a). This is close to the *Meno*'s formula. Socrates first tests a **"dream" theory**: complexes are knowable, but their simple elements cannot be explained, and so cannot be known. Objection: the syllable "SO" cannot be known if its letters are not. Then three senses of **account** fail in turn: speaking one's thought aloud; listing the parts; giving a **mark that distinguishes** the thing. The last fails because the mark must itself be **known**, which is circular.

**It ends in aporia.** Why did Plato leave it there? Some read it as showing knowledge needs **Forms**, which are never mentioned. Others read it as genuine inquiry without that theory. **Disputed.**

**Why it matters.** "Justified true belief" became the textbook analysis, and **Edmund Gettier**'s three-page paper (1963) showed with counterexamples that it is not enough, much as the jury case undid definition 2.
The Parmenides and the Third Man argumen:
In the *Parmenides* Plato does something remarkable: he has **Parmenides** (Stage 2), aged about sixty-five, take apart the theory of Forms, put in the mouth of a **young Socrates**, about twenty. The setting is fictional, a visit to Athens for a festival with **Zeno**.

**The objections to the Forms, in order:**

1. **Which Forms?** (130b–e). Socrates accepts Forms of likeness, justice and beauty; hesitates over man, fire and water; and thinks Forms of **hair, mud and dirt** absurd. Parmenides says that when he is older and philosophy has gripped him, he will not despise such things.
2. **The whole-part dilemma** (131a–e). If a thing participates in a Form, does it get the **whole** Form or a **part**? If the whole, one Form is in many separate things, and so separate from itself. If a part, then a thing is large by a **part of Largeness**, which is smaller than Largeness. Socrates suggests a Form is like **a day**, in many places at once; Parmenides replaces the day with **a sail** spread over many people, each covered by a part.
3. **The Third Man** (132a–b), below.
4. **Forms as thoughts** (132b–c). If a Form is only a thought, it must be a thought **of** something, which would be the Form.
5. **Forms as patterns** (132d–133a). If things participate by **resembling** the Form, the Form resembles them too, and a further Form is needed for their likeness: the regress again.
6. **The greatest difficulty**, as Parmenides calls it (133b–134e). If the Forms are wholly separate, they relate only to each other. Then **we cannot know them**, and the gods, who know them, **cannot know us**.

**The Third Man argument**, set out. It concerns the Form of Largeness; the name "Third Man" comes from **Aristotle**, who used a version with the Form of Man.

1. **One over many:** whenever many things are large, there is **one Form**, Largeness, by which they are large.
2. **Self-predication:** Largeness is **itself large**.
3. **Non-identity:** what makes things large is **not one of them**.
4. Then the large things **plus Largeness** are a new set of many large things.
5. By (1), there is a **second Form**, Largeness 2, by which they are large. By (2) and (3), it is large and distinct from them; and so on.
6. **So there is not one Form of Largeness but infinitely many**, contradicting the theory's claim that each Form is one.

**Gregory Vlastos** (1954) showed that the premises are **inconsistent** with each other: (2) and (3) together already deny that Largeness is unique. The question is which Plato should drop.

**The main readings:**

- **Plato saw the theory was in trouble**, and the late dialogues are a revised metaphysics.
- **Plato kept the Forms** and meant the objections as exercises; the fault is in a **misunderstanding**, most often **self-predication** read as "Largeness is a large thing". On a better reading, "Largeness is large" means "**being large is what Largeness is**", and the regress does not start.
- **The second half of the dialogue**, a long, baffling series of arguments about **the One**, is the gymnastics Parmenides says Socrates needs. What it shows is among the **most disputed** questions in Plato scholarship.

**Where the field stands.** It is **agreed** that the argument is valid given the three premises, and that Plato, at least, was aware of it. Whether the theory survives depends on how the Forms are read.
The Sophist: not-being and the greatest:
The *Sophist* continues the *Theaetetus* the next day. Socrates says little. The leader is a **Stranger from Elea**, Parmenides' home town, a follower of his school. The task: define **the sophist**, and so tell him apart from the philosopher.

**The method of division.** The Stranger practises by defining an **angler**: an art that **acquires** rather than makes; by **hunting**; living prey; water creatures; fish; by striking, with a hook, from below. Each step **divides a kind into two** and follows one branch. Applied to the sophist, division gives six different definitions, among them a paid hunter of rich young men, a merchant of learning, and an expert in refutation. The seventh and last: **a maker of images**, of the **false appearance** of wisdom.

**The problem this raises.** To call the sophist a maker of falsehoods is to say **false statements exist**. A false statement says **what is not**. And **Parmenides** (Stage 2) taught that **what is not cannot be said or thought at all**. So the sophist can hide behind Parmenides: there is no such thing as falsehood.

**To catch him, the Stranger must do "parricide"**: in Jowett's translation he asks Theaetetus not to **"regard me as a parricide"** for laying hands on **"my father Parmenides"**.

**First, being is as puzzling as not-being.** The Stranger reviews the **battle of gods and giants**:

| Side | Claim |
| --- | --- |
| **The giants** (materialists) | only what can be touched, bodies, is real |
| **The friends of the Forms** | only unchanging Forms are real; bodies are mere becoming |

Against the giants: justice and wisdom are real, and not bodies. The Stranger offers a mark of being (247e; translated by Benjamin Jowett, first published 1871; text from Project Gutenberg): **"the definition of being is simply power"**, the power to affect or be affected. Against the friends of Forms: knowing is a kind of **acting on**, so Forms that are known are affected, and so changed in some way. **Being must include both rest and change.**

**The greatest kinds** (254b–259b). Five Forms that **blend** with each other:

1. **Being**
2. **Change** (motion)
3. **Rest**
4. **Sameness**
5. **Difference**

Change **is** (it shares in being) but **is not** being itself. It is the **same** as itself and **different** from rest. So **"is not" can mean "is different from"**. **Not-being is difference**, and it is everywhere: each kind is not countless others.

**False statement solved** (261c–263d). A statement weaves a **name** with a **verb**. "Theaetetus sits" is true. "Theaetetus flies" is false: it says of Theaetetus things that **are**, flying exists, but are **different from** the things that are true of him. Falsehood is no longer saying **nothing**; it is saying **what is other than what is**.

**Why it matters, and the disputes.**

- This is the first analysis of the structure of a **sentence**, subject and predicate, and of **falsity**. Modern philosophy of language starts close to here.
- Did Plato here **distinguish senses of "is"**: identity ("change is not rest") from predication ("change is")? Some scholars say yes, and see a major logical discovery; others deny that Plato needed or made the distinction. **Disputed.**
- Is the "power" mark meant as a **definition** of being, or a provisional offer to the giants? **Disputed**; the text calls it a proposal.
- Does the theory of Forms survive in revised form, with Forms now **blending**? The standard reading says it has been **developed**, not abandoned.
The Timaeus: the craftsman and the likel:
The *Timaeus* is Plato's account of the origin of the **cosmos** (Greek: the ordered world), of the soul, and of the human body. Its speaker, **Timaeus** of Locri in southern Italy, an astronomer, is otherwise unknown and may be invented. The dialogue also opens with the story of **Atlantis**, told as history but generally agreed to be **Plato's invention**.

**The starting point** (27d–29d). Distinguish:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **being** | what always is and never becomes; grasped by thought; the eternal **model** |
| **becoming** | what comes to be and passes away; grasped by opinion with sensation |

The visible world **became**, since it is bodily. Whatever becomes has a **cause**. Its maker, the **Demiurge** (Greek *dēmiourgos*, "craftsman"), looked to the **eternal model** and made the world as like it as possible.

**Why he made it** (29e; translated by Benjamin Jowett, first published 1871; text from Project Gutenberg):

> "He was good, and the good can never have jealousy of anything. And being free from jealousy, he desired that all things should be as like himself as they could be."

**The "likely story."** Because the world is only an **image**, an account of it can only be **likely**, not exact. In Jowett's words, as being is to becoming, **"so is truth to belief"**, and we must be content with **"probabilities as likely as any others"**.

**The main contents:**

1. **The world is one living creature**, with a body and a **world soul**, made of mixed sameness, difference and being, divided by musical ratios, which moves the heavens.
2. **Time** is made with the heavens: in Jowett's phrase, **"a moving image of eternity"**, measured by the planets.
3. **Reason meets necessity.** The craftsman does not make from nothing. He works on a third kind besides being and becoming: the **receptacle** (*chōra*, "space" or "place"), which Plato calls the nurse of becoming, where images of the Forms appear and pass.
4. **Geometrical elements.** Fire, air, water and earth are built from **triangles** into solids: fire the **tetrahedron**, air the **octahedron**, water the **icosahedron**, earth the **cube**. This is the most mathematical physics of antiquity.
5. **The human being**: an immortal rational soul made by the craftsman, mortal parts and body made by lesser gods. Sight was given us so that, watching the orderly heavens, we could order our own souls.

**The great dispute: was there a beginning?** Read literally, the world **came to be** at some moment. **Aristotle** read it so, and objected (Stage 4). Plato's first successors in the Academy said the creation story was a **teaching device**, as a geometer draws a figure step by step though it is timeless. Scholars still **divide** over this.

**Is the craftsman God?** Plato's craftsman orders pre-existing chaos and works under necessity; he is not the creator from nothing of later Jewish, Christian and Muslim thought. How the two pictures relate is a question for Stages 6–7 and the **Theology curriculum**.

**Why it matters.** For about eight centuries the *Timaeus* was **the only Plato most of the Latin West could read**, in part, through the Latin translation and commentary of **Calcidius** (4th century AD). Medieval cosmology was largely built on it.
The Laws: the second-best city:
The *Laws* is Plato's **longest** and probably **last** work, reported to have been left unrevised at his death and copied out from wax tablets by his pupil **Philip of Opus**. It is the only dialogue without **Socrates**.

**The setting.** Three old men walk on a long summer day from Knossos to the cave of Zeus on Crete: an **Athenian Stranger**, **Clinias** of Crete and **Megillus** of Sparta. Clinias is to help found a new colony, and the three design its laws. The text calls it the city of the **Magnesians**, so readers call it **Magnesia**.

**Second-best, and why.** The Athenian still says the best city is one where **friends have all things in common** (Laws V), but that city is for gods or children of gods. Magnesia is the **second-best**: private families and private land, but strictly limited.

**Its main features:**

| Feature | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| **Size** | **5,040** households, a number divisible by every number from 1 to 10 |
| **Property** | land in equal, inalienable lots; wealth allowed to vary only within limits, no more than four times the smallest |
| **Constitution** | a **mixed** constitution, between monarchy and democracy, since Persia had too much of one and Athens of the other |
| **Officials** | elected, with **Guardians of the Laws** and auditors to check them |
| **Education** | public, lifelong, for **girls and boys**; even controlled **drinking parties** as a training in self-control |
| **The Nocturnal Council** | a meeting of the wisest, before dawn, to study the purpose of the laws and keep them sound |

**The rule of law.** The *Republic* put knowledge above law; the *Laws* makes **law** sovereign, and rulers its **servants**. The likeliest reading is that Plato came to think no ruler can be trusted with unchecked power. Whether this is a **change of mind** or the same view applied to a less ideal case is **disputed**.

**Preambles.** Each law comes with a **preamble** (*prooimion*) that **persuades** before it threatens: a free doctor explains his treatment to a free patient; a slave doctor just gives orders. Laws should be like the first. This is the first theory of **why laws should give reasons**.

**Book X: the argument against atheism.** The Athenian names three errors: there are **no gods**; the gods **do not care** about us; they can be **bought off** with sacrifice. Against the first he gives an argument from motion:

1. Some things move others, having been moved; some **move themselves**.
2. A chain of things moved by others must start from **a self-mover**.
3. A self-mover is what we mean by a **soul**.
4. So **soul is prior to body**, and the heavens' orderly motion is caused by a **good soul** or souls.

It is the ancestor of **Aristotle's** unmoved mover (Stage 4) and the cosmological arguments of Stage 7. **Objections:** step 2 assumes there cannot be an infinite chain; step 3 identifies self-motion with soul by definition; and step 4 moves from soul to goodness.

**The penalties.** Impiety is to be punished, and the incurable atheist, after at least five years in what Jowett translates as the **"House of Reformation"**, put to **death**. Readers have noted the irony in a book by Socrates' pupil.

**Why it matters.** The *Laws* was long neglected beside the *Republic*. It is now read as Plato's most practical political philosophy, and the source of later ideas of **mixed constitutions** and the **rule of law**.
Looking back: what Socrates and Plato le:
Stage 2 asked what the world is made of. In this stage the questions turned to **how to live**, **what we can know** and **what is most real**, and almost every later question in Western philosophy got its first serious statement.

**What was established, in the sense of widely accepted ever since:**

- **The method.** Asking for definitions, testing them by counterexample, and following the argument where it leads: the **elenchus** is now simply how philosophy is done.
- **Knowledge is more than true belief.** The *Meno* and *Theaetetus* showed this, with the jury case and the runaway statues. Everyone since has accepted it; what the "more" is remains open.
- **Knowledge is not perception.** The *Theaetetus*' argument that the mind, not the senses, grasps being, sameness and number is widely accepted in some form.
- **The Euthyphro question is real.** Any account of ethics that grounds it in a will, divine or human, has to answer it.
- **Some Platonic arguments fail.** There is broad agreement that **none of the *Phaedo*'s arguments** proves immortality, that the **Book I** arguments against Thrasymachus are weak, and that the **Third Man** is valid against the theory's crudest form.

**What was left open:**

| Question | Where it goes next |
| --- | --- |
| **Are there Forms**, universals apart from things? | Aristotle puts forms **in** things (Stage 4); the medieval problem of universals (Stage 7) |
| **Is justice good for the just?** Glaucon's challenge | the Stoics (Stage 5), Hobbes (Stage 8), and the "why be moral?" question to this day |
| **Is virtue knowledge**, and is akrasia possible? | Aristotle's answer in the *Ethics* (Stage 4), the Stoics (Stage 5) |
| **What is the soul**, and does it survive? | Aristotle's soul as the form of the body (Stage 4); Plotinus (Stage 5); Augustine and Aquinas (Stages 6–7) |
| **Who should rule**: the wise, or the law? | Aristotle's *Politics* (Stage 4); Popper's attack and its critics (Stage 12) |
| **Did the world begin?** | Aristotle's eternal world; the medieval debate (Stages 6–7) |

**The scholarly disputes to remember.** Whether Plato's early dialogues give the historical Socrates; whether Plato's thought **developed** or was one system from the start; whether he speaks through his characters; what the Good beyond being is; whether he held self-predication; whether he ever gave up the Forms.

**A famous verdict, and its limits.** **Alfred North Whitehead** wrote (1929, paraphrased here, since the text is in copyright) that the safest general description of European philosophy is a **series of footnotes to Plato**. It is an exaggeration, and Whitehead meant the abundance of ideas scattered through the dialogues, not a system everyone accepts. But no other writer has set so much of the agenda.

**Socrates and Plato, in one sentence each.** Socrates showed that **examining our beliefs** is part of living well, and died for it. Plato argued that the examination leads beyond the changing world, to **unchanging truths that make knowledge and goodness possible**, and spent fifty years testing his own answer.

**What Stage 4 picks up.** **Aristotle** arrived at the Academy at seventeen, in 367 BC, and stayed twenty years. He kept Plato's questions and rejected many of his answers: the Forms come down into things, ethics becomes the study of **character and practical wisdom**, and logic becomes, for the first time, a formal science. Stage 4 begins with him.
Context: Athens, Macedon and the Academy:
Aristotle lived from 384 to 322 BC, and almost every year of that life was shaped by one fact: **the age of the free Greek city was ending, and he watched it end from close up.**

**The world he was born into.** Athens had lost the Peloponnesian War to Sparta in 404 BC. In 399 it executed Socrates. The fourth century was a time of shifting leagues between Athens, Sparta and Thebes, none strong enough to rule the rest. To the north sat **Macedon**, a kingdom the southern Greeks thought half-barbarian. Under **Philip II** (king 359–336 BC) it became the strongest power in Greece. At **Chaeronea in 338 BC** Philip beat Athens and Thebes, and the cities lost their independence in all but name.
