His son **Alexander** (356–323 BC) then conquered the Persian Empire as far as India.

**Aristotle was tied to both sides.** His father was court doctor to the Macedonian king; he himself tutored Alexander. Yet he did his life's work in Athens, as a resident foreigner who could not own land there. The man who wrote that humans are by nature creatures of the *polis* (the self-governing city) wrote it as the polis was being swallowed by empires.

**The intellectual inheritance.** Three things pressed on him:

| Inheritance | The question it left |
| --- | --- |
| **Parmenides and Zeno** (Stage 2) | Can anything really change or come to be, or is change an illusion? |
| **The Sophists** (Stage 2) | Is anything true or good by nature, or only by custom? |
| **Plato** (Stage 3) | If true knowledge is of unchanging Forms, can there be knowledge of this changing world at all? |

**The Academy.** Plato had founded his school, the **Academy**, outside Athens in about 387 BC. Aristotle arrived at seventeen and stayed about twenty years. It was a place of argument, mathematics and dialectic, and Plato's own late dialogues (Stage 3) show it criticising the theory of Forms from within. **Aristotle's whole philosophy can be read as a long, respectful quarrel with his teacher**: he kept Plato's conviction that knowledge is of what is universal and necessary, and rejected the idea that the universal exists apart from the things that have it.

**What was new.** Greek medicine (the Hippocratic writers) had shown that careful observation could yield general knowledge of the body. Greek mathematics was building proofs from first principles. Aristotle took both as models. His bet was that **the world we see, touch and live in can be known**, in every department, by observing it carefully and reasoning about it rigorously.

**What this stage covers.** His logic (the *Organon*), his natural philosophy (*Physics*), his "first philosophy" (*Metaphysics*), his account of life and mind (*On the Soul*, the biology), his ethics and politics, and his books on persuasion and on tragedy. No single philosopher has covered so much ground, and for some two thousand years, in the Islamic world and in Latin Europe alike, he was simply called **"the Philosopher"**.
Aristotle's life, the Lyceum and the sur:
**Aristotle was born in 384 BC at Stagira**, a small Greek town in the Chalcidice peninsula of northern Greece, which is why he is sometimes called "the Stagirite". His father, **Nicomachus**, was physician to King Amyntas III of Macedon. Both parents died while he was young.

**The life in five stages:**

| Years (BC) | Where | What |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **367–347** | Athens | student, then teacher, in **Plato's Academy**, until Plato's death in 348/347 |
| **347–343** | Assos, then Lesbos | at the court of **Hermias**, ruler of Atarneus, whose relative **Pythias** he married; then on Lesbos with **Theophrastus**, studying marine life |
| **343/342–about 335** | Macedon | tutor to the teenage **Alexander**, at Philip II's invitation |
| **335/334–323** | Athens | founds his own school in the **Lyceum**, a public gymnasium |
| **323–322** | Chalcis, Euboea | leaves Athens after Alexander's death; dies there in **322 BC**, aged about 62 |

**Why he left Athens.** When Alexander died in 323, anti-Macedonian feeling flared. Diogenes Laertius (writing about the third century AD) reports that a priest brought a charge of impiety against him. A later tradition has him saying, in paraphrase, that he left so that Athens would not sin against philosophy a second time, the first being Socrates; the saying may well be a later embellishment.

**The Lyceum.** His school was nicknamed the **Peripatos**, after a covered walkway there, and his followers were called **Peripatetics**. It collected books, specimens and data on a scale no Greek school had tried: the constitutions of 158 cities, lists of victors at the games, the history of medicine. **Theophrastus** (about 371–287 BC) succeeded him as head.

**His will.** Diogenes preserves a will. It provides for his partner **Herpyllis**, mother of his son Nicomachus, and for his daughter Pythias; it frees several named slaves and directs that others be freed when grown, if they deserve it, while still treating people as property to be bequeathed. Keep that in mind for the *Politics*.

**The corpus: what survived is not what he published.** Aristotle wrote polished dialogues for the public (the "exoteric" works). Cicero praised their style as a flowing river of gold (his image, paraphrased here). **They are lost**, except for fragments. What survives are the "**esoteric**" works: **treatises written for teaching**, dense, repetitive, full of cross-references and second thoughts. That is why Aristotle reads so differently from Plato.

**How they came down.** An ancient story (in Strabo and Plutarch) tells of his manuscripts lying in a cellar for generations before reaching Rome. Whatever the truth of it, **Andronicus of Rhodes edited and arranged the treatises in the first century BC**, and our collection descends from his edition. The grouping of the logical works as the *Organon* ("tool") and the title *Metaphysics* are editorial, not Aristotle's.

**How to cite him.** References like **NE 1094a1** use the page, column and line of **Immanuel Bekker's Berlin edition of 1831**. Every modern translation prints them in the margin.
Aristotle's Categories: substance and th:
The *Categories* is a short work, traditionally placed first in the *Organon*. It asks a simple-sounding question: **when we say something about something, what kinds of thing can we be saying?** Its answers shaped Western thought for two thousand years. (Its authenticity has occasionally been doubted; most scholars accept it.)

**The ten categories.** Take Socrates in the marketplace, yesterday, arguing. Everything you can say of him falls under one of ten heads:

| Category | Example |
| --- | --- |
| **Substance** | a man, a horse |
| **Quantity** | five feet tall |
| **Quality** | pale, wise |
| **Relation** | double, older than Plato |
| **Place** | in the marketplace |
| **Time** | yesterday |
| **Position** | sitting |
| **Having** | wearing sandals |
| **Acting** | arguing, cutting |
| **Being affected** | being cut, being refuted |

**Substance comes first.** The Greek is *ousia*, literally "being-ness". Aristotle's definition (Categories 5, translated by E. M. Edghill, 1928):

> "Substance, in the truest and primary and most definite sense of the word, is that which is neither predicable of a subject nor present in a subject; for instance, the individual man or horse."

**Two tests lie behind that.** Something is **"said of" a subject** if it tells you what the subject is: "man" is said of Socrates. Something is **"in" a subject** if it exists only in another thing without being part of what it is: this paleness is in Socrates. The individual man passes neither test: he is not said of anything, and he is not in anything. He is what everything else is said of or is in.

**Primary and secondary substance.** The individual (this man) is **primary substance**. The species and genus it belongs to (man, animal) are **secondary substances**. Everything else depends on primary substances: **if there were no individual things, there would be nothing for qualities, quantities and the rest to belong to.**

**Why this is a revolution.** For Plato, the most real things were the Forms: Man Itself, Beauty Itself, existing apart. For the Aristotle of the *Categories*, **the most real things are the ordinary individuals you can point to**: this horse, that tree, Socrates. Universals exist, but only as said of individuals.

**Other doctrines in the book.** Substances have no contraries (nothing is the opposite of a man) and **can take on contraries while staying one and the same**: Socrates becomes pale, then tanned, and is still Socrates. That is the germ of his whole account of change.

**Objections.**
- *Why ten?* Aristotle gives no derivation. Kant (Stage 10) complained that he simply picked them up as he found them. Elsewhere Aristotle himself often lists only eight, or fewer.
- *Is it about words or things?* Scholars have long disputed whether the categories classify **expressions**, **concepts** or **beings**. Most now say it classifies beings, discovered by attending to how we speak.
- *Is the individual really first?* In the *Metaphysics* (later lessons) Aristotle himself reopens the question, and the answer there is more complicated.
Aristotle's logic: the square of opposit:
In *On Interpretation* and the *Prior Analytics* Aristotle invented **formal logic**: the study of which arguments are valid **because of their form alone**, whatever they are about.

**Four kinds of statement.** Every statement in his system links a subject term (S) to a predicate term (P). Medieval logicians labelled the four forms with vowels, A, E, I, O:

| Label | Form | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **A** | All S are P | All dogs are mammals |
| **E** | No S is P | No dog is a fish |
| **I** | Some S is P | Some dogs are brown |
| **O** | Some S is not P | Some dogs are not brown |

**The square of opposition** arranges them by how their truth depends on each other:
- **Contradictories** (A and O; E and I): **exactly one is true**. If "all dogs are brown" is false, "some dog is not brown" must be true.
- **Contraries** (A and E): **cannot both be true, can both be false**.
- **Subcontraries** (I and O): cannot both be false.
- **Subalternation**: A implies I; E implies O.

**A modern objection.** Today's logic reads "all unicorns are horned" as true if there are no unicorns. Then A does not imply I, and the square partly breaks. **Aristotle's system assumes its terms are not empty**, and with that assumption the square holds. Scholars dispute exactly how he handled empty terms.

**The syllogism.** His definition (Prior Analytics I.1, translated by A. J. Jenkinson, 1928):

> "A syllogism is discourse in which, certain things being stated, something other than what is stated follows of necessity from their being so."

That is a definition of a **valid deduction** in general. His theory then studies one kind: **two premises sharing a middle term (M), yielding a conclusion linking the other two.** The model, later named *Barbara*:

1. All M are P. (All mammals are warm-blooded.)
2. All S are M. (All whales are mammals.)
3. So all S are P. (All whales are warm-blooded.)

**Figures and moods.** The **figure** is where the middle term sits; Aristotle recognised three, and a fourth was added later. A **mood** is the pattern of A, E, I and O in it. He showed which combinations are valid, proved the first-figure ones "perfect" (obviously valid), **reduced** the rest to them, and showed invalid ones invalid by **counterexamples**. He was **the first logician to use letters as variables**, which is the decisive step toward formal logic.

**The sea battle.** *On Interpretation* 9 asks whether a statement such as *there will be a sea battle tomorrow* is already true or false today. If so, he argues, everything happens of necessity. His answer is disputed: many read him as saying such statements are **not yet true or false**, which would limit his logic's rule that every statement is one or the other.

**How long it lasted.** Kant wrote in 1787 that logic had not advanced a step since Aristotle (a paraphrase). **That was too strong**: the Stoics (Stage 5) and medieval logicians added much. But only **Frege's *Begriffsschrift* (1879)** superseded it, because syllogistic **cannot handle relations**. It cannot prove that if every horse is an animal, every head of a horse is the head of an animal, an example usually credited to Augustus De Morgan.
Aristotle's Posterior Analytics: demonst:
If the *Prior Analytics* says what makes reasoning valid, the *Posterior Analytics* says **what makes it knowledge**. It is the first theory of science in the West.

**What scientific knowledge is.** The Greek is *epistēmē*. Aristotle says we know something scientifically when we know **its cause** (why it is so) and know that **it cannot be otherwise**. Knowing *that* the moon is eclipsed is not yet science. Knowing that it is eclipsed **because the earth blocks the sun's light** is.

**Demonstration.** Science is set out as **demonstration** (*apodeixis*): a syllogism whose premises meet strict conditions. In G. R. G. Mure's translation (1928), they "must be true, primary, immediate, better known than and prior to the conclusion, which is further related to them as effect to cause." **The middle term gives the cause.** Why does the moon lose its light? Because of the earth's screening; and the screening is the middle term linking "moon" and "loses its light".

**The regress problem** (Posterior Analytics I.3). If every piece of knowledge must be proved from premises, and those premises must be known, then:

1. Either the chain of proofs goes on forever, and **nothing is ever known**;
2. or it goes in a circle, and **a thing is proved from itself**;
3. or it stops at premises that are **known without proof**.

Some in his day took option 1 (sceptics) and some option 2. **Aristotle takes option 3**: there are **first principles** (*archai*) of each science, known but not demonstrated. They include definitions, the assumption that the subject exists, and axioms common to all sciences, such as the principle of non-contradiction.

**How first principles are known** (Posterior Analytics II.19). Not by proof, and not by being born with them. Perception leaves **memory**; many memories of the same thing make **experience**; from experience the mind grasps **the universal**. His image, in paraphrase: it is like a rout in battle, where one soldier makes a stand, then another, until the line is restored. This process is **induction** (*epagōgē*). The state of grasping first principles is called ***nous***, often translated "intellect" or "understanding".

**Why it matters.** This is the ancestor of **foundationalism**: the view that knowledge rests on basic truths that need no further support. Euclid's *Elements* (about 300 BC) is the nearest thing to a science built on this model.

**Objections and replies.**
- *Most real science is not like this.* Modern science is fallible and revisable, and few of its laws are necessary. **Reply:** Aristotle describes how a **finished** science would be **set out and taught**, not how discovery works; much of his own research looks quite different.
- *Nous seems like a magic guarantee.* How do we know our grasp of a first principle is not a mistake? This is a real gap. **Scholars dispute** whether *nous* is a kind of intuition or a settled understanding reached at the end of long inquiry.
- *Induction cannot give necessity.* Seeing many white swans never proves all swans are white, a problem Hume (Stage 9) made famous. Aristotle seems to think induction reveals essences, not just regularities; whether it can is still debated.
Aristotle's Topics: dialectic and reason:
Demonstration starts from first principles. But **how do you argue about first principles themselves**, which cannot be proved? And how do you argue about ethics, politics, or anything where certainty is not available? Aristotle's answer is **dialectic**, set out in the *Topics* and its appendix, *On Sophistical Refutations*.

**What dialectic was.** In the Academy, dialectic was a practised game. One person, the answerer, defends a thesis ("pleasure is the good"). The other, the questioner, asks only yes-or-no questions, trying to lead the answerer into contradicting himself. The *Topics* is a handbook for this game: it lists hundreds of argument patterns, or "places" (*topoi*), where arguments can be found.

**Reasoning from endoxa.** Demonstration reasons from true and primary premises. **Dialectic reasons from *endoxa***, reputable opinions. Aristotle's definition (Topics I.1, translated by W. A. Pickard-Cambridge, 1928): those opinions are "generally accepted" which are "accepted by every one or by the majority or by the philosophers". They are not certainly true, but they are the best place to start.

**Three uses** (Topics I.2):
1. **Training** the mind.
2. **Conversation** with ordinary people, starting from what they believe.
3. **Philosophy itself**: by working through the puzzles on both sides of a question, we see more easily where the truth lies, and **dialectic is the way to examine the first principles of every science.**

**The four predicables.** Whatever you say of a subject in such an argument is one of four things: its **definition**, a **property** peculiar to it but not its essence (like a human's capacity to learn grammar), its **genus**, or an **accident** that may or may not belong to it.

**The method in action.** Aristotle's treatises often follow a pattern he states in the *Nicomachean Ethics* (VII.1): set out the **appearances** (*phainomena*, which includes what people say), work through the **puzzles** (*aporiai*), and **preserve as many reputable opinions as possible**, explaining why those you reject seemed true. Watch for this in the *Physics*, the *Metaphysics* and the *Ethics*: each opens by surveying what earlier thinkers said.

**Sophistical Refutations.** This short work is **the first catalogue of fallacies**: arguments that look valid but are not. Aristotle names thirteen, six depending on language (like **equivocation**, using one word in two senses) and seven not (like **begging the question** and **treating many questions as one**). Several of Stage 1's fallacies get their names from this list.

**Objections and replies.**
- *Starting from opinion is conservative.* If most people and the wise share a prejudice, dialectic will preserve it. **Reply:** Aristotle says the opinions must be **tested** against each other and the facts; the method can overturn as well as preserve. Critics answer that in practice, as with slavery, it sometimes did not.
- *Is dialectic really a route to first principles?* **Scholars dispute** how far Aristotle thought dialectic, rather than induction and *nous*, establishes first principles. One influential reading, by G. E. L. Owen (1961), argued that much of Aristotle's actual method is dialectical.
Aristotle's Physics: nature as an inner:
The Greek *physis* means **nature**, and Aristotle's *Physics* is not physics in our sense. It is **the philosophy of nature**: what it is for something to be natural, what change is, and what causes, place and time are.

**The definition of nature** (Physics II.1). Some things exist **by nature**: animals and their parts, plants, and the simple bodies (earth, water, air, fire). Others exist **by art** or other causes: beds, cloaks, houses. The difference is this:

**A natural thing has within itself a source (*archē*) of change and of rest.** An acorn grows into an oak by itself. A stone falls by itself. A bed does nothing as a bed; whatever it does, it does because of what it is made of.

**The bed that sprouts.** Aristotle borrows an example from the Sophist Antiphon: **if you buried a wooden bed and it rotted and sent up a shoot, what came up would be wood, not a bed.** Antiphon took that to show that nature is the **matter**, the wood, and the bed's shape is mere surface. Aristotle agrees the shape of a bed is not natural, but for a different reason: **the bed's form comes from outside, from the carpenter.** In a living thing, the form is passed on from within: **man begets man**.

**So nature is both matter and form, but form more.** Flesh and bone are not yet fully natural until they have the form of a living thing. **A thing's nature is above all what it is when it is complete**: the nature of an acorn is to become an oak.

**The elements and natural places.** In Aristotle's picture, each element has a natural motion: **earth moves down toward the centre of the cosmos, fire up, water and air in between.** A stone falls because it is going home. The heavens are made of a fifth element (*aithēr*) that moves naturally in circles, forever. This is set out in *On the Heavens*.

**Two kinds of motion.** **Natural motion** comes from a thing's own nature, like a stone falling. **Violent** (forced) motion goes against it, like a stone thrown upward. Violent motion needs a continuing mover, which leaves Aristotle puzzled about thrown things: what keeps an arrow going after it leaves the bow? His answer, that the air pushes it along, was criticised by **John Philoponus** in the sixth century AD and later abandoned.

**What survived and what did not.**
- **Overturned:** natural places, the fifth element, the distinction between natural and violent motion. Galileo and Newton (Stage 8) replaced them with inertia: **a moving body keeps moving unless something stops it**. This is not disputed.
- **Still argued over:** the central idea that **living things have natures**, inner principles that make them develop and act as they do. Biologists still speak of an organism's development "going right" or "going wrong". Whether that talk is ultimately reducible to physics and chemistry is a live question in the philosophy of biology.

**Why it matters.** The *Physics* is Aristotle's answer to Parmenides and to Plato: **the changing world is not illusion, and it is not a shadow of something else. It has its own principles, and they can be known.**
Aristotle's four causes and the case for:
To understand a thing, Aristotle says, is to know **why** it is. The Greek word is *aitia*, usually translated "cause", but it means something closer to **"the because"**: anything that answers a why-question. In Physics II.3 he lists four kinds.

**The four causes** (Physics II.3, translated by R. P. Hardie and R. K. Gaye, 1930):

> "In one sense, then, (1) that out of which a thing comes to be and which persists, is called 'cause', e.g. the bronze of the statue... In another sense (2) the form or the archetype, i.e. the statement of the essence... Again (3) the primary source of the change or coming to rest; e.g. the man who gave advice is a cause, the father is cause of the child... Again (4) in the sense of end or 'that for the sake of which' a thing is done, e.g. health is the cause of walking about."

| Cause (later Latin name) | Question | Bronze statue | Oak tree |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Material** | What is it made of? | bronze | wood, sap, cells |
| **Formal** | What is it? What is its form or definition? | the shape of Pericles | the structure of an oak |
| **Efficient** (moving) | What started the change? | the sculptor | the parent oak |
| **Final** | What is it for? | to honour Pericles | to be a mature, seed-bearing oak |

**In nature, three often coincide.** The form of an oak, the end of the acorn's growth, and the source (a parent oak, which has that form) are the same in kind. **Only the matter stands apart.**

**The case for final causes** (Physics II.8). Earlier thinkers like Empedocles said that what looks purposeful is chance: animals with parts that happened to fit together survived; the rest perished. Aristotle states the objection himself, with an example: **rain does not fall in order to make the corn grow; it falls because water vapour cools.** If it ruins the harvest, it was not for that either. Why not say the same of teeth: the front ones just happen to come up sharp and the back ones broad?

**His reply, set out:**
1. Chance produces things that happen **rarely** and unpredictably.
2. Teeth, and natural things generally, come about **always or for the most part** in the same useful way.
3. So they are not the result of chance.
4. If not chance, then **for the sake of something**.
5. So there are ends in nature.

**He adds:** nature works like art, but **without deliberating**. A swallow builds its nest and a spider its web without thinking about it. **Aristotle's nature has no designer**; purpose is built into each kind of thing.

**Objections and replies.**
- *Premise 4 is a false dilemma.* Darwin's theory of natural selection (1859) gives a third option: **non-random selection of random variations**, which produces regular, useful results without anything being "for" anything. This is widely taken to undercut Aristotle's argument. **Reply:** many philosophers of biology still say an eye is *for* seeing, and explain that function claim through evolutionary history. The dispute is whether that is Aristotle's teleology or a replacement for it.
- *Final causes are idle.* Bacon and Descartes (Stage 8) dismissed them from science. **Reply:** in biology, asking "what is it for?" is still how organs are understood.
- *A scholarly dispute.* Does Aristotle think rain *does* fall for the sake of crops? Most read II.8 as saying no. **David Sedley** has argued for a more cosmic, partly human-centred teleology. This remains open.
Aristotle on change: potentiality, actua:
Parmenides (Stage 2) argued that change is impossible: a thing would have to come from what is (but then it already is) or from what is not (but nothing comes from nothing). Aristotle's answer is his most influential pair of concepts.

**The three principles of change** (Physics I.7). In every change there is:
1. **a subject** (or substrate) that persists,
2. **a form** it gains, and
3. **a privation**: the lack of that form it had before.

An unmusical man becomes musical. The **man** persists; **musicality** is gained; **unmusicality** is lost. So the musical man comes from what is not musical, not from sheer nothing. **Parmenides' dilemma assumed "what is not" meant nothing at all; it means only "what is not yet such-and-such."**

**Potentiality and actuality.** The deeper version of that answer:
- **Potentiality** (*dynamis*): a real **capacity** to be or do something. The acorn is potentially an oak; the sleeping geometer is potentially doing geometry.
- **Actuality** (*energeia*, or *entelecheia*, roughly "being at the end"): **the capacity realised**. The oak; the geometer actually proving.

A potentiality is not nothing: an acorn is potentially an oak and not potentially a horse. **Change is the passage of something from potentiality to actuality.**

**The definition of motion** (Physics III.1, Hardie and Gaye, 1930):

> "The fulfilment of what exists potentially, in so far as it exists potentially, is motion".

Take bricks being built into a house. They are potentially a house. **The building is the actualising of that potential while it is still a potential.** Once the house stands, the potential is fully realised, and the motion is over.

**Actuality is prior** (Metaphysics IX, called Theta). Aristotle argues that actuality comes before potentiality in definition (a capacity is defined by what it is a capacity *for*), in being (the oak's form is what the acorn tends toward), and in a sense even in time (**an acorn comes from an actual oak**). This will matter for the unmoved mover.

**Two kinds of activity** (Theta 6). Some activities are complete at every moment: **as soon as you see, you have seen**. Others are incomplete until they finish: you are building a house, and have not yet built it. Aristotle calls the first *energeia* in a strict sense, the second *kinēsis* (motion). Happiness, in the *Ethics*, will be the first kind.

**Objections and replies.**
- *The Megarians* (a school of his day) said a thing has a capacity only **while exercising it**. Aristotle's reply (Theta 3): then a builder not building is no builder, and nothing is hot or sweet unless someone is feeling it, which is absurd.
- *The definition is empty.* John Locke (Stage 9), in 1690, held up the scholastic Latin form of it (*actus entis in potentia quatenus in potentia*) as an example of words that explain nothing (a paraphrase). **Reply:** defenders, such as L. A. Kosman, argue it is precise: it picks out the peculiar **incomplete** reality of something in process, which is neither its starting point nor its end.
- *Is potentiality real?* The debate over **dispositions** and **powers** (is fragility a real property of glass before it breaks?) is very much alive in metaphysics today, and many now defend an Aristotelian answer.
Aristotle on the infinite, place, void a:
Books III and IV of the *Physics* take on four concepts every account of nature needs, and Aristotle's analyses of each stood for nearly two thousand years.

**The infinite** (Physics III.4–8). Is anything infinite, without limit? Aristotle's answer is the distinction that shaped Greek mathematics:
- **An actual infinite**, a completed, existing infinity of things, **does not exist**. There is no infinitely large body, and no actual infinity of parts in a line.
- **A potential infinite does.** Numbers can always be **added to**; a magnitude can always be **divided further**. The process never ends, but at no point is there an infinite collection.

**This answers Zeno** (Stage 2). Zeno argued that to cross a distance you must first cross half, then half the rest, and so on forever, and you cannot complete infinitely many tasks. Aristotle replies (Physics VI and VIII) that **the halves are only potential divisions**; the runner crosses a continuous distance, not an actual infinity of points. Mathematicians since Cantor (late nineteenth century) accept actual infinities, and most today answer Zeno with the mathematics of convergent series instead; **whether that fully answers him is still debated.**

**Place** (Physics IV.1–5). Place is not a body's shape or its matter. After working through the alternatives, Aristotle concludes (Hardie and Gaye, 1930): place is "the boundary of the containing body at which it is in contact with the contained body", and more precisely "the innermost motionless boundary of what contains". The place of the wine is the inner surface of the jar.

**The void** (Physics IV.6–9). Is there empty space? The atomists (Stage 2) said there must be, or nothing could move. **Aristotle denies it.** His argument assumes that a body moves faster the lighter the medium it passes through; in a void there is no resistance, so motion would be **infinitely fast**, which is impossible. **That assumption is false**, and Philoponus in the sixth century and Galileo in the seventeenth rejected the dynamics behind it.

**Time** (Physics IV.10–14). Time is not motion, since motions can be fast or slow and time cannot; but there is no time without change, since when we notice no change, we notice no time passing. His definition (Hardie and Gaye, 1930):

> "For time is just this-number of motion in respect of 'before' and 'after'."

**Time is the countable aspect of change**: what we measure when we say an hour has passed. He then raises a puzzle that runs through later philosophy: **if there were no soul to count, would there be time?** He leaves the answer guarded.

**Objections and replies.**
- *Newton's absolute time and space* (1687) were defined as existing independently of anything in them, the opposite of Aristotle's view. **Reply:** Leibniz (Stage 8) defended a relational view against Newton, and Einstein's physics made space and time inseparable from what happens in them. **Relational views like Aristotle's are again respectable**, though not in his form.
- *The finite cosmos.* Aristotle's place theory implies the outermost heaven is not in any place. Later thinkers found this hard to accept; medieval critics asked what would happen if you stood at the edge and stretched out your arm.
Aristotle's Metaphysics: first philosoph:
**The *Metaphysics* is a collection of fourteen books**, not a single planned treatise. The title is not Aristotle's: *ta meta ta physika* means "the books after the *Physics*", probably the place an ancient editor put them. Aristotle's own names for its subject were **"first philosophy"**, **"wisdom"** and **"theology"**.

**How it opens** (Metaphysics I.1, translated by W. D. Ross, 1908):

> "ALL men by nature desire to know. An indication of this is the delight we take in our senses; for even apart from their usefulness they are loved for themselves; and above all others the sense of sight."

Book I then traces a ladder: **perception, memory, experience, art, science**. The wisest person knows the **first causes and principles** of things. Book I also surveys earlier thinkers' causes, and Book III (Beta) lays out the puzzles the rest will address.

**A science of being as being** (Book IV, Gamma). Every other science studies one part of what there is: number, living things, the stars. **First philosophy studies being as being** (*being qua being*): what belongs to anything just insofar as it **is**.

**The problem.** It seemed impossible. Aristotle himself held that **being is said in many ways**: a substance is, a quality is, a quantity is, in different senses. And a science needs one subject-matter. If "being" is ambiguous, there is no one thing to study.

**The solution: focal meaning.** Consider **"healthy"**. A diet is healthy (it produces health), a complexion is healthy (it shows health), a walk is healthy (it preserves health). The senses differ, but **all point to one central thing, the health of a body.** The word is neither univocal (one meaning) nor merely equivocal (unrelated meanings). It is *pros hen*, "related to one". G. E. L. Owen (1960) called this **focal meaning**.

**"Being" works the same way.** In Ross's translation (1908) of Gamma 2: "There are many senses in which a thing may be said to 'be', but all that 'is' is related to one central point, one definite kind of thing, and is not said to 'be' by a mere ambiguity." Qualities, quantities, places are beings because they are qualities, quantities, places **of substances**. So **the science of being is first of all the science of substance.** The question "what is being?" becomes the question **"what is substance?"**, which Books VII–IX take up.

**Four senses of "being"** (Book V, Delta, a philosophical dictionary, and VI.2):
1. being **accidentally** (the musician happens to be pale),
2. being **true** (it *is* so),
3. being in the **categories** (being a substance, a quality and so on),
4. being **potentially** or **actually**.

**A scholarly dispute that runs through the book.** In Book VI (Epsilon), first philosophy is **theology**, the science of unchanging, separate substance, which is, in Ross's words, "universal in this way, because it is first". So is metaphysics the general study of **everything that is** (ontology), or the study of **the highest being** (theology)? Scholars still disagree about how Aristotle meant to join the two, and medieval philosophers (Stages 6–7) fought over it.

**Why it matters.** The questions of this book, what there is, what it is to be a thing, how the many senses of "is" connect, **define the subject still called metaphysics.**
Aristotle's defence of the principle of:
In Metaphysics IV (Gamma) 3–4, Aristotle names **the firmest of all principles**. It is the bedrock of logic and of every science.

**The principle** (Metaphysics IV.3, translated by W. D. Ross, 1908):

> "It is, that the same attribute cannot at the same time belong and not belong to the same subject and in the same respect".

So a door cannot be both open and not open, at the same time, in the same respect. **The qualifications matter**: a door can be open now and shut later, or open at the top and shut at the bottom (a stable door). Aristotle gives versions about **things** (as here), about **belief** (no one can really believe a contradiction) and about **statements** (contradictory statements are not both true).

**It cannot be proved.** Any proof would have to use premises, and reasoning from premises already assumes the principle. **Demanding a proof of it shows a lack of training**, he says; not everything can be proved, or there would be an infinite regress (see the *Posterior Analytics* lesson).

**But it can be defended by refutation.** This is his famous "elenctic" (refutative) argument. Suppose someone denies the principle. Then:

1. The opponent must **say something**; if he says nothing, there is nothing to argue with, and (in Ross's words) "such a man, as such, is from the start no better than a vegetable."
2. If he says something, his words must **signify something definite** both to him and to us: "man", say, must mean *this* and not also *not this*.
3. But to signify something definite is to **exclude its opposite**.
4. So in the very act of saying anything meaningful, **the opponent uses the principle he denies**.

**The force of this** is that it does not beg the question: it does not assume the principle as a premise, but shows that **the opponent's own speech presupposes it**.

**Further arguments.** Aristotle adds several more. If contradictories were all true, everything would be one thing: a man would be a trireme and a wall. And **no one acts as if they believed it**: a person who denies the principle still walks to Megara rather than into a well.

**His targets.** Heraclitus (as some read him), Protagoras's relativism (Stage 2), and anyone who says the same thing both is and is not.

**Objections and replies.**
- *The refutation proves too little.* Jan Łukasiewicz (1910) argued Aristotle's arguments fail: at most they show **some** statements must be meaningful and determinate, not that **no** contradiction can be true. Many scholars agree some of the further arguments are weak.
- *True contradictions.* **Dialetheists**, most prominently Graham Priest (*In Contradiction*, 1987), hold that a few contradictions are true, such as the liar sentence "this sentence is false". They use **paraconsistent logics** in which a contradiction does not imply everything. **Reply:** even Priest accepts the principle for almost all ordinary cases, and most logicians still reject dialetheism; but it is no longer thought absurd.
- **The standard verdict:** the principle itself is accepted by nearly every philosopher. Whether Aristotle's defence of it works is genuinely disputed.
Aristotle's Metaphysics Zeta: substance,:
Book VII (Zeta) is the hardest and most argued-over text in Aristotle. It asks: **what is the substance of a thing**, that which makes it the thing it is? The answer the *Categories* gave, "the individual", is not enough, because an individual turns out to have parts: **matter and form**.

**Form and matter (hylomorphism).** From the Greek *hylē* (matter) and *morphē* (form or shape). A bronze statue is **bronze** (matter) **arranged in a shape** (form). A house is bricks and timber (matter) **organised to shelter** (form). **The individual is a compound of the two.** Matter is what is potentially the thing; form is what makes it actually that thing.

**Four candidates for substance** (Zeta 3). The substance of a thing might be its **substrate** (what underlies it), its **essence**, its **universal**, or its **genus**.

**Why not the substrate?** Strip away from a thing every property, and then its shape and size, and you are left with something with no character of its own: **mere matter**. If substance were the substrate, **matter would be substance**. But a substance must be **separable** (able to exist on its own) and **a "this"** (a definite individual), and bare matter is neither. So matter is not primarily substance. (Whether Aristotle believed in a **"prime matter"** with no properties at all is itself a scholarly dispute.)

**Essence.** Aristotle's phrase is *to ti ēn einai*, literally **"the what-it-was-to-be"** a thing. **The essence of a thing is what its definition states**: for a human, perhaps "rational animal". Zeta argues that things which are primary have their essence **identically**: Socrates' soul and what-it-is-to-be-Socrates' soul are not two things.

**Why not the universal?** (Zeta 13–16). This is his **attack on Plato's Forms**. A universal ("man") is common to many things; but the substance of each thing is **peculiar to it**. And if universals were substances, a substance would be made up of other substances, which leads to absurdity. **So no universal is a substance.**

**Form is substance** (Zeta 17). A syllable is not just its letters: "BA" and "AB" have the same letters. It is the letters **plus their arrangement**, which is not another element. In the same way, **flesh is not just fire and earth but those arranged**, and that arrangement, the form, is **the cause of the matter being a definite thing**. So substance, in the primary sense, is **form**.

**The great puzzle this leaves.** Zeta says (a) form is substance; (b) no universal is substance; and (c) definition, which states the form, is of the universal. **So is form universal or particular?**
- **Particular forms:** each person has their own form, Socrates' and Callias's being distinct (defended by Michael Frede and Günther Patzig, 1988).
- **Species forms:** the form is shared, and is "universal" in a looser sense than the one Zeta 13 rejects.

**Scholars have not settled this**, and it matters: it determines whether Aristotle's world is fundamentally of individuals or of kinds.

**Why it matters.** Hylomorphism is still defended today as a theory of objects and of persons (see the *On the Soul* lessons), and the question of essences, revived by Saul Kripke in 1970 (Stage 12), is central in metaphysics again.
Aristotle's unmoved mover: Physics VIII:
Aristotle's god is not a creator, not a lawgiver and not a person who answers prayers. **It is the end of an argument about motion.** The argument begins in Physics VIII and is completed in Metaphysics XII (Lambda).

**The argument, set out as its defenders would:**
1. **Motion has always existed.** Time cannot have a beginning, since any "first moment" would need a "before"; and time is the number of motion, so motion is eternal too.
2. **Whatever is in motion is moved by something.**
3. The chain of movers **cannot go back to infinity**; there must be a **first mover**.
4. A first mover that was itself moved would need a mover, so the first mover is **unmoved**.
5. To cause motion **eternally**, it must have **no potentiality** (anything potential might fail to be), so it is **pure actuality**.
6. What is pure actuality has **no matter** (matter is potentiality), so it has no body, no size and no parts.

**How it moves** (Lambda 7). Not by pushing. The heavens rotate eternally, and they rotate **toward** it, the way a lover is drawn by what he loves. In Ross's translation (1908), the final cause "produces motion as being loved", and "there is something which moves without being moved, being eternal, substance, and actuality."

**What it does** (Lambda 9). It must be engaged in the best activity, which is **thinking**. And it must think the best object, which is itself. So, in Ross's words, "its thinking is a thinking on thinking." **God is thought thinking itself**, eternally, in perfect happiness.

**How many?** In Lambda 8, Aristotle uses the astronomy of his day (Eudoxus and Callippus) to suggest there are **47 or 55** unmoved movers, one for each heavenly sphere. Whether he kept this view, and how these relate to the first mover, is unclear.

**Objections and replies.**
- *Premise 2 is false.* After Galileo and Newton, **motion does not need a continuing mover**: a body in uniform motion keeps moving on its own (inertia). This is widely agreed to undercut the physics of the argument. **Reply:** defenders such as **Edward Feser** restate it as an argument about **change from potential to actual** in general, which they say inertia does not touch.
- *Premise 1 is unproven.* Philoponus in the sixth century, and later many Muslim, Jewish and Christian philosophers (Stages 6–7), argued against the **eternity of the world**. Kant (Stage 10) argued that reason can prove neither a beginning nor its absence.
- *Premise 3 is challenged.* Why could the chain not be infinite? Aristotle's reply is that the series is of **simultaneous**, not successive, movers: like a hand moving a stick moving a stone, which needs a first.
- *A god who knows only itself.* Does such a god know the world at all? **Scholars dispute** whether thinking itself excludes knowing other things. Later philosophers, from Avicenna to Aquinas, worked to show it does not.

**What came of it.** This argument is the ancestor of **Aquinas's First Way** (Stage 7). What believers made of it as theology belongs to the Theology curriculum; here the question is only **whether the argument holds**.
Aristotle's On the Soul: the soul as the:
For Aristotle, **"soul" (*psychē*) is not a ghost inside a body. It is what makes a living thing alive.** Plants have souls; so do oysters, horses and people. *On the Soul* (*De Anima*, in Latin) is his general theory of life, and only partly a theory of mind.

**The two views he rejects.**
- **Plato's dualism** (Stage 3): the soul is a separate thing that can exist without the body, is imprisoned in it, and survives death.
- **The materialism of the atomists** (Stage 2): the soul is a body itself, made of fine round atoms spread through the flesh.

**His definition** (De Anima II.1, here in paraphrase). The soul is **the first actuality of a natural body that has life potentially**; or, since such a body has organs, **the first actuality of a natural organic body**.

**Unpacking it.**
- **Actuality** = **form** (see the *Metaphysics* lessons). So **the soul is the form of the body**, and the body is the soul's matter. A living thing is a hylomorphic compound, like the statue, with soul as form.
- **First actuality.** A person asleep still has the capacities of a living, thinking being, without using them. That is like **knowing** geometry while not doing it. Using them, actually perceiving or thinking, is **second actuality**. **The soul is the first kind: a set of capacities**.
- **A body that has life potentially**: not a corpse, but a body organised so that it can live.

**Three images Aristotle uses** (II.1, in paraphrase):
1. **The wax and the seal.** It is pointless to ask whether soul and body are one, he says, just as it is pointless to ask whether the wax and the shape stamped on it are one.
2. **The axe.** If an axe were a natural body, its "axe-ness", its power to cut, would be its soul. Take that away and it would be an axe only in name.
3. **The eye.** If the eye were an animal, **sight would be its soul**. An eye that cannot see is an eye only in name, like an eye in a painting or a statue.

**What follows.** A dead body is not a human body, strictly, but a body that **was** human, **in name only**. And the soul is **not separable** from the body, **at least most of it**. Aristotle adds a hedge: nothing prevents some parts from being separable, if they are not the actuality of any bodily part. That hedge leads to the active intellect (a later lesson).

**Objections and replies.**
- *Is this just materialism in other words?* Some modern philosophers (Hilary Putnam and Martha Nussbaum, 1992) have read Aristotle as an early **functionalist**: mental states are defined by what they do, not what they are made of. **Myles Burnyeat** replied (in a paper published in 1992) that Aristotle's physics is so unlike ours that his view **cannot be revived** as a modern theory. The dispute continues.
- *What about personal survival?* If the soul is the form of this body, it seems **the individual person does not survive death**. Aristotle seems to accept that, except perhaps for the intellect. Medieval Christian, Jewish and Muslim philosophers, who believed in resurrection or immortality, had to wrestle with it (Stages 6–7; the theology is in the Theology curriculum).
- *Is it still credible?* Contemporary **hylomorphists** argue that it avoids both the "ghost in a machine" of Descartes (Stage 8) and the view that a person is only a heap of particles. Critics answer that "form" does no explanatory work that physics and biology do not already do.
Aristotle's ladder of souls: nutrition,:
Living things differ in what they can do. **Aristotle sorts their capacities into a ladder, each rung including those below.**

| Level of soul | Capacities | Who has it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Nutritive** | taking in food, growing, reproducing | all living things, including plants |
| **Perceptive** | perception, at least touch; with it **pleasure, pain and desire**; in most, movement from place to place | animals |
| **Rational** | thinking, understanding, deliberating | humans (and, in another way, god) |

**The capacities nest**, as Aristotle puts it, like geometrical figures: **a square contains a triangle** (draw a diagonal), and a rational soul contains the perceptive and nutritive. Humans do not have three souls, but one soul with all three powers.

**Nutrition comes first** because it is the precondition of everything else. Its purpose is not just survival but **reproduction**: by making another like itself, a mortal thing shares, as far as it can, in **the eternal and divine** (De Anima II.4, in paraphrase).

**Perception** (II.5–III.2). Aristotle's general formula: **perception is receiving the form of the thing perceived without its matter**, as wax takes the imprint of a signet ring without taking in the gold or iron of the ring. When I see a red apple, my eye takes on the red, but not the apple.

- **Five senses**, each with its **proper object**: colour for sight, sound for hearing, and so on. About these, he says, the senses are rarely wrong.
- **Common sensibles**: motion, rest, number, shape, size, perceived by more than one sense.
- **The common sense**: a capacity by which we perceive **that we see**, and tell **white from sweet**, which no single sense can do.

**A famous dispute about perception.** When the eye "takes on" red, what happens?
- **Literalists** (Richard Sorabji): the jelly of the eye **literally** becomes red, at least in some way. This would make perception a **physiological change**.
- **Spiritualists** (Myles Burnyeat): nothing physical need happen; the eye simply becomes **aware** of red.
**This is genuinely unsettled**, and it decides whether Aristotle was close to modern theories of mind.

**Imagination** (*phantasia*, III.3) is what remains after perception, the source of dreams and memory and the **images without which**, Aristotle says, **the soul never thinks**.

**Thought** (III.4). The mind thinks forms the way the senses perceive them. But since it can think **all** things, it **can have no nature of its own** except a capacity: before it thinks, it is **actually nothing**. Aristotle compares it to a **writing tablet on which nothing is yet written**. (This image, in Latin *tabula rasa*, was later taken up by Locke, Stage 9.)

**Desire and movement** (III.9–11). An animal moves because it **desires** something that perception or thought presents as good. In humans, desire can follow reason (**wish**) or go against it (**appetite**), which is the starting point for his ethics of **akrasia**.

**Why it matters.** The ladder was the standard framework of Western psychology until the seventeenth century, and the idea that **thought always needs images** has returned in recent cognitive science.
Aristotle's active intellect: the contro:
De Anima III.5 is **one of the shortest and most argued-over passages in the history of philosophy**, about fifteen lines long. Wars of interpretation were fought over it for a thousand years.

**The problem it addresses.** Thought (III.4) is the mind taking on forms. But **something must make the forms actually thinkable**, and actualise the mind's potential to think, just as anything that changes needs a cause. So Aristotle distinguishes **two aspects** of mind:
- a mind that **becomes all things** (the passive or "potential" intellect), and
- a mind that **makes all things**, like **light**, which makes potential colours actual colours (the **active** or **agent intellect**, Latin *intellectus agens*).

**What he says about the second** (paraphrase of III.5): it is **separable, unaffected and unmixed**, being **in its essence activity**. It does not think at one time and not at another. **Only this, once separated, is immortal and eternal**; we do not remember (its former activity), because the passive intellect is perishable; and **without it nothing thinks**.

**The question.** Is the active intellect **part of each human soul**, or something **outside** us?

**The main readings:**

| Reader | Date | Reading |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Alexander of Aphrodisias** | about AD 200 | the active intellect is **God**, the unmoved mover, acting on human minds |
| **Avicenna** (Ibn Sina) | 980–1037 | it is a **separate intelligence**, the lowest of the heavenly ones, which "gives" forms to human minds |
| **Averroes** (Ibn Rushd) | 1126–1198 | there is **one intellect for all humankind**, and even the potential intellect is single and shared |
| **Thomas Aquinas** | about 1225–1274 | **each human has their own** active and potential intellect, as powers of an individual soul (*On the Unity of the Intellect*, 1270) |
| **Many modern scholars** | | some aspect of **each human mind**; others revive a divine reading |

**Why so much was at stake.**
- **Immortality.** If the immortal part is God or a single shared intellect, **no individual person survives death**; only something impersonal does. If each person has their own active intellect, perhaps something personal does. This is why the debate mattered so much to Muslim, Jewish and Christian philosophers (Stages 6–7, and the Theology curriculum for what they believed).
- **Who thinks?** If thinking happens in one shared intellect, Aquinas objected, then **"this man thinks"** would be false, which is absurd. Averroes' followers replied that the individual is linked to the shared intellect through his own images.
- **The nature of mind.** Is thinking something no body can do? III.5 is the main text behind the long tradition that **intellect is immaterial**.

**Where things stand.** **There is no consensus on what Aristotle meant**, and many scholars think the text is too compressed, and possibly incomplete, to settle it. The honest verdict is that III.5 shows **Aristotle believed something about the mind escapes his own hylomorphism**, without telling us clearly what.
Aristotle the biologist: the History and:
**A large share of Aristotle's surviving writing is biology**, and for centuries it was the most neglected part of his work. Today it is often called his greatest scientific achievement.

**The works.**
- ***History of Animals*** (*Historia animalium*): the facts, organised by parts, ways of life and character. ("History" means **inquiry**, as with Herodotus.)
- ***Parts of Animals***: why animals have the parts they do, explained by their functions.
- ***Generation of Animals***: reproduction and development.
- Shorter works on **movement**, **sleep**, **youth and old age**, **respiration**.

**Where it was done.** Much of the marine work seems to come from his years on **Lesbos** (about 345–343 BC), around the lagoon of Pyrrha. He describes **some five hundred kinds of animal**, many from personal observation and dissection, others from fishermen, hunters and travellers' reports.

**The method.** Not a list of curiosities but a search for **causes**. First gather the facts (*that*), then explain them (*why*). The explanation is usually **functional**: a bird has a beak shaped for what it eats; ruminants have several stomachs because their food is hard to digest.

**His defence of studying "lowly" animals** (Parts of Animals I.5, translated by William Ogle, first published 1882):

> "Every realm of nature is marvellous: and as Heraclitus, when the strangers who came to visit him found him warming himself at the furnace in the kitchen and hesitated to go in, reported to have bidden them not to be afraid to enter, as even in that kitchen divinities were present, so we should venture on the study of every kind of animal without distaste; for each and all will reveal to us something natural and something beautiful."

**Famous successes.**
- **The octopus's mating arm** (the hectocotylus), described by Aristotle, was dismissed as fable until zoologists confirmed it in the nineteenth century.
- **The smooth dogfish** bears live young nourished through a **placenta-like** structure, as Aristotle said; Johannes Müller confirmed it in 1842.
- His division of animals into those **with blood and without** roughly corresponds to **vertebrates and invertebrates**. He classed **dolphins with the animals that breathe air and suckle their young**, not with fish.
- He opened **hens' eggs at stages of incubation** and described the developing chick's heart beating.

**Famous failures.**
- He thought **the heart, not the brain, is the seat of perception and thought**, and the brain mainly **cools the blood**.
- He accepted **spontaneous generation** for some insects and shellfish.
- In reproduction he held that **the male supplies the form and the female only the matter**, and described the female as, in effect, a deformed or incomplete male (a paraphrase of Generation of Animals II.3). This view is false, and **it fed centuries of claims that women are naturally inferior.**

**Darwin's verdict.** In an 1882 letter to William Ogle, thanking him for his translation, Darwin wrote (in paraphrase) that Linnaeus and Cuvier had been his gods, but that they were mere schoolboys compared to old Aristotle.

**Why it matters for the philosophy.** Aristotle's ideas of **form, nature, function and final cause** are not abstractions imported into biology. **They were largely formed by doing biology.** That is the strongest case for them, and the reason they lost force once physics, not biology, became the model science.
Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics: eudaimon:
The *Nicomachean Ethics* is probably named after Aristotle's son Nicomachus, perhaps as its editor. A second ethics, the *Eudemian Ethics*, also survives, and **three books are shared between them** (NE V–VII = EE IV–VI). Which came first is disputed; most think the *Eudemian* is earlier.

**The question.** Not "what is my duty?" but **"what is the best life for a human being?"** Ancient ethics generally begins here.

**The opening argument** (NE I.1–2):
1. Every action and pursuit aims at **some good**.
2. Some goods are pursued **for the sake of others**: bridles for horsemanship, horsemanship for war, war for victory.
3. The chain cannot go on forever, or desire would be "empty and vain".
4. So there is **some end we desire for its own sake**, and for which we desire everything else: **the chief good**.

**A famous objection**, pressed by many modern readers: premise 4 does not follow. That every chain ends somewhere does not show **all chains end in the same place**, just as "everyone has a mother" does not mean "there is someone who is everyone's mother". **Reply:** Aristotle may not be inferring it; he goes on (I.7) to argue separately that one end, happiness, meets the conditions.

**Its name: *eudaimonia*.** Everyone agrees, he says, that the chief good is ***eudaimonia***, usually translated **"happiness"**, better **"flourishing"** or **"living well and doing well"**. It is not a feeling but **a whole life going well**. **People disagree about what it consists in.**

**Three lives** (I.5):

| Life | Its good | Aristotle's verdict |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Of pleasure** | enjoyment | a life fit for cattle |
| **Of politics** | honour | too dependent on others; we want honour for our virtue, so virtue is higher |
| **Of contemplation** | understanding | to be discussed (Book X) |

**Against Plato's Form of the Good** (I.6). Aristotle argues that **"good" is said in as many ways as "being"**, so there is no single Form; and even if there were, it would be useless for a doctor or a general. **Ethics is about the good that humans can do and achieve.**

**Its marks** (I.7). The chief good must be **final** (chosen for itself, never for anything else) and **self-sufficient** (it makes a life lacking in nothing). Happiness fits both. Then comes the **function argument**, read closely in the next lesson.

**Precision.** Ethics, he warns (I.3), cannot be as exact as mathematics. It deals with things that are, in Ross's phrase, "only for the most part true", and a well-educated person looks for only as much precision as the subject allows.

**A dispute that runs through the whole book.**
- **The inclusive reading** (J. L. Ackrill, 1974): eudaimonia is a **package** of all the intrinsic goods: virtuous action, friendship, contemplation.
- **The dominant reading** (W. F. R. Hardie, 1965, who coined the terms): eudaimonia is **one supreme good**, contemplation, which Book X will crown.
**Both have strong textual support**, and the debate is not settled.

**External goods.** Aristotle insists (I.8–10) that the happy life needs some **friends, wealth, health and good fortune**: a man ugly, low-born, childless or alone is not quite happy, and **Priam**, king of Troy, who lost everything in old age, cannot be called happy. This sets him against both Socrates and the Stoics (Stage 5), who said virtue alone is enough.
Reading: Aristotle's function argument (:
The most famous argument in Aristotle's ethics, in **W. D. Ross's translation (1908)**, from the Internet Classics Archive. Aristotle has just shown happiness is final and self-sufficient.

**1. The question restated.**

> "Presumably, however, to say that happiness is the chief good seems a platitude, and a clearer account of what it is still desired. This might perhaps be given, if we could first ascertain the function of man."

**"Function"** translates *ergon*: a thing's **work**, its characteristic activity. The idea: to know what a good knife is, ask what a knife is **for**.

**2. The analogy.**

> "For just as for a flute-player, a sculptor, or an artist, and, in general, for all things that have a function or activity, the good and the 'well' is thought to reside in the function, so would it seem to be for man, if he has a function."

Note **"if he has a function"**. He supports it with questions: carpenters and tanners have functions, "and has man none?" And if **eye, hand and foot** each have one, does the whole human not?

**3. Finding it by elimination.**

> "Life seems to be common even to plants, but we are seeking what is peculiar to man. Let us exclude, therefore, the life of nutrition and growth. Next there would be a life of perception, but it also seems to be common even to the horse, the ox, and every animal. There remains, then, an active life of the element that has a rational principle".

This is the **ladder of souls**. The human function is what is **peculiar** (*idion*) to us: **activity involving reason**, either reasoning or obeying reason, as trained desires do.

**4. The conclusion.**

> "human good turns out to be activity of soul in accordance with virtue, and if there are more than one virtue, in accordance with the best and most complete."

**"Virtue"** translates *aretē*, **excellence**: whatever makes a thing do its work well. A good knife's excellence is sharpness. **Human excellence is what makes us do the work of reason well.**

**5. The qualification.**

> "But we must add 'in a complete life.' For one swallow does not make a summer, nor does one day; and so too one day, or a short time, does not make a man blessed and happy."

**The argument in outline:**
1. The good of anything with a function lies in performing that function well.
2. Humans have a function.
3. It is activity of soul involving reason.
4. Doing it well is doing it in accordance with virtue.
5. So the human good is rational activity in accordance with virtue, over a complete life.

**Objections and replies.**
- ***Premise 2.*** Flute-players and eyes have functions because of **a role or a larger whole**. Why think a human as such has one? **Reply:** Aristotle's biology: every living kind has a **characteristic form of life**, so the claim is no stranger than "a good wolf hunts in packs".
- ***Uniqueness.*** Why should what is **peculiar** to us be what is **best** for us? Only humans write tax law or torture for fun. **Reply:** the function is the activity that **organises** the whole life, not just any distinctive trick; critics answer that this already assumes the conclusion.
- ***Fact to value.*** Hume (Stage 9) argued you cannot derive an "ought" from an "is". **Reply:** for Aristotle, "good knife" already mixes the two; **neo-Aristotelians** (Philippa Foot, *Natural Goodness*, 2001) defend this.
- ***Ambiguity.*** "the best and most complete" virtue is where the **inclusive and dominant readings** part ways.

**Verdict.** The argument is widely regarded as **incomplete as it stands**, but no one doubts it set the agenda for **virtue ethics**, revived in the twentieth century (Stage 14).
Aristotle on virtue as a mean:
Having defined happiness as activity in accordance with virtue, Aristotle must say **what virtue is**. Books II–V answer for the **virtues of character**.

**Two kinds of virtue** (NE I.13, II.1). Corresponding to the two rational parts of the soul: **intellectual virtues** (like wisdom), acquired mostly by teaching; and **virtues of character** (*ēthikē aretē*, from *ēthos*, character, itself related to *ethos*, habit), acquired by **habituation**.

**We become what we do** (II.1, translated by W. D. Ross, 1908):

> "men become builders by building and lyreplayers by playing the lyre; so too we become just by doing just acts, temperate by doing temperate acts, brave by doing brave acts."

So **upbringing matters enormously**. In Ross's words: "It makes no small difference, then, whether we form habits of one kind or of another from our very youth; it makes a very great difference, or rather all the difference." The virtuous person **acts knowingly, chooses the act for its own sake, from a firm character** (II.4), and **enjoys it**. Doing right while straining against temptation is only self-control.

**The definition** (II.6, Ross):

> "Virtue, then, is a state of character concerned with choice, lying in a mean, i.e. the mean relative to us, this being determined by a rational principle, and by that principle by which the man of practical wisdom would determine it."

**The doctrine of the mean.** In every area of feeling and action, one can go wrong **by excess or by deficiency**. Virtue hits the target between.

| Sphere | Deficiency | **Virtue** | Excess |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| fear and confidence | cowardice | **courage** | rashness |
| bodily pleasures | insensibility | **temperance** | self-indulgence |
| giving money | meanness | **generosity** | prodigality |
| anger | lack of spirit | **good temper** | irascibility |
| honour, on a large scale | small-souledness | **greatness of soul** | vanity |
| telling the truth about oneself | false modesty | **truthfulness** | boastfulness |

**"Relative to us."** The mean is not arithmetical. If ten pounds of food is too much and two too little, the trainer does not order six for everyone: six is too little for **Milo** the wrestler and too much for a beginner. **The mean is the right amount, at the right time, toward the right people, for the right reason, in the right way.**

**It is not moderation.** Sometimes the right amount of anger is a great deal. And some things have **no mean**: there is no right amount of adultery, theft or murder. In Ross's words, "men are good in but one way, but bad in many" (II.6).

**Objections and replies.**
- *Empty.* The mean is fixed by "the person of practical wisdom". But who is that? The one who finds the mean. **Reply:** Aristotle never meant a formula; ethics is learned by **training perception**, as a doctor learns to judge cases. Critics answer that this gives no help when wise people disagree.
- *Some virtues do not fit.* Justice (Book V) is not a mean between two feelings, and Aristotle himself strains to fit it.
- *Kant's objection* (Stage 10, paraphrased): the difference between virtue and vice is **one of principle, not of degree**; lying is not too much truthfulness.
- *Culturally narrow?* Greatness of soul looks like a Greek aristocrat's ideal, and **humility** has no place on the list.

**What stands.** The idea that virtue is **a trained disposition of feeling as well as action**, and that **good judgment cannot be reduced to rules**, is at the centre of modern virtue ethics.
Aristotle on voluntary action and choice:
**We praise and blame only what people do voluntarily.** So in NE III.1–5 Aristotle gives the first systematic theory of **moral responsibility**, useful too, he says, to lawgivers assigning honours and punishments.

**Two things make an act involuntary** (III.1):
1. **Force**: the moving principle is outside the agent, who contributes nothing, as when **a wind carries you off**, or men who have you in their power.
2. **Ignorance** of the **particulars**: who you are acting on, what you are doing, with what, for what result. A man who lets off a catapult not knowing it was loaded; Merope in the play, who nearly kills her son thinking he is an enemy.

**So the voluntary is what has its origin in the agent, who knows the particular circumstances.** Animals and children act voluntarily, though they do not choose.

**Mixed actions.** What about things done under pressure? Aristotle's example (III.1, translated by W. D. Ross, 1908):

> "Something of the sort happens also with regard to the throwing of goods overboard in a storm; for in the abstract no one throws goods away voluntarily, but on condition of its securing the safety of himself and his crew any sensible man does so. Such actions, then, are mixed, but are more like voluntary actions".

The captain **chooses**; the origin of the act is in him. And **some things one must never do under any pressure**: one should rather die.

**Ignorance that does not excuse.**
- **Ignorance of the universal**, not knowing that theft is wrong, does not excuse; **it is what makes someone bad**.
- **Acting in ignorance is not always acting by reason of ignorance.** A drunk man acts in ignorance, but his ignorance is his own doing, so he is blamed. Some lawgivers, he notes, **doubled penalties** for drunken offences.
- One who acted through ignorance and **regrets it** acted involuntarily; one who does not regret it acted only **non-voluntarily**.

**Choice** (*prohairesis*, III.2–3). Narrower than the voluntary. Choice is **deliberate desire for things in our power**. We deliberate about **what leads to our ends**, not the ends themselves: a doctor does not deliberate whether to heal, but how. **Scholars dispute** whether this means only **means** (instruments) or also **what an end consists in** (what health or happiness would be, here and now).

**Responsibility for character** (III.5). An objector says: "the bad man cannot help it; that is just how he is." Aristotle's answer:

1. We become unjust or self-indulgent **by repeatedly acting** unjustly or self-indulgently.
2. Those acts were **voluntary**, and anyone not utterly senseless knows that activities build character.
3. So we are **partly responsible for our characters**, even if, once formed, they are hard to change, **like a stone that, once thrown, cannot be called back**.

**Objections and replies.**
- *Moral luck and upbringing.* Character is set long before adulthood by parents, laws and fortune, which **Aristotle himself stresses** in Book II. So how far can the adult be responsible? **Reply:** Aristotle claims only that we are, in some way, **partial causes** of our characters. Critics, such as Bernard Williams and Thomas Nagel (1976), pressed the problem of **moral luck** (Stage 14).
- *Determinism.* Aristotle's theory does not ask whether actions are causally determined. Some read him as an early **compatibilist** (responsibility needs the origin to be "in us", not freedom from all causes); **whether that is anachronistic is debated**.
Aristotle on practical wisdom and akrasi:
Two questions from Books VI and VII of the *Ethics*: **what kind of knowledge does a good person have?** And **how can someone know what is best and do the opposite?**

**Practical wisdom** (*phronēsis*, NE VI). Aristotle distinguishes five intellectual excellences:

| Excellence | Concerned with |
| --- | --- |
| **Scientific knowledge** (*epistēmē*) | what is necessary, by demonstration |
| **Art or craft** (*technē*) | making things |
| **Intellect** (*nous*) | first principles |
| **Wisdom** (*sophia*) | the highest things: *nous* plus *epistēmē* |
| **Practical wisdom** (*phronēsis*) | **acting well in human life** |

**Practical wisdom is the ability to deliberate well about what is good for living well overall.** It needs grasp of **universals** (what courage requires) and, above all, of **particulars** (what courage requires *here, now*). So **the young can be good mathematicians but not practically wise**: it needs experience. Its model is the statesman **Pericles**.

**Not mere cleverness.** **Cleverness** (*deinotēs*) is skill at finding means to any goal, good or bad; a skilled con-man has it. Practical wisdom is cleverness **aimed by virtue at the right end**.

**The unity of the virtues** (VI.13). **Virtue makes the goal right; practical wisdom makes the means right.** Full virtue of character is impossible without practical wisdom, and practical wisdom impossible without virtue. So **whoever has practical wisdom has all the virtues**. (Critics doubt it: cannot someone be brave but unjust?)

**Akrasia** (NE VII). The Greek means **"lack of mastery"**, translated **incontinence** or **weakness of will**: knowingly acting against one's own better judgment. The dieter who resolves to skip dessert, and eats it.

**Socrates said it was impossible** (Plato's *Protagoras*, Stage 3): no one does wrong knowingly; apparent akrasia is ignorance. Aristotle's response (VII.2, translated by W. D. Ross, 1908):

> "Now this view plainly contradicts the observed facts, and we must inquire about what happens to such a man; if he acts by reason of ignorance, what is the manner of his ignorance?"

**His solution** (VII.3), using the **practical syllogism**: reasoning that ends in action. In Ross's translation, "the universal opinion is present in us forbidding us to taste", but there is also "the opinion that 'everything sweet is pleasant', and that 'this is sweet'", and appetite is present.

Appetite follows the second opinion. The akratic **has** the knowledge that he shouldn't, but **does not actively use it**, like someone **asleep, mad or drunk** who can recite verses of Empedocles without understanding them. So Aristotle ends by granting, he says, that **the position Socrates sought seems to result** after all: the knowledge that passion drags about is not knowledge in the full sense.

**Four characters:**

| Character | Desire | Action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Virtuous** | right | right, gladly |
| **Self-controlled** (*enkratēs*) | wrong | right, by struggle |
| **Akratic** | wrong | wrong, against judgment, with regret |
| **Vicious** | wrong | wrong, by conviction, without regret |

**The akratic is better than the vicious**: his principle is still sound.

**Objections and replies.**
- *Has Aristotle conceded too much to Socrates?* If the akratic doesn't fully know, is there real akrasia? **Scholars dispute** whether Aristotle allows **"clear-eyed" akrasia**, acting against judgment in full knowledge. Many modern philosophers (Donald Davidson, 1970) insist it happens and needs explaining.
Aristotle on friendship:
**Two of the ten books of the *Ethics* are about friendship**, more than on any single virtue. Book VIII opens (translated by W. D. Ross, 1908): "without friends no one would choose to live, though he had all other goods".

**What *philia* covers.** The Greek is wider than "friendship": it includes **family love**, the bond of **fellow citizens**, of **business partners**, of fellow travellers and soldiers. **Any relationship of mutual, recognised goodwill** counts.

**The definition** (VIII.2). Friends **wish each other well for the other's sake**, **each knows it**, and the goodwill is **returned**. You can wish wine well (that it keep), but not for its own sake, and it cannot wish you well back.

**Three kinds**, by what the friend is loved for (VIII.3):

| Kind | Loved for | Typical of | Lasts |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Of utility** | usefulness | the old, business, alliances | while useful |
| **Of pleasure** | enjoyment | the young, lovers | while pleasant |
| **Of character** (or of virtue) | **who the friend is** | good people alike in virtue | **long, stable** |

**Only the third is friendship in the full sense.** The friends love each other for **what each essentially is**, a good person, not for something incidental. It is also useful and pleasant, but that is a by-product. It is **rare** and takes **time**: in Ross's version (VIII.3), "men cannot know each other till they have 'eaten salt together'".

**A friend is "another self"** (IX.4). A good person relates to his friend as he relates to himself, "for his friend is another self" (Ross). He wishes him to live, wishes him well, shares his joys and sorrows.

**Friendship and justice.** Friendship holds cities together, and **lawgivers care more for it than for justice**: if people were friends, they would not need justice, but just people still need friendship (VIII.1, in paraphrase).

**Unequal friendships** (VIII.7). Father and son, ruler and ruled, husband and wife. These work if **the better party is loved more**, in proportion. Aristotle, who held women inferior, counted marriage among these. If the gap grows too wide, as between humans and gods, friendship ends.

**Does the happy person need friends?** (IX.9). If he is self-sufficient, why? Aristotle's answers: (1) the good person needs people **to do good to**; (2) **we see ourselves more clearly in another**, and can observe a friend's good actions as our own more easily than we observe ourselves; (3) human life is **living together**, which for humans means, in Ross's words, "sharing in discussion and thought" and not, as with cattle, "feeding in the same place".

**Objections and replies.**
- *Egoism.* If my friend is "another self", do I love him only as an extension of me? And IX.8 praises **self-love**. **Reply:** Aristotle distinguishes vulgar self-love (grabbing money and pleasure) from the good person's, which is love of **the best in himself**, and which leads him to **give up wealth, honour and even life for friends**. Critics still find the structure self-centred.
- *Partiality.* Modern impartial ethics (Stages 9 and 14) asks whether special concern for friends is fair. Aristotle's view is a classic **defence of partiality**.
- *Too exclusive.* The highest friendship is open only to the good, and so to few. Whether this makes it **elitist** or simply **realistic** is still argued.
Aristotle on contemplation and the happi:
Book X of the *Ethics* ends with a surprise. After nine books on courage, generosity, justice and friendship, Aristotle says **the happiest life is the life of contemplation** (*theōria*: study, the activity of understanding the highest truths).

**First, pleasure** (X.1–5). Pleasure is not the good, but not bad either. It is not a process (like filling an empty stomach), but **complete at every moment**, like seeing. And it **perfects an activity**, as he puts it, like the bloom on the young, something added. So the best pleasures are those of the best activities.

**The argument for contemplation** (X.7). If happiness is activity in accordance with the highest virtue, it is the activity of **the best thing in us**, the intellect. And contemplation is:
1. **The highest activity**: of the highest part, about the highest objects.
