> "Men seek retreats for themselves, houses in the country, sea-shores, and mountains ... it is in thy power whenever thou shalt choose to retire into thyself."

**Recurring themes:**

| Theme | What he tells himself |
| --- | --- |
| **Impermanence** | all things flow; Alexander and his mule-driver end in the same dust |
| **The view from above** | look down on human affairs from a great height: how small the quarrels look |
| **Providence or atoms** | whether the world is ordered by reason or is a chaos of atoms, his duty is the same |
| **Social duty** | what is not good for the hive is not good for the bee |
| **The present** | the present moment is all anyone loses or has |

**"Providence or atoms"** is philosophically notable: Marcus repeatedly allows that **the Epicureans might be right**, and argues that Stoic conduct is the right response either way.

**Objections and questions:**

- **The record.** Persecution of Christians occurred under him, notably at Lyon in 177; how much he directed is debated by historians. And he made Commodus his heir. Admirers and critics weigh this against the book differently.
- **Is it gloomy?** Many readers find a weariness in it. Others, such as Pierre Hadot (next lesson), argue the repetition is **training**, not mood: the work of keeping one's principles ready.

**Why it matters.** The *Meditations* is the most widely read work of ancient philosophy today, and the best evidence we have of what living Stoicism from the inside was like.
Hadot: ancient philosophy as a way of li:
A French scholar of the twentieth century changed how the ancients are read, arguing that their philosophy was first a practice, a way of living, and only second a set of theories.

**Who.** **Pierre Hadot** (1922–2010) was a French historian of ancient philosophy, a specialist in Plotinus and Marius Victorinus, and from 1982 professor at the Collège de France. His essays ***Exercices spirituels et philosophie antique*** (1981; in English, selected and expanded, as ***Philosophy as a Way of Life***, 1995) and ***What Is Ancient Philosophy?*** (1995; English 2002), with his study of Marcus, ***The Inner Citadel*** (1992; English 1998), made the case. His books are in copyright, so what follows is paraphrase.

**The thesis.**

1. For the ancients, to be a philosopher was to **choose a way of life**: Epicurean, Stoic, Platonist, Cynic.
2. The theories (physics, logic) served that choice: they justified and sustained it.
3. Philosophy was practised through **spiritual exercises**: deliberate practices of attention, memory and imagination meant to **transform the person**, not merely inform them.
4. So we misread the ancient texts if we read them as modern treatises; their repetition and their direct address to the reader are **therapy and training**.

Hadot chose "spiritual" because no other word covers the whole: the exercises engage thought, imagination and feeling together. He did not mean religious.

**Examples of exercises:**

| Exercise | Example |
| --- | --- |
| **Attention** (*prosochē*) | constant watchfulness over one's judgements, in the present moment |
| **Premeditation of evils** | rehearsing loss, exile and death in advance, so they find you ready |
| **The view from above** | imagining the earth from the heavens to see human concerns in proportion |
| **Examination of conscience** | reviewing one's day at night, as Seneca describes |
| **Writing to oneself** | Marcus's *Meditations* |

**Hadot on Marcus.** In *The Inner Citadel* he argued that the *Meditations* are organised by Epictetus's three areas of training (lesson 17): desire, action, assent.

**Objections and replies:**

| Objection | Reply |
| --- | --- |
| **John Cooper**, *Pursuits of Wisdom* (2012): ancient philosophy was a way of life **led by reason and argument**; Hadot overstates the role of non-rational exercises and blurs philosophy into religion | Hadot always said the exercises included reasoning; disagreement is partly about emphasis |
| It fits the Hellenistic schools better than Aristotle or the late Neoplatonist commentators | Hadot argued even they saw the theoretical life as a life |
| It makes modern academic philosophy look like a loss | Hadot thought it was one, and said so |

**Michel Foucault**, who drew on Hadot for his late work on "the care of the self", was criticised by Hadot for making the ancient self too aesthetic, a work of art, rather than a self aligned with universal reason.

**Why it matters.** Hadot's reading lies behind the modern revival of practical Stoicism, and it raises a question this curriculum keeps asking: **what is philosophy for?**
Middle Platonism and Philo of Alexandria:
Between the end of the sceptical Academy and Plotinus lay three centuries in which Platonism became a dogmatic system again, and in which a Jewish thinker in Alexandria read the Bible through it.

**The name.** "**Middle Platonism**" is a modern label for Platonist thought from about **80 BC to about AD 250**: after Antiochus of Ascalon turned the Academy away from scepticism, and before Plotinus. It was not one school but many teachers, in many cities.

**Some figures:**

| Thinker | Dates | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Eudorus** of Alexandria | 1st century BC | stressed a supreme One above other principles |
| **Plutarch** of Chaeronea | about 45–about 120 | priest at Delphi; essays and the *Lives*; read the *Timaeus* literally |
| **Alcinous** | perhaps 2nd century | author of the *Handbook of Platonism* (*Didaskalikos*), a textbook summary |
| **Numenius** of Apamea | 2nd century | a "first god" and a craftsman "second god"; read Plato alongside Pythagoras |

**Shared doctrines:**

1. **A supreme god, a mind**, beyond the world.
2. **The Forms are the thoughts of god.** Plato's Forms (Stage 3) move inside a divine intellect, perhaps borrowing from Aristotle's god who thinks.
3. A gap between that god and matter, bridged by intermediaries: a world soul, a craftsman, daemons.
4. The goal of life is **becoming like god, as far as possible**, Plato's phrase in the *Theaetetus*.

**A live question: was the world made in time?** Plato's *Timaeus* describes a craftsman making the world. Most Platonists read this as a teaching device: the world depends eternally on its cause. **Plutarch and Atticus read it literally**: the world had a beginning. The debate will matter to Christian, Jewish and Muslim philosophers (Stage 6).

**Philo of Alexandria** (about 20 BC–about AD 50) was a leader of the large Jewish community of Alexandria. In AD 39/40 he went on an embassy to the emperor Gaius (Caligula) to plead for his people. He wrote dozens of treatises, mostly reading the **Torah**, the five books of Moses, as philosophy.

**His method: allegory.** Beneath the literal story lies a philosophical meaning. Philo is read here **as a philosopher**; his significance for theology belongs to the **Theology curriculum**.

**His philosophical ideas:**

- **God's existence can be known, his essence cannot.** We know *that* God is, from the order of the world, but not *what* he is. This is an early form of **negative theology**, knowing God by what he is not.
- **The *Logos*.** Between God and the world stands God's Word or Reason, the place of the Forms and the instrument of creation. Philo combined Stoic and Platonic senses of the term.
- **Creation.** In *On the Creation of the World* he defends a world made by God, against Aristotle's eternal world.

**Objections.** Allegory can make a text mean anything; a Platonised Moses may be more Plato than Moses. Philo's reply is that both reason and scripture come from one source, so they cannot finally disagree. **Whether he was more Platonist or more Jewish is a long scholarly dispute**; most now see him as fully both.

**Why it matters.** Philo is the first serious attempt to join Greek philosophy and a scriptural religion, the project of much of the next two stages.
Plotinus: the One, Intellect and Soul:
Plotinus rebuilt Plato's philosophy into a single vision of all reality, flowing from one source and returning to it. It is the last great system of pagan antiquity, and it shaped Christian, Jewish and Muslim thought for a thousand years.

**Who.** **Plotinus** (204/5–270) was born in Egypt. At about twenty-eight he found his teacher in Alexandria, **Ammonius Saccas**, and stayed eleven years. He joined the emperor Gordian III's expedition against Persia in 242–243, hoping to learn **Persian and Indian** philosophy; the emperor was killed and Plotinus escaped. From **244** he taught in **Rome**. He began to write in about 253 and died in Campania in 270. His pupil **Porphyry** wrote the ***Life of Plotinus*** and edited his 54 treatises into six sets of nine: the ***Enneads*** (*ennea* is "nine"), published about **301**.

**The *Life* opens memorably**: Plotinus, Porphyry says in his first sentence, was like a man ashamed to be in a body (paraphrase), would not sit for a portrait, and would not tell his birthday.

**Three "hypostases"** (*hypostasis*, an underlying reality):

| Level | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| **The One** (also **the Good**) | absolutely simple; beyond being and beyond thought; the source of all |
| **Intellect** (*nous*) | eternal mind thinking itself; contains all the Forms |
| **Soul** (*psychē*) | life and movement; the world soul and individual souls; shapes bodies in time |

Below Soul lies the physical world and, at the bottom, **matter**.

**Why there must be a One.** An argument he gives in several forms:

1. Whatever exists is **one** thing: an army, a house, a body is something only by being unified.
2. Whatever is **composite** (made of parts) depends on its parts and on what unifies them.
3. Intellect is not perfectly simple: in thinking it is two, thinker and thought, and its Forms are many.
4. A chain of dependence cannot go back forever, and must end in something **wholly simple**.
5. **So there is a first principle, the One, beyond all multiplicity**, and so beyond being and thought, which always involve some duality.

He draws on Plato's *Republic*, which calls the Good "beyond being".

**Emanation.** How does the many come from the One? Not by choice or labour, but as **light from the sun**, heat from fire, water from an overflowing spring. The One, being perfect, **overflows**, and what flows out turns back to contemplate its source, and so becomes the next level. This movement is **procession and return**. The One **gives without being diminished**.

**Objections and replies:**

| Objection | Reply |
| --- | --- |
| If the One is beyond thought and being, how can Plotinus say anything of it? | He admits we can only say what it is **not**; "One" and "Good" point rather than describe |
| If the One produces by necessity, it is not free | In *Ennead* 6.8 he argues the One is supremely free, because it is exactly what it wills to be; **interpreters dispute how this squares with necessity** |
| Why should unity be the deepest principle? | This is the heart of the system; many philosophers reject its premise that being depends on being unified |

**Why it matters.** Augustine, Pseudo-Dionysius, Avicenna and others (Stage 6) all took Plotinus's structure and changed it. **Neoplatonism** is a modern name; Plotinus thought he was simply explaining Plato.
Plotinus on evil as privation and the as:
Plotinus's universe flows down from the Good. Two questions follow at once: where does evil come from, and how does a soul get back?

**The problem of evil.** If everything comes from the Good, why is there evil? Plotinus's answer, in *Ennead* 1.8, *On What Evils Are*:

1. Evil cannot be a **thing** with its own form, for all forms come from the Good and are good.
2. So evil is a **lack**: an absence of form, measure and good.
3. At the bottom of the procession, where the outflow is exhausted, lies **matter**: utterly formless, **the absence of every form**.
4. **So matter is evil itself**, the "primary evil", not as a positive force but as **pure privation** (*sterēsis*, the absence of what should be there).
5. Bodies and souls are evil only so far as they are mixed with, or turned toward, matter.

**Evil as privation**, the idea that evil is not a substance but **an absence of good**, as blindness is an absence of sight, became **Augustine's answer** (Stage 6) and the standard view in medieval philosophy.

**A puzzle and a dispute.** Is matter produced by the One? If so, the Good produces evil. If not, there is a second principle, which Plotinus denies. **Scholars dispute what Plotinus held**; the most common reading is that matter is the last, indefinite product of the procession, evil only as the point where goodness gives out. Plotinus also attacked the **Gnostics**, who held the world was made by an evil or ignorant power, in *Ennead* 2.9: **the world is the best image of the intelligible that a physical thing can be.**

**The ascent.** The soul came down into a body but can return. The steps:

| Stage | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| **Purification** | the civic virtues order the soul; the purifying virtues detach it from the body |
| **Turning inward** | "withdraw into yourself and look" (a paraphrase of *Ennead* 1.6) |
| **Beauty** | love of bodily beauty leads up to beauty of soul, then to the Forms in Intellect, as in Plato's *Symposium* |
| **Intellect** | the soul thinks as Intellect thinks, knowing the Forms directly |
| **Union** | beyond thought, the soul is one with the One, in a moment that cannot be described |

In *On Beauty* (*Ennead* 1.6) he argues, in paraphrase, that **no eye ever saw the sun without becoming sun-like**, and no soul sees beauty without becoming beautiful. Porphyry reports that Plotinus reached union with the One **four times** while Porphyry was with him.

**The undescended soul.** Plotinus held that **part of each soul never descends**: it stays in Intellect, even while we are unaware of it (*Ennead* 4.8). The ascent is waking up to what we already are. Later Neoplatonists rejected this (next lesson).

**Objections and replies:**

| Objection | Reply |
| --- | --- |
| Calling matter evil insults the physical world | Plotinus calls the cosmos beautiful; matter is evil only as pure absence, and nothing physical is pure matter |
| A privation cannot do anything, yet evil seems active: cruelty, malice | Defenders say malice is a will turned from the good, its harm the loss it brings. **Many find this unconvincing for terrible suffering**; the debate continues in philosophy of religion (Stage 14) |
| Mystical union cannot be checked | Plotinus offers it as the goal of a discipline, not as an argument's premise |
Porphyry, Iamblichus and Proclus: the la:
After Plotinus, his followers made his vision into a school with a curriculum, a commentary tradition and, increasingly, a religion.

**Porphyry** of Tyre (about 234–about 305) studied with Plotinus in Rome from 263, edited the *Enneads*, and wrote on everything. Three works matter most here:

| Work | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| ***Isagoge*** (Introduction) | a short introduction to Aristotle's *Categories*, on genus, species, difference, property and accident |
| ***Against the Christians*** (15 books) | the most learned ancient attack on Christianity; later burned on imperial orders, known only in fragments |
| *Life of Plotinus* | our main source for Plotinus |

**The *Isagoge* opens with three questions it declines to answer**: do genera and species (kinds like "animal" and "human") exist in reality or only in the mind? If they exist, are they bodies or not? Are they separate from things or in them? **Boethius translated this into Latin (Stage 6), and it became the medieval problem of universals (Stage 7).** Porphyry also made Aristotle's logic the entrance to the Platonist curriculum, so that Aristotle and Plato were taught as harmonious.

**Iamblichus** of Chalcis in Syria (about 245–about 325) studied with Porphyry and broke with him. He held:

1. **The soul descends wholly** into the body. Against Plotinus, no part stays above.
2. So **reason alone cannot lift us back**. The soul needs **theurgy**, "divine work": rituals, prayers and sacred objects through which the gods act on the soul. In *On the Mysteries* he argues that it is not thinking that unites us with the gods, but the rites themselves (paraphrase).
3. The levels of reality **multiply**: many intermediate orders between the One and the world.

**Objection**: theurgy looks like magic replacing philosophy. Porphyry had raised just this doubt in his *Letter to Anebo*. Iamblichus's reply: if the soul has truly fallen, it cannot climb by its own thought, and the gods' gift is needed. **Scholars now treat theurgy as a serious response to a real problem in Plotinus**, whether or not they find it convincing. The emperor **Julian** (ruled 361–363), who tried to restore pagan worship, followed Iamblichus.

**Hypatia** of Alexandria, mathematician and Platonist teacher, was murdered by a Christian mob in **415**. Her works are lost.

**Proclus** (412–485), born in Constantinople, headed the Platonist school in **Athens** for nearly fifty years. He was the great systematiser. His ***Elements of Theology*** sets out Neoplatonism in **211 propositions**, each proved from earlier ones, like Euclid. Its central pattern:

| Moment | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Remaining** (*monē*) | every effect stays in its cause |
| **Procession** (*proodos*) | it goes out from its cause |
| **Reversion** (*epistrophē*) | it turns back to its cause |

He also wrote the ***Platonic Theology*** and huge commentaries on Plato and Euclid.

**His long reach.** A Christian writer of about 500 who wrote under the name of **Dionysius the Areopagite** drew heavily on Proclus (Stage 6). An Arabic reworking of the *Elements*, known in Latin as the ***Book of Causes***, was long thought to be Aristotle's until Aquinas spotted its source (Stage 7).
Justinian and 529: the end of the Atheni:
The year 529 is often used to mark the end of ancient philosophy. What happened is less tidy than the date suggests.

**The school.** By the fifth century, the Platonist school at Athens was a private foundation, funded by endowments, teaching a fixed course: Aristotle first, then Plato, then the *Chaldean Oracles*, a sacred text of theurgy. Proclus had headed it; its last head was **Damascius** (about 458–after 538), a sharp critic of Proclus. His pupil **Simplicius** (about 490–about 560) wrote the great commentaries on Aristotle that preserve many fragments of the Presocratics (Stage 2).

**The edict.** The Christian emperor **Justinian** (ruled 527–565) issued laws against pagans and heretics. A chronicler, **John Malalas**, records that in **529** the emperor sent a decree to Athens ordering that **no one should teach philosophy** or explain the laws there. The decree's text does not survive; other laws of the period barred pagans from teaching and confiscated property.

**The journey to Persia.** The historian **Agathias** tells that about 531, **seven philosophers, among them Damascius and Simplicius**, went to the court of the Persian king **Khosrow I**, hoping for a philosopher-king. They were disappointed. In the peace treaty of **532**, Khosrow had it written that they could return home and live by their own beliefs unmolested.

**What we do not know.** **Where they went next is disputed.** One hypothesis places Simplicius and others at **Harran**, in upper Mesopotamia, a pagan centre where a school might have continued; many scholars think the evidence too thin. Nor is it clear how fully teaching in Athens stopped. Some historians, notably Alan Cameron (1969), argued it may have struggled on.

**What did not end.** Philosophy did not die in 529:

| Where | What continued |
| --- | --- |
| **Alexandria** | a school under **Ammonius son of Hermeias** and his successors, including the Christian **John Philoponus** (about 490–about 570), who in **529** itself published *Against Proclus on the Eternity of the World*, arguing the world had a beginning |
| **Constantinople** | Aristotle and Plato read and copied throughout the Byzantine centuries (Stage 7) |
| **Syriac and then Arabic** | Greek logic and philosophy translated, then carried into the Islamic world (Stage 6) |

**Why the date stuck.** Edward Gibbon and later historians made 529 a symbol of the end of the classical world, the more so because 529 is also the traditional date of Benedict's monastery at Monte Cassino. **It is a convenient marker, not a clean break**: the pagan schools ended, and their texts, methods and problems passed into Christian, Jewish and Muslim hands.

**A question to hold.** Philoponus's book of 529 is a sign of what came next: **philosophers arguing with the Greeks, using Greek methods, from new starting points.** That is the subject of Stage 6.
Looking back: the schools, the sceptics:
Eight centuries, from Diogenes's jar to Justinian's decree. What did they settle, what did they leave open, and what does the next stage take up?

**What became common ground.**

1. **Philosophy is for living.** Every school offered a way of life, with exercises to match. Even those who reject the Stoics or Epicureans accept that ethics must answer the question of how to live, not just what is right.
2. **Emotions involve judgements.** The Stoic analysis, that fear and anger rest on beliefs about good and bad, is widely accepted in some form in philosophy and psychology.
3. **Logic is more than syllogisms.** The Stoics founded propositional logic.
4. **Justification has a structure problem.** Agrippa's trilemma — regress, assumption or circle — is still a starting point in the theory of knowledge.

**The great debates left open:**

| Question | The sides here | Where it returns |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Is death bad for the one who dies?** | Epicurus and Lucretius said no; the deprivation view says yes | Stage 14 |
| **Is freedom compatible with determinism?** | Chrysippus (yes); Epicurus and Alexander of Aphrodisias (no) | Stages 9, 11, 14 |
| **Is virtue enough for happiness?** | Stoics and Cynics (yes); Epicureans (pleasure is the good); Aristotelians (virtue plus some external goods) | Stages 7, 14 |
| **Can anything be known?** | Stoics (yes, by cataleptic impression); Academics and Pyrrhonists (suspend judgement) | Stages 6, 8, 9 |
| **Is the world matter alone, or ordered by mind?** | Epicurus (atoms and void); Stoics (a rational body); Platonists (a hierarchy from the One) | every stage |
| **Is evil a thing or an absence?** | Plotinus: privation; the Gnostics: a power | Stages 6, 14 |

**The shape of the period.** The Hellenistic schools began by **narrowing** philosophy to the self, its calm and its freedom, in a world of kings. The later Platonists **widened** it again to the whole of reality, a ladder from matter to the One. Both were answers to the same need: **a life that can be lived well whatever happens outside.**

**Arguments worth re-stating from memory:**

- Epicurus's argument that death is nothing to us, and the deprivation objection.
- Lucretius's symmetry argument, and why our position in time may break the symmetry.
- The Stoic argument that virtue is the only good, and the "preferred indifferent" objection.
- Chrysippus's cylinder, and Alexander's reply.
- Arcesilaus's argument against the cataleptic impression.
- Agrippa's five modes.
- Plotinus's argument for a first principle that is wholly simple.

**What the next stage picks up.** Christian, Jewish and Muslim thinkers inherited all of this. **Augustine** (Stage 6) began as a reader of Cicero, passed through Academic doubt, and found in "the books of the Platonists" the idea of evil as privation and of an immaterial God. **Boethius** translated Porphyry and wrote the *Consolation of Philosophy* in Stoic and Platonist terms. **Avicenna** and the Arabic philosophers took Neoplatonic emanation into a new frame; and **Philoponus**'s argument that the world began opens the long debate over creation. The tools were Greek; the starting points were new.
Context: philosophy in a world of three:
Between about 300 and 1200, Greek philosophy did not die. It moved house, and it changed its hosts' religion three times over.

**The world, in a few dates:**

| Date | What happened |
| --- | --- |
| **312–313** | Constantine wins power and grants Christians toleration |
| **380** | Theodosius makes Nicene Christianity the religion of the empire |
| **410** | Alaric's Goths sack Rome |
| **476** | the last Western emperor is deposed; the Latin West breaks into kingdoms |
| **529** | Justinian forbids pagans to teach; the Platonist school at Athens closes soon after |
| **about 570–632** | the life of Muhammad; within a century Islam rules from Spain to Central Asia |
| **762** | the Abbasid caliphs found Baghdad, where Greek books are put into Arabic |
| **1085** | Christian Castile takes Toledo, and Arabic books start going into Latin |

**Philosophy now spoke four languages.** **Greek** in Constantinople and Alexandria, where the old schools carried on. **Latin** in the West, where little Greek was read and the texts were few. **Syriac**, the language of Christians in Mesopotamia, which became the bridge. And **Arabic**, which from about 800 held the richest philosophy anywhere.

**The new fact was scripture.** Christians, Muslims and Jews each believed God had spoken in a book. Each found that the Greeks, above all Plato and Aristotle, had worked out a way of thinking about God, the soul and the world that was close to theirs in places and flatly against it in others. So the same questions came up in all three faiths, often in the same words:

1. **Faith and reason.** If revelation tells us the truth, what is philosophy for? Can reason prove what scripture says, and what happens when they seem to clash?
2. **Was the world made?** Aristotle taught that the world had no beginning. Scripture says it was created. Can either be proved?
3. **What is God like?** If God is utterly one and simple, can we say anything about him at all?
4. **Evil and freedom.** If a good God made everything, where does evil come from? If God knows the future, are we free?
5. **The soul.** Is the self the body, or something that could exist without it?
6. **Universals.** Do kinds such as "human" or "horse" exist in things, in minds, or on their own?

**A word on method.** These thinkers were believers, and much of what they wrote is theology, which belongs to the separate Theology curriculum. **This stage reads them as philosophers**: what they argued, from premises a non-believer could weigh, and whether the arguments hold. Several of their arguments, such as Anselm's proof of God, Avicenna's flying man and al-Ghazali's doubts about causes, are still argued over in philosophy journals today.
Athens and Jerusalem: Justin, Clement, O:
The first Christian thinkers had to decide what to make of Greek philosophy. Their answers range from open arms to a slammed door.

**The door slammed.** Tertullian of Carthage (about 155–about 220) asked, in a famous line paraphrased here, **what Athens has to do with Jerusalem**: philosophy breeds heresy, and the believer needs nothing beyond the gospel. He is the patron of every later thinker who distrusts philosophy.

**The open arms.** **Justin Martyr** (about 100–about 165), a convert who had tried the Stoics, Aristotelians, Pythagoreans and Platonists in turn, kept wearing the philosopher's cloak after baptism. His idea was the **Logos**: Greek for "word" and "reason". Christ is the divine Logos, and every human mind shares a seed of it (the *logos spermatikos*, "seed-bearing word"). So any truth the pagans found came from the same source. In his *First Apology* (about 155) he goes as far as this:

> "those who lived reasonably are Christians, even though they have been thought atheists; as, among the Greeks, Socrates and Heraclitus, and men like them"

(*First Apology* 46, translated by Marcus Dods and George Reith, *Ante-Nicene Fathers* vol. 1, 1885.) He died a martyr in Rome.

**Clement of Alexandria** (about 150–about 215) said, in his *Stromateis* ("Patchwork"), that **philosophy was to the Greeks what the Law was to the Jews: a tutor leading them towards Christ.** It is a preparation, not a rival.

**Origen** (about 185–about 254), also of Alexandria, was the most systematic mind of the early Church, and a student of Platonism. His *On First Principles* argued that **souls are free rational beings** whose choices explain why the world is unequal, and he hoped that **all might finally be restored** to God. These views were condemned centuries later, in the sixth century. His *Against Celsus* (about 248) answers a pagan philosopher's attack point by point, and is one of the best records of the pagan case against Christianity.

**The Cappadocians**, three bishops of the 300s from what is now central Turkey, were trained in the best Greek schools: **Basil of Caesarea** (about 330–379), **Gregory of Nazianzus** (about 329–390) and **Basil's brother Gregory of Nyssa** (about 335–about 395). Gregory of Nyssa matters most to philosophy:

- **God is infinite**, and the infinite is a perfection, not a defect. For most Greeks the unlimited was formless and imperfect. Some scholars, notably Ekkehard Mühlenberg, call Gregory the first to make infinity a positive divine attribute; others find earlier hints.
- So **the soul's journey into God never ends.** Perfection is endless progress (*epektasis*, "straining forward"), not arrival.
- In a homily on Ecclesiastes he attacked **slavery** itself, asking who can put a price on a being made in God's image. It is usually counted the most outspoken condemnation of slavery that survives from antiquity.

**Why it matters.** Justin's question (does truth found outside the faith belong to it?) runs through this whole stage. Al-Kindi in Baghdad, Maimonides in Cairo and Aquinas in Paris all answered it as Justin did.
Augustine: the restless life behind the:
Augustine is the most influential philosopher between Aristotle and Aquinas, and he told his own story better than anyone else could.

**The life.**

| Date | |
| --- | --- |
| **354** | born at Thagaste, North Africa (now Souk Ahras, Algeria); mother Monica a Christian, father a pagan |
| **373** | at nineteen, reads Cicero's lost *Hortensius* and falls in love with **wisdom** |
| **about 373–382** | a **Manichee**: a follower of a religion teaching that the world is a battle between two equal powers, good and evil |
| **383–384** | teaches rhetoric in Rome, then wins the public chair of rhetoric at **Milan** |
| **386** | reads "**certain books of the Platonists**" (Pusey's wording: Plotinus and Porphyry in Latin) and, that August, is converted in a garden in Milan |
| **387** | baptised by Ambrose at Easter; Monica dies at Ostia |
| **395 or 396** | bishop of **Hippo** (now Annaba, Algeria) until his death |
| **430** | dies on 28 August, with the Vandals besieging the city |

**The Confessions** (written about 397–401) is thirteen books addressed to God in the second person. *Confessio* means both admitting fault and praising. Books I–IX tell his life to his conversion. X examines memory, XI time, and XII–XIII the opening of Genesis. **It is often called the first autobiography**, and it is certainly the first to make the inner life the subject.

**Three escapes, each a philosophical problem:**

1. **From Manichaeism**, over the problem of evil. The Manichees said evil was a substance, a dark stuff. Augustine came to think evil is no thing at all (the lesson on privation).
2. **From scepticism.** For a time he was drawn to the **Academic sceptics**, Plato's later school, who said nothing can be known (Stage 5). His first surviving work, *Against the Academicians* (386), answers them.
3. **From materialism.** He could not think of anything that was not a body, even God. **Plotinus taught him that the most real things are not bodies**: truth, the mind, God. This is the debt he names.

**The garden.** In Book VIII he hears a child's voice from a neighbouring house, in Pusey's translation: **"Take up and read; Take up and read."** He opens Paul's letters at random, reads a line against the life of the flesh, and his long hesitation ends. The scene is famous; whether it happened just as told, or is shaped as a literary set piece, is debated by scholars.

**Why read him as a philosopher.** Nearly every problem in this stage gets its first Latin form from Augustine: the certainty of the self, the nature of evil, the freedom of the will, how we know unchanging truths, what time is, and how to judge a political order. **His method is to start from the inside**: from what the mind finds in itself. Descartes, twelve centuries later, starts the same way.

The doctrines Augustine argued over as a bishop, such as grace, original sin and predestination, are theology, and the Theology curriculum takes them up.
Augustine: si fallor, sum, and the light:
Twelve centuries before Descartes, Augustine found a truth the sceptic cannot touch, and then asked how the mind knows any truth at all.

**The sceptic's challenge.** The Academic sceptics said that for any belief you hold, you might be mistaken: dreaming, mad, deceived by the senses. So suspend judgement on everything.

**Augustine's answer**, in *The City of God* XI.26 (begun 413), translated by Marcus Dods (1871):

> "What if you are deceived? For if I am deceived, I am. For he who is not, cannot be deceived; and if I am deceived, by this same token I am."

In Latin, ***si fallor, sum***: "if I am mistaken, I exist". Set out:

1. Suppose I am deceived in thinking that I exist.
2. Only something that exists can be deceived.
3. So if I am deceived, I exist.
4. So I cannot be deceived in thinking that I exist.

He adds that I equally know that I am alive, that I understand, and that I love this knowing. The same argument appears in *On Free Choice of the Will* (II.3) and *On the Trinity* (X.10).

**Is this the cogito?** Descartes's "I think, therefore I am" (1637) has the same core, and Descartes's contemporaries told him so. **The difference is use.** Descartes made it the foundation for rebuilding all knowledge. Augustine uses it to refute scepticism and then to look inward for a likeness of God in the mind. Scholars still argue over how much Descartes owed him.

**The objection.** It proves less than it seems. It shows that something is doing the doubting, not what that something is: not that it is a soul, or that it lasts from moment to moment. Augustine does go on to argue that the mind knows itself with certainty and so is not a body; that further step is much more disputed.

**Illumination: the second question.** Some truths are **necessary and unchanging**: seven plus three is ten; wisdom is better than folly. My mind changes, and so do the things I see. So where do unchanging truths come from?

- **Not from the senses**, which show only changing particular things.
- **Not from teachers.** In *The Teacher* (*De magistro*, 389), written as a dialogue with his son Adeodatus, he argues that words only prompt us. When I learn that something is true, **I see it for myself.**
- So he concludes: **we see such truths in a light from God**, as the eye sees things in the light of the sun. God is the "inner teacher".

This is **divine illumination**. It replaces Plato's recollection: Augustine came to reject the idea that souls lived before birth.

**What did he mean? This is a real dispute.** Readings include:

| Reading | Claim |
| --- | --- |
| **Content** | God puts the ideas themselves into the mind |
| **Standard** | God supplies the rules by which we *judge* what the senses give us |
| **Ontologist** | we see the truths in God's own mind, and so in a way see God |

Medieval Franciscans such as Bonaventure kept illumination; Aquinas replaced it with Aristotle's theory of abstraction (Stage 7).
Augustine: evil is not a thing but a lac:
If a good God made everything, where does evil come from? Augustine's answer, that **evil has no being of its own**, held the field for a thousand years.

**The problem.** As a young man Augustine accepted the Manichee answer: there are **two principles**, a good one and an evil one, and evil is a real dark substance at war with the light. It explains evil neatly. The cost is that God is not all-powerful and the world is a battlefield.

**The argument** (*Confessions* VII.12, Pusey's translation, 1838): whatever can be corrupted must have some good in it, because corruption takes good away. If a thing lost all its good, it would cease to exist. So:

> "So long therefore as they are, they are good: therefore whatsoever is, is good. That evil then which I sought, whence it is, is not any substance: for were it a substance, it should be good."

Set out:

1. Everything that exists, insofar as it exists, is good (God made it, and being is itself good).
2. Evil is the corruption of a good: blindness in an eye, sickness in a body, injustice in a will.
3. Corruption is the **loss** of something a thing should have.
4. So evil is not a thing but **a privation**: an absence of a good that ought to be there.

**"Privation" is the key term.** It is not a mere absence: a stone's not seeing is no evil. It is the absence of what belongs to a thing's nature. Blindness is evil in a man because a man should see. The idea comes from Plotinus (Stage 5), but Augustine made it the standard Christian and Latin view.

**Where does the privation come from?** From **the will turning away** from a higher good to a lower one. In *The City of God* XII.7 (translated by Dods, 1871) he says the evil will has no efficient cause, that is no cause that produces it:

> "for it is not efficient, but deficient, as the will itself is not an effecting of something, but a defect."

Looking for its cause, he adds, is like trying to see darkness or hear silence.

**The objections.**

- **It is only words.** Pain hurts. Cruelty is a positive act, with planning and pleasure. Calling these "lacks" seems to change the label, not the fact. **Reply:** the claim is about what evil *is*, not how it feels. The cruel man's acts are real; their evil is what is missing from them, namely justice and love.
- **It does not answer the real question.** Even if evil is a lack, why does an all-powerful God permit so much of it? **Reply:** Augustine agreed. Privation answers "what is evil?", not "why is it permitted?". For the second he turns to free will and to the order of the whole.
- **Natural evil.** Earthquakes and disease involve no will. Augustine traced them to the Fall, a theological claim many modern readers do not accept.

**Where things stand.** The privation theory is still defended, especially by Thomists, and widely rejected by philosophers of religion as a full answer to the problem of evil. **Most agree it is at least coherent; the dispute is whether it is enough.**
Augustine: free choice of the will:
Augustine is often credited with giving the West its idea of **the will**: a power of the mind, distinct from reason and desire, by which we consent or refuse.

**The work.** *On Free Choice of the Will* (*De libero arbitrio*), a dialogue with his friend Evodius, begun in Rome in 388 and finished in Africa about 395. It opens with Evodius's question: **is God not the cause of evil?**

**The argument for free will as a gift:**

1. A world with beings who can freely do right is better than one without them.
2. To do right freely, they must be able to do wrong.
3. So God gave a free will that can be misused.
4. The misuse is ours. The gift, like hands or eyes, is good even though it can be used badly.

This is the ancestor of every later **free-will defence** against the problem of evil.

**Why do we sin?** Nothing outside the will forces it. **The will is the cause of its own turning.** If something compelled it, the act would not be a sin. Hence the "deficient cause" of the last lesson.

**Foreknowledge.** Evodius presses: God knows I will sin, so I must sin. Augustine's answer (*De libero arbitrio* III, and *The City of God* V.10):

- Knowing something will happen does not **cause** it. Your memory of the past does not make the past happen; God's foreknowledge does not make the future.
- God foreknows **that I will choose freely**. If my act were not free, his knowledge would be false.

Boethius will sharpen both the objection and the answer.

**Is "the will" new?** **This is a real scholarly dispute.** Albrecht Dihle (*The Theory of Will in Classical Antiquity*, 1982) argued that Augustine invented the concept. Michael Frede (*A Free Will*, 2011) argued that it was already in the Stoics, especially Epictetus. Others place the key step with Maximus the Confessor.

**The later Augustine.** In his fights with Pelagius after 411, Augustine came to say that **since the Fall, the will cannot choose the good without grace**, and that God chooses whom to save. Many readers think this sits badly with *On Free Choice*; Augustine himself denied any contradiction. **That is a theological debate**, followed in the Theology curriculum.

**The objections to the philosophy:**

- **Is a cause-less choice really free, or just random?** If nothing explains why the will turned, the turning looks like chance, not control. This is the "luck objection" still pressed against libertarian free will.
- **Could God not have made free beings who always choose well?** J. L. Mackie (1955) asked this; Alvin Plantinga (1974) replied that God cannot guarantee what free creatures will freely do.

**What stays.** The vocabulary: free choice (*liberum arbitrium*), consent, the divided will (the inner struggle of *Confessions* VIII, where he both wills and does not will the same thing). The modern free-will debate starts here.
Reading: Augustine, Confessions XI, on w:
The most famous pages ever written on time, read slowly. All quotations are from *Confessions* Book XI, translated by E. B. Pusey (1838), Project Gutenberg. Section numbers are those of modern editions.

**The question behind it.** Opponents asked: *what was God doing before he made heaven and earth?* Augustine refuses the old joke answer, "He was preparing hell (saith he) for pryers into mysteries" (XI.12), and gives a real one. **There was no "before"**, because time is itself something God made: "time itself Thou madest" (XI.13). Then he asks what this thing, time, is.

**The puzzle** (XI.14.17):

> "What then is time? If no one asks me, I know: if I wish to explain it to one that asketh, I know not"

| Phrase | What it tells you |
| --- | --- |
| **"If no one asks me, I know"** | we use the concept every day without trouble |
| **"if I wish to explain it... I know not"** | but we cannot define it. Wittgenstein quotes this as the mark of a philosophical problem |

**The argument that time hardly exists.** The past is no more. The future is not yet. Only the present is. But a present year is not all present: most of its months are past or to come. Nor is a month, a day or an hour. He presses down to the instant (XI.15.20):

> "If an instant of time be conceived, which cannot be divided into the smallest particles of moments, that alone is it, which may be called present... The present hath no space."

So: **past and future do not exist, and the present has no length.** Yet we say "a long time" and we measure times. What can we be measuring?

**His answer** (XI.20.26). It is not properly said that there are three times, but perhaps:

> "there be three times; a present of things past, a present of things present, and a present of things future." For these three do exist in some sort, in the soul, but otherwhere do I not see them; present of things past, memory; present of things present, sight; present of things future, expectation.

**This is the turn.** Past and future do exist, but **in the mind**, as memory and expectation. When I measure how long a syllable lasted, I measure what it left behind in me (XI.27.36):

> "It is in thee, my mind, that I measure times."

Earlier he guessed that time is "nothing else than protraction; but of what, I know not; and I marvel, if it be not of the mind itself?" (XI.26.33). The Latin is *distentio animi*, **a stretching-out of the mind.**

**Weighing it.**

- **Aristotle had said** that time is the number, that is the measure, of motion (Stage 4). Augustine rejects this: we measure a body's rest by time as well as its motion (XI.24.31).
- **The obvious objection:** if time is in the mind, was there no time before minds? Did the dinosaurs not last? **Scholars dispute** whether Augustine meant that time is only in the mind, or only that our *measuring* of time is done there.
- **His legacy is large.** Husserl's lectures on the consciousness of time, Heidegger, and Bergson begin from these pages. In physics, the question whether the "flowing present" is real or only how minds experience time is still open.

**Note the tone.** "I confess to Thee, O Lord, that I yet know not what time is" (XI.25.32). The argument is carried on as a prayer, and the confession of ignorance is part of the method.
Augustine: the City of God and the two c:
In 410 the Goths sacked Rome. Pagans said the city had fallen because it abandoned its old gods. Augustine's reply grew into twenty-two books and a philosophy of history and politics.

**The work.** *The City of God* (*De civitate Dei*), written from 413 to about 426. Books I–X demolish the pagan case: the gods never protected Rome, and the philosophers, even the Platonists he admires, could not save. Books XI–XXII tell the story of two cities from creation to the end.

**The central idea** (XIV.28, translated by Dods, 1871):

> "two cities have been formed by two loves: the earthly by the love of self, even to the contempt of God; the heavenly by the love of God, even to the contempt of self."

**The two cities are not places.** They are not the Church and the State. They are **two kinds of people, sorted by what they love most**, mixed together in every society until the end of time. A people, he redefines, is **a multitude united by agreement about what it loves** (XIX.24).

**Politics without illusions:**

1. **No earthly state is truly just.** Cicero had defined a commonwealth by justice. By that standard, Augustine argues, Rome was never one, since true justice gives God his due.
2. **Without justice, kingdoms are great robber bands.** In IV.4 (paraphrased here) he tells of a pirate captured by Alexander the Great. Asked what he meant by troubling the sea, the pirate replied: the same as you mean by troubling the whole world; I do it with one small ship and am called a robber, you with a great fleet and are called an emperor.
3. **Yet earthly peace is a real good.** Order, food, safety: both cities use them. "The peace of all things is the tranquillity of order" (XIX.13, Dods). Christians should obey and serve earthly rulers while not placing final hope in them.

**Against the cycles.** Many Greeks held that history repeats in great cycles. Augustine attacks this in Book XII: **history is a line with a beginning and an end, and each event happens once.** This linear view shaped how Europe thought about history and progress.

**The verdict and the disputes.**

- **Realists** read him as the founder of political realism: states run on power and self-love, and expecting virtue from politics is naive. Reinhold Niebuhr in the twentieth century took this line.
- **Others** read him as a theocrat, since medieval writers used him to put popes over kings ("political Augustinianism"). Most scholars now think this misreads him: he sets the heavenly city above every earthly order, the Church's included.
- **His defence of coercion** against the Donatists, a schismatic church in Africa, became a precedent for religious persecution. It is the part of his politics most often condemned.

**What stays.** The thought that **a society is defined by what it loves**, and that politics can secure peace but not salvation, is still argued over in political theory.
Boethius: the Consolation of Philosophy:
A Roman senator, condemned to death for treason, writes a dialogue in which Philosophy herself visits his cell. It became one of the most read books of the Middle Ages.

**Who.** Anicius Manlius Severinus **Boethius** (about 480–524 or 525), of an old Roman family, lived under **Theodoric**, the Ostrogothic king of Italy. He was **consul in 510**, and his two sons were made consuls together in 522, a rare honour. Then he defended a senator accused of plotting with Constantinople, was himself accused, and was imprisoned and **executed near Pavia** without a proper trial. He wrote the *Consolation* in prison.

**His life's plan.** Boethius meant to **translate all of Plato and Aristotle into Latin** and show that they agreed. He got through much of Aristotle's logic and Porphyry's introduction. For six hundred years almost all the Aristotle the Latin West had was his.

**The book.** Five books, alternating prose and verse. Boethius is weeping and writing poems when a tall woman appears: **Lady Philosophy**. She drives off the Muses of poetry, who only feed his grief, and begins the cure in stages, mild remedies first.

**Fortune speaks** (Book II, translated by H. R. James, 1897). Philosophy lets Fortune make her own case:

> "This is my art, this the game I never cease to play. I turn the wheel that spins. I delight to see the high come down and the low ascend."

And Philosophy's comment: "if it takes to standing still, it ceases to be the wheel of Fortune."

**The argument of Books II and III**, set out:

1. Everyone seeks happiness, the complete good that leaves nothing to be wanted.
2. Wealth, office, power, fame and pleasure can all be taken away, and none satisfies on its own.
3. A good you can lose cannot make you secure, since you must always fear losing it.
4. So true happiness lies in a good that cannot be lost: **the highest good, which is God**, and the wise share in it by becoming good.

**Book IV**: the wicked look powerful, but **evil is weakness**; they fail to reach the good everyone wants, and are punished by being what they are. The echo of Plato's *Gorgias* (Stage 3) is direct.

**Why Christianity is absent.** **The *Consolation* never mentions Christ**, though Boethius also wrote short theological treatises on the Trinity. Scholars have long debated why. The usual answer is that he chose to show how far reason alone can go; a minority once doubted that he was a Christian at all. It reads as Platonism with a Stoic temper.

**The objections.**

- **Is it a consolation?** The argument shows that external goods cannot make one happy. It does not show that their loss does not hurt, and the man is about to die.
- **"The wicked are weak"** depends on a Platonic sense of power as the ability to reach the true good. In the ordinary sense, tyrants plainly can do what they like.

**Its life afterwards.** King Alfred, Chaucer and Elizabeth I all translated it. **The wheel of Fortune** became one of the commonest images in medieval art.
Boethius: God's foreknowledge and human:
Book V of the *Consolation* sets out the problem of foreknowledge more sharply than anyone before, and answers it with an idea of **eternity** that has been argued over ever since.

**The problem**, as Boethius puts it to Philosophy:

1. God knows infallibly everything that will happen.
2. If God knows that I will do X tomorrow, then I cannot fail to do X, or God would be wrong.
3. What cannot fail to happen happens necessarily.
4. So everything I do is necessary, and I am not free.
5. Then praise, blame, reward, punishment and prayer are all pointless.

**Augustine's answer is not enough**, says Boethius. Augustine said knowledge does not *cause* the event. Fine; but if the knowledge is certain, the event is still *fixed*.

**First step: knowledge depends on the knower.** Things are known according to the power of the knower, not the nature of the thing. Sense, imagination, reason and intelligence grasp the same thing in different ways. So the question is not what the future is like, but **what God's way of knowing is like**.

**Second step: eternity.** The definition, in James's translation (1897):

> "eternity is the possession of endless life whole and perfect at a single moment."

**Eternal does not mean lasting forever.** A world with no beginning and no end, as Aristotle thought, would still live one moment after another. God's life has no before and after. So **God does not foreknow; he sees**. Everything, our tomorrow included, is present to him at once, as things below are present to someone looking down from a height.

**Third step: two kinds of necessity:**

> "So, then, there are two necessities--one simple, as that men are necessarily mortal; the other conditioned, as that, if you know that someone is walking, he must necessarily be walking."

If I see you walking, you must be walking, but **my seeing does not force you to walk.** God's seeing your free act in his eternal present makes it necessary only in this conditioned way, the way any known fact must be as it is known.

**The objections.**

- **Is a timeless God coherent?** If God is outside time, can he act, respond to prayer, or know what time it is *now*? Philosophers such as Nicholas Wolterstorff argue that God must be in time. Eleonore Stump and Norman Kretzmann (1981) worked out Boethius's view as "eternalism" and defended it.
- **Does it remove the problem?** If my act is eternally seen, it is still settled. Some argue that **the same dilemma returns** with "God eternally knows" in place of "God foreknows", though defenders reply that the seeing depends on the act, not the act on the seeing.
- **Is the distinction valid?** Most logicians accept that "necessarily, if God knows X then X" does not imply "X is necessary". The logical point is widely agreed; whether it settles the problem is not.

**Where it stands.** Boethius's answer is still one of the three or four main options in the debate, alongside **Ockhamism** (Stage 7) and **open theism**, the view that God does not know free future acts. Theology's use of it is in the Theology curriculum.
Boethius and Porphyry: the problem of un:
One short paragraph, in a beginner's handbook to logic, set the Middle Ages its most argued-over question. Boethius passed it on.

**The source.** **Porphyry** (about 234–about 305), Plotinus's pupil and editor, wrote the ***Isagoge*** ("Introduction"), a short guide to five terms needed to read Aristotle's *Categories*: genus, species, difference, property, accident. At the start he raises three questions, and then declines to answer them as too deep for an introduction:

1. Do **genera and species** (kinds such as "animal" and "human") exist in reality, or only in the mind?
2. If they exist, are they **bodies or not bodies**?
3. Do they exist **apart from sensible things, or in them**?

**What a universal is.** A **universal** is what many things have in common: the "human" that Socrates and Plato both are, the "red" shared by all red things. A **particular** is an individual: this man, this apple. The question is what sort of thing, if any, a universal is.

**Boethius's commentaries.** He wrote **two commentaries** on the *Isagoge*: the first on an older Latin version by Marius Victorinus, the second on his own translation. In the second he answers Porphyry's questions.

**First, the argument that universals cannot be things:**

1. A universal must be **one and the same** in many things at once.
2. But nothing that is one can be **wholly in many** separate things at the same time; it would be divided.
3. So a universal cannot be a single real thing.

**Second, the argument that they cannot be mere thoughts:**

1. If universals are only in the mind, either they match something real or not.
2. If they match nothing, they are **empty, false thoughts**, and all science, which is about kinds, would be about nothing.

**His solution: abstraction.** To think of something **otherwise than it is** is not always to think falsely.

- Putting together what is not together in reality (a horse and a man into a centaur) is false.
- But **considering apart what is together in reality** is not false. A geometer thinks of a line without its body, though no line exists without a body.

So the mind **considers the likeness** that is really in many individuals, apart from those individuals. **Universals exist in sensible things, but are understood apart from them.** In his words, paraphrased: they subsist in sensibles, and are understood outside bodies.

**A caution.** Boethius says he gives the answer of Aristotle as read by Alexander of Aphrodisias, **because the book introduces Aristotle**, not because he has decided Aristotle is right against Plato. **Scholars debate** how much of a position of his own it is.

**The three later answers**, which Stage 7 takes up:

| Name | Claim |
| --- | --- |
| **Realism** | universals are real things, in or beyond particulars |
| **Conceptualism** | universals are concepts, grounded in real likeness |
| **Nominalism** | only particulars exist; universals are names or signs |

Boethius's answer sits between the first two. Abelard and Ockham will push towards the third.
John Philoponus: the world had a beginni:
In 529, the year Justinian banned pagan teaching, a Christian in Alexandria published a book attacking the most respected doctrine in Greek philosophy: that the world has always existed.

**Who.** **John Philoponus** (about 490–about 570), also called John the Grammarian, worked in the Neoplatonist school of Alexandria under Ammonius, editing his teacher's lectures on Aristotle. *Philoponus* means "lover of work".

**The target.** Aristotle had argued that motion and time can have no first moment, so **the world is eternal**. The Neoplatonist **Proclus** (412–485) gave eighteen arguments that the world, though caused by God, had no beginning. Philoponus answered in ***Against Proclus on the Eternity of the World*** (529), and then in ***Against Aristotle on the Eternity of the World***, which survives only in quotations by his opponent Simplicius.

**His arguments from infinity.** Aristotle himself said that **an actual infinite**, an infinite number of things all real at once or completed, cannot exist. Philoponus turned this against him:

1. **The traversal argument.** If the world had no beginning, an infinite number of days has already passed. But an infinite series cannot be gone through to the end. So we could never have reached today. So the past is finite.
2. **The addition argument.** If the past is infinite, then each new year adds to an infinite number. But nothing can be greater than the infinite. So the past is not infinite.
3. **The multiplication argument.** Saturn takes about thirty years to circle the heavens, the Sun one year. If the past were infinite, the Sun would have made thirty times an infinite number of circuits. That is absurd. So the past is finite.

**The replies.**

- **Aristotelians**, such as Simplicius: the past days do not exist together. **They are a potential infinite**, never complete at any one time, so Aristotle's rule against actual infinites does not apply.
- **Modern mathematics.** Since Cantor in the 1870s and 1880s, infinite sets are well understood, and **an infinite set can be added to without getting larger** in number: the even numbers are as many as all the whole numbers. So **arguments 2 and 3 are now generally held to fail.**
- **The traversal argument is still argued over.** It needs a starting point infinitely far back, and there is none; an infinite past, critics say, has no first day to cross from. Defenders such as William Lane Craig, who revived it as the "*kalām* cosmological argument" in 1979, reply that there is still something absurd in a completed infinite series.

**Philoponus the physicist.** He also broke with Aristotle's physics:

- A thrown stone keeps moving not because the air pushes it but because **the thrower gives it an inner force**. This is the ancestor of the medieval **impetus** theory.
- **Heavy and light bodies dropped together fall in nearly the same time**, contrary to Aristotle. He says this from observation, about a thousand years before Galileo.

**Afterwards.** His arguments passed into Arabic, to **al-Kindi** and the theologians of *kalām*, and from there to **Saadia** and **Bonaventure**. The question whether the world's beginning can be *proved* runs through the rest of this stage.
Pseudo-Dionysius: negative theology as p:
A Syrian monk, writing about 500 under a borrowed name, gave Christian thought its most radical account of what language cannot say.

**The name.** The author calls himself **Dionysius the Areopagite**, the Athenian converted by Paul (Acts 17:34). He was taken at his word for a thousand years, which gave his writings almost apostolic weight. Doubts began in the Renaissance. In **1895 Hugo Koch and Josef Stiglmayr**, working separately, showed that he **borrows closely from Proclus** (412–485). So he wrote around 500, probably in Syria. **Who he was remains unknown**; the writings are first quoted in the 520s and 530s.

**The works.** *The Divine Names*, *The Mystical Theology* (five short chapters), *The Celestial Hierarchy*, *The Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, and ten letters.

**Three ways of speaking about God.**

| Way | Greek term | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Affirmation** | *kataphasis* (cataphatic) | God is good, wise, living, because God causes goodness, wisdom, life |
| **Negation** | *apophasis* (apophatic) | God is not good, not wise, not being, as these words are meant of creatures |
| **Eminence** | the prefix *hyper-* | God is "super-good", "super-essential": beyond the thing named, not below it |

**The argument behind negation:**

1. Our words and concepts are drawn from created things, which are limited.
2. God is the cause of all things, and is not one more thing among them.
3. A word that marks off one thing from others cannot fit what is not one of the things.
4. So each affirmation is, strictly, false of God, and must be denied.
5. Denial brings us nearer the truth, until even the denials are left behind.

**The end of *The Mystical Theology*** (chapter 5, translated by C. E. Rolt, 1920):

> "nor does It belong to the category of non-existence or to that of existence... nor can any affirmation or negation apply to it"

**Even "not" fails.** God is beyond both "is" and "is not". What is left is **"unknowing"** (Greek *agnōsia*), which he presents as a higher knowing, not mere ignorance.

**The roots.** This is Plotinus's One (Stage 5), "beyond being", made Christian. The debt is real; so is the difference: Dionysius's God is personal and creates freely.

**The objections.**

- **Self-refutation.** "Nothing can be said of God" is itself something said of God. **Reply:** the negations are a ladder, a practice of correcting our speech, not a set of theses about God's nature.
- **Emptiness.** If every predicate is denied, what is the difference between this God and nothing at all? An empty concept cannot be worshipped or reasoned about. Maimonides, later in this stage, faces this objection directly.
- **Why affirm anything?** If affirmations are false, scripture's language is false. **Reply:** they are true as to what God causes, false as to how they mean.

**Afterwards.** Eriugena translated him into Latin in the 860s. Aquinas quotes him constantly. Modern philosophy of religion still argues whether **apophatic theology is a coherent position or a polite refusal to have one**. Its spiritual side is taken up in the Theology curriculum.
Maximus the Confessor: the natural will:
A seventh-century monk lost his tongue and his right hand for saying that Christ had two wills. The argument behind it is one of the subtlest accounts of the will in ancient thought.

**Who.** **Maximus the Confessor** (about 580–662). Where he was born is disputed: a Greek life says Constantinople, a hostile Syriac one Palestine. A monk who wrote in Greek, he spent years in North Africa and Rome. He opposed **Monothelitism**, the imperial compromise teaching that Christ had **one will**. He was tried in Constantinople, mutilated, and died in exile in the Caucasus in 662. The Council of Constantinople of 680–681 took his side. The theology belongs to the Theology curriculum; **the philosophy is a theory of what a will is.**

**The question underneath: does the will belong to nature or to person?** A **nature** is what kind of thing something is (human); a **person** is who it is (Peter). If the will belongs to the person, one person has one will. If it belongs to the nature, anyone who has a full human nature has a human will.

**Maximus's answer:**

1. Every rational nature has a **natural will** (*thelēma physikon*): a built-in drive towards its own good, towards being, life and understanding.
2. So the will belongs to **nature**. What belongs to the **person** is the *way* the will is used: willing *this* rather than *that*.
3. A full human nature without a human will would not be a full human nature.

**The deliberating will.** Maximus calls it the **gnomic will** (*thelēma gnōmikon*), from *gnōmē*, a settled disposition or opinion formed by deliberation. We deliberate, weigh, hesitate and choose because **we do not see the good clearly**, and our natural drive is confused.

**The striking consequence.** Deliberation is not the height of freedom; **it is a sign of its limits.** A being that saw the good perfectly would not hesitate between options. It would move towards the good without obstacle, and that would be the most free. Maximus came to deny Christ a gnomic will for this reason, while insisting on his natural human will.

**Objections and replies.**

- **Freedom means alternatives.** If a perfect being cannot choose evil, is it free? Most modern libertarians say freedom needs the ability to do otherwise. **Reply:** that confuses freedom with indecision; nobody thinks a person less free for being unable to want to torture a child. The modern debate over whether freedom needs alternatives (Harry Frankfurt, 1969; Susan Wolf's *Freedom within Reason*, 1990) is a distant echo.
- **Is a "natural will" a will at all?** A drive towards one's good sounds like appetite, not will. **Reply:** for Maximus it is *rational* appetite, the desire of a mind, not of a stomach.

**His analysis of the act.** Using Aristotle and the bishop Nemesius (about 400), Maximus separates the stages of a human act: wishing, inquiring, deliberating, judging, choosing, acting. Through **John of Damascus** (about 675–749), whose summary reached Latin about 1150, this list reached **Aquinas**.

**Who first had the idea of will? This is disputed.** Some historians credit Augustine (see the lesson on free choice); others credit Maximus with the first full account of will as a faculty of rational nature.
Eriugena: the Periphyseon and the divisi:
In the ninth century, at a Frankish court where little Greek was known, an Irishman wrote the most ambitious system of philosophy between Augustine and Aquinas.

**Who.** **John Scottus Eriugena** (about 800–about 877). Both names mean "Irish". He taught at the court of **Charles the Bald**, king of the West Franks, from the 840s. He was one of very few in the West who read Greek well.

**His career in three acts.**

| Date | |
| --- | --- |
| **851** | *On Predestination*, against the monk Gottschalk; it was condemned by councils at Valence (855) and Langres (859) |
| **about 860–862** | translates **Pseudo-Dionysius** into Latin, then Maximus and Gregory of Nyssa |
| **about 864–866** | writes the ***Periphyseon*** ("On Natures"), a dialogue in five books between a teacher and a student |

**Reason and authority.** In *On Predestination* he says that true philosophy is true religion, and true religion true philosophy. In the *Periphyseon* (paraphrased) he argues that **authority comes from true reason, but reason never from authority**: an authority not backed by reason is weak. He is still a believer reading scripture; but he reads it with the confidence of a philosopher.

**The four divisions of nature.** "Nature" for Eriugena means **everything that is and everything that is not**. He divides it four ways:

| | Creates | Is created |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1. God as source** | yes | no |
| **2. The primordial causes** (the patterns of things in God's mind) | yes | yes |
| **3. The world of things in space and time** | no | yes |
| **4. God as the end to which all returns** | no | no |

**The great cycle.** Everything **goes out** from God (1) through the causes (2) into the world (3), and **returns** to God (4). The scheme is Neoplatonic: Plotinus's procession and return (Stage 5), through Dionysius and Maximus.

**God as nothing.** Taking negative theology to the end, Eriugena says God is ***nihil*, "nothing"**, by excellence, not by lack: God is not any of the things that are. **Creation "from nothing"** then means creation from God's own unknowable depth. Creation is a **theophany**: God appearing.

**The charge of pantheism**, the view that God and the world are the same. Read this way, God "creates himself" in things, and things return into God. In **1225 Pope Honorius III condemned the *Periphyseon*** and ordered copies burned.

**Was he a pantheist? This is a real dispute.** Against the charge: he insists that God transcends everything created and that creatures keep their being in the return. For it: the cycle seems to make the world a stage in God's own life. Most recent scholars think "pantheist" misreads him, and some prefer "panentheist": the world is in God, but God is more than the world.

**Why read him.** He shows what happens when Greek Neoplatonism is taken seriously in Latin. He had almost no followers for centuries; his translations of Dionysius were his real legacy. Hegel's admirers in the nineteenth century rediscovered him.
Anselm: the ontological argument of the:
An eleventh-century monk claimed to prove God's existence from the bare idea of God. Philosophers have been trying to say exactly what is wrong with it, or right, for nine hundred years.

**Who.** **Anselm** (1033–1109), born at Aosta in northern Italy, became a monk at Bec in Normandy and its abbot in 1078, then **Archbishop of Canterbury** from 1093. His motto was *fides quaerens intellectum*, **faith seeking understanding**: start from belief and try to understand it by reason.

**The works.** The *Monologion* (1076) argued for God from degrees of goodness. Dissatisfied with its chain of arguments, he looked for **a single argument** that would need nothing else. The ***Proslogion*** (1077–1078) is the result. The name "ontological argument" was given to arguments of this kind much later, by Kant.

**The text** (*Proslogion* 2, translated by S. N. Deane, 1903):

> "we believe that thou art a being than which nothing greater can be conceived... And assuredly that, than which nothing greater can be conceived, cannot exist in the understanding alone. For, suppose it exists in the understanding alone: then it can be conceived to exist in reality; which is greater."

**The argument, set out:**

1. God is **that than which nothing greater can be conceived**.
2. Even "the fool" of Psalm 14, who says there is no God, understands this phrase. So it exists **in the understanding**.
3. Suppose it existed in the understanding **alone**.
4. Then we could conceive it existing **in reality** as well.
5. **Existing in reality is greater** than existing in the understanding alone.
6. So we could conceive something greater than that than which nothing greater can be conceived. That is a contradiction.
7. So it exists **both in the understanding and in reality**.

**The painter.** Anselm's own illustration: a painter has the picture in his mind before he paints it, but does not yet think it exists. To have something in mind is not to think it real.

**A second argument** (*Proslogion* 3). A being that **cannot be conceived not to exist** is greater than one that can. So God cannot even be conceived not to exist. This is the seed of the modern **modal** versions, which argue about necessary existence (Norman Malcolm, 1960; Alvin Plantinga, 1974).

**The main objections**, the first in the next lesson:

| Objector | Objection |
| --- | --- |
| **Gaunilo** (soon after) | the same form "proves" a perfect island |
| **Aquinas** (1260s) | not everyone understands "God" this way; and even granted the meaning, it only follows that God is *thought* to exist |
| **Kant** (1781) | existence is not a property that makes a thing greater: a hundred real thalers contain no more than a hundred imagined ones |
| **Frege and Russell** | "exists" is not a predicate of things but says that a concept has instances |

**Where it stands.** **There is broad agreement that the argument as Anselm gave it fails**, and very little agreement on why. Russell remarked, in a passage paraphrased here, that it is easier to feel sure it must be fallacious than to find where the fallacy lies. Plantinga's modal version is generally judged **valid**; the dispute is over whether its key premise, that such a being is possible, can be known without assuming the conclusion.

**Cur Deus Homo**, briefly. In *Why God Became Man* (finished 1098) Anselm tried to show by "necessary reasons" (*rationes necessariae*) why the Incarnation was fitting. It is a landmark of theology, followed in the Theology curriculum.
Gaunilo's lost island and Anselm's reply:
The first and still the most famous objection to the ontological argument came from a monk at the other end of France, and Anselm had it copied with his own reply.

**Who.** **Gaunilo**, a monk of Marmoutier near Tours, wrote *On Behalf of the Fool* soon after the *Proslogion*. Almost nothing else is known of him. Anselm asked that the objection and his *Reply* be **copied with the *Proslogion* from then on**, a remarkable act of fairness.

**The parody** (translated by S. N. Deane, 1903). Imagine an island in the ocean, "more excellent than all other countries", called the **lost island** because no one can find it. Someone argues:

> "You can no longer doubt that this island which is more excellent than all lands exists somewhere, since you have no doubt that it is in your understanding."

The reasoning has exactly Anselm's form. Gaunilo's verdict: either the speaker is joking, or "I know not which I ought to regard as the greater fool: myself, supposing that I should allow this proof; or him".

**The logic of the parody.** If an argument of a given form leads from true premises to an absurd conclusion, **the form is bad**. So something must be wrong with Anselm's, even if we cannot say what.

**Gaunilo's second objection is deeper.** **We do not really understand** "that than which nothing greater can be conceived". I can hear the words, but I have no concept of such a being, any more than of the island's riches. The first premise, that it is "in the understanding", already claims too much.

**Anselm's replies:**

1. **The argument works only for "that than which nothing greater can be conceived"**, not for "the greatest island". An island is greatest only *among islands*. Its greatness is limited by being an island, and a limited thing can always be conceived not to exist.
2. **We do understand the phrase.** We understand it the way we understand "ineffable": enough to reason with, even if we cannot picture what it names.
3. Gaunilo attacks "greater than all", but Anselm's phrase is "**than which nothing greater can be conceived**", which says nothing about comparison with existing things.

**Modern restatements.**

- **Plantinga** (1974): the qualities that make an island great, more palm trees, more beaches, **have no maximum**. There can always be one more coconut. So "the greatest possible island" is incoherent. Greatness in the divine sense (knowledge, power, goodness) has an intrinsic maximum.
- **The parodists reply:** then build the parody on a concept with a maximum, such as "the greatest possible evil being", or "a being than which nothing *worse* can be conceived". If the same form "proves" an evil god, the form is still at fault.
- **Another reply** points out that the parodies all assume **existence adds greatness**; once Kant's point is accepted, both Anselm's argument and the parodies fall together.

**Where it stands.** Most philosophers think Gaunilo was right that something is wrong; most also think his island, as he stated it, does not show what. The parody remains the **standard test** for any new version of the argument: if it also proves the island, something has gone wrong.

**Why this exchange matters.** It is one of the first open, written philosophical debates in the medieval West, conducted as argument against argument, with both sides preserved together.
Falsafa: Greek philosophy goes into Arab:
Between about 750 and 1000, nearly all of Aristotle and much of Greek science and medicine were translated into Arabic. It was one of the largest transfers of learning in history.

**The setting.** In 750 the **Abbasid** family took the caliphate and moved its centre east. In **762** Caliph al-Mansur founded **Baghdad**. Its people included Persians, Arabs, Syriac-speaking Christians, Jews and Zoroastrians, and Greek learning had long been studied in Syriac in Christian schools.

**Why translate?** Several reasons worked together:

- **Practical**: medicine, astronomy, astrology, mathematics, engineering.
- **Argument**: Muslim theologians debated Christians, Jews and Manichees, and needed **Aristotle's logic** to do it.
- **Prestige**: caliphs, especially **al-Ma'mun** (ruled 813–833), presented themselves as heirs of ancient wisdom.

**The "House of Wisdom."** Al-Ma'mun's *Bayt al-Hikma* in Baghdad is often described as a great translation academy. **Historians now doubt this.** Dimitri Gutas (*Greek Thought, Arabic Culture*, 1998) argued that it was chiefly a palace library, and that the movement was carried by many patrons over two centuries.

**The translators.** The greatest was **Hunayn ibn Ishaq** (809–873), a Nestorian Christian physician, often working **Greek to Syriac to Arabic**, with his son Ishaq and nephew Hubaysh. He collected manuscripts from several sources and compared them before translating. Most translators were Christians.

**Two mistakes that shaped everything.** Two Neoplatonist works passed as Aristotle's:

| Title | What it really was |
| --- | --- |
| ***The Theology of Aristotle*** | a paraphrase of parts of Plotinus's *Enneads* IV–VI |
| ***The Book of the Pure Good*** (Latin *Liber de causis*) | an Arabic reworking of Proclus's *Elements of Theology* |

So **"Aristotle" in Arabic came with Plotinus's One, emanation and return** built in. Much of the Neoplatonic flavour of Arabic philosophy comes from this.

**Two words.**

- ***Falsafa*** is the Arabic borrowing of Greek *philosophia*. A ***faylasuf*** (plural *falasifa*) was someone who worked in the Greek tradition: logic, physics, metaphysics, ethics.
- ***Kalam*** ("speech", "discussion") was **dialectical theology**: reasoning from the Qur'an, using argument to defend it. Its practitioners, the *mutakallimun*, were often opponents of the *falasifa*: they held that the world was created in time and is made of atoms that God re-creates at every instant.

**The two camps argued for three centuries.** The *falasifa* said demonstration, in Aristotle's sense, gives the highest knowledge. The theologians said the philosophers' conclusions, an eternal world, a God who knows only universals, contradicted revelation. That quarrel reaches its climax with **al-Ghazali and Averroes**, later in this stage.
