Aquinas's ethics joins two ideas: Aristotle's **virtue**, the excellence that makes a life go well, and the Stoic and Roman idea of a **natural law**, a moral order that reason can read in human nature.

**Four kinds of law.** In the "Treatise on Law" (*Summa theologiae* I-II, questions 90 to 97), law is defined as **an ordinance of reason for the common good, made by whoever has care of the community, and promulgated**. Then:

| Law | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| **Eternal law** | God's reason governing the whole universe |
| **Natural law** | the rational creature's **share** in the eternal law: what reason can grasp of how to act well |
| **Human law** | particular rules made by rulers, applying natural law to circumstances |
| **Divine law** | the law revealed in Scripture (for the Theology curriculum) |

**The first precept.** In I-II question 94, article 2, Aquinas argues that, as the first principle of thought is non-contradiction, so the first principle of practical reason is, in paraphrase: **good is to be done and pursued, and evil avoided.** It is self-evident; nobody acts except for some good.

**What counts as good?** Reason grasps as goods the things to which humans have a **natural inclination**:

1. **Life**, which we share with all substances: to preserve ourselves.
2. **Mating and raising children**, which we share with animals.
3. **Knowing the truth** (including about God) and **living in society**, which belong to us as rational.

The precepts of natural law are the reasoned **protection and pursuit of these goods**.

**Human law and its limits.** Human law binds because it derives from natural law, either as a **conclusion** (do not murder) or as a **determination** (drive on the left: some rule is needed, and this one is chosen). A human law that contradicts natural law is, he says, no longer a law but a **corruption of law** (I-II q. 95 a. 2; paraphrased). Martin Luther King Jr. invoked Aquinas on unjust law in 1963.

**The virtues.** A **virtue** is a stable good **habit** of the soul. Aquinas takes Aristotle's moral and intellectual virtues and orders them under the four **cardinal virtues** (from *cardo*, hinge), on which the moral life turns:

| Virtue | Perfects | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Prudence** | practical reason | knowing what to do here and now |
| **Justice** | the will | giving each their due |
| **Fortitude** (courage) | the irascible appetite | holding firm against fear |
| **Temperance** | the desiring appetite | moderating pleasure |

Above these he places the **theological virtues**, faith, hope and charity, which he held are given by God; they belong to the Theology curriculum.

**The objections.**

- **Is to ought.** Hume (Stage 9) argued that no "ought" follows from an "is". Natural law seems to infer **what we should do** from **what we are inclined to**. Reply: Aquinas does not infer the good from inclinations; reason **grasps** the goods as good, self-evidently, and the inclinations are how they first appear.
- **Which inclinations?** Humans are also inclined to greed. Reply: only those proper to our **rational** nature reveal goods. Critics say this smuggles in the conclusions.
- **A real dispute among interpreters.** The **"new natural law" theory** of Germain Grisez and John Finnis (from the 1960s) reads Aquinas as grounding ethics in self-evident basic goods **without** first needing a metaphysics of nature. Traditional Thomists (for example, Ralph McInerny and Russell Hittinger) argue that this misreads him. The disagreement is live.
Siger of Brabant and the Latin Averroist:
In the 1260s and 1270s a group of masters in the Paris arts faculty read Aristotle **as a philosopher reads him, wherever that led**. They are called the **Latin Averroists** or **radical Aristotelians**, and their leader was Siger of Brabant.

**The man.** **Siger of Brabant** (about 1240 to about 1284) was a master of arts at Paris. His views were among those condemned in **1270**; in **1276** he was summoned before the French inquisitor and fled, apparently to the papal court. He died at **Orvieto**, reportedly stabbed by a deranged secretary. Strikingly, **Dante** put him in Paradise (*Paradiso*, canto 10), praised there by Aquinas himself, his great opponent. With him worked **Boethius of Dacia** (active about 1270s), author of *On the Eternity of the World*.

**The method: philosophy speaks as philosophy.** Siger's working principle was that the task of a philosopher is to state **what Aristotle and reason conclude**, not what is true by faith. Where they differ, he would report the philosophical conclusion, and add that the truth lies with faith.

**The unity of the intellect.** His most notorious thesis followed **Averroes**'s reading of Aristotle's *On the Soul*:

1. The intellect grasps **universals**, which are immaterial.
2. So the intellect is **immaterial**, not the form of any body.
3. What is immaterial cannot be **many** in one species, for matter is what divides one individual from another of the same kind.
4. So there is **one intellect for all humans**, and individual humans think by being joined to it through their own images.

The conclusion: **no individual intellect survives death**.

**Aquinas's reply.** In *On the Unity of the Intellect, against the Averroists* (1270), Aquinas argued two things:

- **It is not Aristotle's view,** read correctly, nor the view of the Greek commentators.
- **It is false by experience:** **this human thinks**. If the intellect were one separate thing, it would not be *I* who understand, any more than I see when someone else sees. Our thinking is ours.

Siger seems to have been moved by this, and his later works shift towards Aquinas's position; how far is disputed.

**The "double truth".** The 1277 condemnation charged certain masters with saying things are true in philosophy but false in faith, as if there were **two contrary truths**. Did anyone hold this? **The standard view now is that none did.** Siger and Boethius of Dacia said rather that a conclusion follows **from Aristotle's principles**, or **from natural causes alone**, while the **simple truth** is with faith. Boethius argued that the natural philosopher, starting from nature, cannot reach creation, which is not a natural process; so he may deny a beginning of the world **as a natural philosopher** without contradicting the believer.

**The objection.** Is this coherent? If you know a conclusion is false, how can you assert it, even "as a philosopher"? Defenders answer that it is like a mathematician deriving a result from axioms she does not hold; **"follows from these premises" is not "is true"**. Critics, then and now, found it evasive.

**Why it matters.** The Averroists asked whether philosophy can be an **autonomous** discipline, judged by its own standards alone. That is a modern question, and they were early to ask it.
Duns Scotus: the univocity of being and:
John Duns Scotus is the most difficult of the great schoolmen, and among the most influential. He was called the **Subtle Doctor**, and he earned it.

**The man.** **John Duns Scotus** (about 1266 to 1308) was a Scottish Franciscan, probably from **Duns** in the Borders. He taught at **Oxford** and **Paris**, and died young at **Cologne** in November 1308. His work survives in several versions of his *Sentences* commentary (the **Ordinatio** is the main one), in questions on Aristotle's *Metaphysics*, and in the treatise ***On the First Principle***, a proof of an infinite being.

**Univocity of being.** Against Aquinas's analogy, Scotus argued that **some concepts are univocal**, the same in meaning, for God and creatures, above all the concept of **being**.

**The argument from doubt** (Ordinatio I, distinction 3):

1. A person can be **certain** that God is a being while **doubting** whether God is finite or infinite, created or uncreated.
2. A concept you are certain of is **different** from concepts you doubt.
3. So the concept of *being* is distinct from both *finite being* and *infinite being*, and common to both.
4. So "being" is **univocal** to God and creatures.

**The argument from proof.**

1. All our concepts come from creatures.
2. An argument from creatures to God needs a **middle term with one meaning**; otherwise it commits the **fallacy of equivocation**.
3. So if we can know anything of God by reason, some concepts are univocal.

**What univocity does not mean.** Scotus did **not** think God and creatures are the same kind of thing. The concept *being* is very thin, and what differs is the **mode**: God is **infinite** being, creatures finite. Infinity is not one more property but the intrinsic degree of God's being, as a colour's intensity is not something added to it.

**The objections.** Thomists replied that a concept "common" to God and creatures puts both under a higher category, which God's transcendence forbids. Scotus answered that *being* is not a category or genus. Some modern theologians (for example in "Radical Orthodoxy" from the 1990s) blame Scotus's univocity for flattening God into one more being and so opening the road to secular modernity. **Most Scotus scholars think this reads him badly**, since univocity is a claim about concepts, not about how God exists. It is a live debate.

**The formal distinction.** Scotus needed a way to say that two things are **distinct but not separable**. Between:

| Distinction | Example |
| --- | --- |
| **Real** | two separable things: Socrates and Plato |
| **Of reason only** | one thing thought of two ways: the morning and evening star, as named |

he placed the **formal distinction**: two **formalities** in one thing, each with its own definition, which **cannot exist apart** but are distinct **prior to any act of the mind**. Examples: God's justice and God's mercy; a human's rationality and animality; a common nature and what makes it *this* one (next lesson).

**The objection.** Is it a third option, or a new name for a contradiction? **Ockham** argued that between real and mental distinction there is no room: if *a* and *b* differ in any way independent of the mind, they are two things. Scotists replied that **definitional distinctness** in reality is not separability. The same question recurs with Palamas, later in this stage.
Duns Scotus: haecceity, and the will tha:
Two more of Scotus's ideas changed philosophy: what makes an individual **this** individual, and what makes the will **free**.

**The problem of individuation.** Socrates and Plato are both human. What makes Socrates **this** human and not another? Earlier answers:

| Answer | Who | Scotus's objection |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Matter** (designated by quantity) | Aquinas | matter is itself general until something makes it *this* matter; the question recurs |
| **Accidents** (size, place) | many earlier thinkers | accidents are **posterior** to the substance; they cannot make it what it is |
| **Mere negation** (not being divided) | some contemporaries | a negation needs something positive behind it |
| **Existence** | others | existence does not distinguish essences |

**Scotus's answer: haecceity.** Each thing has a positive, unrepeatable principle of **thisness**, which in some works he calls **haecceity** (from Latin *haec*, "this"; elsewhere he calls it the "ultimate reality of the being"). It is **formally distinct** from the common nature.

**The common nature.** Scotus also held, against nominalism, that the nature **human** in Socrates has a **less than numerical unity**: it is not one thing, but it is not merely a concept. That is why Socrates and Plato can be really alike. Haecceity contracts that nature to *this* one.

**The argument, simplified.**

1. A **singular** thing is incompatible with being divided into many things each identical to it.
2. This incompatibility must have a **positive** ground in the thing.
3. It is not the nature (shared), nor matter, quantity, accidents or existence (by the objections above).
4. So there is a distinct positive entity, the **haecceity**.

**Objections.** We can never **know** a haecceity: no concept captures pure thisness. Scotus accepted this, which some find a fatal cost. And Ockham asked: why not say every thing is **simply individual by itself**, so no principle is needed? That is the nominalist answer. The debate is still alive in modern metaphysics as the question of **bare particulars** and **primitive thisness**.

**The will.** Scotus held that the will is a **rational power** in a strict sense: it is open to **opposites**. The intellect, given its evidence, cannot help assenting; nature acts one way; only the will, at the very moment it chooses, **could have chosen otherwise** (the theory called **synchronic contingency**: at the same instant the alternative remained possible).

**The two affections.** Building on Anselm (Stage 6), Scotus said the will has two inclinations:

- the **affection for the advantageous** (*affectio commodi*): seeking one's own happiness;
- the **affection for justice** (*affectio iustitiae*): loving a good **for its own sake**, as it deserves, even against one's advantage.

Free choice is possible because the second can **moderate** the first. A will that only sought its own happiness, Scotus thought, would not be free.

**Ethics.** Scotus held that the commands to love God are necessary, but that most of the moral law about our neighbour, though fitting, depends on **God's free will**. Scholars dispute how far he is a **divine command theorist**: some read him as one, others stress that he thought these laws highly fitting to human nature. **Objection**, from Thomists then and since: this makes morality **arbitrary**. The reply depends on that dispute.
Ockham: the razor and nominalism:
William of Ockham cut medieval metaphysics down to size. His tool was a principle of economy, and his result was the most thorough **nominalism** of the Middle Ages.

**The man.** **William of Ockham** (about 1287 to 1347) was an English Franciscan, from Ockham in Surrey. He studied at Oxford and lectured on the *Sentences*, but never became a full master; he was later called the **Venerable Inceptor** (a beginner in the degree). In **1324** he was summoned to the papal court at **Avignon** to answer charges about his teaching. In **1328**, after a quarrel with Pope John XXII over Franciscan poverty, he fled to the emperor **Louis of Bavaria**. He spent his last years in **Munich** writing on politics, and died there about 1347. His chief philosophical work is the ***Summa of Logic*** (about 1323).

**The razor.** The principle called **Ockham's razor** says: **do not posit more things than you need to explain the facts.** Ockham stated it in several forms, for example that plurality should not be posited without necessity. (The famous Latin slogan about not multiplying entities is a later formula, not found in his works.) He did not invent it, but he used it more ruthlessly than anyone.

What counts as "necessity", for Ockham? Three things only: **what is self-evident**, **what is known by experience**, and **what is required by Scripture** or the Church's teaching.

**Nominalism: only individuals exist.** Ockham held that **everything that exists outside the mind is individual**. There are no common natures, no "less than numerical unity", no formal distinctions in creatures. Against Scotus:

1. If the nature *human* in Socrates were **really** distinct from his individuality, they would be two things, and could in principle be separated. Then there could be a human nature that belonged to no one.
2. If it were distinct **only in the mind**, then outside the mind Socrates is **simply singular**.
3. A third option, the formal distinction, is either real (and then 1 applies) or mental (and then 2 applies).
4. So outside the mind there is **nothing common**, and the razor removes the need for any.

**Then what are universals?** They are **signs**. Ockham developed a theory of **mental language**: concepts are **natural signs** of things, as smoke signifies fire, and are combined into mental sentences, as spoken words are combined into spoken ones. The concept *human* is a universal because it **signifies many individuals** at once. Universality is a property of **signs**, not things.

**The categories cut down.** Aristotle had ten categories (Stage 4). Ockham argued that, among created things, only **substances** and **qualities** are real things. Quantity, relation, place and time are not extra entities; "Socrates is to the left of Plato" is made true by Socrates and Plato and where they are, with no third item called *being-to-the-left*.

**The objections.**

- **Why do concepts fit?** If nothing common exists, why do our concept *human* and the world line up so well? Why can we not classify Socrates with stones? Ockham's answer: individuals can be **more or less alike** in themselves, and likeness is not a further thing. Realists reply that likeness **in a respect** requires a respect, which is a common nature by another name.

**Where the arguments stand.** The modern debate between realism and nominalism about properties (Stage 14) runs very close to this one, and "Ockham's razor" remains a working principle in science and philosophy, though **what counts as "simpler"** is itself contested.
Ockham: God's absolute and ordained powe:
Ockham's theology of God's power turned into a tool for philosophy: a way of testing what is **necessary** and what only **happens to be so**.

**The distinction.** It did not begin with Ockham: thirteenth-century theologians used it, and the 1277 condemnation gave it force. God's power can be considered two ways:

| | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| **Absolute power** (*potentia absoluta*) | everything God **could** do: anything that **does not involve a contradiction** |
| **Ordained power** (*potentia ordinata*) | what God **has in fact chosen** to do, the order He has set up and keeps |

Ockham stressed that this is **not two powers**, but one power considered two ways.

**The use in philosophy.** The distinction gives a test of what depends on what:

1. Whatever God does by means of a secondary cause, He **could** do directly, by absolute power.
2. Whatever is **really distinct** from something else could, by absolute power, exist without it.
3. So if *a* and *b* are two things, God could make *a* without *b*.

This argument lets Ockham ask of any supposed link, **is it necessary or contingent?** The answer, very often, is contingent.

**Intuitive cognition of what does not exist.** Ockham held that the mind has **intuitive cognition**, direct awareness of a thing as present, from which we judge that it exists. Then:

1. The act of awareness is a **thing really distinct** from its object, the star I see.
2. So God could, by absolute power, keep the act in being **without the star**.
3. So it is possible to have an intuitive cognition of a star that **does not exist**.

Ockham added that, in such a case, the intuition would lead us to judge **correctly** that it does not exist. Later Ockhamists were less sure, and the case raised a **sceptical worry** three centuries before Descartes (Stage 8): if God could cause the appearance without the thing, how do I know the thing is there?

**Causation without necessity.** For the same reason Ockham held that the link between a natural cause and its effect is **known by experience**, not by reason alone: God could make fire touch cotton without burning it. (Al-Ghazali made the same point in the eleventh century; Stage 6.) This anticipates Hume (Stage 9), though Ockham did not doubt that causes are real.

**Ethics.** Ockham said that God could, by absolute power, command even that a creature **hate God**, and then it would be right; this is one of his most debated claims. He also said that a good act requires following **right reason**. **Scholars dispute** whether he is a pure divine command theorist, or held that, in the order God has actually made, right reason is a real and sufficient guide.

**The objections.**

- **Scepticism.** If God could deceive us at any moment, knowledge of the world seems lost. Reply: what God *can* do is not what He *does*; in the ordained order, our faculties are reliable. Critics answer that knowledge needs more than reliability we cannot check.
- **Arbitrariness.** If God could make hatred of God good, goodness is God's whim. Reply: God's commands are not whims, since God is good; but then, critics ask, is goodness prior to God's will after all? This is **the Euthyphro dilemma** (Stage 3) in medieval dress.

**A large historical thesis, disputed.** Some historians (for example, Hans Blumenberg and Michael Gillespie) argue that the Ockhamist God of **unlimited will** broke the medieval link between reason and the world and set the stage for modernity. Others think this greatly overstates the role of one school.
John Buridan: the via moderna in the art:
John Buridan shows what nominalism could do in the hands of a philosopher who was **not a theologian**. He spent his whole career teaching logic and natural philosophy, and his influence ran through the universities of Europe.

**The man.** **John Buridan** (about 1300 to about 1361) was a master of arts at **Paris** for over thirty years, twice rector of the university, and, unusually, never moved on to the theology faculty. He was a secular cleric, not a friar. He wrote a logic textbook, the ***Summulae de dialectica***, and question-commentaries on most of Aristotle.

**The via moderna.** Buridan agreed with Ockham that **only individuals exist** and that universals are concepts, though he was independent of Ockham on many points. Their way of doing philosophy, by careful **logic of terms** and economy of entities, was called the **modern way** (*via moderna*), against the **old way** (*via antiqua*) of Aquinas, Scotus and their followers.

**Logic: supposition.** Medieval logicians developed **supposition theory**: an account of what a term **stands for** in a sentence. In "Man is running", "man" stands for individual men; in "Man is a species", it stands for the concept; in "Man has three letters", for the word. Buridan's *Summulae* is one of the most refined treatments, and modern logicians have found in it ideas close to the modern theory of **reference** (Stage 12).

**Impetus.** Aristotle said a thrown stone keeps moving because the **air** pushes it. Buridan, building on earlier critics (John Philoponus in the sixth century had a similar idea), argued against this:

1. A spinning top or a smith's wheel keeps turning **in the same place**, where no air can push it from behind.
2. A javelin sharpened at the back flies no worse than one blunt at the back, though air would have less to push on.
3. So the air does not keep projectiles moving.
4. Instead, the thrower gives the stone an **impetus**, a quality that carries it on until resistance and weight wear it down.

He suggested that God might have given the heavens an impetus at creation, so that they need no angels to turn them. **Impetus is not inertia**: it is a force inside the body, not a state that needs no cause. But historians see it as a **step towards** Galileo's physics.

**Buridan's ass.** The famous puzzle of a donkey **starving between two equal bales of hay**, unable to choose, is **not found in Buridan's surviving works**. It is probably a later critics' parody of his view of the will. Buridan held that the will, faced with two goods it judges equal, can **suspend** choice to deliberate further; a version of the case appears in Aristotle's *On the Heavens*, about a man equally hungry and thirsty. Its philosophical point remains: **can a rational agent choose without a reason to prefer?** Leibniz (Stage 8) said no; many modern philosophers say choosing at random is rational when the options are equal.

**The liar.** Buridan offered a solution to the **liar paradox** ("This sentence is false"): every sentence, he argued, **implicitly claims its own truth**, so the liar sentence claims both that it is true and that it is false, and is simply false. Whether this works is still discussed.

**Influence.** Through his pupils and his books, Buridan's way became standard in the new universities of central Europe, Prague, Vienna, Kraków and Heidelberg, in the later fourteenth and fifteenth centuries.
Byzantine philosophy: Photios, Psellos a:
While the Latins rebuilt philosophy from translations, the Greek-speaking Christian empire of **Byzantium**, with its capital at **Constantinople**, read Plato and Aristotle in their own language without a break. Its central question was the same as the Latins': **how far may a Christian follow the ancient philosophers?**

**The setting.** In Byzantium, philosophy was taught as part of a general higher education, together with rhetoric. There were no universities in the Latin sense; there were teachers, sometimes paid by the emperor, and a church that drew a line between **"outside" learning** (Greek philosophy) and **"inside" learning** (Christian doctrine). Most Byzantine philosophy is in **commentaries**, letters and short treatises.

**Photios** (about 810 to about 893), twice patriarch of Constantinople (858 to 867 and 877 to 886), was the greatest scholar of his age. His ***Bibliotheca*** (*Library*) summarises and judges **279** books he had read, many now lost. He also wrote on Aristotle's *Categories*, and discussed the problem of universals, apparently taking a broadly moderate realist view in which genera and species exist in individuals. He represents **learned conservatism**: the classics preserved, judged by Christian standards.

**Michael Psellos** (1018 to about 1078, though some date his death later) was a court politician, historian (his *Chronographia* is a vivid memoir of the emperors), and the boldest Platonist of Byzantium. About **1045** the emperor Constantine IX named him **"consul of the philosophers"**, head of philosophical teaching in the capital. Psellos revived the study of **Plato, Plotinus and Proclus** (Stage 5), whom earlier Byzantines had treated with suspicion. He insisted that he took from them only what agreed with Christian truth, and said he loved philosophy as the queen of the sciences. Critics then and since have wondered how sincere these limits were; scholars still debate how far he was a **Christian Neoplatonist** and how far a Neoplatonist in Christian dress.

**John Italos** (about 1025 to after 1082), Psellos's pupil and successor as consul of the philosophers, went further. He used **dialectic**, Aristotle's logic, on theological questions, and was accused of teaching that **souls exist before bodies**, that **the world is eternal**, and that the **Platonic Forms** exist. In **1082**, under the emperor Alexios I Komnenos, he was tried and condemned.

**The anathemas.** The verdict on Italos was added to the ***Synodikon of Orthodoxy***, a text read aloud in churches every year. Its key clause, in paraphrase, condemns those who study Greek learning **not merely for education** but who **accept its doctrines as true**, against Christian teaching. This set the Byzantine line: **philosophy is allowed as training, not as a source of doctrine.**

**Compare the West.** The Latin West condemned propositions in 1270 and 1277 but went on teaching all of Aristotle in the arts faculty. Byzantium kept philosophy in its schools too, but the Synodikon made its place **subordinate** in principle. Whether this limited Byzantine originality, or simply directed it, is a question historians argue.

**What Byzantium gave.** Byzantine scholars preserved most of the Greek philosophical texts we have, and in the fifteenth century, as the empire fell, Greek scholars carried them to **Italy** (the next stage).
Palamas and Barlaam: the hesychast contr:
The last great Byzantine controversy began with a dispute about monks at prayer and became a debate on a philosophical question: **can a perfectly simple God have real distinctions within Him?**

**The setting.** **Hesychasm** (from *hesychia*, stillness) was a practice of monks, especially on Mount Athos, of silent prayer with controlled breathing. The monks claimed that at its height they saw a **divine light**, the same light the apostles saw at Christ's **Transfiguration** on Mount Tabor. (The practice and its theology belong to the Theology curriculum; this lesson takes up only the philosophical claim.)

**The critic.** **Barlaam of Calabria** (about 1290 to 1348), a Greek monk from southern Italy and a learned Aristotelian, attacked the monks from about **1336**. Two arguments:

1. **God is unknowable in essence.** Following Pseudo-Dionysius (Stage 6), God's nature is beyond all knowledge. So whatever the monks saw, it was **not God**. It must be a **created** light, or an illusion.
2. **Demonstration about God is limited.** Barlaam argued that apodictic (strictly demonstrative) proofs about divine things are not available to us, since we do not grasp God's essence.

**The defender.** **Gregory Palamas** (about 1296 to 1359), an Athonite monk, later archbishop of Thessaloniki, answered in the ***Triads in Defence of the Holy Hesychasts*** (about 1338 to 1341).

**Palamas's distinction.** He agreed that God's **essence** (*ousia*) is utterly unknowable and cannot be shared by creatures. But God also has **energies** (*energeiai*, activities or operations), which are:

- **uncreated**: they are truly God, not something He made;
- **distinct** from the essence;
- **participable**: creatures can genuinely share in them.

So the light the monks saw was **God's own energy**, truly God, while God's essence stays beyond them.

**The argument, as a defender states it.**

1. Creatures can truly **know and share in God** (else union with God, which both sides accepted, is empty).
2. Creatures can **never** know or share in God's **essence** (both sides accepted this too).
3. If whatever creatures share in were **created**, they would not be sharing in God.
4. So there is something **uncreated**, truly God, that is **not the essence**: the energies.

**The objection, from Barlaam and later Gregory Akindynos and Nikephoros Gregoras.** God is **simple**, without parts. A real distinction between essence and energies makes God **composite**, or makes two Gods. Palamas replied that the distinction is not between two **things**: the energies are **of** the essence, as rays of the sun are of the sun, and their distinction does not divide God's being.

**The philosophical question.** Is there coherent room for a distinction that is **neither a distinction between things nor merely in our minds**? This is exactly the question raised by **Scotus's formal distinction** a few decades earlier in the West, and by Aquinas's insistence that God's attributes are **identical** with His essence. Scholars dispute how close Palamas and Scotus are, and how Palamas's distinction should be classed.

**The outcome.** Councils at Constantinople in **1341, 1347 and 1351** upheld Palamas. Barlaam left for Italy, became a bishop there, and taught Greek to **Petrarch**. In the Orthodox Church Palamas's teaching became standard; Latin theologians long criticised it. Whether it is coherent is still argued, on both sides, as philosophy.
Nicholas of Cusa: learned ignorance and:
Nicholas of Cusa stands at the end of the Middle Ages and the start of the Renaissance, and fits neither neatly. He took the old Neoplatonic idea that **God is beyond all concepts** and turned it into a method.

**The man.** **Nicholas of Cusa** (Cusanus, 1401 to 1464) was born at Kues on the Moselle, studied law at Padua, and became a churchman, diplomat and, from 1448, a **cardinal**. He travelled to Constantinople in 1437 to bring Greek delegates to the council of union with the Latin Church. On the voyage back, he said, the idea of **learned ignorance** came to him. He finished ***On Learned Ignorance*** (*De docta ignorantia*) in **1440**. Other works include ***On the Vision of God*** (1453) and ***On the Peace of Faith*** (1453), written after the fall of Constantinople, imagining a council of religions.

**Learned ignorance.** The argument:

1. We know by **comparing**: we measure the unknown against the known, by **proportion**.
2. Between the **finite** and the **infinite** there is **no proportion**.
3. So the infinite, God, **cannot be known** by comparison.
4. But we can **know that we do not know**, and know **why**. That knowing is not empty: it is **learned** ignorance, the highest knowledge available to us.

**The image.** A polygon inscribed in a circle: add sides, and it comes closer and closer to the circle, but **never becomes it**, however many sides it has. Our knowledge of truth is like that polygon.

**The coincidence of opposites.** In the finite world, things are greater or less, and opposites exclude each other. In the **infinite**, Cusanus argued, opposites **coincide** (*coincidentia oppositorum*). His mathematical illustrations:

- As a circle grows infinitely large, its curve becomes **straight**: the infinite circle and the infinite line coincide.
- God is the **absolute maximum**, than which nothing can be greater, and also the **absolute minimum**, than which nothing can be smaller: in the infinite they are one.

**The universe without a centre.** Applying the same logic to the cosmos, Cusanus argued that the universe has **no fixed centre and no edge**, that the earth is **not at rest at the middle**, and that from any place it would seem that one is at the centre. This was not modern astronomy, which needs observation and calculation; but it broke with the closed cosmos of Aristotle **a century before Copernicus**.

**The objections.**

- **The law of non-contradiction.** If opposites coincide in God, is not reason itself abandoned? Cusanus answered that the coincidence is **beyond** reason, not against it; reason, which works by distinguishing, cannot reach it, but **intellect**, a higher seeing, can. The theologian **John Wenck** of Heidelberg attacked the book on just this point, and Cusanus replied in his *Defence of Learned Ignorance* (1449). Critics since have asked whether "beyond reason" is just a way of saying "contradictory".
- **The mathematics.** The illustrations are suggestive, not proofs: an infinitely large circle is not a well-defined object in the geometry he used. Defenders say they were meant as **images for thought**, not demonstrations.

**Why he matters.** He looked back to Pseudo-Dionysius and Eriugena (Stage 6) and forward to the infinite universe of **Giordano Bruno**, who admired him, and to the speculative philosophers of the next stage.
Looking back: the via antiqua, the via m:
By 1450 the schools had argued for three and a half centuries, and the arguments had hardened into **schools of thought**, each with its own masters, textbooks and university.

**The two ways.** In the fifteenth century, universities split between:

| | **Via antiqua** (the old way) | **Via moderna** (the modern way) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Masters** | Aquinas, Albert, Scotus, read through their followers (Thomists, Albertists, Scotists) | Ockham, Buridan and their followers |
| **On universals** | some form of **realism**: common natures are real | **nominalism**: only individuals exist |
| **Method** | metaphysics of natures and essences | logic of terms and signs; economy of entities |
| **Strongholds** | **Cologne**, Leuven, many Dominican houses | Paris for a time, **Erfurt**, Vienna, Heidelberg, Tübingen |

Some universities had **both ways** taught side by side, with separate lectures. In **1474** King Louis XI of France banned nominalist teaching at Paris; the ban was lifted in **1481**. The young **Martin Luther** was trained at Erfurt in the via moderna, a fact historians link, in disputed ways, to his later attacks on scholastic theology (for the Theology curriculum).

**What was settled, more or less:**

1. **The method.** State the question, give the other side first, answer every objection. This is still how philosophy is written.
2. **Logic** reached a sophistication not matched again until the nineteenth century: supposition theory, theories of consequence (valid inference), and solutions to the liar paradox.
3. **Philosophy as a discipline,** with its own standards, distinct from theology, even if under it. Albert said so, the Averroists pressed it, and the universities built it into their faculties.

**What was left open:**

| Question | The positions on the table |
| --- | --- |
| **Universals** | Abelard's status, Aquinas's moderate realism, Scotus's common nature, Ockham's signs |
| **Talk of God** | Aquinas's analogy against Scotus's univocity; Cusanus's learned ignorance; Palamas's energies |
| **Individuation** | matter (Aquinas), haecceity (Scotus), nothing needed (Ockham) |
| **The soul** | form of the body that subsists (Aquinas), one intellect for all (Averroists), several forms (Franciscans) |
| **The will** | following the intellect (Aquinas), free to choose against it (Scotus), the relation of God's will to the good (Ockham) |
| **Proofs of God** | the Five Ways and Scotus's infinite being, against Ockham's doubt that so much can be proved |

**What the next stage picks up.** The humanists of the Renaissance turned against the schoolmen's Latin and their questions, and went back to **ancient texts** (Plato newly in full, Cicero, the Sceptics). Descartes, trained by Jesuits in late scholastic philosophy, rejected its physics of forms but kept many of its problems: the soul and body, the proofs of God, the will and the intellect, the worry that God might deceive us. Locke and Hobbes inherited Ockham's nominalism. The schoolmen were dismissed, and **read**, by nearly everyone who came after.

**A fair verdict.** For centuries "scholastic" meant pedantic. The twentieth century, through historians of logic and philosophers reviving Aquinas and Scotus, reversed much of that judgement. **Most historians of philosophy now rank the period among the most rigorous in its history**; whether its framework of natures and forms can be revived is a live question, not a settled one.
Context: Europe from the Renaissance to:
Between about 1400 and 1715 the ground under European thought moved more than at any time since the Greeks. This stage follows the philosophers who felt it move.

**Five shocks, in rough order:**

| Shock | When | What it unsettled |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **The recovery of ancient texts** | from the 1400s; Greek scholars reach Italy, especially after the fall of Constantinople in **1453** | the schoolmen's Aristotle was now one ancient voice among many: Plato, Plotinus, the Stoics, Epicurus, the sceptic Sextus Empiricus |
| **Printing** | Gutenberg's press, about **1450** | books became cheap and fast, so disputes spread across a continent in months |
| **The Reformation** | Luther, from **1517** | who decides what is true in religion? Scripture, the Church, or the individual conscience? |
| **The wars of religion** | French wars 1562–98; the Thirty Years' War **1618–48**; the English Civil War 1642–51 | if reasonable people kill each other over doctrine, what can ground peace, law and certainty? |
| **The new science** | Copernicus **1543**, Galileo, Kepler, then Newton's *Principia* **1687** | the Earth moves; the heavens are not perfect; nature is written in mathematics |

**The questions these pressed on philosophers:**

1. **What can we know for certain?** If authorities disagree and the senses deceive, is there a foundation nothing can shake? (Montaigne doubts it; Descartes tries to supply one.)
2. **What is the world made of?** The new science pictured nature as **matter in motion**, like a vast machine. Where, then, do minds, freedom and God fit?
3. **What makes political power legitimate?** Not inherited sacred order, but something else: success (Machiavelli), or agreement (Hobbes).
4. **Can reason still reach God?** Some said yes, by proof (Descartes, Leibniz); some said reason must give way to the heart (Pascal); one identified God with nature itself (Spinoza).

**Two new terms you will meet constantly:**
- **Rationalism**: the view that **reason alone, without the senses, can give us substantial knowledge** of how things are. Descartes, Spinoza and Leibniz are the "rationalists".
- **Empiricism**: the view that **all knowledge of the world comes from experience**. Bacon and Hobbes lean this way; the full empiricists (Locke, Berkeley, Hume) are Stage 9.

The labels are later tidyings-up, and historians now warn that they hide a great deal: Descartes did experiments, and Leibniz was steeped in observation. Use them as a rough map, not a fence.

**Where it ends.** By 1715 Leibniz was arguing with Newton's spokesman Samuel Clarke about space and God, and Locke's empiricism was already in print. The Enlightenment had begun.
Humanism and the revival of Plato: Ficin:
The Renaissance began as a movement about books and teaching, and became a new picture of what a human being is.

**Humanism** meant, first, the *studia humanitatis*: grammar, rhetoric, poetry, history and moral philosophy, studied from the ancient classics in their original languages. **Petrarch** (1304–1374) is its usual founder. Humanists wanted elegant Latin, recovered Greek, and texts cleaned of medieval errors. **Lorenzo Valla** (1407–1457) showed by its anachronistic Latin that the "Donation of Constantine", a document giving the popes power over the West, was a forgery (1440). Philology became a weapon.

**The revival of Plato.** The medieval West had read little Plato directly. At the **Council of Florence (1438–39)** the Byzantine philosopher **Gemistos Plethon** lectured on Plato, and the Medici rulers of Florence took notice. **Marsilio Ficino** (1433–1499), a doctor's son, was given a villa and manuscripts by Cosimo de' Medici. He produced:
- the first complete **Latin translation of Plato** (printed **1484**), and later of **Plotinus** (1492);
- a translation of the *Corpus Hermeticum*, writings he thought very ancient (they date from the early Christian centuries);
- his own *Platonic Theology* (written about 1469–74, printed 1482), arguing at length for the **immortality of the soul**.

Ficino believed Plato and Christianity taught one truth, an "ancient theology" handed down from Hermes and Pythagoras to Plato. He is credited with the phrase **"Platonic love"**: love that rises from beauty in a body to beauty itself (Stage 3's *Symposium*). Whether there was a formal "Platonic Academy" in Florence is **disputed**; many historians now think it was an informal circle, not an institution.

**Giovanni Pico della Mirandola** (1463–1494) went further. In **1486** he proposed to defend **900 theses** in Rome, drawn from Plato, Aristotle, Arab and Jewish thinkers, and the Jewish Kabbalah, claiming all wisdom agrees at bottom. A papal commission found thirteen of them unacceptable, Pope Innocent VIII then condemned the whole set (1487), and the debate never took place.

His opening speech, printed after his death and later titled the ***Oration on the Dignity of Man***, contains the most famous image of the age. In paraphrase: God gave every creature a fixed nature but the human being none, placing him at the centre of the world and telling him he may **shape himself into whatever he chooses**, sink to the beasts or rise to the angels.

**Why it matters, and the objection.** **The human being is defined by freedom, not by a fixed place in a hierarchy.** That idea runs from Pico to the existentialists of Stage 13. The objection is that humanism produced more eloquence than argument: Ficino and Pico assembled harmonies between authorities rather than testing claims. Scholars also warn against reading Pico as a modern secular individualist; his freedom serves an ascent to God, which is a subject for the **Theology** curriculum.
Machiavelli: The Prince and the effectua:
The most notorious book in political philosophy, and one of the most argued over.

**Niccolò Machiavelli** (1469–1527) served the Florentine republic as a diplomat and secretary from 1498 to 1512. When the Medici returned to power he lost his post, was imprisoned and tortured on suspicion of conspiracy (1513), and retired to a farm outside Florence. There he wrote ***The Prince*** (written **1513**, printed **1532**), and the longer ***Discourses on Livy*** (written about 1513–19, printed 1531), a study of the Roman republic.

**The new method.** Earlier "mirrors for princes" told rulers to be just, merciful and pious. Machiavelli says in chapter 15 he will follow the **"effectual truth"** (*verità effettuale*) of things, how men actually live, not imagined republics. A ruler who always does what is good will be ruined among so many who are not good. So **a prince must learn how not to be good, and use that knowledge as necessity requires.**

**The central claims:**
1. **Appearance matters more than reality.** A prince should *seem* merciful, faithful, humane and religious, and be ready to act otherwise.
2. **Fear is more reliable than love.** In W. K. Marriott's translation (1908) of chapter 17: "it is much safer to be feared than loved, when, of the two, either must be dispensed with." Love depends on the subjects; fear depends on the prince. But he must **avoid being hated**, above all by not seizing property or women.
3. **Cruelty well used** is quick, done at once and for security (chapter 8); cruelty badly used grows with time.
4. ***Virtù* against *fortuna*.** *Virtù* is not moral virtue but **energy, skill and boldness**; *fortuna* is chance, which Machiavelli compares to a flooding river that can be held back by dykes built in calm weather (chapter 25). His model of *virtù* is **Cesare Borgia** (chapter 7).

**What is he doing? Four readings, still disputed:**

| Reading | Claim |
| --- | --- |
| **Teacher of evil** | he deliberately detaches politics from morality (Leo Strauss, 1958) |
| **Scientist of politics** | he describes, neutrally, how power works |
| **Two moralities** | Isaiah Berlin (1972): he sets the pagan civic morality of Rome against Christian morality and shows **they cannot both be lived**; his originality is to show values can genuinely conflict |
| **Republican** | read with the *Discourses*, he loves free republics; *The Prince* is advice for founding or emergency, or even (Spinoza and Rousseau thought) a warning to the people |

**The strongest objection** is that his realism is self-defeating: a world of rulers who keep faith only when convenient is the world in which nobody can trust anyone, which makes ruling harder. The reply is that he never claims otherwise; he only says a single ruler cannot afford to be the one honest player. Hobbes, later in this stage, takes up exactly that problem.
Montaigne and the new scepticism:
The man who made doubt a way of life, and handed it to Descartes as a problem.

**Michel de Montaigne** (1533–1592), a nobleman of Bordeaux, retired in 1571 to a tower on his estate to read and write. He later served as mayor of Bordeaux (1581–85). His ***Essays*** (books I–II in **1580**, book III added in **1588**, with a fuller edition printed in 1595 after his death) invented the form: *essai* means "attempt" or "trial". He tests his judgement on everything, from cannibals to thumbs, and his main subject is himself.

**The recovery of ancient scepticism.** Pyrrhonism, the scepticism of Pyrrho as written up by **Sextus Empiricus** (Stage 5), was printed in Latin in **1562** (Henri Estienne's translation of the *Outlines of Pyrrhonism*). Pyrrhonists answer every argument with an equally strong counter-argument, and **suspend judgement** (*epoché*), hoping for tranquillity.

**"Apology for Raymond Sebond"** (*Essays* II.12), his longest essay, is the key text. Nominally a defence of a fifteenth-century book of natural theology, it becomes an assault on human reason:
1. **Animals often outdo us**, and we have no neutral standpoint from which to rank ourselves above them.
2. **Customs and laws differ endlessly** between peoples, and each thinks its own natural.
3. **The senses deceive** and vary with health, age and mood; reason can check the senses only with reasoning, which needs its own check, **and so without end**.
4. Therefore we have **no criterion of truth** that does not beg the question.

He took as his emblem a balance in equilibrium, with the motto that Charles Cotton's translation (1685–86) renders as **"What do I know?"** (*Que sais-je?*).

**Fideism.** Montaigne concludes that since reason cannot reach the truth, we should keep the customs and religion we were born into and **receive faith as a gift**, not as the product of argument. This position, faith over reason because reason fails, is called **fideism**. Whether Montaigne meant it sincerely or as a shield for a quieter unbelief is a **long-standing scholarly dispute**; most current scholars take him to be a sincere, if unusual, Catholic.

**Why it matters.** The historian Richard Popkin argued that the revival of Pyrrhonism caused a **"sceptical crisis"** in early modern thought: if the Reformation showed that doctrine had no agreed criterion, Montaigne extended the problem to all knowledge. On this reading, Descartes's *Meditations* is an answer to Montaigne and his follower **Pierre Charron** (*De la sagesse*, 1601). Popkin's thesis is influential and also debated.

**The objection** to Montaigne's scepticism is old: the claim that we know nothing seems itself a claim to know. The Pyrrhonist reply, which Montaigne uses, is that sceptical arguments work like a purge that carries itself away along with what it expels. They report how things seem; they assert nothing.
Bacon: the idols and the new induction:
The prophet of science as organised, cooperative inquiry, and the first great diagnostician of bias.

**Francis Bacon** (1561–1626) was a lawyer and politician who rose to **Lord Chancellor** of England in 1618 and fell in 1621, convicted of taking bribes. His plan was a *Great Instauration*, a total renewal of knowledge. Its best-known parts are ***The Advancement of Learning*** (1605) and ***Novum Organum*** ("New Instrument", **1620**), named against Aristotle's logical works, the *Organon*. His fable ***New Atlantis*** (printed 1627) imagines a state-funded research institute, an inspiration for the Royal Society (1660).

**The complaint.** Scholastic science, Bacon says, leaps from a few observations to the most general principles and then deduces from them; it argues well and discovers nothing. He compares three kinds of thinker: **the ant**, who only collects; **the spider**, who spins webs out of itself; and **the bee**, who gathers material and transforms it. Science should be the bee.

**The idols.** Before the mind can learn, it must be cleared of false images. In the edition of Joseph Devey (1902), aphorism I.39 reads: "Four species of idols beset the human mind, to which (for distinction's sake) we have assigned names, calling the first Idols of the Tribe, the second Idols of the Den, the third Idols of the Market, the fourth Idols of the Theatre."

| Idol | Source | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Tribe** | human nature itself | we notice confirming cases and ignore the rest; we see more order than exists |
| **Den** (or Cave) | each person's upbringing and temperament | one mind loves differences, another resemblances |
| **Market**place | **words**, formed in common talk | names for things that do not exist, or vague names for things that do |
| **Theatre** | received philosophical systems | dogmas staged like plays, Aristotle's above all |

The Idols of the Tribe are what psychologists now call **confirmation bias**, about 350 years early.

**The method.** Bacon's induction is not simple counting of cases. Studying heat, he draws up **tables**: of cases where heat is present, cases similar but where it is absent, and cases where it varies in degree. Then he **excludes** every candidate nature not always present with heat. Negative cases matter most: one counter-instance outweighs many confirmations. His provisional result ("the first vintage") was that **heat is a kind of motion**, which turned out right.

**Objections.** (1) Bacon **underrated mathematics and bold hypothesis**; Galileo and Newton advanced by daring theories tested against nature, not by tables. (2) His method seems to need a finite list of possible "natures" to exclude, which nature does not supply. The reply is that his emphasis on **disconfirmation** and on guarding against bias anticipates Popper (Stage 12), and that he is the philosopher of science as a **public, cumulative, cooperative enterprise**.
The scientific revolution's challenge to:
The philosophers of this stage worked inside a revolution in the picture of nature. This lesson sets out what was overturned.

**The Aristotelian picture** (Stage 4), as taught in the universities:
- The Earth sits **motionless at the centre**; the heavens above the Moon are perfect, unchanging, made of a fifth element.
- Each thing has a **substantial form**, an inner nature that makes it what it is and directs its activity.
- Explanation names **four causes**, including the **final cause**, the goal a thing tends towards. A stone falls because its natural place is the centre.
- Qualities we sense, heat and colour, are **real qualities in things**, much as we perceive them.

**What broke it:**

| Who | When | What |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Copernicus** | *On the Revolutions*, **1543** | the Sun at the centre, the Earth a moving planet |
| **Kepler** | *New Astronomy*, 1609 | planets move in **ellipses**, not perfect circles |
| **Galileo** (1564–1642) | *Starry Messenger*, **1610** | the telescope shows mountains on the Moon, moons around Jupiter; later, the phases of Venus |
| Galileo | *Dialogue*, 1632; condemned by the Inquisition, **1633**; *Two New Sciences*, 1638 | laws of falling bodies; motion described mathematically |
| **Newton** | *Principia*, **1687** | one set of laws for heaven and earth |

**The new philosophy of nature** that grew up with this work is called the **mechanical philosophy**: nature is **matter in motion**, and every change is explained by the size, shape and motion of particles pushing on one another, like the parts of a clock. Descartes, Gassendi, Hobbes and Robert Boyle (1627–1691) all held versions of it.

Three consequences mattered for philosophy:
1. **Final causes were expelled from physics.** Things do not move to reach goals; they are pushed.
2. **Mathematics became the language of nature.** Galileo wrote in *The Assayer* (1623), in paraphrase, that the book of the universe is written in mathematics, its letters triangles and circles.
3. **Primary and secondary qualities.** Galileo argued that tastes, smells and colours exist only in the perceiver, while size, shape, number and motion are in the things. (The labels "primary" and "secondary" come later, from Boyle and Locke.) **The world as we experience it was split in two**: the mathematical world science describes, and the coloured world in the mind.

That third point creates the problem of the next twelve lessons. **If matter is only extension and motion, what is the mind that sees colour?** Descartes's answer is that it is something else entirely.

**A caution.** Historians now resist the tidy story of light against darkness. Many late scholastics were sophisticated natural philosophers; the new scientists were often deeply religious (Kepler, Boyle, Newton); and Galileo's trial was as much about politics and his handling of the Pope as about astronomy. That the Aristotelian physics of natural places failed, though, is not disputed.
Descartes: the method of doubt and the e:
The man usually called the father of modern philosophy began by trying to doubt everything.

**René Descartes** (1596–1650) was born in La Haye in Touraine (the town is now called Descartes), schooled by the Jesuits at La Flèche, and trained in law. On **10 November 1619**, in Germany, he had three dreams he took as a call to rebuild all knowledge. He settled in the Dutch Republic in 1628, a mathematician of genius (the coordinate geometry of his *Geometry*, 1637, is why graphs have Cartesian axes). After Galileo's condemnation he withheld his physics, *The World*. He published the ***Discourse on Method*** (**1637**), the ***Meditations on First Philosophy*** (**1641**), the ***Principles of Philosophy*** (1644) and ***The Passions of the Soul*** (1649). He died in **Stockholm in February 1650**, having gone to teach Queen Christina.

**The project.** His beliefs are like a house built on sand; rather than repair them one by one, he will **knock out the foundations** and rebuild on rock. The method: **withhold assent from anything that admits the slightest doubt**, as if it were false. The point is not to *believe* the doubts. It is to find out whether anything survives them.

**Meditation I: three waves of doubt.**

1. **The senses sometimes deceive** (a tower looks round far off). But surely not about my sitting here by the fire in my dressing gown?
2. **The dreaming argument.** I have dreamed exactly such things. **There are no sure signs by which waking can be told from sleep.** So any particular perception might be a dream. But even dreams seem built from simpler elements, shape, number, extension, and arithmetic holds asleep or awake: two and three make five.
3. **The deceiving God, then the evil demon.** Might an all-powerful being make me go wrong even when I add two and three? To keep this doubt alive in his mind, Descartes imagines, in John Veitch's translation (1853), "some malignant demon, who is at once exceedingly potent and deceitful", who has "employed all his artifice to deceive me". Now **even mathematics is doubtful**, and so is the existence of my body.

**Hyperbolic doubt.** This kind of doubt is called **hyperbolic** (exaggerated): it is deliberately pushed beyond any doubt a sensible person would feel in daily life. Descartes says so himself; no one, he notes, has seriously doubted that he has a body. The doubt is a **tool**, used once in a lifetime, to test foundations.

**Objections.**
- **Can you really doubt at will?** Belief does not obey the will. Reply: Descartes asks only that we *withhold assent* and keep the doubt before the mind by an imaginative effort; that is why he invents the demon.
- **The doubt undermines its own tools.** If the demon can corrupt my reasoning, it can corrupt the reasoning of Meditation I too. This becomes the problem of the Cartesian circle, three lessons on.
- **The dreaming argument.** Some reply that a dream is identified only by contrast with waking life, so the possibility that *all* experience is dream is not even coherent. The **brain in a vat** of later philosophy (Putnam, 1981) is the demon's modern descendant.
Descartes: the cogito and the thinking t:
One certainty survives the demon, and Descartes builds everything on it.

**The argument (Meditation II).** Even if the demon deceives me about everything, **he cannot make me be nothing while I think I am something**. To be deceived, I must exist. So "I am, I exist" is necessarily true whenever I think it.

In the ***Discourse*** (1637), Part IV, the same thought appears in the form everyone knows. In Veitch's translation (1850): "this truth, I think, therefore I am (COGITO ERGO SUM), was so certain and of such evidence that no ground of doubt, however extravagant, could be alleged by the sceptics capable of shaking it". The Latin *cogito ergo sum* appears in the *Principles* (1644). The *Meditations* themselves say only "I am, I exist".

**What does "think" cover?** Not just reasoning. *Cogitatio* means **any conscious state**: doubting, understanding, affirming, denying, willing, refusing, imagining, and even *seeming* to see and feel. **I may be wrong that I see a light; I cannot be wrong that it seems to me that I do.**

**What am I?** Descartes next asks what this "I" is. Not a body (that is still in doubt). Not a soul that nourishes or walks. **Only a thinking thing**, a *res cogitans*: a mind. Whether that thinking thing might *also* turn out to be a body he leaves open here; the proof that mind and body are distinct comes in Meditation VI.

**Is it an inference?** "Therefore" suggests a syllogism:
1. Everything that thinks exists.
2. I think.
3. Therefore I exist.

But premise 1 is a general principle that the demon might have shaken. Descartes replied (Second Replies) that he grasps it **by a simple intuition of the mind**, seeing in his own case that thinking requires existing. Whether the cogito is an inference, an intuition, or (Jaakko Hintikka, 1962) a **performance** that refutes its own denial whenever anyone attempts it, is **disputed**.

**Objections.**
- **Gassendi:** why not "I walk, therefore I am"? Reply: because I may only dream I walk; but "I seem to walk" is a thought, and does work.
- **Lichtenberg** (18th century), in paraphrase: we should say "it thinks", as we say "it lightens". **Thinking is certain; that there is a single, lasting "I" doing it is not.** This is the most serious objection; Hume (Stage 9) presses it.
- **Augustine anticipated him** (*City of God* XI.26, "if I am mistaken, I exist"), as Arnauld noticed. Descartes acknowledged the likeness and said he used it differently: as the first link of a chain, not as a stand-alone refutation of sceptics.

**Why it matters.** **The cogito moves the starting point of philosophy from the world to the first-person mind.** Much of what follows, for three centuries, is an argument about whether you can get back out again.
Reading: Descartes's Meditation II, the:
The most famous six pages in modern philosophy, read closely. All quotations are from John Veitch's translation (first published 1853, reprinted 1901), as given on Wikisource; the paragraph numbers are Veitch's.

**1. The swimmer.** Meditation II opens in distress: "just as if I had fallen all of a sudden into very deep water, I am so greatly disconcerted as to be unable either to plant my feet firmly on the bottom or sustain myself by swimming on the surface." The doubts of Meditation I are not a game; they have left him without footing. He wants, like **Archimedes**, "only a point that was firm and immovable".

**2. The cogito, under the demon (para. 3).**

> "let him deceive me as he may, he can never bring it about that I am nothing, so long as I shall be conscious that I am something. So that it must, in fine, be maintained, all things being maturely and carefully considered, that this proposition (pronunciatum) I am, I exist, is necessarily true each time it is expressed by me, or conceived in my mind."

Notice three things. There is **no "therefore"** here. The certainty is **tied to the moment**: "each time it is expressed by me". And the demon is not refuted; he is shown to be **powerless on this one point**, because being deceived is itself a way of existing.

**3. "But how often?" (para. 6).** "I am—I exist: this is certain; but how often? As often as I think". Then the conclusion that matters most for what follows: "I am therefore, precisely speaking, only a thinking thing, that is, a mind". The word "precisely" carries weight. He means that **thinking is all he can be certain belongs to him**, not yet that nothing else does.

**4. What a thinking thing is (para. 8):** "It is a thing that doubts, understands, [conceives], affirms, denies, wills, refuses; that imagines also, and perceives." The square brackets are in Veitch's text. Perceiving survives as *seeming*: "it is certain that I seem to see light, hear a noise, and feel heat; this cannot be false".

**5. The wax (para. 11).** He now turns to a body, to show that even bodies are known by the mind. A piece of wax fresh from the hive has taste, smell, colour, shape, size, hardness; it "sounds when struck upon with the finger". Put it by the fire: every one of those qualities changes. "Does the same wax still remain after this change? It must be admitted that it does remain".

**The argument laid out:**
1. Every quality I sensed in the wax has changed.
2. The same wax remains.
3. So what I knew the wax to be was **none of the sensed qualities**.
4. What remains is only "something extended, flexible, and movable" (para. 12).
5. The wax can take **infinitely many** shapes, more than imagination can run through.
6. So the wax is grasped "by the mind alone", an "intuition (*inspectio*) of the mind".

**6. Hats and cloaks (para. 13).** Looking from a window, we say we *see* men in the street, yet "what do I see from the window beyond hats and cloaks that might cover artificial machines, whose motions might be determined by springs?" **We judge, and call it seeing.**

**7. The payoff (para. 15).** Every act by which I know the wax proves more surely that I, who know it, exist. So the mind is **better known than the body**, reversing common sense.

**Questions to carry away.** Does the wax show that bodies are *really* just extension, or only that our *concept* of a body outruns any one sensation? Gassendi pressed the second; the next lessons follow the argument out.
Descartes: the trademark argument for Go:
Locked inside his own mind, Descartes needs a way back to the world. His first bridge is a proof of God from the idea of God (Meditation III).

**Some scholastic machinery first.** Descartes distinguishes two kinds of reality an idea can have:
- **Formal reality**: the reality a thing has simply by existing. My idea of the Sun has the small formal reality of a mental event.
- **Objective reality**: the reality an idea *represents*. My idea of the Sun represents a substance, and so has more objective reality than my idea of a colour.

Reality comes in **degrees**: an infinite substance has more than a finite substance, which has more than a mode (a quality or state).

**The argument, as its best defender would put it:**
1. I have an idea of God: **an infinite, perfect substance**.
2. **The cause of anything must have at least as much reality as its effect.** This holds for the objective reality of ideas too: what an idea represents must come from a cause with at least that much formal reality. (Something cannot come from nothing, nor more from less.)
3. The idea of God has infinite objective reality.
4. I am finite and imperfect: I doubt, and doubting is an imperfection.
5. So I cannot be the cause of this idea. Only an actually infinite being can.
6. **Therefore God exists.**

Why "trademark"? Because Descartes concludes, in Veitch's translation (1853), that God implanted the idea "that it might serve, as it were, for the mark of the workman impressed on his work".

**A second argument** in the same Meditation: I could not keep myself in existence from one moment to the next, nor could my parents; so I depend on a being that **conserves** me, and that being must be God.

**The objections:**

| Objection | Who | The point |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **We have no idea of God** | Hobbes, Third Objections | we have only the word, or an image built from finite things; "infinite" just means "not finite" |
| **The idea is built up** | Gassendi, Fifth Objections | we amplify finite perfections, knowledge, power, without limit |
| **The causal principle is doubtful** | many, then Hume (Stage 9) | why must ideas have causes with as much "reality" as they represent? The degrees of reality are themselves contested metaphysics |
| **I might be the cause** | Descartes raises it himself | perhaps I am potentially infinite, growing towards perfection |

**The replies.** To Hobbes and Gassendi, Descartes said **the infinite is prior to the finite**: I recognise myself as limited and doubting only by comparison with an idea of something perfect. Amplifying would never reach actual infinity; and a merely potential perfection, always growing, is by definition not the actual perfection I conceive.

**Where it stands.** This argument has **few defenders today**, chiefly because premise 2, applied to objective reality, looks like a piece of scholastic metaphysics the cogito did not earn. Its importance is structural: **everything after Meditation III depends on God not being a deceiver**, which is why the next two lessons matter. The argument's theology belongs to the **Theology** curriculum.
Descartes: the ontological argument:
In Meditation V Descartes gives a second, shorter proof of God, from the very concept of God. It is a cousin of Anselm's argument (Stage 6).

**The argument.**
1. Whatever I clearly and distinctly perceive to belong to the **nature** (essence) of a thing truly belongs to it. (The angles of a triangle equal two right angles, whether or not any triangle exists.)
2. I clearly and distinctly perceive that God is **a supremely perfect being**.
3. **Existence is a perfection.**
4. So existence belongs to the nature of God.
5. **Therefore God exists.**

In Veitch's translation (1853): "the existence can no more be separated from the essence of God, than the idea of a mountain from that of a valley, or the equality of its three angles to two right angles, from the essence of a [rectilinear] triangle".

**Descartes answers the first objection himself.** I cannot conceive a mountain without a valley, but it does not follow that any mountain exists, only that mountain and valley go together *if* they exist. So perhaps God, *if* he exists, exists necessarily? Descartes replies that the cases differ: existence is not attached to God conditionally, it is **part of what God is**. A mountain's essence does not include existence; God's does. And he insists I am **not free** to build a God without existence, as I am free to imagine a horse with or without wings.

**Anselm's and Descartes's versions compared:**

| | Anselm (1077–78) | Descartes (1641) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Concept | that than which nothing greater can be thought | supremely perfect being |
| Form | reduction to absurdity: if it existed only in the mind, a greater could be thought | direct: existence is in the essence, as properties are in a triangle |

**The objections.**
- **Caterus** (First Objections), following Aquinas: even granting that the concept of God includes existence, **it follows only that the concept includes existence**, not that anything in reality answers to it.
- **Gassendi** (Fifth Objections): **existence is not a perfection.** It is not one property among others but the condition of having any properties at all. A thing that does not exist lacks not a perfection but everything.
- **Kant** (*Critique of Pure Reason*, 1781; Stage 10) made Gassendi's point famous: **"being" is not a real predicate.** Adding "and it exists" to the concept of a hundred coins adds nothing to the concept. To say something exists is to say the concept is instantiated, not to enrich it.

**Replies.** Defenders say Kant shows only that existence is not an *ordinary* predicate; **necessary existence** might still be a perfection. In the twentieth century Alvin Plantinga (1974) recast the argument in modal logic: if it is *possible* that a maximally great being exists, then it exists. Critics answer that the possibility premise is exactly as strong as the conclusion.

**Where it stands.** Most philosophers think **some version of the Gassendi–Kant objection defeats Descartes's form** of the argument. Whether any ontological argument works is still argued; the modal versions are taken seriously, and few people are moved by any of them. That combination, a proof hard to refute and hard to believe, is part of its fascination.
Descartes: the Cartesian circle:
Descartes's own most famous critic noticed that his whole system might be arguing in a circle.

**What Descartes needs God for.** By the end of Meditation III he has proved, to his satisfaction, that God exists and is **no deceiver**, because deception springs from a defect. From this he draws his **truth rule**: **whatever I clearly and distinctly perceive is true.** A *clear* perception is one present and open to an attentive mind; a *distinct* one is so sharply separated from all others that it contains only what is clear. If God made me so that even my clearest perceptions were false, he would be a deceiver.

**The objection.** **Antoine Arnauld** (1612–1694), a young theologian, put it in the Fourth Objections (1641). In paraphrase:

1. We can be sure that what we clearly and distinctly perceive is true **only because God exists** and is no deceiver.
2. We can be sure that God exists **only because we clearly and distinctly perceive** the premises of the proof.
3. So the argument assumes what it is meant to prove.

This is the **Cartesian circle**. If it holds, the demon of Meditation I has never been dismissed.

**Descartes's reply** (Fourth Replies, and Second Replies): he distinguished between **what we perceive clearly now** and **what we remember having perceived clearly**. While I attend to a clear perception, I cannot doubt it; God is not needed for that. God is needed for **conclusions I hold without attending to their proofs**, when the demon doubt could creep back in.

**Four ways scholars read the reply** (a genuine and lasting dispute):

| Reading | Claim | Difficulty |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Memory** | God guarantees memory of past proofs, not present perceptions | Descartes rejects this as the whole story elsewhere; and memory is not the problem in Meditation I |
| **Present perception** | present clear perceptions are self-certifying; God secures them when no longer attended to | then why did Meditation I doubt arithmetic, which is clear and distinct? |
| **Psychological certainty** | the aim is unshakeable conviction, not truth: once we see God is no deceiver, no reason for doubt remains (Harry Frankfurt, 1970) | that seems to give up on truth |
| **Consistency** | reason is shown to be self-consistent: it does not undermine itself | consistency is not truth either |

**What is broadly agreed.** That **Descartes's argument faces a serious circularity problem** is almost universally accepted; whether his texts contain an escape is disputed. Many think any attempt to validate reason by reason must at some point trust reason, and that the real lesson is about the limits of foundationalism.

**Foundationalism** is the view that knowledge rests on basic beliefs that need no support from others, with everything else built on them. Descartes is its classic exponent. Its critics, from Hegel to Quine (Stages 10 and 12), propose instead that beliefs support one another like the planks of a ship repaired at sea.
Descartes: mind-body dualism and the rea:
Descartes's most influential and most disputed conclusion: that the mind is a different thing from the body.

**Terms.** A **substance** is something that can exist on its own, not as a quality of something else. Each substance has a principal **attribute**, its essence: for minds, **thought**; for bodies, **extension** (length, breadth, depth). **Substance dualism** is the view that there are two fundamentally different kinds of substance, minds and bodies. (It differs from **property dualism**, the view that one kind of substance has two irreducibly different kinds of property.)

**The conceivability argument (Meditation VI):**
1. I can clearly and distinctly conceive of myself as a thinking, unextended thing, existing without a body.
2. I can clearly and distinctly conceive of body as an extended, unthinking thing.
3. **Whatever I can clearly and distinctly conceive apart can be made to exist apart, at least by God.**
4. Things that can exist apart are really distinct.
5. **Therefore my mind is really distinct from my body, and can exist without it.**

In Veitch's translation (1853): "it is sufficient that I am able clearly and distinctly to conceive one thing apart from another, in order to be certain that the one is different from the other".

**The divisibility argument (also Meditation VI):**
1. The body is divisible into parts.
2. The mind is not: I cannot conceive half a mind; willing, understanding and sensing are activities of one and the same mind.
3. So mind and body have different properties, and are not the same thing.

**Animals and machines.** In the *Discourse* (Part V) Descartes argued that animals are complex **automata**, and that two tests would unmask a machine built to look human: it could not **use language** to respond to whatever is said, and it could not **act flexibly** across all situations. These are early forms of the questions in Stage 14's lessons on AI.

**The objections.**
- **Arnauld's triangle** (Fourth Objections): someone may clearly conceive a right-angled triangle without conceiving that the square on its hypotenuse equals the squares on the other sides. It does not follow that the triangle could lack that property. **What I can conceive apart may not be apart in reality**; my conception may be incomplete. Descartes replied that mind and body are each conceived as **complete things**, which the triangle and its property are not.
- **The masked man fallacy.** I can doubt my body exists but not my mind; so, it seems, they differ. But I can doubt that the masked man robbed the bank while being certain my father did not, even if my father is the masked man. **Differences in what I know do not show differences in things.** (Descartes's main argument does not, in fact, rest on doubt alone; whether it escapes the fallacy is disputed.)
- **The divisibility premise** is challenged by split-brain cases and by the thought that mental unity might be a property of a physical system.

**Where it stands.** Most philosophers of mind today are **physicalists** of some kind, and the conceivability step is widely thought to need more than Descartes gives it. But descendants of his argument (Kripke, 1980; Chalmers's zombies, 1996; Stages 12 and 14) are alive. And Descartes himself said, in Meditation VI, that he is not in his body merely "as a pilot in a vessel" but intimately joined to it. How, is the next lesson.
Descartes: the pineal gland and Elisabet:
If mind and body are utterly different, how do they act on each other? A princess asked the question that still has no agreed answer.

**Descartes's account.** The body is a machine: nerves are tubes, and **animal spirits**, a very fine fluid made from the blood, flow through them and move the muscles. The soul is joined to the whole body, but exercises its functions chiefly in one small organ deep in the brain, the **pineal gland** (*conarion*). His reasons (*Passions of the Soul*, 1649, articles 31–32; and the *Treatise of Man*, written in the early 1630s and printed after his death):
- it is **single**, while most brain parts come in pairs, so it can unite the double images from two eyes;
- it is **central** and hangs among the cavities through which the spirits flow;
- it is **mobile**: the soul tilts it, redirecting the spirits; and the spirits move it, producing sensations in the soul.

**Elisabeth of Bohemia** (1618–1680), daughter of the exiled "Winter King" of Bohemia, living at The Hague, wrote to Descartes in **May 1643**. In paraphrase her question was: **how can the soul, which is only a thinking substance, move the bodily spirits to perform voluntary actions?** Every motion, she observes, seems to need pushing and contact, and contact needs extension. The soul has none.

**Her argument set out:**
1. Bodies are moved only by contact (being pushed).
2. Contact requires extension and surface.
3. The Cartesian soul is unextended.
4. So the soul cannot move a body.

**Descartes's replies** (21 May and 28 June 1643):
