- There are **three primitive notions**: of thought, of extension, and of **the union** of the two. We go wrong by explaining the union with notions that belong to body alone. We understand it best not by metaphysics but **through the senses and ordinary life**.
- He compared it with how scholastics thought heaviness moves a body without contact, a notion he thought false for bodies but which shows how we conceive the mind's action.

Elisabeth was not satisfied. In paraphrase, she replied that it would be easier for her to grant the soul matter and extension than to grant that an immaterial thing could move and be moved by a body. That is, she suggested **giving up dualism** rather than accept a union nobody can explain.

**Why it matters.** This is **the interaction problem**, usually ranked the gravest objection to substance dualism. Later answers form much of this stage: Malebranche says **God does the causing** (occasionalism); Spinoza says mind and body are **one thing under two descriptions**; Leibniz says they **never interact** but are pre-arranged to agree.

**A further problem.** Leibniz later claimed Descartes thought the soul changes the **direction** of the spirits without adding motion, and that the conservation of momentum rules even that out. Whether Descartes held this is **disputed**.

**Elisabeth's place.** Their correspondence ran until Descartes's death. He dedicated the *Principles* (1644) to her, and *The Passions of the Soul* grew out of their letters on the emotions. She ended her life as Abbess of Herford. She is now read as **a philosopher in her own right**, not just an interlocutor.
Gassendi, Arnauld and the Objections and:
The *Meditations* were published with their own criticism bound in, the first great peer review in philosophy.

**How it worked.** Descartes's friend **Marin Mersenne** (1588–1648), a Minim friar at the centre of Europe's learned letter-writing network, circulated the manuscript. The first edition (Paris, **1641**) printed the text with **six sets of Objections** and Descartes's **Replies**; the second (Amsterdam, 1642) added a seventh. Together they are longer than the *Meditations* themselves.

| Set | Author | Main thrust |
| --- | --- | --- |
| First | **Caterus**, a Dutch priest | the ontological argument proves only a concept |
| Second | theologians gathered by **Mersenne** | could an atheist have certain knowledge? |
| Third | **Thomas Hobbes** | the thinker may be a body; we have images, not an idea of God |
| Fourth | **Antoine Arnauld** | the circle; the triangle against dualism |
| Fifth | **Pierre Gassendi** | the empiricist case against the whole project |
| Sixth | various | animals, mathematics, freedom |
| Seventh (1642) | **Pierre Bourdin**, a Jesuit | ridicule of the method of doubt |

**Pierre Gassendi** (1592–1655) was a priest, astronomer and from 1645 professor of mathematics at the Collège Royal in Paris. His life's work was to **revive the atomism of Epicurus** (Stage 5) in a form a Christian could hold: atoms created and set moving by God, an immortal soul added. His *Syntagma philosophicum* was printed after his death (1658). Against Aristotle and Descartes alike he held a moderate **empiricism**: **all our ideas come through the senses**, and our knowledge reaches appearances, not the hidden essences of things.

**Gassendi's objections:**
1. **"Why not 'I walk, therefore I am'?"** Any action shows existence. (Descartes: only if the walking is a thought, a seeming to walk.)
2. **The wax.** We never perceive a bare extended "substance" beneath the qualities; we know things **only through their qualities**. Strip them away and nothing knowable remains.
3. **The idea of God** is built up from finite ideas.
4. **Existence is not a perfection.**
5. **How can an unextended mind be united to an extended body**, or receive images from it? (Elisabeth's question, two years earlier.)

**The tone.** Gassendi addressed Descartes as "O Mind"; Descartes replied to "O Flesh". The exchange grew bitter, and Gassendi expanded his answers into the *Metaphysical Disquisition* (1644).

**Arnauld** (1612–1694) was the most respected objector. A leading theologian of **Port-Royal** and the **Jansenist** movement, he later co-wrote the *Port-Royal Logic* (1662), the standard logic textbook for two centuries, and argued with both Malebranche and Leibniz.

**Why this lesson matters.** Nearly every standard objection to Descartes taught today was **put to him in his lifetime and answered in print**. Reading the Replies is the best way to see the arguments at their strongest. Bennett's modernised version on Early Modern Texts includes them.
Hobbes: materialism and the mechanical m:
Where Descartes split the world in two, Hobbes said there is only one thing: body in motion.

**Thomas Hobbes** (1588–1679) was born in Malmesbury, Wiltshire, educated at Oxford, and spent most of his life as tutor and secretary to the **Cavendish** family. According to his friend John Aubrey, at about forty he chanced on Euclid's *Elements* and fell in love with geometry's method of building from definitions. He met Galileo in Italy (1636), joined Mersenne's circle in Paris, and wrote the Third Objections. Fearing arrest for his royalist writings, he lived in Paris from **1640** to 1651. His works include *The Elements of Law* (circulated 1640), *De Cive* (1642), ***Leviathan*** (**1651**) and *De Corpore* (1655). He died at Hardwick Hall in 1679, aged 91.

**The metaphysics: materialism.** **Materialism** is the view that **everything that exists is material**. For Hobbes, the universe is the aggregate of bodies; the phrase "incorporeal substance" is as contradictory as "a round square". All change is motion, and all motion is caused by the motion of a contiguous body.

**The mind as motion.**
- **Sensation** is motion pressed from objects through the organs to the brain and heart, and the brain's resistance outward. Colour and sound are not in things; they are how motion appears to us.
- **Imagination** is what remains when the object is gone. In the original *Leviathan* (1651), chapter 2: "Imagination therefore is nothing but Decaying Sense".
- **Reasoning** is calculation: adding and subtracting names and their consequences, "reckoning", as he puts it in chapter 5.
- **Desire** and **aversion** are small inner motions towards and away from things. "Good" names what a person desires.

**Freedom without free will.** Hobbes held that every act, including every act of will, is **necessitated** by prior causes. Yet we are free: **liberty is the absence of external impediments** to doing what we will, as water is free to flow downhill when no bank stops it. This view, that freedom and determinism are compatible, is called **compatibilism**. His debate with **Bishop John Bramhall**, published as *Of Liberty and Necessity* (1654), is its first great statement. Bramhall replied that without real alternatives, praise, blame and sin make no sense. The argument has not stopped since.

**God.** Hobbes insisted he was no atheist, and late in life argued that **God is a body**, a very pure and fine one. Whether he was a sincere if eccentric believer or a concealed atheist is **disputed**; his contemporaries mostly assumed the second.

**Objections.**
1. **The problem of consciousness.** Motion in the brain explains motion; it does not seem to explain *how things feel*. Leibniz's mill (later this stage) is aimed at exactly this.
2. **Self-refutation.** If reasoning is only motion, why trust it to be true rather than merely to happen?
3. **Meaning.** Can "reckoning with names" explain what makes a name *about* anything?

**Why it matters.** Hobbes is the first great modern **materialist**, and **the ancestor of the view that the mind is a computer**: reasoning as rule-governed manipulation of symbols. His politics, next, is built on this psychology.
Hobbes: the state of nature, the social:
The founding argument of modern political philosophy, written as England fought a civil war.

**The setting.** *Leviathan* appeared in **1651**, two years after the execution of Charles I. Hobbes wanted to show, from premises about human nature alone, why people must obey a government, and why rebellion is the worst of evils.

**The state of nature** (chapter 13) is a thought experiment: **life without any government** to make and enforce rules. Hobbes argues:

1. **Humans are roughly equal**: the weakest can kill the strongest, by trickery or alliance.
2. So any two who want the same thing become enemies, and nobody can feel secure.
3. "So that in the nature of man, we find three principall causes of quarrel. First, Competition; Secondly, Diffidence; Thirdly, Glory." (*Diffidence* means distrust.) Men invade for gain, for safety and for reputation.
4. **The rational policy for each is to strike first.**
5. Hence, without "a common Power to keep them all in awe", there is "such a warre, as is of every man, against every man".

No farming, building, trade, arts or letters can survive this, "and which is worst of all, continuall feare, and danger of violent death; And the life of man, solitary, poore, nasty, brutish, and short." (All quotations are from the original English of 1651, spelling unchanged.)

**There is no injustice in the state of nature.** Justice and property exist only where there is law; and law exists only where there is a power to enforce it. Each person has a **right of nature**: the liberty to use any means to preserve themselves, even to another's body.

**The way out: the laws of nature** (chapters 14–15). These are rules reason discovers for self-preservation:
- **First:** seek peace when you can get it; when you cannot, use all the advantages of war.
- **Second:** be willing to **lay down your right to all things**, provided others do the same.
- **Third:** keep the agreements you make.

**The social contract** (chapter 17). Agreements between people who distrust each other are worthless without enforcement: "Covenants, without the Sword, are but Words". So everyone covenants with everyone else to **hand their right of self-government to one person or assembly**, the **sovereign**. The sovereign is not party to the contract and so cannot break it. The resulting state is the great **Leviathan**, a "mortal god", pictured on the title page as a giant made of all its citizens.

**The sovereign's power** must be nearly absolute: divided power (king against parliament, church against state) leads straight back to civil war. One limit remains: **no one can give up the right to defend their own life**.

**The objections.**
- **Locke's** (Stage 9): it is foolish to escape polecats and foxes by being devoured by lions. **An absolute sovereign is a greater danger than one's neighbours.**
- **The "Fool"** (Hobbes's own, chapter 15): why keep a covenant when breaking it pays? Hobbes's reply: you cannot count on getting away with it, and anyone known to break faith will be shut out of the alliances everyone needs.
- **Was there ever a state of nature?** Hobbes admits it was perhaps never general. The argument does not need it to be historical; it asks what *would* happen if government fell away, as it did in his own country.

**Why it matters.** **Political authority rests on the consent of the governed, given for their own protection.** Locke, Rousseau and Rawls all start from Hobbes's question, even while rejecting his answer.
Pascal: the wager:
A mathematician's argument that it is rational to bet on God, and the birth of decision theory.

**Blaise Pascal** (1623–1662) was born in Clermont, in the Auvergne. As a teenager he wrote on conic sections; at about nineteen he built a calculating machine; his experiments on the vacuum (the Puy de Dôme, 1648, carried out by his brother-in-law) helped overturn the Aristotelian claim that nature abhors a vacuum; and his letters with **Fermat in 1654** founded the mathematics of **probability**. On the night of **23 November 1654** he had a religious experience he recorded and sewed into his coat (the *Memorial*). He defended the Jansenists of Port-Royal in the *Provincial Letters* (1656–57). His notes for a defence of Christianity were published after his death as the ***Pensées*** ("Thoughts", **1670**).

**The wager** (fragment 233 in Brunschvicg's numbering, used by the translation below; 418 in Lafuma's). Its setting: reason cannot prove or disprove God. So suppose a coin is tossed: God is, or is not. Must we bet?

In the translation by W. F. Trotter (Dutton edition, 1958, Project Gutenberg): "Yes; but you must wager. It is not optional. You are embarked." Then: "Let us weigh the gain and the loss in wagering that God is. Let us estimate these two chances. If you gain, you gain all; if you lose, you lose nothing. Wager, then, without hesitation that He is."

**The argument in decision-theory form.** **Expected value** is the value of an outcome multiplied by its probability, summed over outcomes.

| | God exists | God does not exist |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Wager for God** | infinite gain | small finite loss (some pleasures) |
| **Wager against** | infinite loss, or at least no gain | small finite gain |

1. You must choose: not choosing is choosing against.
2. Reason cannot settle whether God exists, so the probability is not zero.
3. Any non-zero chance of an **infinite** reward outweighs any finite cost.
4. **So the rational choice is to wager for God.**

**The objections, in order of fame:**
- **Many gods.** The table has two columns, but there are many possible gods, some of whom might punish Christian belief. Diderot made the point in the 18th century. Defenders reply that not all hypotheses are equally live, and that the argument is addressed to someone already choosing between Christianity and unbelief.
- **You cannot believe at will.** Pascal answers this himself: act as if you believe, go to Mass, use holy water, and **belief will follow habit**. Critics find that a recipe for self-deception.
- **The infinity problem.** If there is even a tiny chance that *any* course of action leads to God, it too has infinite expected value. So **infinite stakes swamp all reasoning**, making every choice equally good (a point developed by Alan Hájek, 2003).
- **The wrong kind of reason.** A belief adopted for profit is not a belief held because it is true; and would a God worth worshipping reward it? William James (Stage 11) and W. K. Clifford divided on exactly this.

**Where it stands.** The wager is a landmark in **decision theory**, the study of rational choice under uncertainty. Most philosophers think **the many-gods and infinity objections defeat it in its simple form**; some defend refined versions. Pascal himself never presented it as a proof that God exists, only as an argument that **unbelief is not the safe default**.
Pascal: the Pensées and the reasons of t:
The *Pensées* are fragments, but their picture of human beings, and of what reason can and cannot do, is among the most piercing in philosophy.

**Greatness and wretchedness.** Pascal's anthropology turns on a contrast. In Trotter's translation (fragment 347): "Man is but a reed, the most feeble thing in nature; but he is a thinking reed." The universe can crush him with a drop of water, yet he is nobler than what kills him, "because he knows that he dies". **Our dignity lies in thought; our misery is that we are tiny, mortal and inconstant.** Neither the Stoic who sees only greatness nor the sceptic who sees only misery has the whole truth.

**Diversion.** Most of life, Pascal says, is spent **escaping ourselves**: hunting, gambling, war, business. Fragment 139: "all the unhappiness of men arises from one single fact, that they cannot stay quietly in their own chamber." We pursue the hare not for the hare but for the chase, which stops us thinking about our condition.

**The infinite.** The new science had opened a boundless universe. Fragment 206: "The eternal silence of these infinite spaces frightens me." Man stands between **two infinities**, the infinitely large and the infinitely small, able to know neither end.

**Two kinds of mind** (fragment 1). The ***esprit de géométrie*** reasons from a few clear principles, far from common use. The ***esprit de finesse*** (intuitive judgement) takes in many delicate principles at a glance, as a good judge of character does. Each fails where the other succeeds.

**The heart.** Fragment 277: "The heart has its reasons, which reason does not know." By **the heart** Pascal does not mean feeling or emotion in our sense. He means **a power of immediate knowing**: we know first principles, that there is space, time, motion and number, **by the heart**, not by proof. Reason then builds on them. So:

1. Reason proves nothing without first principles.
2. First principles are not proved; they are known directly ("by the heart").
3. So it is no objection to a belief that reason cannot demonstrate it.

This is aimed **against both the sceptic and the rationalist**. Against the Pyrrhonist: we cannot doubt in practice what the heart knows. Against Descartes, whom one fragment (78) dismisses as "useless and uncertain": **reason is not the only, or the first, way of knowing**.

**The three orders** (fragment 793): **bodies**, **minds** and **charity** (love). Each is infinitely above the one below, and invisible to it, as Archimedes's genius means nothing to a conqueror.

**Objections.** The appeal to the heart can be used to defend anything: whose heart, and how do we tell its reasons from wishful thinking? Defenders reply that Pascal limits the heart's knowledge to first principles and to what the whole person discerns, not to any feeling. Pascal's case for Christianity itself is a matter for the **Theology** curriculum.

**Why it matters.** Pascal is the first great **critic of rationalism from within the new science**, and a forerunner of Kierkegaard and the existentialists (Stages 11 and 13), for whom the human condition, not the cogito, is where philosophy starts.
Spinoza: substance monism and Deus sive:
The most radical system of the century: there is only one thing, and it is God, or Nature.

**Baruch (Benedict) de Spinoza** (1632–1677) was born in Amsterdam to a family of Portuguese Jews who had fled the Inquisition. In **1656**, aged 23, he was placed under a ***cherem***, a ban of expulsion, by the Amsterdam synagogue, for reasons never stated but surely his views. He lived quietly, grinding lenses for microscopes and telescopes, and turned down a professorship at Heidelberg (1673). The only book he published under his own name was an exposition of Descartes (1663). The ***Ethics*** appeared after his death in **1677**.

**The definitions.** Spinoza sharpens Descartes's terms:
- **Substance**: that which is **in itself and conceived through itself**; it needs nothing else to exist or to be understood.
- **Attribute**: what the intellect perceives as the essence of a substance (Descartes's thought and extension).
- **Mode**: a state of a substance, which exists in and is conceived through something else. **You, this table and this thought are modes.**

Descartes had admitted that strictly only God is independent; Spinoza takes the admission seriously.

**The argument for monism** (*Ethics* Part I):
1. Two substances cannot share an attribute (proposition 5): if they did, nothing could distinguish them.
2. A substance cannot be produced by another, so it exists **by its own nature**; existence belongs to it (proposition 7).
3. **God**, defined as a substance with **infinitely many attributes**, necessarily exists (proposition 11).
4. Since God has every attribute, any other substance would share an attribute with God, which premise 1 forbids.
5. Therefore, in R. H. M. Elwes's translation (1883): "Besides God no substance can be granted or conceived" (I.14), and "Whatsoever is, is in God, and without God nothing can be, or be conceived" (I.15).

**Deus sive Natura.** In Part IV Spinoza speaks of "the eternal and infinite Being, which we call God or Nature" (Elwes's rendering of *Deus sive Natura*). God is not a person outside the world who plans and judges; God **is** the one infinite substance, of which the world is the expression. He distinguishes ***natura naturans*** (nature *naturing*, God as active cause) from ***natura naturata*** (nature *natured*, the modes that follow).

**Mind and body.** Thought and extension are two attributes of one substance. So **a mind and its body are one and the same thing**, conceived first under thought, then under extension: "The order and connection of ideas is the same as the order and connection of things" (II.7, Elwes). **There is no interaction problem**, because there are not two things to interact.

**The objections.**
- **Leibniz:** premise 1 fails. Two substances might share one attribute and differ in another. Spinoza's proof works only if each substance has a single attribute, or none share. This is widely regarded as **a genuine gap**.
- **Is it pantheism, or atheism?** **Pantheism** says God and the universe are identical. Contemporaries read Spinoza as an atheist in disguise; the Romantics called him "God-intoxicated". Scholars still **dispute** whether Spinoza's God is the whole of nature, or only *natura naturans*, or something whose infinite attributes far exceed the world we know.
- **How can a finite mode follow from the infinite?** Spinoza's account of this is notoriously obscure.

His biblical criticism comes in two lessons' time; its theology is for the **Theology** curriculum.
Spinoza: the geometric method, determini:
How Spinoza wrote, why he thought nothing could have been otherwise, and what he thought a human being is.

**The geometric method.** The *Ethics* is set out like Euclid: **definitions, axioms, propositions, proofs**, with explanatory scholia (notes). Its full title is *Ethics, Demonstrated in Geometrical Order*. The form expresses a conviction: **reality is as rational as geometry**, so its truths can be deduced as a triangle's properties are.

**Necessitarianism.** In Elwes's translation (1883), I.29: "Nothing in the universe is contingent, but all things are conditioned to exist and operate in a particular manner by the necessity of the divine nature." And I.33: "Things could not have been brought into being by God in any manner or in any order different from that which has in fact obtained." This is stronger than determinism. **Determinism** says each event is fixed by prior causes and laws; **necessitarianism** says the whole world, laws included, could not have been different.

**Free will is an illusion.** In a letter of 1674 Spinoza imagined, in paraphrase, a stone set moving by an outside push that became conscious and thought it moved by its own choice. **Humans think they are free because they are conscious of their desires and ignorant of the causes** that determine them.

**No final causes.** The Appendix to Part I is a blistering attack on the idea that nature or God acts for purposes. We call things good or bad, ordered or confused, as they suit us, and project our purposes onto God. The will of God becomes, in Elwes's phrase, "the sanctuary of ignorance".

**The conatus.** Part III, proposition 6, in Elwes's translation (1883): "Everything, in so far as it is in itself, endeavours to persist in its own being." This striving, the ***conatus***, is **the essence of each thing**. In a human being, conscious of itself, it is **desire**. The emotions are its fluctuations: **joy** is the passage to greater power of acting, **sadness** to lesser. Love is joy accompanied by the idea of its cause; hatred, sadness accompanied by the idea of its cause.

**What freedom is.** Not uncaused choice, but **acting from one's own nature, understood**. We are in bondage when moved by passions, confused ideas of outside causes. **Understanding a passion transforms it**: to grasp the necessity of an event weakens grief and anger over it. At the summit (Part V) is the ***intellectual love of God***, the joy of understanding all things as following from God or Nature, and a kind of eternity of the mind.

**The argument for calm, set out:**
1. Everything happens necessarily.
2. The mind that understands this ceases to rage against what could not have been otherwise.
3. Passions rooted in confused ideas lose force when understood.
4. So **knowledge is the path to freedom and peace of mind**.

**Objections.**
- **Necessitarianism seems false**: surely the world could have had one more grain of sand. Leibniz drew back from it on exactly this ground.
- **Responsibility.** If no one could have done otherwise, how can anyone be blamed? Spinoza's reply: we restrain the dangerous whether or not they are blameworthy, as we restrain a mad dog; praise and blame are tools, not verdicts.
- **Egoism.** If everything strives only to preserve itself, is all virtue self-interest? Spinoza's answer is that nothing is more useful to a person than another person living by reason, so **rational self-interest leads to cooperation**.
Spinoza: the Tractatus Theologico-Politi:
The book that made Spinoza notorious in his lifetime: a critique of Scripture and a defence of free thought.

**The book.** The ***Theological-Political Treatise*** (*Tractatus Theologico-Politicus*) was published **anonymously in 1670**, with a false place of publication. It was condemned by Reformed church synods and banned by the authorities of Holland in 1674. Its subtitle states the aim: to show that **freedom to philosophise** not only can be granted without harm to religion or peace, but cannot be taken away without destroying them.

**The context.** The Dutch Republic was the most tolerant state in Europe, but its leader Johan de Witt was under pressure from Calvinist preachers allied with the House of Orange. In **1672** de Witt and his brother were lynched by a mob in The Hague.

**The method of interpreting Scripture** (chapter 7): **interpret the Bible from the Bible alone**, like nature from nature. Study its language, the history of each book, who wrote it, when, for whom. Do not read philosophical truths into it, as Maimonides (Stage 6) had done, nor read it as dictated by a reason it does not contain.

**The results he drew:**

| Topic | Spinoza's claim |
| --- | --- |
| **Prophecy** | prophets had vivid **imaginations** and moral seriousness, not superior knowledge; their teachings fit their times and temperaments |
| **Authorship** | the Pentateuch was **not written by Moses**; much of the Hebrew Bible was compiled much later (he credits hints in the medieval commentator Ibn Ezra) |
| **Miracles** | nothing can happen against nature, which is God's own necessity; "miracles" are events whose natural causes people did not understand |
| **Scripture's message** | at its core, simple: **obey God by loving justice and charity towards one's neighbour** |

**The separation of faith and philosophy.** If Scripture teaches **obedience**, not truth about nature, then **faith and reason do not compete**. Theology has no authority over philosophy, and philosophy none over piety.

**The politics** (chapters 16–20). Like Hobbes, Spinoza begins from a state of nature in which **right extends as far as power**, and a contract for security. Unlike Hobbes, he argues that **the purpose of the state is freedom** (chapter 20, paraphrased): not to turn people into beasts or puppets, but to let them use their reason safely. **Thought cannot be commanded**, so a state that tries only breeds hypocrites and rebels. Actions may be regulated; opinions and speech, as far as possible, should be free. He judged democracy the most natural form of state.

**Objections.**
- Religious critics: Spinoza reduces revelation to morality and imagination, assuming in advance that miracles are impossible. Whether his method is neutral or presupposes his metaphysics is **a fair question**.
- Liberal critics: his toleration is pragmatic. Since right equals power, the sovereign *may* restrict speech; Spinoza only argues it is unwise to.

**Why it matters.** The *Treatise* is a founding text of **modern biblical criticism** and of the **liberal defence of free speech**. Its theology belongs to the **Theology** curriculum; here, note how directly it extends Spinoza's metaphysics into politics.
Malebranche and occasionalism:
If minds cannot move bodies, perhaps nothing created moves anything, and God does it all.

**Nicolas Malebranche** (1638–1715) was a priest of the **Oratory** in Paris. In 1664 he read Descartes's *Treatise of Man*, and the story goes that his excitement gave him palpitations. His main work is ***The Search after Truth*** (1674–75); others include the *Treatise on Nature and Grace* (1680) and the *Dialogues on Metaphysics and on Religion* (1688). He fought a long public battle with Arnauld.

**Occasionalism** is the view that **God is the only true cause**. What we call causes, fire burning cotton, my will raising my arm, are only **occasions** on which God acts according to general laws. The idea has earlier forms: al-Ghazali (Stage 6) argued that fire does not burn cotton, God does; and Cartesians before Malebranche, such as Louis de La Forge and Géraud de Cordemoy, used it to solve the interaction problem. Malebranche made it a system.

**Three arguments:**

1. **The necessary connection argument** (*Search* VI.2.3):
   1. A true cause is one between which and its effect **the mind perceives a necessary connection**.
   2. We perceive no necessary connection between one ball striking another and the second moving, nor between willing and the arm rising.
   3. We perceive a necessary connection only between **the will of an infinitely powerful being** and its effects.
   4. So only God is a true cause.
2. **The ignorance argument.** I do not know which nerves and animal spirits must move for my arm to rise. **How can I do what I do not know how to do?**
3. **Continuous creation.** Descartes held that God keeps the world in being by recreating it at every moment. But in recreating a body God must put it *somewhere*; so **God, not other bodies, puts it where it moves to**.

**Vision in God.** Malebranche also argued that our ideas are not states of our own minds but are in God, and **we see all things in God**. Arnauld attacked this in *On True and False Ideas* (1683): ideas, he said, are simply our perceptions.

**Objections.**
- **Leibniz:** occasionalism makes nature **a perpetual miracle**. God must intervene at every instant.
- **Moral responsibility.** If God moves my arm when I strike someone, is God the author of the blow? Malebranche: God acts by **general volitions**, simple laws, and my will supplies the occasion. This simplicity also explains evil: God chose the simplest laws, not a world free of every harm. (The *Treatise on Nature and Grace* belongs as much to the **Theology** curriculum.)
- **Is it even coherent** to call God a cause and deny that anything else is, when our concept of cause comes from creatures?

**The irony.** Malebranche's first premise was taken over by **Hume** (Stage 9): we never perceive necessary connection between events. Hume simply dropped God from the picture, and **causation became the great problem of empiricism**.

**Where it stands.** Occasionalism has few defenders today, but it is **not dismissed as absurd**; it follows rigorously from widely held premises, which is why it is studied.
Leibniz: monads and pre-established harm:
The last and most ingenious of the great rationalists: a world made of minds, each a mirror of all the rest.

**Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz** (1646–1716) was born in Leipzig. A lawyer, diplomat and court historian to the House of Hanover, he was also among the most wide-ranging minds in history: he **invented the calculus** independently of Newton (his version published 1684, with the notation still used), designed a calculating machine, worked on binary arithmetic and planned a universal logical language. His philosophy is scattered through letters and short essays: the *Discourse on Metaphysics* (1686), the *New System* (1695), the ***Theodicy*** (1710, the only philosophical book he published), and the ***Monadology*** (written **1714**, printed after his death). He died in Hanover in 1716, largely neglected by the court.

**Why monads?** Leibniz argues (*Monadology* 1–3, in Robert Latta's translation, 1898, from Wikisource):
1. There are compound things.
2. A compound is "nothing but a collection or *aggregatum* of simple things".
3. So there must be **simple substances**, without parts.
4. What has no parts has no extension, shape or divisibility.
5. So the ultimate constituents of reality are **not atoms of matter**, but unextended, simple substances, which he calls **monads** (Greek *monas*, "unit").

**What a monad is like.** Since it has no parts, its only states are **perceptions** (representations of the rest of the universe) and **appetitions** (tendencies from one perception to the next). Every monad **mirrors the whole universe** from its own point of view, mostly confusedly. Leibniz's image (§57): the same town looked at from different sides. Monads range from the barely-perceiving ones that make up a stone, through animal souls, to rational minds capable of self-awareness, which he calls **apperception**. Matter, as it appears to us, is a **well-founded phenomenon**: the way aggregates of monads show up to perceivers.

**"No windows."** Monads cannot act on one another (§7): "The Monads have no windows, through which anything could come in or go out." Each unfolds entirely from its own nature, like a program running on its own.

**The mill** (§17). Perception cannot be explained mechanically. Imagine a thinking machine enlarged "so that one might go into it as into a mill". Inside "we should... find only parts which work one upon another, and never anything by which to explain a perception." This is aimed at Hobbes, and is an ancestor of the modern **hard problem of consciousness** (Stage 14).

**Pre-established harmony.** If nothing acts on anything, why does my arm rise when I will it? Because **God set up all monads from the start so that their states correspond**. In §78: "The soul follows its own laws, and the body likewise follows its own laws; and they agree with each other in virtue of the pre-established harmony". Leibniz compared it to **two clocks** made so perfectly that they always agree, without any link between them. Malebranche's God adjusts the clocks at every moment; **Leibniz's God set them right once, at creation**.

**Objections.** It sounds fantastic: a universe of windowless perceivers synchronised by God. It **leaves no room for genuine interaction**, which most people take as plain fact. Leibniz replied that it is the only account that respects both the mechanical laws of bodies and the unity of minds, without constant miracles. Whether he was an **idealist** (only minds exist) or allowed some reality to bodies is **disputed** among scholars.
Leibniz: the principle of sufficient rea:
Two principles do most of the work in Leibniz's philosophy, and both are still argued about.

**Two great principles.** Leibniz says (*Monadology* 31–32, Latta's translation, 1898) that our reasonings rest on "two great principles": **contradiction**, by which we judge false whatever involves a contradiction, and **sufficient reason**, "in virtue of which we hold that there can be no fact real or existing, no statement true, unless there be a sufficient reason, why it should be so and not otherwise, although these reasons usually cannot be known by us."

**The Principle of Sufficient Reason (PSR): nothing is without a reason why it is so rather than otherwise.** It applies to facts, events, and the existence of the world as a whole.

**Two kinds of truth** follow:
- **Truths of reason** (necessary): their opposite is contradictory. They can be proved by analysis in finitely many steps. 2+2=4.
- **Truths of fact** (contingent): their opposite is possible. Their reasons involve an **infinite analysis** that only God completes. Caesar crossed the Rubicon.

**Complete concepts.** In the *Discourse* (§8, 13) Leibniz holds that the concept of each individual contains **everything that will ever be true of it**: Caesar's concept contains crossing the Rubicon. How, then, is Caesar's act free and contingent? Because its reason **inclines without necessitating**, and its denial is not a contradiction. Many readers, Arnauld first, thought this **collapses into fatalism**, and whether Leibniz escapes is a lasting dispute.

**The identity of indiscernibles.** If two things were exactly alike in every respect, God would have **no sufficient reason** to put one here and the other there. So (*Monadology* 9) "in nature there are never two beings which are perfectly alike". Leibniz told the story, in his letters to Clarke, of a gentleman who searched a garden for two leaves exactly alike and could not find them.

**Two principles that are easily confused:**

| Principle | Statement | Status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Indiscernibility of identicals** ("Leibniz's Law") | if x and y are the same thing, they share every property | almost universally accepted |
| **Identity of indiscernibles** | if x and y share every property, they are the same thing | **disputed** |

**The objections.**
- **Black's spheres.** Max Black (1952), in paraphrase: imagine a universe containing only **two exactly similar iron spheres**, a fixed distance apart. Nothing distinguishes them, yet there are two. Defenders reply that each sphere has a property the other lacks, *being identical with this sphere*; critics answer that counting such properties makes the principle trivial.
- **Against the PSR.** Is there a reason why there is something rather than nothing? If the PSR is true, the chain of reasons seems to make **everything necessary**, as in Spinoza. Quantum mechanics offers apparent events without sufficient reasons, though how to interpret it is itself disputed. Some, following Hume and Kant, treat the PSR as a demand of reason rather than a known truth about the world.

**Why it matters.** These principles generate the rest: Leibniz's argument for monads, the best world, and his case against absolute space, all run on them. **To accept or reject the PSR is to decide much of metaphysics.** Recent philosophers (for example Michael Della Rocca) have defended it strongly; most remain cautious.
Leibniz: the best of all possible worlds:
Leibniz's answer to the problem of evil, and the joke Voltaire made of it.

**The problem of evil.** If God is all-good, all-knowing and all-powerful, why is there evil? Pierre Bayle's *Historical and Critical Dictionary* (1697) had argued that reason cannot answer the question, and faith must accept what reason cannot reconcile. Leibniz's ***Theodicy*** (**1710**) is his reply. He coined the word: Greek *theos*, "God", and *dikē*, "justice", **the justification of God**.

**The argument from sufficient reason:**
1. God, in his understanding, surveys **infinitely many possible worlds**, each a complete, consistent history.
2. Only one can be actual, so there must be a **sufficient reason** for choosing it (*Monadology* 53).
3. God is perfectly wise and good; the only reason fitting such a being is **that the chosen world is the best**.
4. So **the actual world is the best of all possible worlds**.

In Latta's translation (1898) of §55: "the actual existence of the best that wisdom makes known to God is due to this, that His goodness makes Him choose it, and His power makes Him produce it."

**What "best" means.** Not the most pleasant for us. The best world contains (§58) "as great variety as possible, along with the greatest possible order". And worlds come whole. Things are **compossible** if they can exist together; you cannot remove one evil without changing the entire world, perhaps for the worse.

**Three kinds of evil** (*Theodicy*):

| Kind | What it is | Why God permits it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Metaphysical** | the imperfection of any created thing, which is finite by being created | creation without it is impossible |
| **Physical** | suffering | often a means to greater good, or punishment |
| **Moral** | sin | God does not will it but permits it as the price of a world with free creatures, which is better overall |

**The objections.**
- **Voltaire's** *Candide* (**1759**), written after the **Lisbon earthquake of 1755**, has the tutor Pangloss insist that all is for the best amid earthquake, war and the Inquisition. The satire is brilliant, but philosophers note that **Leibniz never claimed that each evil is good**, only that the whole is the best possible.
- **Is there a best world?** Perhaps for any world there is a better one, as for any number there is a larger. Then no choice is the best, and Leibniz's argument fails. This is the most serious philosophical objection.
- **God's freedom.** If God must choose the best, is creation necessary? Leibniz: God's choice is **morally**, not metaphysically, necessary; choosing worse is possible, but would be unworthy of him. Critics find the distinction thin.
- **The scale of suffering.** Could any variety and order outweigh the suffering of, say, one tortured child? Dostoevsky's Ivan Karamazov (1880) presses this.

**Where it stands.** Philosophers of religion today mostly defend the weaker claim that God may have **morally sufficient reasons** we cannot see, not that this is the best world. The theological side belongs to the **Theology** curriculum; here, note that the argument is a strict application of the PSR.
Leibniz and Clarke: space, God and the c:
The last great debate of the age, conducted through a princess, between Leibniz and Newton's champion.

**The correspondence.** In 1715 Leibniz wrote to **Caroline, Princess of Wales**, criticising Newton's natural philosophy as dangerous to religion. She passed the letter to **Samuel Clarke** (1675–1729), an Anglican priest and philosopher, who replied, with Newton's help, it is generally believed. **Five letters each** were exchanged in 1715–16. Leibniz died in November 1716 before answering Clarke's fifth; Clarke published the whole in **1717**.

**The issues:**

**1. God the clockmaker.** Newton had suggested that the solar system would gradually fall out of order without God's occasional correction. Leibniz mocked this: Newton's God must **wind up his watch from time to time**, a poor workman. Clarke replied that a God who never acts in the world is a step towards a God who does nothing, and so to atheism; **God's ongoing governance is providence, not repair**.

**2. Absolute or relational space.**
- **Newton and Clarke: absolute space.** Space is a real, infinite container, existing independently of bodies, and in some sense an attribute of God.
- **Leibniz: relational space.** **Space is only the order of coexisting things**, as time is the order of successive things. Without bodies there is no space.

**Leibniz's argument from the PSR:**
1. If space were absolute, God could have placed the whole universe **ten feet east** of where it is (or rotated it, or begun it a year earlier).
2. The two universes would be **indiscernible**: every relation between bodies the same.
3. So God would have **no sufficient reason** to choose one over the other.
4. But God does nothing without sufficient reason.
5. So the supposition is incoherent, and **space is not absolute**.

**Clarke's reply:** God's **will alone** can be a sufficient reason. A free agent can choose between equal options, as someone choosing between two identical coins. Leibniz retorted that a choice without reasons is not freedom but chance.

**Absolute motion.** Clarke also appealed to Newton's *Principia* (1687): rotation produces observable effects, such as water climbing the sides of a spinning bucket, so there is **real motion** that is not just change of relation between bodies. Leibniz's reply here was weakest; historians generally judge this **Newton's strongest point**.

**3. Gravity and miracles.** Newtonian gravity acts across empty space with no mechanism. Leibniz called that an occult quality or **a perpetual miracle**. Clarke replied that gravity is a law of nature whose cause is unknown, not a miracle.

**4. Freedom.** Clarke defended a **liberty of indifference**: the power to choose without decisive reasons. Leibniz held that reasons **incline without necessitating**.

**Who won?** Opinion has swung. Eighteenth-century physics followed Newton. After **Einstein's relativity** (1905, 1915) and with Ernst Mach's earlier criticism of the bucket argument, relationalism regained ground, though general relativity does not straightforwardly vindicate either side. The question whether spacetime is a substance or a set of relations is **still open** in philosophy of physics.
Anne Conway: one substance, alive throug:
A philosopher who answered Descartes, Hobbes and Spinoza with a system of living spirit, and was nearly forgotten.

**Anne Conway** (1631–1679), née Finch, was born in London and raised in the house now called Kensington Palace. Without formal education, she learned philosophy by correspondence with the Cambridge Platonist **Henry More** (1614–1687). From her teens she suffered **crippling headaches**, which no doctor could relieve. The physician and Kabbalist **Francis Mercury van Helmont** came to treat her in 1670 and stayed for the rest of her life. Through him she studied the Jewish Kabbalah and met Quakers; she became a Quaker shortly before her death.

**Her book.** Her only surviving treatise, written in her last years, was published anonymously in a Latin translation at Amsterdam in **1690**, and translated back into English in **1692** as ***The Principles of the Most Ancient and Modern Philosophy***.

**Three kinds of being.**

| Species | Nature |
| --- | --- |
| **God** | infinite, unchangeable, perfectly good |
| **Christ, the "middle nature"** | the link between God and creatures: changeable only towards good. Conway treats this as a metaphysical category; its theology is for the **Theology** curriculum |
| **Creatures** | changeable, for better or worse |

**Her central claim: all created things are one kind of substance.** **Body and spirit are not two substances but two ends of a scale**: body is condensed, sluggish spirit; spirit is subtle, active body. Everything created is alive and perceives, to some degree.

**Her arguments against dualism:**
1. If spirit and body were wholly different in nature, as Descartes says, **they could not affect each other**, yet the soul feels the body's pain and moves its limbs.
2. **Sympathy and union require likeness of nature.**
3. So body and spirit must share a nature, differing only in degree.

This is Elisabeth's objection turned into a positive system.

**Against the materialists and Spinoza.** Hobbes made everything dead matter; Spinoza made creatures parts of God. Conway calls both errors: **matter is not dead**, and **creatures are distinct from God**, because they change and God does not.

**Change and perfectibility.** Creatures can change into others: over long ages a stone might become an animal, an animal a human being. Suffering is **medicinal**, it purifies; hence, she argued, all creatures will eventually be restored to good, and punishment is never eternal.

**Leibniz.** Leibniz owned a copy of her book, probably a gift from van Helmont, and **praised it**, recognising its affinity with his own views: simple, perceiving, living units making up the world. Whether Conway actually **influenced** Leibniz's monadology (the case Carolyn Merchant made in 1979) or simply anticipated it is **disputed**.

**Objections.** Her conclusions draw heavily on premises about God's goodness that a non-theist will not grant. Her "spirit particles" each contain infinitely many others, which some readers find hard to make coherent. And the argument from interaction cuts both ways: a materialist can accept premise 3 and conclude that everything is body.

**Why she matters.** Conway offers **a vitalist monism** (one kind of substance, living throughout), a road not taken by the mechanists. Her rediscovery since the 1980s is part of a wider recovery of **early modern women philosophers**, with Elisabeth, Margaret Cavendish, Mary Astell and Damaris Masham.
Looking back: from Renaissance doubt to:
Three centuries of argument, from Ficino's Plato to Leibniz's monads. What was settled, what was left open, and where it goes.

**What changed for good.**
1. **Philosophy no longer answered to Aristotle.** By 1700 the scholastic synthesis of forms and final causes no longer framed natural philosophy, and has never recovered that role. Nature was **matter in motion described by mathematics**.
2. **The starting point moved inside.** After Descartes, philosophy began, for a long time, with **the mind and its ideas**, and asked how we know the world beyond.
3. **Political authority became a problem to be justified.** After Machiavelli and Hobbes, nobody could simply assume rulers are ordained; they had to be shown legitimate, most often by **consent**.
4. **Scepticism became a permanent companion.** Montaigne's question, "What do I know?", has never been dismissed, only answered in different ways.

**The great unsolved problem: mind and body.**

| Thinker | Answer |
| --- | --- |
| Descartes | two substances that interact |
| Hobbes | only body |
| Malebranche | two substances; God does the causing |
| Spinoza | one substance under two attributes |
| Leibniz | only simple, perceiving substances, pre-arranged to harmonise |
| Conway | one created substance, spirit and body by degrees |

**Every option on the modern menu, physicalism, dualism, idealism, dual-aspect monism, panpsychism, was on the table by 1700.** None won agreement then, and none has since. Elisabeth's question is still the sharpest form of the problem.

**What was left open.**
- **Can reason alone reach substantial truths about reality?** The rationalists said yes, and built proofs of God, the soul and the structure of the world. Their systems contradicted one another, which was itself a reason for doubt.
- **The cogito and the circle.** Is there a foundation that guarantees knowledge? Or must knowledge be justified some other way?
- **Causation.** Malebranche's point that we never *perceive* necessary connection waited for Hume.
- **Freedom and necessity.** Hobbes and Spinoza denied free will in the usual sense; Leibniz tried to save contingency; Clarke defended liberty of indifference. The debate continues, unresolved.
- **Proofs of God.** The trademark, ontological and cosmological arguments, the wager and the theodicy were each pressed hard. Most philosophers now think the trademark argument fails and the ontological argument at least in Descartes's form; the others remain live controversies.

**What Stage 9 picks up.** The empiricists answer the rationalists. **John Locke** (*Essay concerning Human Understanding*, 1689) denies innate ideas and traces all knowledge to experience; **Berkeley** drops matter altogether; **Hume** turns Malebranche's argument and Montaigne's scepticism against causation, the self and reason itself. **Kant** (Stage 10) will try to reconcile both sides, arguing that the rationalists and the empiricists each saw half the truth.

**A last thought.** This stage contains more ambitious systems than any other: Descartes's tree of knowledge, Spinoza's geometry of God, Leibniz's monads. **Their ambition is their importance.** Even where their proofs fail, they show with great clarity what follows from premises many people still hold.
Context: the new science, a bloodless re:
Stage 8 ended with the rationalists, Descartes, Spinoza and Leibniz, who trusted reason to reach the deep structure of the world. This stage follows the other great current of the century from 1690 to 1790: **empiricism**, the view that **all our ideas and all our knowledge of the world come from experience**. It also follows the movement around it, the **Enlightenment**: the effort to rebuild knowledge, morals and politics on reason and evidence rather than on authority and custom.

**Four things pressed on these thinkers.**

| Pressure | What it did |
| --- | --- |
| **The new science** | The Royal Society (1660), Robert Boyle's chemistry, Newton's *Principia* (1687). Nature turned out to be matter in motion, obeying laws. What, then, are colour, taste and the mind? |
| **The wars of religion** | A century of killing over doctrine. Could people who disagreed about God live in one state? |
| **The Glorious Revolution** (1688–89) | England replaced James II with William and Mary, and Parliament set limits on the crown. When may a people remove its ruler? |
| **The growth of print and the public** | Coffee houses, journals, salons, the Scottish universities. Philosophy was now written for readers, not only for schools |

**Locke**, in the preface to his *Essay* (1689), described himself, in paraphrase, as an **under-labourer** clearing rubbish from the ground so that scientists like Boyle and Newton could build. That modest job turned out to be enormous. If every idea comes from experience, what can we really know about matter, cause, self and God?

**The arc of the stage is a slide toward doubt, and then a recovery.** Locke builds the empiricist programme. **Berkeley** pushes it until matter disappears. **Hume** pushes further, until causation, induction and the self all look unsupported by reason, and then argues that nature, not reason, keeps us believing. **Reid** answers that the whole road started from a mistake.

**Morals and politics run alongside.** If morality is not stamped on the mind at birth, where does it come from? Shaftesbury, Hutcheson, Butler, Hume and Adam Smith answer: from feeling, conscience and sympathy. In France, **Voltaire** and **Diderot** turn philosophy into a campaign, and **Rousseau** asks what could make any government legitimate. The stage ends in the 1790s, with **Burke** and **Wollstonecraft** arguing over the French Revolution.

**A warning about labels.** "The British empiricists" (Locke, Berkeley, Hume) against "the continental rationalists" is a scheme drawn up by later historians. It is useful, but none of these men thought of himself as on a team, and the lines blur: Locke used reason heavily, and Leibniz cared about experience.
Locke: the attack on innate ideas:
**John Locke** (1632–1704) was an Oxford-trained physician and the secretary of the first Earl of Shaftesbury, a leader of the opposition to the Stuart kings. He spent 1683 to 1689 in exile in Holland and returned after the Revolution. His *Essay Concerning Human Understanding* came out in December 1689 (dated 1690) and went through four editions in his lifetime.

**Book I attacks innate ideas.** An **innate idea** or principle is one the mind has from birth, built in rather than learned: for example "whatever is, is", or "God exists", or "parents must be honoured". Many in Locke's day held that such principles were stamped on the soul and guaranteed its knowledge.

**The argument from universal consent, and Locke's reply:**

1. If a principle were innate, every human being would assent to it.
2. There is no principle to which every human being assents. Children and people with severe mental disabilities have no notion of "whatever is, is"; whole nations have lacked the idea of God; moral rules vary from people to people.
3. So no principle is innate.

**Locke adds that universal consent would not prove innateness anyway**, since there might be another explanation of why everyone agrees.

**The defender's best reply: innate means "there to be found", not "already in view".** A truth can be in the mind without being thought of, and people come to know it when they reach the use of reason. Locke answers that this makes the claim empty. If "innate" only means "the mind is able to come to know it", then **every truth anyone ever learns is innate**, including the whole of geometry.

**Locke's positive picture comes in Book II**, in his own words from the Gutenberg text: "Let us then suppose the mind to be, as we say, white paper, void of all characters, without any ideas". Where does it get its furniture? "To this I answer, in one word, from EXPERIENCE." (The Latin phrase *tabula rasa*, "scraped tablet", is the traditional name for this picture, though Locke's word is "white paper".)

**The strongest answer came from Leibniz**, in his *New Essays on Human Understanding* (written about 1704, published 1765). The mind is not a blank but **like a block of marble with veins in it** that mark out a statue: ideas are innate as **dispositions**, which experience brings out. Locke would say this is still only a capacity. Whether a capacity with this much built-in shape deserves the name "innate" is the real issue, and it is still argued, for example over Chomsky's claim (Stage 12 and after) that the grammar of language is inborn.

**A dispute about the target.** Locke names few opponents. Scholars disagree whether he was fighting Descartes, the Cambridge Platonists, Lord Herbert of Cherbury (whom he does criticise), or ordinary teachers who used "innate principles" to forbid questions.
Locke: simple and complex ideas, and whe:
**For Locke an idea is whatever the mind is aware of when it thinks**: a sensation of red, a memory of a smell, the thought of a triangle, the notion of justice. Book II of the *Essay* sets out to show that every such idea comes from experience.

**Two sources of experience.**

| Source | What it gives |
| --- | --- |
| **Sensation** | ideas of outside things: yellow, hot, hard, bitter |
| **Reflection** | ideas of the mind's own workings, noticed from within: thinking, doubting, willing, believing |

**Simple ideas** are the atoms: one quality, one appearance, which cannot be broken down further. The mind is **passive** in receiving them. It cannot invent a new simple idea, just as a man born blind cannot form the idea of scarlet.

**Complex ideas** are built by the mind from simple ones, by combining, comparing and abstracting. Locke divides them into:

- **Modes**: ideas of things that do not exist on their own, such as a dozen, a triangle, murder, gratitude.
- **Substances**: ideas of things that do, such as gold, a horse, a man. They are bundles of simple ideas (yellow, heavy, malleable) together with a confused idea of something that holds them together.
- **Relations**: ideas got by comparing, such as cause, older than, the same as.

**Abstraction** makes general ideas. From many particular triangles the mind keeps what they share and drops the rest, and the word "triangle" stands for that general idea.

**Book IV asks how far knowledge goes.** Locke defines **knowledge** as the perception of agreement or disagreement between ideas. It comes in three grades: **intuitive** (seen at once, as that white is not black), **demonstrative** (reached by steps, as in geometry), and **sensitive** (that some particular thing outside me exists now, which falls short of the other two but is enough for life). Beyond these lies **probability**, or judgement, on which nearly all science and daily life depend.

**Locke's distinction between real and nominal essence** follows. The **nominal essence** of gold is the set of features by which we sort things as gold. The **real essence** is the hidden structure of tiny particles that causes those features. We know the first and, in Locke's time, not the second, so natural science must stay probable.

**The standard objection: the veil of ideas.** If the mind is aware only of its own ideas, how can it ever check that they match the world? We would be shut behind a veil, like someone who sees only photographs and can never compare them with the scene. Berkeley and Hume will press this hard.

**A genuine scholarly dispute.** Some interpreters read Locke as holding that ideas are inner objects we perceive *instead of* things (a "representative" theory). Others, such as John Yolton, argue that for Locke an idea is simply the *act* of perceiving a thing, so the veil objection misreads him.
Locke: primary and secondary qualities,:
**Is the redness in the tomato, or in you?** Locke's answer, drawn from Boyle's science of tiny particles ("corpuscles"), became one of the most influential distinctions in philosophy.

**A quality** is a power a body has to produce an idea in a mind. Locke sorts them:

| Kind | Examples | The idea in us |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Primary** | solidity, extension (size), shape, motion or rest, number | **resembles** the quality in the body |
| **Secondary** | colour, sound, taste, smell, heat | **does not resemble** anything in the body; the body has only a power, from the arrangement of its particles, to cause that sensation |

**So the tomato really is round and solid, but it is "red" only in the sense that its surface particles cause a sensation of red in a seeing creature.** Take away eyes, and the shape remains; the redness, as we experience it, does not.

**Locke's arguments for the distinction:**

1. **Science explains secondary qualities by primary ones.** Motion of particles explains heat; the texture of a surface explains its colour. The reverse never happens.
2. **Primary qualities cannot be removed from a body.** Divide a grain of wheat as often as you like: each part still has some size, shape and solidity.
3. **The lukewarm water.** Warm one hand and chill the other, then put both in the same bowl of water. It feels cold to one hand and hot to the other. The water cannot be both, so the heat felt is in us. Equally, a pounded almond changes colour and taste without anything but its particles being rearranged.

**Berkeley's objection** (next lessons) is that every one of these arguments works as well for the primary qualities. Shape and size also look different from different places, and nobody can even imagine a shape that has no colour at all. If colour is only in the mind, so is shape. Locke's defenders reply that he is not arguing from how things feel but from **what the best science needs to explain the appearances**, which is a different and stronger kind of argument.

**Substance: "something, I know not what".** When we gather the ideas of yellow, heavy and malleable into the idea of gold, we suppose something underneath that holds them together, a **substratum** or support. Locke admits we have no clear idea of it: it is only "something" that supports qualities. He compares this to the story of the Indian who said the world rests on an elephant, the elephant on a tortoise, and the tortoise on something he knew not what.

**Is Locke mocking substance or keeping it?** Scholars divide. One reading has Locke a quiet sceptic about substance, preparing the way for Berkeley and Hume. Another, now common, says he keeps substance as a real thing and only admits that our idea of it is thin.

**Thinking matter.** In Book IV Locke remarked that, for all we can prove, God could give some systems of matter the power to think. That aside caused a long controversy with Bishop Edward Stillingfleet, and it still sits at the centre of the philosophy of mind.
Locke: personal identity and memory:
**What makes you the same person as the child in your old photographs?** Not the same matter, which has been replaced; not, Locke argued, even the same soul. His chapter "Of Identity and Diversity" (Book II, chapter xxvii) was added in the second edition of 1694, and it began the modern debate.

**Locke separates three questions** that had been run together:

| Same what? | What makes it the same |
| --- | --- |
| **Same substance** (body or soul) | the same stuff, continuing |
| **Same man** (human animal) | one continuing life, organised as one body, like an oak through its growth |
| **Same person** | sameness of **consciousness** |

**A person**, in Locke's words from the Gutenberg text, is "a thinking intelligent being, that has reason and reflection, and can consider itself as itself, the same thinking thing, in different times and places". And personal identity reaches "as far as this consciousness can be extended backwards to any past action or thought".

**The prince and the cobbler.** Suppose the soul of a prince, carrying his memories, entered the body of a cobbler. Everyone else would see the same cobbler, the same man. But the person would be the prince, since he would remember being the prince and be conscious of the prince's deeds as his own.

**Why it matters: "person" is a forensic term**, Locke's word, meaning a term of the law courts. It answers to praise, blame, reward and punishment. You can justly be punished only for what you can own as your own act. Locke even ties the Last Judgement to it.

**Objection 1: circularity** (Joseph Butler, 1736). Memory cannot *make* me the person who did a deed, because a genuine memory already *presupposes* that I did it. "I remember robbing the bank" counts as memory only if I was the robber. Defenders reply that we can define a weaker relation, an apparent memory caused in the right way by the past experience (later called **quasi-memory**), which does not presuppose identity.

**Objection 2: the brave officer** (Thomas Reid, 1785). A boy is flogged for stealing apples. As a young officer he captures an enemy standard and remembers the flogging. As an old general he remembers the battle but has forgotten the flogging. By Locke's test, the general is the officer and the officer is the boy, but the general is not the boy. Identity is transitive (if A is B and B is C, A is C), so Locke's theory contradicts itself. **There is broad agreement that this objection refutes the memory theory in its simple form.**

**The reply that survives.** Later philosophers replaced direct memory with **overlapping chains** of psychological connection: the general is linked to the boy through the officer. This "psychological continuity" view, developed by Derek Parfit and others, is taken up in Stage 14.

**Also forgotten in Locke's day: forgetting.** Locke accepted the result that if I lose all memory of a deed, I am not the person who did it, though the law may still punish the man. Many find that too strong; others think it correct.
Molyneux's problem: would the newly sigh:
**William Molyneux** (1656–1698) was a Dublin scientist and politician who wrote a treatise on optics, *Dioptrica Nova* (1692). He first sent Locke a puzzle in 1688; Locke printed it in the second edition of the *Essay* (1694, Book II, chapter ix), introducing "the learned and worthy Mr. Molineux". In the Gutenberg text the question runs:

> "Suppose a man BORN blind, and now adult, and taught by his TOUCH to distinguish between a cube and a sphere of the same metal, and nighly of the same bigness, so as to tell, when he felt one and the other, which is the cube, which the sphere. Suppose then the cube and sphere placed on a table, and the blind man be made to see: quaere, whether BY HIS SIGHT, BEFORE HE TOUCHED THEM, he could now distinguish and tell which is the globe, which the cube?"

**Molyneux answered no, and Locke agreed.** The man knows how a cube *feels*, with its corners pressing his hand. He has no experience yet of how a cube *looks*. The link between the two must be learned.

**Why the question matters.** It tests whether the senses share any ideas. Is there a single idea of shape that sight and touch both give us, or two quite different ideas that we have learned to connect?

| Answer | Who | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **No** | Molyneux, Locke, Berkeley (*New Theory of Vision*, 1709) | the ideas of sight and of touch are different, joined only by experience. Berkeley makes this his central thesis |
| **Yes** | Leibniz, in the *New Essays* | the man could reason it out: a cube has corners, a sphere has none, and he can find the corners by sight if he thinks about it |
| **It depends** | various later writers | perhaps yes after a little looking, no at the very first glance |

**The question became an experiment.** In 1728 the surgeon William Cheselden reported on a boy born with cataracts whose sight he restored; the boy could not at first tell shapes apart by sight. Philosophers argued over what this proved, since newly restored eyes see poorly in any case.

**A modern result.** In 2011 a team led by Richard Held, working with children in India treated for congenital blindness, reported that immediately after surgery subjects **could not** reliably match an object seen to one felt, but **learned to do so within days**. That supports a "no" to Molyneux's exact question. It does not settle the philosophy: defenders of "yes" say the subjects' vision was not yet good enough to test the real issue, and that the speed of learning suggests a shared structure was waiting.

**The lesson for empiricism.** Molyneux's problem is a case where a philosophical question about where ideas come from can be partly answered by observation. That itself is very much in the empiricist spirit.
Locke: the Two Treatises, property and t:
**Locke's political writings appeared in 1689 too**, the *Two Treatises of Government* anonymously. The **First Treatise** demolishes Sir Robert Filmer's *Patriarcha* (published 1680), which claimed that kings inherit their power from Adam's authority over his children. The **Second Treatise** builds Locke's own theory. Peter Laslett argued in 1960 that most of it was written years before 1688, as a case for resistance to Charles II.

**The state of nature** is the condition of people with no common government. Unlike Hobbes's war of all against all (Stage 8), Locke's has a **law of nature**, known by reason. In the Gutenberg text: "being all equal and independent, no one ought to harm another in his life, health, liberty, or possessions". Everyone has the right to punish breaches of it.

**Property.** How can anyone own part of a world God gave to all in common? Locke's answer (Second Treatise, section 27): "every man has a property in his own person", and so in his labour. Whatever a person takes from nature "he hath mixed his labour with", and makes it his own, provided there is "enough, and as good, left in common for others", and provided he takes no more than he can use before it spoils. Money, by consent, later lets people store wealth without spoiling and so accumulate unequally.

**Government by consent.** Because judging one's own case is unreliable, people agree to form a society and set up a government to protect their "lives, liberties and estates, which I call by the general name, property" (section 123). Government holds power on **trust**. If it violates that trust, the people may resist and replace it.

**Objections, in their strongest form:**

1. **Consent.** Almost nobody ever agreed to their government. Locke's reply is **tacit consent**: whoever enjoys the protection of a state, even by travelling on its roads, consents to it. Hume answered (in "Of the Original Contract", 1748) that this is like telling a man carried aboard a ship asleep that he consented by not leaping into the sea.
2. **Labour-mixing.** Robert Nozick (Stage 14) asked: if I pour my can of tomato juice into the sea, do I own the sea, or have I lost my juice? Why should mixing gain rather than waste?
3. **Who benefits.** C. B. Macpherson (1962) read Locke as justifying unlimited capitalist accumulation; others, such as James Tully, deny it. Scholars also debate how far Locke's remarks on America as "waste" land served the seizure of Native land; he was involved in the government of the Carolina colony and invested in the slave-trading Royal African Company. These are matters of record; how they bear on the theory is disputed.

**Toleration.** Locke's *Letter Concerning Toleration* (Latin, 1689) argues that the state's business is civil goods (life, liberty, property), and that **force cannot produce belief**: you can make a man say a creed, not believe it. So persecution is useless as well as wrong. The Anglican Jonas Proast replied (1690) that force can make people *consider* arguments they would otherwise ignore, a sharp objection Locke spent years answering. Its limits: no toleration for atheists, whose oaths he thought worthless, nor for churches owing allegiance to a foreign prince, usually read as aimed at Roman Catholics.
Berkeley: immaterialism and esse est per:
**George Berkeley** (1685–1753) was an Irish clergyman, a fellow of Trinity College Dublin, and later Bishop of Cloyne (from 1734). In his twenties he published *An Essay towards a New Theory of Vision* (1709), the *Treatise concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge* (1710) and *Three Dialogues between Hylas and Philonous* (1713). His thesis was startling: **there is no matter.**

**Immaterialism** is the view that nothing exists except **minds** (Berkeley calls them spirits) and **ideas** (what minds perceive). Tables, trees and mountains are real, but they are collections of ideas, not lumps of an unthinking stuff outside all minds.

**The slogan is Latin: *esse est percipi*, "to be is to be perceived".** In the Gutenberg text of the *Principles* (section 3), after saying that the table he writes on exists means he sees and feels it: "Their ESSE is PERCIPI, nor is it possible they should have any existence out of the minds or thinking things which perceive them."

**The core argument (Principles, section 4), set out:**

1. Houses, mountains and rivers are things we perceive by sense.
2. What we perceive by sense are only our own ideas and sensations.
3. Ideas and sensations cannot exist unperceived.
4. So houses, mountains and rivers cannot exist unperceived.

**Against Locke's matter, Berkeley adds three more blows.**

- **Likeness.** Locke said our ideas of primary qualities resemble qualities in matter. But, in Berkeley's words, "an idea can be like nothing but an idea". A colour can only be like a colour, a shape seen only like a shape seen.
- **The primary qualities fall with the secondary.** Every argument Locke used for colour (it varies with the observer) applies to shape and size, and nobody can conceive a shape with no colour. So all qualities are in the mind.
- **Matter is idle.** Even Locke's matter is "something I know not what". It explains nothing that God acting directly could not explain better, and it breeds scepticism and atheism.

**Berkeley insists he is on the side of common sense.** Ordinary people believe the things they see and touch are real; they do not believe in an invisible, colourless substratum behind them. It is the philosophers who doubt that the things we see are the real things.

**The strongest objections:**

1. **Premise 2 is the weak point.** It assumes we perceive ideas, not things. Reid (later in this stage) will say that is exactly the error of the whole "way of ideas".
2. **Act and object.** G. E. Moore (1903) argued that Berkeley confuses the *act* of perceiving blue, which is mental, with the *blue* perceived, which need not be.
3. **The famous kick.** James Boswell reports that in 1763 Samuel Johnson, told that Berkeley's argument could not be refuted, kicked a large stone and said, in substance, that he refuted it thus. Berkeley would reply that he never denied the stone is hard; he only denied that its hardness exists outside all minds.

**A note on reading.** Berkeley is *not* saying that things are dreams, or that they vanish when you look away. That is the subject of the next lesson.
Berkeley: the master argument and God as:
**The master argument** is the name later scholars gave to a short passage (*Principles*, sections 22–23, and the first of the *Three Dialogues*) in which Berkeley stakes everything on one test. In the Gutenberg text: "I am content to put the whole upon this issue:—If you can but CONCEIVE it possible for one extended movable substance, or, in general, for any one idea, or anything like an idea, to exist otherwise than in a mind perceiving it, I shall readily give up the cause."

**The argument, set out:**

1. Try to conceive a tree that exists unperceived and unconceived.
2. In doing so, you are conceiving it.
3. So the tree is not, after all, unconceived; you have only formed an idea in your own mind and failed to notice yourself doing it.
4. So it is impossible to conceive of anything existing unconceived.
5. What is inconceivable is impossible (or at least has no meaning for us). So nothing exists unconceived.

**The standard objection: content and act.** Most commentators think the argument fails, and they agree on why. There is a difference between **conceiving a tree that is unconceived** (the content of my thought is a tree with no one thinking of it) and **the tree's being conceived by me** (a fact about my act). I can conceive of my own funeral without conceiving that I am absent from my thinking about it. Berkeley's step 3 slides from one to the other. Defenders, a minority, reply that for an empiricist, conceiving just *is* having an image, and every image is had by someone, so the distinction cannot be drawn in the way the objectors want.

**So what keeps the world in being when no one is looking?** If to be is to be perceived, does the tree in the empty garden blink out of existence?

**Berkeley's answer is God.** Two arguments run through his work:

| Argument | The idea |
| --- | --- |
| **From passivity** (*Principles*, section 29) | I can call up ideas of imagination at will, but I cannot choose what I see when I open my eyes. Those ideas must be caused by another spirit, powerful, wise and regular: God. The **laws of nature** are just the regular order in which God gives us ideas |
| **From continuity** (*Three Dialogues*) | sensible things exist when no finite mind perceives them; so there must be an infinite mind that perceives them always |

**Scholars dispute** how much weight Berkeley puts on the second, continuity argument. Jonathan Bennett argued it plays almost no role in the *Principles*, where the passivity argument does the work; others disagree.

**Objections to the theistic step.** The passivity argument shows that my sense ideas have *some* cause beyond my will, not that the cause is a mind, let alone one God. And if God perceives the tree, are my tree-ideas and God's the same ideas? Berkeley struggled with this. The arguments for God here are assessed as arguments; the theology of creation belongs to the Theology curriculum.

**Berkeley and science.** In *De Motu* (1721) he argued that Newton's "forces" are useful mathematical fictions, not real causes. That **instrumentalist** view of science has had a long life.
Hume: impressions, ideas and the copy pr:
**David Hume** (1711–1776) was born in Edinburgh. In his twenties he wrote *A Treatise of Human Nature* (Books 1 and 2 in 1739, Book 3 in 1740). Late in life he said, in substance, that it fell dead from the press. He recast its first book as the *Philosophical Essays concerning Human Understanding* (1748), retitled *An Enquiry concerning Human Understanding* in 1758, and its third as the *Enquiry concerning the Principles of Morals* (1751). Suspected of atheism, he was twice refused a university chair, at Edinburgh (1745) and Glasgow (1751), and won fame instead with his *History of England*.

**His project is a "science of man"**: to do for the mind what Newton did for nature, explaining thought by a few principles drawn from experience.

**Perceptions** is Hume's word for every content of the mind. They divide into two kinds, differing in **force and vivacity**, that is, liveliness:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Impressions** | sensations, passions and emotions as they first strike us: seeing red, feeling anger |
| **Ideas** | the fainter copies of these in memory, thought and imagination |
