| **Two-aspect** (Gerold Prauss; Henry Allison, *Kant's Transcendental Idealism*, 1983) | One set of things, considered in two ways: as they appear, and as they are apart from our knowing | Critics say it shrinks the doctrine into a modest point about method, and fails to explain what Kant says about things in themselves |

Many recent readings sit somewhere between, holding that there is one world but that it has properties we cannot know.

**The affection problem.** Kant says things in themselves **affect** our senses and so give rise to appearances. But *affect* is a causal notion, and Kant has just argued that causality applies only within experience. **Friedrich Jacobi** made this complaint in 1787: without the thing in itself he could not get into the system, and with it he could not stay there. (This is a paraphrase of his well-known remark.)

**Replies.** Kant's defenders say that thinking of things in themselves as grounds of appearances is permitted, since we may think what we cannot know, so long as we claim no knowledge of how the grounding works. Critics answer that this is a promissory note that can never be cashed.

**Why it mattered.** This one problem drove the next generation. **Fichte** concluded that the thing in itself should be dropped, and that the mind produces all its objects. Hegel concluded that the very idea of something wholly unknowable is incoherent, because to draw a limit is already to stand on both sides of it. Both moves are taken up later in this stage.
Kant's paralogisms: the illusion of a kn:
The second half of the *Critique*, the **Transcendental Dialectic**, is about **illusion**. Reason (*Vernunft*), in Kant's narrow sense, is the faculty that seeks the unconditioned: the complete series of conditions behind anything conditioned. That drive is natural and unavoidable. But it tempts us to treat ideas that can never be met in experience as if they were objects we could know. Kant calls this **transcendental illusion**, and compares it to the way the moon looks larger near the horizon: you can learn it is an illusion, but you never stop seeing it.

**The three ideas of reason**, and the three pretended sciences built on them:

| Idea | Pretended science | Kant's chapter |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **The soul** | rational psychology | the Paralogisms |
| **The world as a whole** | rational cosmology | the Antinomies (next lesson) |
| **God** | rational theology | the Ideal of Pure Reason (the lesson after) |

**The target here.** **Rational psychology** claimed, from the mere thought "I think", to prove four things about the soul: that it is a **substance**; that it is **simple** (without parts, so it cannot decompose, which was the classic argument for immortality); that it is **one and the same** person through time; and that its relation to bodies in space is only problematic. Descartes and the Wolffians argued roughly this.

**A paralogism** is a fallacious syllogism, an argument that looks valid but is not. Kant's diagnosis of the first:

1. What cannot be thought otherwise than as subject exists only as subject, and is substance.
2. A thinking being, considered merely as such, cannot be thought otherwise than as subject.
3. **Therefore a thinking being exists only as subject, that is, as substance.**

**The trick** is a shift of meaning in the middle term. In premise 1, "subject" means a real thing that underlies properties. In premise 2, it means only the logical subject of a thought: the "I" that must be able to accompany every representation. **That the I is always the subject of my thoughts says nothing about what kind of thing does the thinking.** The "I think" is a form of consciousness, not an intuition of an object, so no categories, substance included, can be applied to it.

**The same diagnosis runs through the rest:** the logical simplicity of "I" is not proof of a simple thing, and the formal identity of "I" across my thoughts is not proof of a persisting substance. Kant offers the image of a series of elastic balls, each passing its motion and states on to the next. A series of substances could pass consciousness along in the same way, and the last would still feel itself to be the same as the first.

**What follows.** **We can neither prove nor disprove that the soul is an immortal substance.** Materialism is just as unfounded as spiritualism. Kant later gave immortality back, but as a postulate of practical reason, not as knowledge (the lesson on the second *Critique*).

**Objections.** Some argue Kant's own "I think" is richer than he admits, that self-awareness does give some knowledge of the self. Others, from the materialist side, say he leaves the soul too open a question. Kant's attack on the old proofs of a simple soul is widely accepted. What we positively know about the self remains disputed.
Kant's antinomies of pure reason:
An **antinomy** (Greek, "conflict of laws") is a pair of opposed claims, each of which seems provable. When reason tries to think **the world as a whole**, as a completed totality, Kant claims it produces four such pairs. Each side has an argument of its own, usually an indirect proof showing that the opposite leads to absurdity.

| | Thesis | Antithesis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | The world has a **beginning in time** and is **limited in space** | The world has **no beginning** and **no limits**; it is infinite |
| **2** | Every composite substance consists of **simple parts** | Nothing is simple; everything is **infinitely divisible** |
| **3** | Besides the causality of nature there is also **causality through freedom** | There is no freedom; **everything happens by laws of nature** |
| **4** | There is an **absolutely necessary being**, as part of the world or as its cause | **No necessary being** exists anywhere |

**A taste of the first antinomy.** *Thesis*: if the world had no beginning, an infinite series of past moments would have been completed by now; but an infinite series can never be completed; so the world began. *Antithesis*: if it began, there was empty time before it; but nothing can come to be in empty time, since no moment of it differs from any other to make it the moment; so it did not begin.

**Why this matters to Kant.** He presented the antinomies as **indirect proof of transcendental idealism.** If the world were a thing in itself, a given whole, one side of each pair would have to be true. Since reason proves both, the assumption that the world is a given whole must be wrong. In a letter to Christian Garve of 1798 Kant said that it was the antinomy, not Hume, that first woke him from his dogmatic slumber.

**Kant's resolution.**

- **The first two, the "mathematical" antinomies: both sides are false.** The world of appearances is never given as a complete whole. It is only ever an indefinite task of going further back in time or further down in division. Asking whether it is finite or infinite is like asking whether a square circle is red: the question presupposes something that does not exist.
- **The last two, the "dynamical" antinomies: both sides may be true**, of different things. In the world of appearances, everything happens by natural causes. But the same agent, considered as a thing in itself, may be free. Freedom is thus shown to be **possible**, not proven actual; for its actuality Kant turns to morality.

**Objections.**

- **The proofs are weaker than Kant thought.** Modern mathematics, with Cantor's theory of infinite sets (from the 1870s), shows that "an infinite series can never be completed" is not a contradiction. Many think the thesis proof of the first antinomy fails, and some of the other proofs too.
- **Modern cosmology** asks whether the universe had a beginning, and answers with physical evidence, not just reasoning. Whether that dissolves Kant's point, or only moves it, is debated.
- **Freedom.** The resolution of the third antinomy puts freedom outside time. Critics ask how a timeless choice can explain an act I perform at a moment, or how I can be responsible for a character I never chose in time. This is a central puzzle of Kant's ethics.

The antinomies are where Kant's method looks most like a diagnosis of reason's own temptations, and they were deeply influential on Hegel's view that contradiction lies at the heart of thought.
Kant's critique of the proofs of God:
In the third part of the Dialectic, the **Ideal of Pure Reason**, Kant argues that **there are only three possible ways of proving God by speculative reason, and none succeeds.** The arguments themselves are set out in the Theology curriculum and in earlier stages (Anselm in Stage 6, Aquinas in Stage 7, Descartes in Stage 8). Here the question is only whether Kant's objections hold as argument.

**1. The ontological argument** (Kant coined the name). It argues from the concept of God alone: God is the most perfect being; existence is a perfection; so God exists. Kant's reply is his most famous objection.

In Meiklejohn's translation (1855): **"Being is evidently not a real predicate, that is, a conception of something which is added to the conception of some other thing."** A **real predicate** is one that adds to the content of a concept, as "red" or "heavy" does. To say a thing exists does not add a feature to it; it says that something answers to the concept. His illustration: **"A hundred real dollars contain no more than a hundred possible dollars."** (Kant wrote *Taler*, a coin.) Being richer is a fact about my bank balance, not about the concept.

**So the argument fails** because you cannot pack existence into a concept and then unpack it. If "God exists" is analytic, it only says that if anything is God, it exists; if synthetic, it cannot be proved from the concept.

**2. The cosmological argument.** Something exists; whatever exists contingently has a cause; so there is a necessary being. Kant argues that it secretly relies on the ontological argument: to get from "a necessary being exists" to "that being is God", one must assume that the concept of the most real being contains necessary existence. And it uses "cause" beyond possible experience, which the Analytic forbids.

**3. The physico-theological argument** (the argument from design). The order of nature looks designed, so it has an intelligent designer. Kant treated it with respect, saying it deserved always to be mentioned with reverence. But at most it gives **an architect working with material, not a creator**, and to reach an infinite and perfect God it again falls back on the cosmological argument, and so on the ontological.

**How the objections are judged.**

- **Existence is not a predicate** is widely accepted in some form. Frege and Russell later analysed existence as a matter of quantifiers, "there is something that is F", which many take to vindicate Kant.
- **But the ontological argument is not dead.** Modal versions (Alvin Plantinga, 1974) argue from the **possibility** of a maximally great being, and do not treat existence as a predicate. Whether they beg the question is disputed (Stage 14).
- **The reduction of the cosmological argument** to the ontological is widely thought to be **Kant's weakest step**. Defenders of Aquinas-style arguments say they reach a necessary being without first defining God into existence.
- **Hume's** *Dialogues* (1779) had made similar points about design.

**Kant was not an atheist.** He thought speculative reason could neither prove nor disprove God. He then argued that **practical reason**, the reason that guides action, gives us a rational basis for belief. That is where the Groundwork and the second *Critique* take over.
Reading: Kant's Groundwork on the good w:
***Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals* (1785)** is Kant's short first book on ethics. *Groundwork* translates *Grundlegung*, "laying the foundation". Thomas Kingsmill Abbott's translation (1873) calls it *Fundamental Principles of the Metaphysic of Morals*, and it is on Project Gutenberg. All quotations here are Abbott's, as fetched.

**1. The opening sentence.**

> "Nothing can possibly be conceived in the world, or even out of it, which can be called good, without qualification, except a good will."

Every word is chosen. "Without qualification" means **unconditionally**: good in every circumstance, not good-if. Kant then runs through rivals. Intelligence, wit, courage and resolution are talents of mind and temperament, and they can become **"extremely bad and mischievous"** if the will using them is bad. A clever, brave murderer is worse than a stupid, timid one. The "gifts of fortune" (power, riches, honour, health, even happiness) can breed pride. So only one thing is good without condition: **the good will**, the settled resolve to do what is right.

**2. Results do not matter to its worth.** If by bad luck the good will achieved nothing at all, Kant writes,

> "then, like a jewel, it would still shine by its own light, as a thing which has its whole value in itself."

**Its usefulness "can neither add nor take away anything from this value."** This is the deepest break with the consequentialists of Kant's time and later, for whom what makes an act good is what it brings about.

**3. Duty and the shopkeeper.** To see what a good will is, Kant turns to **duty**, the will acting under moral constraint. He asks us to tell apart acting **in accordance with duty** and acting **from duty**:

> "it is always a matter of duty that a dealer should not over charge an inexperienced purchaser; and wherever there is much commerce the prudent tradesman does not overcharge, but keeps a fixed price for everyone, so that a child buys of him as well as any other."

The shopkeeper does the right thing, but **"his own advantage required it"**. His act accords with duty, but it was not done from duty, and so it has no **moral worth**. Kant goes on to the harder case of a person naturally sympathetic, who helps others because he enjoys it. Such help is "proper" and "amiable", Kant says, but its worth only shows when that person helps from duty even after his sympathy has died.

**4. The definition.**

> "Duty is the necessity of acting from respect for the law."

**Respect** (*Achtung*) is the one feeling Kant allows into the motive of morality, because it is produced by recognising the moral law, not by any object we want.

**What to take from the passage.**

1. Moral worth lies in the **will**, not in outcomes.
2. The will is good when it acts **from duty**, not from inclination or self-interest.
3. Duty is defined by **law**, which is why the next step is to ask what form a moral law has: the categorical imperative.

**The obvious objection.** Does Kant think helping a friend out of love is worse than helping from duty? The poet Schiller mocked the idea in a short verse: the man who serves his friends gladly must learn to despise them first, and then do with disgust what duty bids (a paraphrase). Many Kantians reply that the passage asks only **what shows** moral worth, in a test case where inclination is absent. It does not say that feeling is bad, and Kant elsewhere praises cultivating sympathy. Whether this reading is generous or correct is disputed.
Kant's categorical imperative: the formu:
**An imperative** is a command, an "ought". Kant divides them in two.

- **Hypothetical imperatives** command conditionally: *if* you want X, do Y. "If you want to pass, study." They bind only those who want the end.
- **The categorical imperative** commands unconditionally: do Y, whatever you want. Moral demands, Kant holds, are of this kind. "Do not lie" does not lapse if lying would serve you.

**A maxim** is the personal rule behind an action, the principle you are actually acting on, such as "When I need money, I will borrow it and promise to repay, though I know I cannot."

**The formula of universal law.** In Abbott's translation (1873): **"Act only on that maxim whereby thou canst at the same time will that it should become a universal law."** And in a variant: **"Act as if the maxim of thy action were to become by thy will a universal law of nature."**

**The test, step by step:**

1. State your maxim.
2. Imagine a world in which everyone acts on it, as a law of nature.
3. Ask whether that world is even conceivable (**contradiction in conception**).
4. If it is, ask whether you could consistently will to live in it (**contradiction in the will**).
5. If either test fails, the act is forbidden.

**Kant's four examples:**

| Case | Test it fails | Kind of duty |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **The false promise** | Conception: if everyone made false promises when in need, no one would believe a promise, so the maxim **"would necessarily destroy itself"** (Abbott) | perfect duty to others |
| **Suicide from self-love** | Conception, Kant argues: a nature that destroyed life by the very feeling meant to preserve it would contradict itself | perfect duty to oneself |
| **Neglecting one's talents** | Will: a rational being necessarily wills that his capacities be developed | imperfect duty to oneself |
| **Refusing to help others** | Will: you will need help yourself, and cannot will a world where none is given | imperfect duty to others |

**Perfect duties** allow no exceptions. **Imperfect duties** leave room for choice about when and how.

**Objections.**

- **Empty formalism.** Hegel argued that the test is only a consistency check. It can show that some maxims contradict themselves, but any content can be made consistent, so it cannot tell us what to do.
- **False positives and negatives.** "I will cross only at 3 p.m. on Tuesdays" seems to pass. Maxims can be tailored so narrowly ("I will lie when my name is Roachi") that almost anything passes. Defenders answer that the maxim must be the agent's real reason, described honestly.
- **The murderer at the door.** Benjamin Constant objected that the rule against lying would forbid lying to a murderer who asks where your friend is hiding. **Kant, in a 1797 essay, accepted the conclusion.** Most readers think this is wrong, and many Kantians argue that Kant misapplied his own theory.

**Replies.** Christine Korsgaard (1985) defends a "practical contradiction" reading: a maxim fails if universalising it would defeat its own purpose. On that reading the false promise fails cleanly. Whether every immoral maxim fails, and every innocent one passes, is still argued.
Kant on humanity, autonomy and the kingd:
Kant gives several **formulations** of the one categorical imperative, and claims they are equivalent: different ways of saying the same law. Which ones are distinct, and whether they really are equivalent, is a scholarly dispute.

**1. The formula of humanity.** Kant argues that **"rational nature exists as an end in itself."** An *end* is something aimed at. Most ends are relative to our wants: a car matters only because I want it. But a rational being, a person, is an end **in itself**, valuable as such. From this comes the most quoted of the formulas (Abbott, 1873):

**"So act as to treat humanity, whether in thine own person or in that of any other, in every case as an end withal, never as means only."**

*Withal* is archaic for "at the same time". Notice the words **"never as means only"**. Kant does not forbid using people as means; we use bus drivers and shopkeepers all the time. He forbids using them **merely** as means: treating them in ways they could not possibly consent to, as when deceiving or coercing them. The false promiser treats the lender as a tool.

**2. The formula of autonomy.** *Autonomy* is Greek for "self-law". Kant's claim is that the moral law is **not imposed from outside**, by God, society or desire. A rational will gives the law to itself. Every rival theory, he says, makes morality **heteronomous**, "law from another": it grounds duty in something the agent happens to want, such as happiness, perfection or the will of God, and so makes it hypothetical. **Only autonomy yields a categorical imperative.** This is Kant's most original idea, and it shaped all later thought about freedom.

**3. The formula of the kingdom of ends.** Imagine a community of all rational beings, each both lawgiver and subject, each treating all others as ends. Act as a member legislating for such a kingdom. Here Kant draws his distinction between **price** and **dignity**: in Abbott's words, **"In the kingdom of ends everything has either value or dignity."** What has a price can be swapped for an equivalent. What has dignity **"admits of no equivalent"**.

**Why it matters.** This is the root of modern talk of **human dignity** and of **rights** that cannot be traded away for the greater good. It is the main rival to utilitarianism (Stage 11), which allows any act if the total good is greater.

**Objections.**

- **Who counts?** Kant ties dignity to rationality. What about infants, people with severe cognitive disabilities, and animals? Kant held that we have only indirect duties concerning animals: cruelty to them coarsens us. Many find this inadequate; Kantians have offered revisions.
- **Autonomy and God.** Theistic critics ask whether a self-legislating will can really bind itself, and whether moral law does not need a lawgiver beyond us (see the Theology curriculum).
- **Vagueness.** What counts as treating someone "merely" as a means? The formula is powerful and widely used in practice, but how to apply it is contested.

**The good will** of the opening of the *Groundwork*, it turns out, is a will that is **autonomous**: it acts on a law it gives itself as a rational being.
Kant's Critique of Practical Reason and:
**The *Critique of Practical Reason* (1788)** is the second Critique. Its job is to show that **pure reason can be practical**: that reason by itself, without any desire, can move the will.

**The "fact of reason."** In the *Groundwork* Kant had tried to prove the moral law from the idea of freedom. Here he reverses the order. **Our awareness of the moral law is simply given**, a "fact of reason": we know that we ought, whatever we want. Kant's illustration: a man ordered by his prince, on pain of death, to give false testimony against an innocent person may not know whether he would refuse. But he knows that he could, and that he should.

**Freedom.** If I know I ought to do something, I must be able to do it ("ought implies can"). So the moral law reveals that I am free. Kant put it neatly: **freedom is the ground of the moral law's being; the moral law is the ground of our knowing about freedom.** The first *Critique* had shown freedom only to be possible (the third antinomy). Now it is affirmed, for practical purposes.

**The highest good.** Morality does not aim at happiness. But reason also demands a whole in which **virtue and happiness are joined**, happiness in proportion to worthiness of happiness. Kant calls this **the highest good** (*summum bonum*). In this life the virtuous often suffer, and the wicked flourish.

**The postulates.** A *postulate* is something we must assume in order to make sense of a duty we really have. Kant names three:

| Postulate | Why reason needs it |
| --- | --- |
| **Freedom** | The moral law commands; so we must be able to obey |
| **The immortality of the soul** | We must strive for complete conformity to the moral law, but no finite being achieves it in a lifetime. So we must assume an endless progress |
| **The existence of God** | Only a moral and all-powerful cause of nature could make happiness match virtue |

**This is not knowledge.** Kant calls it **rational faith** or belief (*Glaube*). The first *Critique* denied that we can know any of these things. The second argues that a moral agent may, and in a sense must, hold them. Hence the earlier slogan about abolishing knowledge "to make room for belief".

**The famous conclusion.** In Abbott's translation: **"Two things fill the mind with ever new and increasing admiration and awe, the oftener and the more steadily we reflect on them: the starry heavens above and the moral law within."**

**Objections.**

- **The moral argument for God.** Does the duty to pursue the highest good really require that it be achievable? Perhaps we need only strive. And critics ask whether this is a disguised appeal to wishful thinking. For the argument as theology, see the Theology curriculum.
- **The fact of reason** strikes many as a retreat: after a whole *Critique* of argument, the foundation of morality is simply asserted. Defenders reply that nothing more basic could ground it without making it heteronomous.
- **Freedom outside time** remains the deep puzzle from the antinomies.
Kant's Critique of Judgment: beauty, the:
**The *Critique of Judgment* (1790)** is the third Critique. It tries to bridge the realm of nature (governed by the laws of the first *Critique*) and the realm of freedom (governed by the moral law of the second). Its bridge is **judgment**: the power of thinking a particular under a universal. When the universal is given, judgment simply applies it (**determining judgment**). When only the particular is given and a universal must be found, it is **reflecting judgment**. Beauty and living things both call for reflecting judgment.

**Part one: the judgment of taste.** "This rose is beautiful." Kant examines it under four headings, or **moments**:

1. **Disinterested.** The pleasure in the beautiful does not depend on wanting the thing to exist or to use it. That separates the beautiful from the **agreeable** (what pleases the senses, like wine) and the **good** (what we value through a concept).
2. **Universal without a concept.** When I call something beautiful, I speak as if for everyone, demanding agreement, yet no rule or concept proves it. You cannot argue someone into finding a rose beautiful.
3. **Purposiveness without purpose.** In J. H. Bernard's translation (1892): **"Beauty is the form of the purposiveness of an object, so far as this is perceived in it without any representation of a purpose."** A beautiful thing looks as if made to fit our powers of knowing, yet serves no purpose we can name.
4. **Necessary.** The judgment claims that everyone **ought** to agree. Kant grounds this in a shared sense, a **sensus communis**, and in the free play of imagination and understanding that he thinks all humans share.

Kant also separated **free beauty** (a flower, a pattern) from **dependent beauty** (a building or a horse, judged against a concept of what it should be).

**The sublime.** Building on Edmund Burke's *Philosophical Enquiry* (1757), Kant distinguished:

- **The mathematical sublime**: something so vast (the starry sky, the pyramids) that imagination cannot take it in as a whole.
- **The dynamical sublime**: nature's overwhelming power, a storm at sea or a volcano, seen from safety.

**The twist.** In both, our senses fail, but we become aware of something in ourselves **greater than nature**: reason's idea of the infinite, and our moral freedom. The sublime is, strictly, in the mind, not in the mountains.

**Part two: teleological judgment.** *Teleology* (from the Greek *telos*, "end") is explanation by purposes. Living things look purposive: in an organism, each part exists for the others and for the whole. Mechanical explanation cannot fully account for this, Kant argued, and he doubted that there could ever be a Newton who explained a blade of grass by mechanical laws alone (a paraphrase). But purpose is a **regulative** principle: a guide for inquiry, not a known fact about nature.

**Objections.** Can a judgment be both subjective (a feeling) and universal? Critics say Kant's "free play" is too thin to ground agreement. And Darwin (1859) offered exactly the mechanical explanation of purposiveness Kant doubted. Whether that answers Kant, or only relocates the question, is still debated.
Kant on enlightenment and perpetual peac:
**"What is Enlightenment?" (1784).** In December 1784 Kant published a short answer to a question raised in a Berlin journal, the *Berlinische Monatsschrift*. Its opening is **paraphrased** here, since no public-domain English translation was fetched to quote from. It runs like this: **enlightenment is humanity's emergence from an immaturity for which it is itself to blame.** *Immaturity* means being unable to use your own understanding without another's guidance. It is self-incurred when the cause is not lack of intelligence but lack of **courage**.

**The motto** Kant adopts is from the Roman poet Horace: ***Sapere aude*, "dare to know"**, or, as Kant glosses it, have courage to use your own understanding.

**Why people stay immature.** It is comfortable. A book thinks for me, a pastor has a conscience for me, a doctor decides my diet. Guardians make the step to maturity look dangerous.

**His distinction:**

- **The public use of reason**: speaking as a scholar to the whole reading public. This, Kant says, **must always be free**.
- **The private use of reason**: what one says in an office or post, as an officer, tax official or clergyman. This may be restricted. An officer must obey an order, but may later publish a criticism of it.

He praises Frederick the Great for a policy summed up as: argue as much as you like, but obey. **We do not live in an enlightened age**, Kant says, but in an **age of enlightenment**: the process is under way.

**Toward Perpetual Peace (1795)** was written after Prussia made a separate peace with revolutionary France at Basel. It takes the form of a mock treaty. After six **preliminary articles** (no secret reservations in peace treaties, no standing armies in the long run, no forcible interference in another state's constitution, among others) come three **definitive articles**, quoted in Mary Campbell Smith's translation (1903):

1. **"The civil constitution of each state shall be republican."** By *republican* Kant means a state with representative government, separation of powers and the rule of law, not necessarily one without a monarch. Citizens who must bear the costs of war will be slow to vote for it.
2. **"The law of nations shall be founded on a federation of free states."** Not a world state, which Kant feared would be a soulless despotism, but a league.
3. **"The rights of men, as citizens of the world, shall be limited to the conditions of universal hospitality."** A stranger may visit, and must not be treated with hostility. Kant attacked European colonial conquest under this head.

**Its afterlife.** The essay is a founding text for the League of Nations, the United Nations and **democratic peace theory**, the observation that established democracies rarely if ever fight each other.

**A dark side, honestly told.** Kant's lectures on anthropology and geography and several essays contain a **racial hierarchy** with white Europeans at the top. Scholars dispute how this relates to his universal ethics. Some argue it exposes the universalism as hollow. Others, notably Pauline Kleingeld, argue that in the 1790s Kant revised his views, with *Perpetual Peace*'s attack on colonialism as evidence. **This is an open and serious debate.**
The first reaction to Kant: Jacobi, Hama:
Kant's *Critique* was at first barely read. It became famous in the later 1780s, helped by Karl Leonhard Reinhold's popular *Letters on the Kantian Philosophy* (1786–87). It was quickly attacked from several sides. Three critics mattered most, and all three were friends of one another and suspicious of reason's claims.

**Friedrich Heinrich Jacobi (1743–1819)** was a businessman, novelist and philosopher.

- **The pantheism controversy.** In 1785 he published *On the Doctrine of Spinoza*, in letters to Moses Mendelssohn, reporting that the great writer Lessing, shortly before his death in 1781, had confessed himself a Spinozist. *Pantheism* is the view that God and nature are one. Spinoza (Stage 8) was then seen as an atheist and fatalist. A storm followed.
- **His argument.** Any consistent rational system, which explains everything by its causes, ends in Spinoza: a necessary chain with no room for a personal God or free will. So reason pursued to the end leads to fatalism and what Jacobi later called **nihilism** (he popularised the word, in a 1799 open letter to Fichte).
- **His alternative**: a leap of **faith** (*Glaube*), an immediate certainty, prior to argument, of God, freedom and the outer world. He called it a *salto mortale*, a somersault.
- **Against Kant**: the thing-in-itself problem from earlier in this stage. Kant's system needs things in themselves that cause sensations, and forbids saying so.

**Johann Georg Hamann (1730–1788)**, also of Königsberg and a friend of Kant, was known as the **"Magus of the North"**. He was a Lutheran thinker whose writings are full of allusion and wit, and are hard to read.

- In his **Metacritique on the Purism of Reason** (written 1784, published 1800) he argued that Kant had tried to purify reason of tradition, experience and **language**. But reason exists only in language, which is historical and bodily. **There is no pure reason to critique.**
- Hamann shaped Herder, and influenced later thinkers including Kierkegaard (Stage 11).

**Johann Gottfried Herder (1744–1803)** was Kant's student in Königsberg in the early 1760s, and later a pastor and court preacher at Weimar.

- **Treatise on the Origin of Language (1772)**: language is not given by God nor invented by convention, but grows out of humanity's distinctive reflective awareness. **Thought and language are inseparable.**
- **Ideas for the Philosophy of History of Humanity (1784–91)**: each people has its own spirit, expressed in its language, songs and customs, and each age must be judged by its own standards, not by ours. This is a founding text of **historicism** and of cultural nationalism. Kant reviewed it harshly in 1785, and the two fell out.

**What they had in common.** Reason is not an abstract, timeless faculty. It lives in **language, history, feeling and faith**. That theme passed into Romanticism, into Hegel's historical reason, and into the whole later tradition of hermeneutics (Stage 13).

**Assessing them.** Their strongest point, that reason is embedded in language and culture, is now widely accepted in some form. Their weakest is that, once reason is put on trial, the critics seem to rely on reason to make their case. Jacobi's leap of faith is criticised as arbitrary; his defenders say every system starts somewhere it cannot prove.
Fichte: the I and the not-I:
**Johann Gottlieb Fichte (1762–1814)** was the son of a poor ribbon-weaver in Saxony. He made his name in 1792 with *Attempt at a Critique of All Revelation*, which was published anonymously and at first mistaken for Kant's own work. Kant corrected the error, and Fichte was famous overnight.

**His career in brief.** Professor at Jena from 1794. Forced out in 1799 after the **atheism controversy**, when an essay identifying God with the moral order of the world was attacked as atheistic. Then Berlin, where during the French occupation he gave the **Addresses to the German Nation** (1807–08), and where he was later rector of the new university.

**His starting point.** Fichte thought Kant's results were right but his system unfinished. Two problems stood out:

1. **The thing in itself.** As Jacobi had said, it is inconsistent to say an unknowable thing causes our sensations. **Fichte dropped it.** All that we can know must be accounted for from the activity of the mind.
2. **No single principle.** Kant had listed forms of intuition, categories and ideas, but never derived them from one source. Fichte wanted **one first principle** from which the whole system of knowledge follows. He called his philosophy the **Wissenschaftslehre**, the "doctrine of science" or of knowledge, first set out in 1794–95.

**The three principles** of the 1794 *Foundation*:

| | Principle | Plain sense |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **The I posits itself** | Self-consciousness is an act, not a thing. The I exists only in its own act of self-awareness |
| **2** | **The I posits a not-I** | To be aware of itself as anything, the I must set something against itself: an object, a world |
| **3** | **The I posits, within itself, a divisible I opposed to a divisible not-I** | The two limit each other. That mutual limitation is the structure of all finite experience |

*Posit* (*setzen*, "to set" or "to place") means to establish something by an act of mind. *Not-I* is everything that is not the self.

**What this means.** The "I" here is not your individual personality. It is the activity of self-consciousness as such. And the not-I is not mere illusion. The world is real for us, as the resistance the I runs into, which Fichte called a **check** (*Anstoss*). **The world exists so that we have something to act on.** Fichte's idealism gives primacy to the **practical**: we are first agents, striving, and only then knowers.

**Its ethics and politics.** Recognition: I become a self only when summoned to freedom by another free being. This idea of **mutual recognition** passed straight to Hegel.

**Objections.**

- **Solipsism.** If the I posits the not-I, is the world the creation of my mind? Fichte denied it, saying the absolute I is not the empirical individual. Critics found the distinction slippery.
- **Kant's verdict.** In an open declaration of 1799, Kant publicly disowned the Wissenschaftslehre, calling it, in paraphrase, an indefensible system: mere logic, which by itself can yield no content and no knowledge of objects.
- **Interpretation.** Fichte rewrote the Wissenschaftslehre many times. What his late versions say, and how far they move from subjective idealism, is a live scholarly field.
Schelling: nature philosophy and the ide:
**Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling (1775–1854)** was a prodigy. At the Protestant seminary in Tübingen, the *Stift*, he shared a room with **Hegel** and the poet **Hölderlin**, both five years older. At 23 he was a professor at Jena (1798), alongside Fichte and close to the Romantic circle of the Schlegel brothers and Novalis. He lived long enough to see his fame eclipsed by Hegel's and then, in a sense, restored.

**His break with Fichte.** Fichte had made nature merely the not-I: the material the I acts on. **Schelling thought this left nature dead.** For Romantics, nature was alive, creative and full of meaning, not a mechanism or an obstacle.

**Nature philosophy (*Naturphilosophie*)**, set out in *Ideas for a Philosophy of Nature* (1797) and *On the World Soul* (1798):

- **Nature is a self-organising, productive whole**, driven by opposed forces (attraction and repulsion, positive and negative charge) that rise through stages: matter, light, magnetism, electricity, chemistry, life, and finally mind.
- **Mind is nature become aware of itself.** Nature is, in effect, spirit that does not yet know itself; spirit is nature that does. (This is a paraphrase of one of his best-known formulas.)
- So **nature need not be derived from mind, as Fichte did. Both are expressions of one underlying reality.**

**The *System of Transcendental Idealism* (1800)** worked the other way, from mind to nature, and ended in **art**. In a work of genius, conscious intention and unconscious creative force are fused. **Art reveals the unity of nature and mind** better than philosophy can.

**The philosophy of identity (from 1801).** The ground of both nature and mind is **the Absolute**: a pure identity, neither subject nor object, from which both emerge as different degrees of one reality. It is grasped by **intellectual intuition**, a direct seeing of the Absolute which Kant said we do not have.

**Hegel's objection.** In the preface to his *Phenomenology* (1807), Hegel mocked an Absolute in which all differences simply vanish, comparing it to the night in which all cows are black (a paraphrase). Hegel's point was that an identity grasped all at once, by intuition, explains nothing; the Absolute must be worked out through its differences, by thought. The two old friends were estranged.

**The late Schelling.** In *Philosophical Investigations into the Essence of Human Freedom* (1809) he asked how real freedom, including the freedom to do evil, could exist in a world grounded in God. In 1841 he was called to Berlin to counter the Hegelians. His lectures were attended by **Kierkegaard, Engels and Bakunin**. He distinguished **negative philosophy**, which deals with what things are, from **positive philosophy**, which deals with the bare fact **that** they exist, which reason cannot derive.

**Assessing him.** Nature philosophy was attacked by working scientists as speculation without experiment, and parts of it were simply wrong. But it also inspired real research: Ørsted, who discovered electromagnetism in 1820, is often cited as one scientist it influenced. Many now credit the late Schelling with anticipating existentialism: thought cannot produce existence. How unified his many systems are is a matter of scholarly dispute.
Hegel: the Phenomenology of Spirit and t:
**Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel was born in Stuttgart on 27 August 1770 and died in Berlin on 14 November 1831**, during a cholera epidemic. His career was slow:

| Years | Where | What |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1788–93 | Tübingen seminary | Rooms with Schelling and Hölderlin; they cheer the French Revolution |
| 1793–1800 | Bern, Frankfurt | House tutor; early writings on religion |
| 1801–07 | Jena | Lecturer; the *Phenomenology* finished as Napoleon defeated Prussia at Jena (October 1806) |
| 1807–16 | Bamberg, Nuremberg | Newspaper editor, then head of a secondary school; *Science of Logic* (1812–16) |
| 1816–18 | Heidelberg | Professor; *Encyclopedia of the Philosophical Sciences* (1817) |
| 1818–31 | Berlin | Professor; *Philosophy of Right* (1820); the most famous philosopher in Germany |

**The *Phenomenology of Spirit* (1807).** *Phenomenology* here means a study of how things appear to consciousness. *Spirit* translates *Geist*, which also means "mind". The book traces **consciousness through a series of shapes**, each one a way of taking the world to be, each one breaking down on its own terms and passing into the next. It starts with the simplest, sense-certainty (the belief that the richest knowledge is just "this, here, now"), and ends with **absolute knowing**. Hegel called the path a **way of despair** (*Weg der Verzweiflung*), since at each stage consciousness loses its certainty.

**The master and slave** (in German *Herrschaft und Knechtschaft*, "lordship and bondage") is the book's most famous section. Its argument, in the standard reading:

1. Self-consciousness wants **recognition**. I can be sure I am a free self only if another self acknowledges me as one. Things cannot do this; only another person can.
2. Two self-consciousnesses meet, each wanting recognition from the other, without giving it. They fight a **struggle to the death**, each proving it is free by risking its life.
3. If one dies, there is no one left to recognise the winner. So one yields from **fear of death**, and becomes the **slave**; the other becomes the **master**.
4. **The master's victory is hollow.** He is recognised only by someone he regards as a thing, which is no recognition at all. He depends on the slave's labour and lives in idle consumption.
5. **The slave, through fear and through work**, shapes the world and sees himself in what he makes. He gains a self-consciousness the master lacks.
6. So **the relation inverts**: the truth of mastery is servitude, and the truth of servitude is a beginning of freedom.

The section then moves on to Stoicism, Scepticism and the "unhappy consciousness", ways of seeking freedom in thought alone.

**How it has been read.** As an account of **individual psychology**, of **history** (ancient slavery and its ending), or of the **logic of recognition** that any free society needs. **Marx** read labour as the key. **Alexandre Kojève's** Paris lectures (1933–39) made it the heart of Hegel for a generation of French thinkers. Many scholars now think Kojève overplayed it. Its place in the book is disputed.

**Objection.** Is mutual recognition really required for self-consciousness, or is Hegel describing only one historical pattern? The modern **politics of recognition** (Charles Taylor, Axel Honneth) builds on Hegel's answer.
Hegel's dialectic, Geist and the Science:
**Spirit (*Geist*).** For Hegel, reality is not ultimately a collection of things, nor the private ideas of one mind. It is **spirit coming to know itself**: a rational structure that develops through nature, human minds, societies and history, and that becomes fully self-conscious in human knowledge. Hegel divides spirit into three:

| Level | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| **Subjective spirit** | the individual mind: sensation, consciousness, thought |
| **Objective spirit** | mind made real in the world: law, morality, family, society, state |
| **Absolute spirit** | spirit knowing itself, in **art**, **religion** and **philosophy** |

**Whether this is metaphysics.** The traditional reading takes Hegel to hold that a cosmic mind, the **Absolute**, is the true reality, which some readers identify with God. A **non-metaphysical** reading (Klaus Hartmann, Terry Pinkard, Robert Pippin) takes him to continue Kant: a theory of the categories of thought and of the social conditions of reason, with no cosmic mind. **This is one of the big disputes in Hegel scholarship.**

**The dialectic, as Hegel did and didn't describe it.**

- **The myth.** The formula "thesis, antithesis, synthesis" is often attributed to Hegel. **He did not use it as a description of his method.** The triad comes from Fichte and Schelling, and was popularised as "Hegel's method" by later writers, including Heinrich Moritz Chalybäus in the 1830s. Gustav Mueller's article "The Hegel Legend of Thesis-Antithesis-Synthesis" (1958) made the point famous.
- **What Hegel described.** A concept is examined on its own terms; it turns out to contain a tension or contradiction; that tension drives it into another; and the outcome both cancels and keeps what came before. Hegel's word is ***aufheben***, which in ordinary German means both "to cancel" and "to preserve", and also "to lift up". It is often translated **"sublate"**.
- **Determinate negation.** When a position fails, the result is not mere nothing. It is a definite new position shaped by exactly how the old one failed. This is why the process has a direction.

**The *Science of Logic* (1812–16)** applies this to pure thought, from the emptiest category to the richest. The opening is famous:

1. **Being**: begin with the most indeterminate concept, pure being, with no qualities at all.
2. But being without any qualities is indistinguishable from **nothing**.
3. Thought passes from being to nothing and from nothing to being. That movement is **becoming**.

From there the *Logic* runs through three parts, **Being, Essence and the Concept**, ending in **the absolute Idea**. Logic, for Hegel, is not just rules of inference. It is the structure of thought, and so of reality, since he holds that the two are not finally separate.

**Objections.**

- **The opening.** Critics, from Trendelenburg in the 1840s onward, say the move from being to becoming smuggles in time and motion that pure thought does not contain.
- **Contradiction.** If Hegel means that real contradictions exist, he seems to break logic, since from a contradiction anything follows. Defenders reply that he means tensions and instabilities in concepts, not true contradictions in the logician's sense.
- **Obscurity.** Schopenhauer called Hegel a charlatan, and analytic philosophers long dismissed him. Since the 1970s there has been a strong Hegel revival, especially in the English-speaking world, and he is again read as a serious thinker about concepts, norms and society.
Hegel's Philosophy of Right and history:
**The *Philosophy of Right* (1820, title page dated 1821)** is Hegel's political philosophy. *Right* (*Recht*) means law, justice and rights together. Its subject is **freedom made real in institutions**.

**Its three parts:**

| Part | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| **Abstract right** | property, contract, crime and punishment: persons as bearers of rights |
| **Morality** | the inner world of conscience, intention and responsibility, Kant's territory |
| **Ethical life** (*Sittlichkeit*) | freedom lived in shared institutions: **family**, **civil society** and **the state** |

**The key move.** Kant's morality, Hegel argued, is the free individual asking what reason demands. But by itself it is empty: the "empty formalism" objection from earlier. **Real freedom needs a social world** in which rational institutions give duties content and people recognise themselves in the laws they live under. **Civil society** is the market and its associations, the sphere of individual needs; Hegel was among the first to analyse it, and saw that it produces poverty it cannot cure. **The state** is the highest form of ethical life. By this he means the whole constitutional community, a constitutional monarchy with representative estates and the rule of law, not just the government.

**The preface** holds two famous, and much argued over, claims, both given here in paraphrase:

- **What is rational is actual, and what is actual is rational.** Conservatives read it as approval of the Prussian state. Hegel's defenders note that by *actual* (*wirklich*) he meant not whatever exists but what fully realises its rational nature.
- **The owl of Minerva flies only at dusk.** Philosophy understands a form of life only once it has matured, and cannot tell the world what it ought to be.

**History as the progress of freedom.** In lectures given in Berlin, published after his death in 1837, Hegel argued that **world history is the progress of the consciousness of freedom.** His scheme, in outline:

1. In the ancient **Oriental** world, as he called it, **one** was known to be free: the despot.
2. In the **Greek and Roman** worlds, **some** were free: citizens, not slaves.
3. In the **Germanic, Christian** world, all are known to be free, as humans.

Individuals pursue their own passions, but through them reason achieves its ends. Hegel called this the **cunning of reason**.

**Objections.**

- **The authoritarian reading.** Karl Popper, in *The Open Society and Its Enemies* (1945), attacked Hegel as a prophet of the totalitarian state. Most Hegel scholars now judge that a caricature: Hegel defended property, conscience, the rule of law and representation. But the debate over how liberal he was continues.
- **Eurocentrism.** The scheme ranks the world with Europe at its peak. Hegel's notorious claim that **Africa has no history** is now almost universally rejected as false, and as prejudice.
- **The end of history.** Does the story stop with his own time? Hegel was careful not to predict, but his successors split over exactly this point.
The Right and Left Hegelians:
**When Hegel died in 1831** his school dominated German universities. Within a decade it had split, over **religion** first and **politics** second. The question was what Hegel's claim that the rational is actual meant in practice. Does it bless the existing order, or demand that the existing order be made rational?

**The labels** come from **David Friedrich Strauss (1808–1874)**. His *Life of Jesus Critically Examined* (1835–36) treated the gospels' miracles as **myth**: the early Church's expression of ideas in the form of stories. It caused a scandal, and cost Strauss his career. Replying to his critics in 1837, he sorted Hegelians into a **Right, Centre and Left**, on the model of the French parliament, according to how they read Hegel on Christ and the gospel history.

**The Right, or Old, Hegelians** held that Hegel's philosophy and Protestant Christianity agree, and that the Prussian state was broadly rational. They included Karl Friedrich Göschel and Hermann Hinrichs. They kept Hegel in the universities, edited his works, and are now little read.

**The Left, or Young, Hegelians** took Hegel's method, the dialectic, as more important than his system, and turned it against religion and the state:

| Thinker | Dates | Contribution |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **David Friedrich Strauss** | 1808–1874 | The gospels as myth |
| **Bruno Bauer** | 1809–1882 | Went further: the gospels as literary invention; open atheism; dismissed from Bonn in 1842 |
| **Ludwig Feuerbach** | 1804–1872 | *The Essence of Christianity* (1841): God is **humanity's own nature projected** outside itself and worshipped |
| **Arnold Ruge** | 1802–1880 | Radical journals; later a democrat in exile |
| **Max Stirner** | 1806–1856 | *The Ego and Its Own* (1844): every ideal (God, Man, the State, morality) is a "spook" the individual should cast off |
| **Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels** | 1818–1883; 1820–1895 | Turned Hegel's dialectic to material and economic history |

**Feuerbach's move** is the key one. Hegel had said that spirit expresses itself in the human world. Feuerbach inverted this: **it is humans who express themselves in the idea of spirit.** Theology, he said, is really anthropology. Marx, in the **Theses on Feuerbach** (written 1845), praised the inversion but said Feuerbach stopped too soon: the task was not only to interpret the world but to change it (a paraphrase). For Feuerbach's argument as an argument about God, see the Theology curriculum.

**Why the split matters.** The same Hegel produced defenders of throne and altar and the founders of revolutionary socialism. Both sides had texts to cite. **Whether Hegel himself was a conservative, a liberal reformer or a closet radical is still disputed.**

**The wider afterlife.** Hegelianism also spread abroad later in the century: to Britain (T. H. Green, F. H. Bradley), to Italy, and to the United States, where a group in St Louis founded the *Journal of Speculative Philosophy* (1867), the first American journal devoted to philosophy. In Germany, by the 1860s, a "back to Kant" movement, **Neo-Kantianism**, was rising against Hegel's grand system.

**Next stage.** Schopenhauer and Kierkegaard rebelled against Hegel from opposite sides. Feuerbach and Marx came out of the Left. That is where Stage 11 begins.
Looking back: what Kant and the idealist:
In about sixty years, from Kant's *Critique* in 1781 to the Hegelian split around 1840, German philosophy changed the questions everyone after it would ask.

**What was broadly settled** (in the sense that few philosophers since have gone back):

- **Mind is not a passive mirror.** Experience is shaped by concepts and forms the mind brings, whether these are fixed (Kant), social and historical (Hegel), or linguistic (Hamann, Herder). Some version of this is now common ground in philosophy and in cognitive science.
- **The old metaphysical proofs were in trouble.** Kant's attacks on rational psychology and on the ontological argument in its classical form are widely accepted, even by those who defend newer versions.
- **Autonomy and dignity.** Kant's idea that persons have a worth beyond price, and that morality is a law reason gives itself, became the backbone of modern talk of human rights.
- **Reason has a history.** After Herder and Hegel it became hard to think about knowledge, morality or politics without asking how they developed.

**What was left open:**

| Question | Where it stands |
| --- | --- |
| **Are there synthetic a priori truths?** | Kant said yes. Logicism, non-Euclidean geometry and Quine pushed against him. Still debated |
| **What is the thing in itself?** | Kant kept it; Fichte dropped it; Hegel called it incoherent. Two-world and two-aspect readings still contend |
| **Did Kant answer Hume?** | The Second Analogy is admired and contested. Many think its main argument does not quite work as stated |
| **Is the categorical imperative a usable test?** | Hegel's empty-formalism charge and the murderer at the door are still discussed. Kantian ethics remains one of the three main theories, beside consequentialism and virtue ethics |
| **Freedom and nature** | Kant placed freedom outside time. Whether that makes sense, or whether freedom must be found within nature, is still argued |
| **Was Hegel a metaphysician?** | Cosmic-spirit and non-metaphysical readings both have strong defenders |
| **Hegel's politics** | Conservative, liberal or radical: the Right–Left split never ended |

**Where these thinkers stand in the long conversation.** Kant is generally ranked with Plato and Aristotle among the most important philosophers; his questions frame most later work, analytic and continental alike. Hegel is more divisive. For one tradition he is the summit of philosophy; for another, a cautionary tale about systems, though his reputation has risen steeply since the 1970s.

**What Stage 11 picks up.**

- **Schopenhauer** took Kant's thing in itself and named it: **will**, blind and striving.
- **Kierkegaard** answered Hegel's system with the existing individual, who cannot be absorbed into any system.
- **Feuerbach and Marx** turned the Left Hegelian critique of religion into a critique of society and economics.
- **Mill and Comte** took the other road, of empiricism and science, and **Nietzsche** asked what is left once the God that Kant made room for is no longer believed in.

**One line to carry forward:** Kant asked what reason can know, and drew a boundary. The next century asked who draws it, in what history, and in whose interest.
Context: Europe after Hegel, from the ra:
Hegel died in Berlin in November 1831. For a few years his system seemed to have finished philosophy: reason, history, religion and the state all fitted into one great story of Spirit coming to know itself. The nineteenth century is largely the story of people walking out of that building, by different doors.

**The world was changing faster than any system could hold.**

| Change | What it pressed on philosophers |
| --- | --- |
| **The industrial revolution** (Britain first, then Belgium, France, Germany) | factories, cities, child labour, a new working class. Who gains from all this wealth, and is the worker free? |
| **Revolutions**: 1830, and the wave of **1848** across Europe | can society be remade by reason, or by force? |
| **The railway, the telegraph, the newspaper** | public opinion becomes a power; the reading public grows |
| **Science's prestige**: chemistry, geology, thermodynamics, and **Darwin's *Origin of Species* (1859)** | is science the only real knowledge? Where does that leave ethics, religion and metaphysics? |
| **Biblical criticism**: David Friedrich Strauss's *Life of Jesus* (1835) | can Christianity survive being read as history and myth? |
| **Mass politics**: wider votes, unions, the "woman question" | who counts, and how far may the majority govern the minority? |

**The Young Hegelians.** In the 1830s and 1840s a group of Hegel's younger German readers (Strauss, Bruno Bauer, Ludwig Feuerbach, and for a while Karl Marx) kept Hegel's method, history moving through conflict, and threw out his conclusion that the Prussian state and Christian religion were reason made real. The "Right Hegelians" kept the conclusion. This split is the seed of Feuerbach and Marx.

**Four questions run through the stage:**

1. **What happens when God is no longer believed in?** Feuerbach and Marx say: humanity reclaims what it projected. Nietzsche says: the floor falls out of morality, and few have noticed. Kierkegaard says: faith was never a matter of the crowd's belief in the first place.
2. **Is the individual swallowed by the system?** Kierkegaard against Hegel; Mill against the tyranny of public opinion; Nietzsche against the herd.
3. **Can ethics be made scientific?** Bentham, Mill and Sidgwick try to put morality on one principle, the greatest happiness. Comte wants a science of society.
4. **What is the mind, and what is truth, once philosophy takes science seriously?** Schopenhauer turns Kant inside out; the American pragmatists ask what difference a belief makes; Brentano founds a descriptive psychology that leads straight into the twentieth century.

**One more change: who philosophers were.** Many of this stage's great names held no university post. Schopenhauer lived on inherited money; Kierkegaard wrote from his flat in Copenhagen; Marx was a journalist and exile in London; Mill worked for the East India Company; Nietzsche retired from his professorship at 34 through ill health. Philosophy was being written for the reading public, and sometimes against the professors.

**The Christian thinkers here** (Kierkegaard, Solovyov, Brentano in his early years) are read as philosophers: what they argued, and whether it holds. Their theology is taken up in the Theology curriculum.
Schopenhauer: the world as will and repr:
**Arthur Schopenhauer** (1788–1860), born in Danzig, son of a merchant, published his main work, ***The World as Will and Representation***, in 1818 (dated 1819; enlarged with a second volume in 1844). It sold almost nothing. In 1820 he lectured in Berlin at the same hour as Hegel, whom he despised; hardly anyone came. Fame arrived only in the 1850s, after the essays of *Parerga and Paralipomena* (1851).

**He began from Kant.** Kant (Stage 10) had argued that we know only **appearances**, things as our minds must shape them in space, time and the categories such as cause, and never the **thing in itself**, things as they are apart from us. Schopenhauer accepted this and pushed it.

**Half one: the world as representation.** A *representation* (German *Vorstellung*, which older translators render "idea") is anything present to a mind. His book opens, in the translation by R. B. Haldane and J. Kemp (1883):

> "The world is my idea:"—this is a truth which holds good for everything that lives and knows

So: no object without a subject. The sun I know is a sun-as-seen. And the whole of science, he said, is governed by one rule, the **principle of sufficient reason** (everything has a ground why it is so rather than not), which applies only inside appearance.

**Half two: the world as will.** Can we ever get behind the appearance? Schopenhauer said yes, at one point: **our own bodies**. I see my arm move as an object among objects; but I also know it from inside, as my **willing**. The act of will and the movement of the arm are not two events, cause and effect; they are **one thing known in two ways**.

His argument, set out:

1. I know my body in two ways: as representation, and from within as will.
2. Everything else in nature appears to me only as representation.
3. If other things have an inner nature at all, the best clue we have to it is the one case known from inside.
4. So the inner nature of everything, the thing in itself, is **will**.

**"Will" here is not conscious choice.** It is blind striving: the pull of gravity, the growth of a plant, the instinct of an animal, the sex drive, the will to live. In us it becomes conscious; in a stone it is not. It is one, not many, since number belongs to space and time, which belong only to appearance.

**Objections:**

- **The leap at premise 4.** Why think a stone has an inner side at all, let alone one like my willing? Critics call this an argument from analogy stretched past breaking. Schopenhauer's reply: the alternative is that everything except me is a mere phantom, which he calls a position no one can refute and no one can hold, except in a madhouse.
- **Inconsistency with Kant.** Kant said the thing in itself cannot be known. If will is known through inner sense, it is known *in time*, so it too is appearance. Schopenhauer partly conceded this in the 1844 second volume: will is the thing in itself **as nearly as we can know it**, not the thing in itself unveiled. How far he retreats is a live scholarly dispute.

**Why it matters:** Schopenhauer put **non-rational striving** at the heart of reality and of the self, before Darwin and before Freud. And he was the first major Western philosopher to read the Upanishads and Buddhist texts closely and with respect, finding in them, he said, his own conclusions.
Schopenhauer: pessimism, art and the den:
If reality is blind will, what is life like? Schopenhauer's answer made him the great philosopher of **pessimism**: the view that existence is, on balance, bad, and that it would have been better not to be.

**The argument from the structure of desire:**

1. To will is to want what one lacks; lack is a kind of pain.
2. When a desire is satisfied, the satisfaction is brief, and either a new desire arises or **boredom** sets in.
3. So life swings like a pendulum **between pain and boredom**.
4. Pleasure is only the momentary removal of a pain: it is **negative**; pain is what is felt as **positive**.
5. And at the level of nature, will devours itself: every animal lives by the death of others.
6. So, on balance, existence is suffering.

**Objections:**

- **Premise 4 is doubtful.** Many pleasures, a taste, a piece of music, the warmth of a friendship, do not seem to be mere relief from a prior pain. Most commentators think this is the argument's weakest step.
- **"On balance" needs a measure** of pleasure against pain, and Schopenhauer offers none. He leans on vivid examples.
- **Nietzsche's later objection** (lesson 24): the judgement "life is bad" is itself a symptom, the verdict of weariness, not a discovery.

**Three ways out, in rising order.**

**1. Art.** In aesthetic contemplation we stop wanting things and simply look. For that moment we become, in Haldane and Kemp's translation, a "pure will-less subject of knowledge", and see not this object but its **Idea** (here in Plato's sense: the eternal type it expresses). Release from willing is release from pain. The arts form a ladder, from architecture (showing gravity and rigidity) up to tragedy. **Music** stands apart: it does not copy Ideas; it **copies the will itself**, which is why it speaks so directly. This made him the philosopher of composers, Wagner above all.

**2. Compassion.** The basis of morality, he argued in *On the Basis of Morality* (1840), is not Kant's duty but **compassion** (*Mitleid*): feeling another's suffering as one's own. Its deep ground is metaphysical: since will is one, the line between you and me belongs only to appearance. The cruel man **does not see through** that line; the compassionate man does.

**3. The denial of the will.** The highest path is to stop willing at all: chastity, poverty, fasting, the life of the ascetic. Schopenhauer saw this in Christian saints, Hindu renunciants and the Buddhist ideal of extinguishing craving. What remains, he ended his first volume, is to us **nothing**; but to those who have turned the will around, our world, with all its suns, is nothing.

**A puzzle he never fully solved:** if the will is everything, what does the denying? And if will is the only force, how can it turn against itself? He called it the one point where freedom breaks into appearance, and admitted it was mysterious. Whether this is a contradiction or an honest limit is disputed.

**Note:** he rejected suicide as a way out, arguing that the suicide *wills life* and is only refusing its conditions; it destroys one appearance and leaves the will untouched.

**Influence:** Wagner, Tolstoy, Thomas Mann, the young Nietzsche, and the young Wittgenstein all read him closely. His ethics of compassion also included animals, which he defended against cruelty with unusual force for his time.
Kierkegaard: the pseudonyms and the thre:
**Søren Kierkegaard** (1813–1855) lived almost his whole life in Copenhagen, on a fortune left by his father, a strict and melancholy Lutheran. In 1840 he became engaged to Regine Olsen and in 1841 broke it off, for reasons he never fully explained. Then, in about twelve years, he wrote a vast body of work and died at 42.

**He wrote against Hegel's "system"**, as taught in Copenhagen, which he thought explained everything except the one thing that matters: how *I*, an existing individual, am to live. You cannot live in a system, he said, any more than in a palace you have built but sleep in the shed beside it.

**The pseudonyms.** Many of his books are signed by invented authors, each with a point of view:

| Book (year) | "Author" |
| --- | --- |
| *Either/Or* (1843) | edited by **Victor Eremita** |
| *Fear and Trembling* (1843) | **Johannes de Silentio** |
| *Philosophical Fragments* (1844) and *Concluding Unscientific Postscript* (1846) | **Johannes Climacus** |
| *The Concept of Anxiety* (1844) | **Vigilius Haufniensis** |
| *The Sickness unto Death* (1849) | **Anti-Climacus** |

He also published "upbuilding discourses" under his own name. **Why the masks?** His word was **indirect communication**. You cannot hand someone a way of existing as you hand them a fact; you can only show them possibilities and leave them alone with the choice. So each pseudonym speaks from inside a way of life, and the reader must judge. **The rule of reading:** do not cite a pseudonym as Kierkegaard's settled view; he asked this himself. How far the pseudonyms speak for him is a central dispute.

**The three stages (or "spheres") of existence:**

**1. The aesthetic.** Life lived for the interesting moment: pleasure, beauty, novelty, the avoidance of boredom. Its figures in *Either/Or* volume 1 are the seducer and the clever young man "A". Its secret is **despair**: it never chooses, so it has no self, only moods. Its trick against boredom is "crop rotation", changing not the field but the way one farms it.

**2. The ethical.** Life of commitment: marriage, work, duty, the universal. In volume 2, Judge William writes to "A" urging him to **choose himself**, to take responsibility for his life as a whole. The title's either/or is this: aesthetic or ethical. And the choice is not argued for from outside; one is either inside the ethical or not.

**3. The religious.** Here the self stands before God as a single individual. Climacus divides it in two: **Religiousness A**, the inward relation to the eternal that any serious person might reach; and **Religiousness B**, Christianity proper, which rests on the **paradox** that the eternal God became a man in time, a thing reason cannot master and faith must embrace.

**How one moves between them:** not by logic but by a **leap**, a choice. The stages are not a ladder everyone climbs, and the earlier ones are not abolished but put in their place.

**Objections:** if the move between stages cannot be reasoned, is the choice arbitrary? Alasdair MacIntyre (*After Virtue*, 1981) pressed this, reading Kierkegaard as making morality a groundless choice. Defenders reply that this misreads him: the higher stage is not chosen blindly but is found by **living the lower one to its end** and meeting its despair.

The Christian claims are taken up in the Theology curriculum; here, the question is whether the analysis of ways of living holds.
Kierkegaard: Fear and Trembling and the:
***Fear and Trembling*** (1843), signed by "Johannes de Silentio" (John of silence), is a meditation on one story: **Genesis 22**, where God commands Abraham to sacrifice his son Isaac, and Abraham rises early, travels three days to Mount Moriah, binds the boy, and raises the knife before an angel stops him.

**Silentio's point: we praise Abraham as the father of faith, and we have not understood what we are praising.** If a man in church went home and did what Abraham did, we would call him a murderer. So either Abraham is a murderer, or there is something higher than ethics.

**The ethical**, here, is **the universal**: duties that apply to everyone and can be explained to anyone (this is close to Kant and Hegel). In the ethical, the individual's task is to express himself in the universal; to put the private above it is temptation.

**Silentio's three "problemata" (problems):**

1. **Is there a teleological suspension of the ethical?** (*Teleological*: for the sake of an end, a *telos*.) That is: can the ethical be set aside, not abolished, for the sake of a higher end, the individual's relation to God?
2. **Is there an absolute duty to God?** If there is, then the individual stands higher than the universal.
3. **Was Abraham right to keep silent** before Sarah, Eliezer and Isaac? In ethics we must explain ourselves; Abraham cannot, because what he does cannot be put in universal terms.

**Silentio's answer:** if faith exists, then **yes** to all three. If not, Abraham is lost.

**The contrast with the tragic hero.** Agamemnon sacrifices his daughter Iphigenia for the sake of the army and the city. Terrible, but understandable: he gives up one ethical duty for a higher **ethical** one, and everyone weeps with him. Abraham has no such higher universal. He acts for God's sake alone, and **no one can understand him**.

**The knight of infinite resignation and the knight of faith.** The first gives up what he loves and makes peace with its loss in the eternal: Silentio says he can do this himself. The knight of faith does that **and also**, by virtue of the absurd (the usual English rendering of his phrase), believes he will receive it back in this life. Abraham gives up Isaac and still believes he will have Isaac. This **double movement** Silentio says he cannot make; he can only describe it from outside.

**The main interpretations (a real dispute):**

- **Divine command reading:** Kierkegaard holds that God's commands override morality.
- **Critique of Hegel and Danish complacency:** the target is a comfortable Christendom that thinks faith is easy and ethics is the highest thing; the book is an alarm, not a policy.
- **The religious as fulfilment:** the ethical is not destroyed but "suspended", relativised and returned, as Isaac is returned.

**The strongest objection** was stated before Kierkegaard by **Kant** (*The Conflict of the Faculties*, 1798): Abraham should have answered that he is quite sure he ought not to kill his innocent son, and far less sure that the voice commanding it is God. Whatever speaks against the moral law cannot be from God. Replies: this assumes ethics is the highest court, which is exactly what is in question; and Silentio's point is that faith carries **fear and trembling** precisely because there is no outside guarantee.

**Why it matters:** few books ask more sharply whether morality is the last word, and what it would mean if it were not. The theological reading of Genesis 22 is for the Theology curriculum.
Kierkegaard: anxiety, despair and the cl:
Three of Kierkegaard's ideas went on to shape twentieth-century existentialism, psychology and theology.

**1. Anxiety.** *The Concept of Anxiety* (1844, "Vigilius Haufniensis", the watchman of Copenhagen) distinguishes **fear**, which has an object (a dog, a cliff), from **anxiety** (Danish *Angest*, often translated "dread"), which has none. Anxiety is the feeling of one's own **freedom**: the dizziness of possibility. The book's image, paraphrased: anxiety is like the giddiness of someone looking down into an abyss, where the eye meets no ground and he senses that he could throw himself in. He describes it, in paraphrase, as an attraction that repels and a repulsion that attracts: we are drawn to and repelled by what we could do. Anxiety comes before sin and is not itself sin. It can ruin us, or educate us toward faith.

**2. Despair.** *The Sickness unto Death* (1849, "Anti-Climacus") opens with a famous definition of the self, paraphrased here: the self is a relation that relates itself to itself, and in doing so relates to the power that established it. A human being is a synthesis of opposites, **finite and infinite, temporal and eternal, necessity and possibility**, and the self is the activity of holding them together.

**Despair** is a misrelation in that self. Its forms:

| Form | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| **Unaware despair** | the most common; the person does not know he has a self to lose |
| **Despair of weakness** | **not willing to be oneself**: wishing to be someone else, or no one |
| **Despair of defiance** | **willing to be oneself**, but on one's own terms, as one's own creator |

The cure, Anti-Climacus says, is that the self, in willing to be itself, **rests transparently in the power that established it**: faith. Despair is not only a feeling; one can be in despair while feeling fine.

**3. "Subjectivity is truth."** In the *Concluding Unscientific Postscript* (1846), Johannes Climacus distinguishes two ways of asking about truth:

- **Objectively:** is what I believe true? This is the question of the scholar and scientist, which can only ever reach **approximation**, never certainty.
- **Subjectively:** am I related to it **truly**? With what passion, inwardness and risk do I hold it?

For the questions that concern one's existence (how to live, how to die, God), Climacus claims, the **how** matters more than the **what**. His famous example, paraphrased: a person in a Christian land who prays to the true God in a false spirit prays in untruth; a person in an idolatrous land who prays with the whole passion of the infinite to an idol prays in truth.

**Is this relativism? The standard reading says no.** Climacus is not saying any passionate belief is true. He is saying that, for existential matters, objective proof is not available, and **the passionate commitment of the whole self under uncertainty** is the only fitting relation. Faith, he says, is holding fast to an objective uncertainty with the most passionate inwardness.

**Objections:** passion is no guide to truth (the fanatic is passionate); and why should the infinitely important question be the one we are least able to settle by evidence? **Reply:** Climacus agrees there is no guarantee; that is the risk he calls faith. Whether his definition then makes all deep commitments equally fitting is debated.

**After him:** Heidegger's anxiety, Sartre's anguish and bad faith, Barth's theology, and Wittgenstein, who is reported to have called him the most profound thinker of the nineteenth century, all draw on these pages.
Feuerbach: theology is anthropology:
**Ludwig Feuerbach** (1804–1872) studied under Hegel in Berlin, then turned against him. His academic career was ended in 1830 by an anonymous pamphlet attacking personal immortality, whose authorship became known; he lived thereafter as a private scholar in a Bavarian village. His great book, ***The Essence of Christianity*** (1841), was translated into English in 1854 by **Marian Evans, who wrote novels as George Eliot**.

**The thesis: the secret of theology is anthropology.** Anthropology here means the study of human beings. When people speak of God, Feuerbach says, they are really speaking about **human nature**, without knowing it.

**How the argument runs:**

1. Animals have consciousness of objects; humans alone have consciousness of their own **species**, of human nature as such: reason, will and love, without limit.
2. The individual feels limited; the species is not. So humans imagine those powers perfected and **set them outside themselves**, as a being: God. This is **projection**.
3. God's attributes are therefore human attributes, idealised: infinite wisdom, infinite love, infinite will.
4. In worshipping God, humans worship **their own nature**, made strange to them.
5. So the more is given to God, the less remains to man: to enrich God, man must become poor.

The English translation, early in the book:

> consciousness of the objective is the self-consciousness of man. We know the man by the object, by his conception of what is external to himself

(*The Essence of Christianity*, tr. George Eliot, 1854.)
