**The conclusion is not despair but recovery.** Feuerbach called himself not an atheist in the destructive sense, but someone who gives back to humanity what it had alienated. The aim is a religion of humanity. In Eliot's text: "Homo homini Deus est", **man is God to man**, and the highest love is the love of one human being for another.

**Alienation.** The key idea, inherited from Hegel and turned around: to be *alienated* is to make something that is yours into something foreign that stands over you. Hegel's Spirit alienates itself in nature and returns; for Feuerbach it is **man** who alienates himself in God, and must return.

**Objections:**

- **The genetic fallacy.** Explaining why people believe something does not show it false. A projection may also be a true perception: people projected a father onto God, but perhaps God is fatherly. Feuerbach's case shows at most that religion **could** arise without God; whether it did is a further question.
- **Which human nature?** Feuerbach speaks of "the species" in the abstract. Marx's complaint (next lessons): real humans live in particular social relations, and religion's roots must be sought there.
- **Theological replies**, notably Karl Barth's in the twentieth century, take Feuerbach seriously as a warning against religion that is only human self-praise, while denying his conclusion. That conversation belongs to the Theology curriculum.

**Why he matters:** Feuerbach is the bridge from Hegel to Marx, and the first full **projection theory** of religion, the ancestor of Marx's and Freud's. Marx's *Theses on Feuerbach* (written 1845, published by Engels in 1888) begins as a tribute and ends with the most famous line in his early work, which in paraphrase says: philosophers have only interpreted the world in various ways; the point is to change it.
Marx: alienated labour in the 1844 Manus:
**Karl Marx** (1818–1883) was born in Trier in the Rhineland, son of a lawyer of Jewish family who had converted to Lutheranism. He studied law and philosophy in Bonn and Berlin, among the Young Hegelians, took a doctorate in 1841 on Democritus and Epicurus, and became a radical journalist. Exiled from Germany, then from Paris and Brussels, he settled in **London in 1849** and stayed there until his death, much of it in poverty, supported by his friend and co-author **Friedrich Engels** (1820–1895), whose family owned a cotton mill in Manchester.

**The *Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844*** were written in Paris and **not published until 1932**. They are the young Marx's attempt to join Hegel, Feuerbach and the British economists. Their central idea is **alienated labour**.

**The starting point:** for Marx, what makes us human is **free, conscious, productive activity**. We are not just consumers. We shape the world by labour and, in doing so, express and develop ourselves; we see ourselves in what we make. He calls humanity's nature its **species-being** (a term from Feuerbach).

**Under capitalism, labour is alienated** in four ways:

| Alienated from | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| **The product** | what the worker makes belongs to someone else and stands over him as a hostile power: capital |
| **The activity** | work is forced, done only as a means to stay alive; the worker feels at home only when not working |
| **Species-being** | the free creative activity that makes us human is reduced to a mere means of survival |
| **Other people** | relations between people become relations between owners and the owned, buyer and seller |

**The parallel with Feuerbach is deliberate.** As in religion the more man puts into God the less he keeps, so in work: the more the worker produces, the poorer he becomes, and the world of things he makes grows in value as he loses it.

**The argument, compressed:**

1. Human flourishing consists in free, conscious, creative activity in community.
2. Under wage labour, workers sell their activity; its product and direction belong to others.
3. So under wage labour, most people are cut off from their own flourishing.
4. This is a result of a **social arrangement**, not of human nature or nature's scarcity.
5. So it can be changed.

**Objections:**

- **Premise 1 is a contested picture of the good life.** Many people find meaning outside work, in family, faith or leisure. Is Marx imposing an artist's or craftsman's ideal on everyone?
- **Is alienation a fact or a feeling?** If a worker is content, is he still alienated? Marx says yes, which makes the concept partly a normative judgement rather than a description.
- **Does abolishing private property cure it?** Critics point to the factories of the twentieth-century communist states, which were no less alienating, and some argue that the division of labour in any industrial society produces it.

**A scholarly dispute:** is there one Marx or two? Louis Althusser (1960s) argued for an **"epistemological break"** about 1845, after which the humanist talk of alienation was replaced by a science of history. Others, including many who read the 1844 texts after 1932, see the same moral concern running all the way through *Capital*. The dispute is unsettled.
Marx: historical materialism, base and s:
In *The German Ideology* (written with Engels, 1845–46, published only in 1932) and above all in a short **Preface** to *A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy* (1859), Marx set out the theory of history Engels later called **historical materialism**.

**"Materialism" here does not mean love of possessions, or only the view that everything is matter.** It means that the **material conditions of producing life**, how people get food, shelter and goods, are the foundation of society and the key to history, rather than ideas. Hegel had history driven by Spirit; Marx, he said, set Hegel back on his feet.

**The theory, in parts:**

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Productive forces** | tools, machines, land, raw materials, and human skill and knowledge |
| **Relations of production** | who owns and controls the forces, and who works for whom: master and slave, lord and serf, capitalist and wage-worker |
| **Mode of production** | the two together: ancient slavery, feudalism, capitalism |
| **The base** (or economic structure) | the sum of the relations of production |
| **The superstructure** | law, politics, and forms of social consciousness: religion, morality, philosophy, art |

**The core claims, as his best defenders state them:**

1. Productive forces tend to **develop** over history, because humans are inventive and want to escape scarcity.
2. A given set of relations of production lasts as long as it helps the forces to develop.
3. When the relations become **fetters** on the forces, an era of social revolution begins, and new relations replace them.
4. The superstructure is shaped by the base: legal and political institutions exist largely because they stabilise the economic structure.
5. So the broad course of history is set by the growth of productive power, and the next stage after capitalism is socialism.

The 1859 Preface's most quoted claim, paraphrased: it is not people's consciousness that determines their being, but their social being that determines their consciousness.

**How strong is "determines"?** This is the main dispute. Engels, in letters after Marx's death (for example to Joseph Bloch, 1890), insisted that the economic factor is decisive only **in the last instance**, and that the superstructure acts back on the base. **G. A. Cohen**, in *Karl Marx's Theory of History: A Defence* (1978), reconstructed the theory as a **functional explanation**: the base has the character it has *because* that character helps the forces grow; the superstructure has its character *because* it stabilises the base. This revived the theory among analytic philosophers.

**Objections:**

- **Unfalsifiable?** **Karl Popper** (*The Open Society and Its Enemies*, 1945) argued that Marx's theory began as a testable prediction (revolution in the most advanced industrial countries), failed the test, and was saved by reinterpretations that made it untestable. This is taken up in Stage 12.
- **Ideas cause too.** **Max Weber** (*The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism*, 1905) argued that religious ideas helped make capitalism possible. Defenders say Weber shows only that the superstructure acts back, which Engels allowed.
- **Where is the line?** Law seems to belong to the base too, since ownership is a legal relation. Cohen's reply: define relations of production in terms of effective power, not legal title.
- **Revolutions happened in the wrong places**: Russia (1917) and China (1949) were mostly peasant countries, not the advanced industrial ones the theory predicted.

**There is broad agreement** that the strong, mechanical version of the theory, with ideas as mere reflections, is false; whether a weaker version is both true and interesting remains disputed.
Marx: class struggle and ideology:
The **Communist Manifesto** (1848), written by Marx and Engels for a small workers' society on the eve of the 1848 revolutions, opens its first section with a sentence that sums up a theory. In Samuel Moore's English translation, edited by Engels (1888):

> The history of all hitherto existing societies is the history of class struggles.

**What a class is.** For Marx a class is defined by its **relation to the means of production**, not by income or manners. Under capitalism there are two main classes:

- the **bourgeoisie**: those who own the means of production (factories, land, capital);
- the **proletariat**: those who own nothing but their ability to work, and must sell it for wages.

Their interests conflict structurally: profits rise as wages fall, whatever any individual employer intends. **Class struggle** is the working-out of that conflict, sometimes hidden, sometimes open.

**The Manifesto's story:** the bourgeoisie was once revolutionary; it destroyed feudalism and created more productive power in a century than all previous generations together. But it calls into being the class that will bury it: the proletariat, concentrated in factories, increasingly organised, with nothing to lose. It ends, in Moore's translation: "WORKING MEN OF ALL COUNTRIES, UNITE!"

**Ideology.** Why don't the exploited simply see their situation and revolt? Marx's answer is **ideology**: ideas that serve the interests of the ruling class while appearing to be neutral, natural or eternal. *The German Ideology* argues, in paraphrase, that the ideas of the ruling class are in every age the ruling ideas, because the class that controls material production also controls the means of producing and spreading ideas.

Examples Marx gives or implies:

- Treating **private property** as a natural right rather than a historical arrangement.
- Treating the **market** as a sphere of free and equal exchange, while hiding the compulsion that drives the worker to it.
- **Religion**, which he called the sigh of the oppressed creature and the opium of the people (paraphrase of the 1844 introduction to his critique of Hegel's philosophy of right): a real consolation for real suffering, which by consoling keeps the suffering in place.

**Note on a phrase:** "false consciousness" is often attributed to Marx; it is in fact **Engels's**, in a letter of 1893 to Franz Mehring.

**The argument of ideology critique, set out:**

1. If a belief is widely held because it serves the interests of a dominant group, and would not be held otherwise, its being held is no evidence of its truth.
2. Many beliefs about society are held for that reason.
3. So they should be suspected, and examined for their social function.

**Objections:**

- **Self-reference.** Isn't Marxism an ideology too, serving the interests of revolutionary intellectuals? Marxists reply that the proletariat's interest, uniquely, is the interest of all humanity; critics find this convenient.
- **The genetic fallacy again.** Showing a belief serves the powerful does not show it is false; premise 1 claims only that its popularity is no evidence. Careful defenders accept this limit.
- **Classes have not polarised** as predicted. The middle classes grew; workers in many countries won votes, unions and welfare states through reform, not revolution.

**Why it matters:** "ideology", "class", and "who benefits from this belief?" became tools used far beyond Marxism, in sociology, history, and the "hermeneutics of suspicion" (Paul Ricoeur's phrase for Marx, Nietzsche and Freud) of Stage 13.
Marx: surplus value as an argument, and:
***Capital***, volume 1, appeared in **1867**; volumes 2 and 3 were edited from Marx's manuscripts by Engels and published in 1885 and 1894. Its central argument claims to show that **capitalism rests on exploitation even when every exchange in it is fair**.

**The puzzle.** In a market, equal values are exchanged for equal values. Yet capitalists end the cycle with more money than they began with. Where does the extra come from, if no one is cheated?

**Marx's tools:**

- **The labour theory of value** (taken from Adam Smith and David Ricardo, Stage 9): the value of a commodity is set by the **socially necessary labour time** needed to produce it.
- **Labour power** versus **labour.** The worker does not sell his labour (his work); he sells his **labour power**, his capacity to work for a period, say a day.
- The value of labour power, like any commodity, is the labour time needed to produce it: what it costs to keep the worker alive and able to work, and to raise the next generation.

**The argument, set out:**

1. Commodities exchange at their values (labour theory of value).
2. The capitalist buys labour power at its value: the cost of the worker's subsistence.
3. Suppose subsistence takes 4 hours of labour to produce, but the working day is 10 hours.
4. In 10 hours the worker produces 10 hours of value, and is paid the value of 4.
5. The remaining 6 hours' worth is **surplus value**, which the capitalist keeps, and from which profit, interest and rent are paid.
6. So exploitation, the taking of unpaid labour, lies at the heart of capitalism, **even though the wage was a fair exchange**.

The ratio of surplus to paid labour (here 6 to 4) Marx calls the **rate of exploitation**.

**The main criticisms:**

- **The labour theory of value.** The **marginalist revolution** of the early 1870s (William Stanley Jevons and Carl Menger in 1871, Léon Walras in 1874) explained prices by **marginal utility** and scarcity, not labour. Most economists today reject the labour theory of value; that is broad agreement within economics, though some Marxist economists dispute it.
- **The transformation problem.** In volume 3, Marx admits that actual prices do not match labour values, because profit rates tend to equalise across industries with different mixes of machines and labour. He offered a way to "transform" values into prices. **Eugen von Böhm-Bawerk** (*Karl Marx and the Close of His System*, 1896) argued this contradicts volume 1. Whether the transformation can be done consistently has been argued over for a century.
- **Other contributions.** The capitalist provides the machines, takes the risk, and waits for returns. Defenders reply that this is the very question: why should ownership of means of production, often inherited, entitle anyone to the product of another's labour?

**An important twentieth-century move.** Analytic Marxists, among them **G. A. Cohen** and **John Roemer** (1980s), argued that the **charge of exploitation does not need the labour theory of value**. It needs only the claim that workers, lacking means of production, are **forced** to work for others, who appropriate part of what the workers make without making a matching contribution. This turns the question from economics into **political philosophy**: is that arrangement unjust? And that question is open, taken up by Rawls and Nozick in Stage 14.

**Why it matters:** whatever the verdict, Marx's argument makes a philosophical point that survives: a system can be built entirely of voluntary, fair-looking exchanges and still be judged unjust as a whole.
Comte: positivism and the law of three s:
**Auguste Comte** (1798–1857), of Montpellier, was for some years secretary to the social reformer Henri de Saint-Simon, then broke with him and, after a mental breakdown in 1826, gave the lectures that became the six-volume ***Course of Positive Philosophy*** (1830–1842). He coined the word **sociology** and, later, the word **altruism**.

**Positivism** is Comte's view that **genuine knowledge is knowledge of observable phenomena and the laws relating them**, reached by the methods of the sciences. Questions about hidden essences, first causes and final purposes are not answered but **set aside** as beyond knowledge. Science asks *how* things happen, by which constant laws, not *why* in the ultimate sense.

**The law of three stages.** Every branch of knowledge, and the human mind as a whole, passes through three stages:

| Stage | How it explains the world | Example: why does fire burn? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Theological** | by the will of gods or spirits; reaches its height in a single God | a god or spirit of fire |
| **Metaphysical** | by abstract forces or essences, which Comte saw as gods turned into abstractions | fire has a burning nature, a vital principle, a "phlogiston" |
| **Positive** | by observed regularities and laws, without asking for ultimate causes | the laws of combustion and chemistry |

The metaphysical stage is a **transition**: it dissolves theology but is itself replaced.

**The hierarchy of the sciences.** Sciences reach the positive stage in order of increasing complexity and decreasing generality: **mathematics, astronomy, physics, chemistry, biology, and finally sociology**, which depends on all the rest. Sociology was the last to be made scientific, and its task was to do for society what physics had done for nature: find its laws of **statics** (order) and **dynamics** (progress), and so end the chaos left by the French Revolution.

**The Religion of Humanity.** After 1845, under the influence of his love for **Clotilde de Vaux** (who died in 1846), Comte's later work, the *System of Positive Polity* (1851–54), proposed a new religion with Humanity as its object of worship, with secular saints and priests of science. **John Stuart Mill**, who had admired and funded him, wrote in *Auguste Comte and Positivism* (1865) that the early Comte was a great thinker and the later one a warning.

**The argument for the law of three stages, as its defenders put it:**

1. In every field where we now have real knowledge, explanation once appealed to divine will.
2. In each, it then passed through talk of essences and forces.
3. Each field that reached laws of phenomena then made reliable predictions and progress; earlier modes did not.
4. So the positive stage is the mature end of inquiry, and other fields, ethics and politics included, should follow.

**Objections:**

- **It is a historical generalisation, not a law**, and the history is tidied. Religious and scientific thinking have coexisted in the same minds (Newton, Pascal) and the same ages.
- **Self-refutation.** "Only knowledge of observable laws is genuine" is not itself a law of observable phenomena. On what basis is it known? This objection returns against the logical positivists in Stage 12.
- **Science needs unobservables.** Atoms, fields and genes go beyond what Comte allowed. He opposed, for instance, speculation about the chemistry of the stars as beyond knowledge; spectroscopy showed it within reach within a few years of his death.

**Why it matters:** "positivism" became a name for a whole attitude, that science is the measure of knowledge, which the **Vienna Circle** of the 1920s revived as logical positivism.
Bentham: the principle of utility and th:
**Jeremy Bentham** (1748–1832), a London lawyer who never practised, spent his long life designing reforms of law, prisons, parliament and education. His ***Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation*** was printed in 1780 and published in 1789. It opens:

> Nature has placed mankind under the governance of two sovereign masters, pain and pleasure. It is for them alone to point out what we ought to do, as well as to determine what we shall do.

(Text as given on Wikisource; Bentham wrote in English.)

**Two claims are packed into that sentence.** **Psychological hedonism**: pleasure and pain in fact determine what we do. **Ethical hedonism**: pleasure and pain determine what we *ought* to do. The two together are the root of his system.

**The principle of utility.** An action is right in proportion to its tendency to increase the happiness of those affected; wrong in proportion to its tendency to diminish it. **Happiness** means pleasure and the absence of pain. **Utility** means the property of a thing to produce benefit or happiness, or to prevent pain. This is the first great form of **utilitarianism**, a kind of **consequentialism**: the view that the rightness of an act depends only on its consequences.

**Each counts for one.** The happiness of everyone affected counts, equally: a lord's pleasure no more than a labourer's. In a famous footnote in chapter 17, Bentham extends this to animals: the question about them, in paraphrase, is not whether they can reason or talk, but **whether they can suffer**.

**The calculus.** To measure a pleasure or pain, Bentham lists its **dimensions**:

| Dimension | Question |
| --- | --- |
| Intensity | how strong? |
| Duration | how long? |
| Certainty | how likely? |
| Propinquity | how soon? |
| Fecundity | will it be followed by more of the same kind? |
| Purity | will it be followed by the opposite kind? |
| Extent | how many people does it reach? |

Sum the pleasures, subtract the pains, for each person affected, and compare acts. Later writers called this the **felicific calculus**; the name is not Bentham's own.

**The argument for utility, as Bentham states it:** he argues that it cannot be directly proved, since it is what proves everything else; but every opponent, he says, is found to appeal to it in the end, or to mere sentiment dressed up as principle (his list of such disguises includes the moral sense, right reason and the law of nature).

**Objections:**

- **Measurement.** Pleasures cannot be put on a single scale, and different people's cannot be compared. Defenders reply that we compare them roughly every day, in deciding whose need is greater.
- **Quality.** All pleasure is the same stuff, for Bentham: he held that, quantity of pleasure being equal, the child's game of push-pin is as good as poetry (paraphrase of *The Rationale of Reward*, 1825). Mill would revise this (next lesson).
- **Justice and rights.** If torturing one innocent person gave enough pleasure to enough others, the calculus seems to approve it. This **is the standing objection** to all simple utilitarianism. Utilitarians reply with rules, side-constraints, or by biting the bullet; the dispute is live.
- **Psychological hedonism** is widely rejected: people sacrifice pleasure for truth, duty, others, and posterity.
Mill: Utilitarianism and the higher plea:
**John Stuart Mill** (1806–1873) was raised by his father, the Scottish philosopher **James Mill**, a close friend of Bentham, as an experiment in education: Greek at three, Latin at eight, logic and political economy before his teens. At twenty, in 1826, he fell into a depression he describes in his *Autobiography* (1873). He recovered in part through poetry, Wordsworth above all, and came to think that Bentham's picture of human nature was too thin.

***Utilitarianism*** appeared in *Fraser's Magazine* in 1861 and as a book in 1863. It is short, written for the general reader, and the most read defence of the theory ever made. Mill states the principle (Gutenberg text):

> The creed which accepts as the foundation of morals, Utility, or the Greatest Happiness Principle, holds that actions are right in proportion as they tend to promote happiness, wrong as they tend to produce the reverse of happiness.

**The objection he set out to answer.** Critics, Mill reports, called utilitarianism "a doctrine worthy only of swine": if pleasure is all that matters, a pig's contented life is as good as a human's.

**Mill's reply: pleasures differ in quality, not only quantity.** Some pleasures, of the intellect, the feelings and imagination, and of moral sentiment, are **higher**: more desirable in kind, so that a small amount can outweigh a large amount of lower, bodily pleasure.

**How do we know which is higher? The test of competent judges.** Of two pleasures, the higher is the one that **almost everyone who has experienced both** decidedly prefers, even knowing it brings more discontent. His most famous lines:

> It is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied; better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied. And if the fool, or the pig, is of a different opinion, it is because they only know their own side of the question.

**The argument, set out:**

1. The only evidence of what is more desirable is what is preferred by those who know the options.
2. Those acquainted with both intellectual and bodily pleasures decidedly prefer the intellectual.
3. So intellectual pleasures are more desirable, even in smaller quantities.
4. So a doctrine of pleasure need not rank the pig's life with Socrates'.

**Objections:**

- **Inconsistency.** If pleasure is the only good, what makes one pleasure "better" except more pleasure? If something else does (dignity, nobility), then pleasure is not the only good, and Mill has left hedonism. This objection, pressed by F. H. Bradley and G. E. Moore, is widely thought to have force; some defenders reply that **quality is a dimension of pleasantness itself**, just as intensity is.
- **The judges.** Are competent judges unbiased? Mill himself admits that many who are capable of higher pleasures sink into lower ones. He answers that they lose the capacity first.
- **Elitism.** The test conveniently favours the tastes of educated Victorians. Mill's reply would be that anyone can become a competent judge, given education, which is why he cared so much about it.

**The rest of the book.** Chapter 2 also answers the objection that there is no time to calculate before acting: we have, he says, the whole past of humanity's experience about which acts tend to cause happiness, stored in **secondary rules** of ordinary morality. Chapter 5 argues that **justice** is the name for the most important and binding class of social utilities, those concerning security. Whether Mill was an **act** utilitarian (judge each act by its consequences) or a **rule** utilitarian (judge acts by rules whose general following maximises happiness) is a **genuine scholarly dispute**.
Mill: the proof of the principle of util:
Chapter 4 of *Utilitarianism* is titled "Of What Sort of Proof the Principle of Utility Is Susceptible." It is three pages long and is one of the most criticised passages in moral philosophy.

**Mill's caveat first.** Questions of ultimate ends, he says, are not amenable to direct proof, in the sense in which a theorem is proved. But considerations may be given that can move the intellect to assent, and this is equivalent to proof.

**The argument itself:**

> The only proof capable of being given that an object is visible, is that people actually see it. The only proof that a sound is audible, is that people hear it: and so of the other sources of our experience. In like manner, I apprehend, the sole evidence it is possible to produce that anything is desirable, is that people do actually desire it.

And then:

> No reason can be given why the general happiness is desirable, except that each person, so far as he believes it to be attainable, desires his own happiness.

(Both from the Gutenberg text of *Utilitarianism*.)

**Set out, it has three stages:**

1. The only evidence that something is desirable is that people desire it.
2. Each person desires his own happiness.
3. So each person's happiness is a good to that person.
4. So the general happiness is a good to the aggregate of all persons.
5. (Further argument) People desire nothing for its own sake except happiness: things like virtue or money, desired for themselves, have become **parts** of happiness.
6. So happiness is the only thing desirable as an end, and the sole criterion of morality.

**Objection 1: the equivocation on "desirable".** **G. E. Moore** (*Principia Ethica*, 1903) charged that *visible* means *able to be seen*, but *desirable* means **worthy of being desired**, not *able to be desired*. So the analogy fails, and Mill commits what Moore called the **naturalistic fallacy**, defining a moral property by a natural one. This is the best-known objection. **Replies:** Mill never says desire *defines* desirability; he says it is the only **evidence** of it, just as seeing is evidence of visibility. Read so, premise 1 is a claim about evidence, not meaning, and is not obviously false, though one may still doubt it.

**Objection 2: the fallacy of composition (steps 3 to 4).** From "each person's happiness is good for that person" it does not follow that "the general happiness is good for everyone", any more than "each man has a mother" gives "all men have the same mother". **Reply:** in a letter of 1868 (to Henry Jones), Mill clarified, in paraphrase, that he meant only this: since A's happiness is a good, B's a good, C's a good, the **sum** of these goods is a good. That avoids the composition fallacy, though it assumes that goods can be summed impartially, which the egoist denies.

**Objection 3: we desire more than happiness** (step 5). We desire knowledge, virtue, our children's welfare, in themselves. Mill's reply is that these become *parts* of happiness. Critics say this stretches "happiness" until the claim is empty.

**The broad verdict.** There is wide agreement that the proof, **read as a deductive proof, fails**. There is no agreement on whether Mill meant it that way, and many recent scholars read it charitably as a **cumulative argument from evidence**, which he warned us it was.

**Why it matters:** the problem Mill faced, how any ultimate standard can be justified without circularity, does not go away by refuting him. Every ethical theory faces it, and Sidgwick takes it up next.
Mill: On Liberty and the harm principle:
***On Liberty*** (1859) appeared the year after the death of **Harriet Taylor Mill**, whom Mill had known since 1830 and married in 1851, and whom he called in its dedication in part its author. It argues for one principle, and has been quoted in courts and parliaments ever since.

**The new danger.** Earlier struggles for liberty had been against kings. In a democracy, Mill says, the danger is **the tyranny of the majority**, and not only through law: through **social pressure** and public opinion, which can enforce conformity more thoroughly than any police.

**The harm principle.** The only purpose for which power can rightfully be exercised over any adult, against his will, is **to prevent harm to others**. His own good, physical or moral, is not enough. (The exact words are read closely in the next lesson.)

**Its three domains of liberty:**

1. **Thought and expression**: conscience, opinion, speech and publication.
2. **Tastes and pursuits**: "framing the plan of our life to suit our own character", even if others think it foolish.
3. **Association**: combining with others for any purpose not harming others.

**The argument for free speech (chapter 2).** Silencing an opinion is wrong in every case:

| If the silenced opinion is… | Why silencing it is wrong |
| --- | --- |
| **true** | we lose the truth; to silence it assumes our own infallibility |
| **false** | we lose the clearer perception of truth that comes from its collision with error |
| **partly true** | we lose the part of the truth it holds, as most opinions are partial |
| (in every case) | a truth never challenged becomes **dead dogma**, held as prejudice, not understood |

**Individuality (chapter 3).** Human beings are not machines built to a model but trees that need to grow on all sides. Experiments in living, and eccentricity itself, are goods.

**The deep ground is utility**, "in the largest sense, grounded on the permanent interests of man as a progressive being". Mill expressly forgoes any appeal to abstract rights.

**The principal objections:**

- **What is "harm"?** Offence? Moral distress? Economic competition? Mill says ruining a rival in fair trade is a harm society tolerates, and offence is not harm, but where to draw the line is the whole difficulty.
- **No act is purely self-regarding.** The drunkard harms his family, his creditors, his employer. Mill answers in chapter 4: society may punish the breach of a definite duty to others, but not the vice itself.
- **Utility and liberty may conflict.** If paternalism (forcing people for their own good) sometimes makes them happier, a utilitarian should approve it. Mill argues that **in the long run** people are the best judges of their own good. Critics doubt the long run always favours him.
- **Morality and law.** **James Fitzjames Stephen**'s *Liberty, Equality, Fraternity* (1873) argued that law rightly enforces morality; the debate was refought in the 1950s and 60s by **Lord Devlin and H. L. A. Hart** over the decriminalisation of homosexuality.
- **The colonial exception.** Mill limits the principle to "civilised" societies and permits despotism over "barbarians" for their improvement; he spent 35 years (1823–1858) at the East India Company. Critics see a principle with an imperial blind spot; defenders say the limit is about the conditions for free discussion, not race. The dispute is real.
Reading: Mill's On Liberty, chapter 1, t:
The passage below is from chapter 1, "Introductory", of *On Liberty* (1859). Mill wrote in English; the text is the Project Gutenberg edition (eBook 34901), from the Walter Scott Publishing Co. edition of 1901.

> The object of this Essay is to assert one very simple principle, as entitled to govern absolutely the dealings of society with the individual in the way of compulsion and control, whether the means used be physical force in the form of legal penalties, or the moral coercion of public opinion.

**Read slowly.** "One very simple principle": Mill's ambition is a single rule. "Govern absolutely": no exceptions within its domain. And note the two means, **law and public opinion**. The essay is as much about social pressure as about the state.

> That principle is, that the sole end for which mankind are warranted, individually or collectively, in interfering with the liberty of action of any of their number, is self-protection. That the only purpose for which power can be rightfully exercised over any member of a civilised community, against his will, is to prevent harm to others.

**Two formulations.** The first says *self-protection*, the second *to prevent harm to others*. They are meant as one principle, but the second became the standard name: **the harm principle**. "Against his will": consent changes everything. "Civilised community" is a limit Mill will spell out shortly.

> His own good, either physical or moral, is not a sufficient warrant. He cannot rightfully be compelled to do or forbear because it will be better for him to do so, because it will make him happier, because, in the opinions of others, to do so would be wise, or even right.

**The rejection of paternalism**, in three steps rising in strength: better for him, happier, even *right*. So Mill rules out enforcing morality as such, not only enforcing prudence. And note "happier": a utilitarian is refusing to force happiness on people. This is the tension the critics seize.

> These are good reasons for remonstrating with him, or reasoning with him, or persuading him, or entreating him, but not for compelling him, or visiting him with any evil in case he do otherwise.

**The line is between persuading and compelling.** Mill is not saying "mind your own business": argue, plead, warn. What is forbidden is force, legal or social ("visiting him with any evil").

> The only part of the conduct of any one, for which he is amenable to society, is that which concerns others. In the part which merely concerns himself, his independence is, of right, absolute. Over himself, over his own body and mind, the individual is sovereign.

**The image of sovereignty.** The language once used of kings is given to each person over himself. "Merely concerns himself": everything turns on the line between self-regarding and other-regarding conduct, which critics say cannot be drawn cleanly.

**Then the limits.** The next paragraph says the doctrine applies only to "human beings in the maturity of their faculties", not to children, and continues:

> Despotism is a legitimate mode of government in dealing with barbarians, provided the end be their improvement, and the means justified by actually effecting that end.

**Do not skip this.** It is part of the text, and it shows the principle's conditions: liberty applies once people can be improved "by free and equal discussion". Whether this is a principled limit or an imperial prejudice is a real dispute (previous lesson).

**And the foundation:**

> I regard utility as the ultimate appeal on all ethical questions; but it must be utility in the largest sense, grounded on the permanent interests of man as a progressive being.

**The puzzle to take away.** Mill claims an *absolute* principle and grounds it on *utility*, which weighs consequences case by case. Can a principle be both? His answer is that, given what people are, a firm rule of non-interference produces more good over time than case-by-case meddling. Whether that holds is the question the whole essay is meant to settle, and readers still divide on it.
Mill: The Subjection of Women:
***The Subjection of Women*** was written in 1861 and published in **1869**. It is the most important argument for the equality of the sexes by a major philosopher before the twentieth century, and Mill said in his *Autobiography* that much of its thinking came from Harriet Taylor Mill (who had published "The Enfranchisement of Women" in 1851) and her daughter Helen Taylor.

**The thesis**, in his own words in the Gutenberg text:

> That the principle which regulates the existing social relations between the two sexes--the legal subordination of one sex to the other--is wrong in itself, and now one of the chief hindrances to human improvement; and that it ought to be replaced by a principle of perfect equality, admitting no power or privilege on the one side, nor disability on the other.

**The situation he attacked.** In Victorian England a married woman's property and earnings passed to her husband; she could not easily leave him, had no right to her children, and could not vote, enter most professions or attend university.

**His arguments:**

1. **The argument from origins.** Women's subordination did not arise from any judgement that it was best. It arose from **men's greater physical strength**, and was then made law. Every other system of rule by force, slavery included, has been abolished or is being; this one survives because it is more intimate.
2. **The argument from "nature".** Defenders say women are naturally suited to subordination. Mill replies: **we cannot know what women's nature is**, because we have only ever seen women raised under subordination, trained from childhood to submissiveness. In his words: "What is now called the nature of women is an eminently artificial thing--the result of forced repression in some directions, unnatural stimulation in others."
3. **The argument from free choice.** If women are naturally unfit for certain work, there is no need to forbid them by law: competition will exclude them. **Laws that forbid what nature already prevents are pointless**; laws that forbid what women could do are unjust.
4. **The argument from consequences** (the utilitarian ground): equality would double the talent available to society; make marriage a school of justice instead of a school of despotism; and give half of humanity the happiness of a free life.

**Marriage** is the centre of the book. Mill compares the wife's legal position, at its worst, to slavery, and argues that the family, the first school of moral feeling, teaches boys that they rule merely by being male. A marriage of equals would teach justice.

**In Parliament.** As MP for Westminster (1865–1868), Mill moved in 1867 to amend the Reform Bill by replacing "man" with "person", to give women the vote. It was **defeated by 196 votes to 73**, but it began the parliamentary campaign that ended, after 1918 and 1928, in equal suffrage.

**Objections and replies:**

- **Natural difference.** Opponents then and now point to real average differences between the sexes. Mill's reply does not deny difference; it denies that **anyone can know** it is large enough to justify legal barriers, and says that if it is real, free competition will show it.
- **Feminist criticisms from the twentieth century**: Mill largely assumes that most married women will choose to manage the household; and his case rests on utility and individual rights, leaving unexamined the economic structure that critics like Engels (*The Origin of the Family*, 1884) blamed.
- **Utility is a fragile ground** for a right: if subordination made people happier, would it be justified? Mill's argument implies it would not, because it never does; critics want a firmer basis.

**Why it matters:** a first-rate philosopher argued, against nearly all his contemporaries, that a universal social arrangement rested on nothing but force and habit, and was proved substantially right.
Mill: the System of Logic, induction and:
Mill's first great book, ***A System of Logic*** (1843), was a textbook for decades in British universities. It is the most thorough nineteenth-century account of **empiricism**: the view that all knowledge comes from experience.

**Logic, for Mill, is the science of proof**, of reasoning from known truths to others. And all real reasoning, he argued, is ultimately **inductive**: from particular cases to general conclusions. (*Induction*: inferring from observed cases to unobserved ones. *Deduction*: inferring what must follow from premises. Stage 1 sets out the difference.)

**Even the syllogism hides an induction.** Take: All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; so Socrates is mortal. If "all men are mortal" already includes Socrates, the argument begs the question. Mill's answer: the real inference is **from particulars to particulars**. We have seen many men die; we infer that Socrates will. The general proposition is a **register** of past inferences, a memorandum, not the ground.

**Even mathematics is empirical.** Mill held, with almost no one before or since, that **2 + 2 = 4** and the axioms of geometry are very well-confirmed generalisations from experience. Frege's attack on this view (*The Foundations of Arithmetic*, 1884) is generally judged decisive, and is met in Stage 12.

**Mill's methods.** For finding causes, he set out five methods, still taught:

| Method | Idea |
| --- | --- |
| **Agreement** | if cases of an effect share only one circumstance, it is probably the cause |
| **Difference** | if a case with the effect and one without differ in only one circumstance, it is the cause, or part of it |
| **Joint method** | agreement and difference together |
| **Residues** | subtract the known causes of part of an effect; what remains is due to what remains |
| **Concomitant variation** | if one thing varies whenever another does, they are causally connected |

**The problem of induction.** Hume (Stage 9) argued that no inference from observed to unobserved can be justified without assuming that **nature is uniform**, that the future will resemble the past; and that assumption can only be supported by induction, so the justification is circular. Mill accepts that every induction rests on the **uniformity of nature**, and he accepts that this principle is itself known by induction: the widest generalisation of all, confirmed by all experience.

**Is this circular?** Mill's reply: not viciously. The uniformity principle is not a premise from which particular inductions are deduced; it is the **summing-up** of countless successful inductions, and each makes the others more trustworthy. Critics say this simply restates Hume's problem without solving it. There is **broad agreement that Mill did not solve Hume's problem**; whether anyone has is open, and Popper's and Goodman's responses come in Stage 12.

**Names.** Mill also distinguished a word's **denotation** (the things it applies to) from its **connotation** (the attributes it implies). "Man" denotes Socrates, Plato and the rest, and connotes being rational, animal, and so on. **Proper names**, he held, denote but **do not connote**: "Dartmouth" names a town even if the river Dart changes course. This view, rejected by Frege and Russell, was revived a century later by **Saul Kripke** (Stage 12).

**Free will.** In Book 6 Mill argues that human actions are caused like any events, yet that this does not mean they are **compelled**: character is a cause, and we can help shape our character. This "compatibilism" (the view that determinism and freedom are compatible) is close to Hume's.
Sidgwick: The Methods of Ethics and the:
**Henry Sidgwick** (1838–1900) was a Cambridge philosopher of exceptional honesty. In 1869 he resigned his fellowship at Trinity College because it required assent to the Thirty-Nine Articles of the Church of England, which he could no longer give in good conscience; the college kept him on as a lecturer, and the religious test was abolished in 1871. He helped found **Newnham College** for women. His ***The Methods of Ethics*** (1874) is regarded by many moral philosophers as the finest work of classical utilitarianism, and as one of the great books of ethics in English.

**The plan of the book.** Sidgwick does not begin by defending a theory. He asks: what **methods** do ordinary people use to decide what they ought to do? He finds three:

| Method | The ultimate aim |
| --- | --- |
| **Egoism** (egoistic hedonism) | my own greatest happiness |
| **Intuitionism** (common-sense morality) | following moral rules known directly to be right: keep promises, tell the truth, be just |
| **Utilitarianism** (universalistic hedonism) | the greatest happiness of all |

He then examines each, patiently, for clarity and consistency.

**Against intuitionism.** The rules of common-sense morality, when pressed, are **vague and conflict** (when may a promise be broken? how much truth is owed to a dying man?), so they cannot be the self-evident first principles they claim to be. But when we look at **how** we resolve their conflicts, we find ourselves appealing to consequences for happiness. So common-sense morality is, in his phrase, **unconsciously utilitarian**.

**But utilitarianism itself rests on intuitions.** A few principles survive as truly self-evident, he argues, among them:

- **Justice**: what is right for me must be right for anyone similar in similar circumstances.
- **Prudence**: a later good is not to be preferred less than a nearer one merely because it is later.
- **Benevolence**: the good of any one individual is of no more importance, from the point of view (as he put it) of the universe, than the good of any other.

From the last, with the assumption that happiness is the good, utilitarianism follows. **Sidgwick thus unites intuitionism and utilitarianism**: utilitarianism rests on rational intuition.

**The dualism of practical reason.** But egoism survives too. It seems equally self-evident to Sidgwick that it is **reasonable for each person to prefer his own happiness**. Reason then gives two supreme commands, to seek the general good and to seek one's own, and **where they conflict, reason has no way to decide**. This he called the **dualism of practical reason**.

**His argument, set out:**

1. It is self-evident that I ought to pursue the general good, impartially.
2. It is also reasonable for me to pursue my own good above others'.
3. In some cases these conflict.
4. Nothing in reason settles which wins.
5. So practical reason is divided against itself, unless some further fact (such as a moral order of the universe, in which duty and interest coincide) reconciles them.

The book's last pages say, in substance, that without such a reconciliation the cosmos of duty is reduced to a chaos. Sidgwick could neither prove such a reconciliation nor believe it guaranteed; his work in psychical research (he was first president of the Society for Psychical Research, 1882) was partly a search for evidence that might supply it.

**Objections and responses:** many reject premise 2 (impartial reason should treat my good as no more important than anyone else's); others, like **Derek Parfit** (Stage 14), worked a lifetime on whether the dualism can be overcome. **Sidgwick's question is still open.**

**Why he matters:** his method of careful comparison of theories, testing them against considered judgements, is the direct ancestor of **reflective equilibrium** in John Rawls (Stage 14), who admired him and wrote a foreword to a 1981 reprint of the *Methods*.
Darwin's challenge to philosophy:
**Charles Darwin** (1809–1882) published ***On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection*** on **24 November 1859**. The idea had been read the year before, on 1 July 1858, at the Linnean Society in London, in a joint presentation with **Alfred Russel Wallace**, who had reached it independently. *The Descent of Man* (1871) applied it to human beings.

**The theory in four steps:**

1. Living things vary, and much of the variation is inherited.
2. More are born than can survive.
3. Those whose variations suit them better to their surroundings tend to survive and reproduce more.
4. Over vast time, this **natural selection** accumulates small changes into new species, all descended from a few common ancestors.

The first edition ends, in the Gutenberg text of 1859:

> There is grandeur in this view of life, with its several powers, having been originally breathed into a few forms or into one; and that, whilst this planet has gone cycling on according to the fixed law of gravity, from so simple a beginning endless forms most beautiful and most wonderful have been, and are being, evolved.

**Five challenges it set philosophy:**

**1. Design.** William Paley's *Natural Theology* (1802) had argued that the eye is like a watch: so intricately fitted to a purpose that it must have a designer. Natural selection offered a **mechanism that produces the appearance of design without a designer**. Hume's *Dialogues* (1779, Stage 9) had attacked the design argument logically; Darwin supplied an alternative explanation, which is what most readers found decisive. The theological side belongs to the Theology curriculum.

**2. Essences and species.** Since Aristotle (Stage 4), species had been read as **fixed kinds**, each with an essence. Darwin made species populations with blurred edges, changing over time. The old question of **natural kinds** had to be reopened.

**3. Purpose in nature.** Aristotle's final causes, explanation by what something is *for*, seemed either abolished or rebuilt. Biology still speaks of functions, but these can be **cashed out by selection history**: hearts pump blood because hearts that did so were selected.

**4. The place of humans.** If humans descend from other animals, is reason, or morality, or the soul, different in kind or only in degree? Darwin argued in *The Descent of Man* that the moral sense grew from **social instincts**, sympathy above all, plus intelligence and habit.

**5. Ethics and evolution.** **Herbert Spencer** (1820–1903) coined "survival of the fittest" (1864) and built an evolutionary ethics: what furthers evolution is good. This became the loose movement later called **Social Darwinism**. Two great objections:

- **T. H. Huxley**, "Darwin's bulldog", argued in his lecture *Evolution and Ethics* (1893) that ethical progress consists not in imitating the cosmic process but in **combating** it (paraphrase).
- **G. E. Moore** (1903) charged Spencer with the **naturalistic fallacy**: from the fact that something is "more evolved" it does not follow that it is better. Most philosophers accept that **an "ought" cannot simply be read off the course of evolution**, which echoes Hume's is–ought gap (Stage 9).

**A sixth challenge Darwin raised himself.** In a letter of 1881 (to William Graham) he wondered, in paraphrase, whether the convictions of a mind developed from the minds of lower animals can be trusted at all. If minds evolved for survival, not truth, why trust our reasoning about metaphysics? This doubt was taken up in the twentieth century by naturalists and their critics (Alvin Plantinga's evolutionary argument against naturalism, Stage 14).

**Why it matters:** the pragmatists, who come later in this stage, were the first school to take Darwin as their starting point. John Dewey's essay "The Influence of Darwin on Philosophy" (1909) argued that he had shifted philosophy's interest from fixed essences to **change, process and adaptation**.
Nietzsche: the madman and the death of G:
**Friedrich Nietzsche** (1844–1900) was born in Röcken in Saxony, son of a Lutheran pastor who died when he was four. A brilliant student of classical philology, he became a professor at **Basel in 1869, aged 24**. Ill health forced him to resign in 1879. For ten years he wandered between Swiss and Italian boarding houses, writing book after book that almost no one bought. In **January 1889** he collapsed in Turin and never recovered his mind; he died in Weimar on **25 August 1900**.

**His books, in order:** *The Birth of Tragedy* (1872); *Human, All Too Human* (1878); *Daybreak* (1881); ***The Gay Science*** (1882, with a fifth book added in 1887); ***Thus Spoke Zarathustra*** (1883–85); ***Beyond Good and Evil*** (1886); ***On the Genealogy of Morals*** (1887); and in his last sane year, 1888, *Twilight of the Idols*, *The Antichrist* and *Ecce Homo*.

**How to read him.** He wrote in aphorisms, numbered sections, parables and polemic, not in treatises. He said things for effect, contradicted himself, and wore masks, like Kierkegaard. His meaning is **unusually disputed**, and every major claim below has rival readings.

**The death of God.** Section 125 of *The Gay Science* tells a parable. In Thomas Common's translation (1910):

> "Where is God gone?" he called out. "I mean to tell you! _We have killed him_,—you and I! We are all his murderers! But how have we done it? How were we able to drink up the sea? Who gave us the sponge to wipe away the whole horizon?

And a little later:

> God is dead! God remains dead! And we have killed him!

The madman's hearers are not believers but unbelievers, who laugh at him. He ends by saying, in paraphrase, that he has come too early: the deed is done, but its news has not yet reached them.

**What "God is dead" means.** It is **not an argument** that God does not exist. It is a claim about **culture**: belief in the Christian God has become unbelievable to educated Europe, through science, history and Christianity's own demand for truthfulness. The madman's images (the sea drunk up, the horizon wiped away, the earth unchained from its sun) say what has been lost: **the fixed point** that gave up and down, value and meaning.

**The consequence: nihilism.** *Nihilism* (from Latin *nihil*, nothing) is the condition in which the highest values devalue themselves, and nothing seems to matter. Nietzsche thought it was coming, as the long shadow of God's death, for perhaps two centuries.

**The unbelievers' mistake.** The laughing atheists think they can drop God and keep Christian morality: compassion, equality, the sanctity of each soul. Nietzsche thinks this is self-deception. In *Twilight of the Idols* he mocks the English, naming George Eliot (Feuerbach's translator), for believing that one can give up the Christian God and hold on all the tighter to Christian morality (paraphrase). Morality, he argues, was a **whole** with belief in God, and pulling out the keystone brings it down.

**The argument, set out as his defenders would:**

1. Our moral values (equality, pity, guilt, the worth of every soul) were grounded in Christian belief.
2. That belief is no longer credible.
3. Values do not stay valid once their ground is removed; they merely persist from habit.
4. So our values are now groundless, and we face nihilism, unless new values are created.

**Objections:** premise 1 is disputed: Kant, the utilitarians and many others argued that equality and kindness can be grounded in reason or happiness, without God. And premise 3 is an example of the genetic fallacy, if read as saying a value is refuted by its origin. Defenders reply that Nietzsche is not refuting values by origin, but showing they **lose authority** once their claimed source is gone.

The question of God itself is for the Theology curriculum; Nietzsche's question here is **what follows for morality**.
Nietzsche: master morality and slave mor:
In *Beyond Good and Evil* (1886, section 260) and the first essay of ***On the Genealogy of Morals*** (1887), Nietzsche offers a history of morality. A **genealogy**, here, is a history of where a value came from, written to change how we see it.

**Two kinds of morality.**

| | **Master morality** | **Slave morality** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Who made it | the strong, noble, ruling classes of the ancient world | the weak, oppressed and ruled |
| Its pair of terms | **good and bad** | **good and evil** |
| What "good" means | "we, the noble": strong, proud, healthy, truthful, generous | the meek, humble, patient, kind |
| The other term | "bad" means low, common, unfortunate: almost an afterthought, said with pity | "evil" means the master: the strong, the proud, the dangerous; said with hatred |
| How it begins | **affirmation**: saying yes to oneself | **negation**: saying no to the other |

**Ressentiment.** Nietzsche uses the French word for the festering resentment of those who cannot act on their hatred. In Horace B. Samuel's translation (Gutenberg, 1913 printing):

> The revolt of the slaves in morals begins in the very principle of _resentment_ becoming creative and giving birth to values--a resentment experienced by creatures who, deprived as they are of the proper outlet of action, are forced to find their compensation in an imaginary revenge.

**The "slave revolt in morality".** The powerless could not defeat their masters, so they **revalued** the masters' values: strength became evil, weakness became goodness, impotence became patience, inability to strike back became forgiveness, and the masters were promised punishment in another world. Nietzsche credits this revolt to the priestly people of ancient Judaism and its completion to Christianity, and says it **won**: modern democratic morality is its heir. (This passage was later abused by antisemites. Nietzsche himself despised antisemitism and said so repeatedly; see lesson 25.)

**The second and third essays** trace **guilt** (in German *Schuld*, also "debt") to the debtor–creditor relation, and **bad conscience** to instincts that, locked inside society, turn against the self. The third asks why the **ascetic ideal**, self-denial as the highest value, has had such power, and answers, in paraphrase, that humans would rather will nothingness than not will at all.

**What is the genealogy meant to show?** A real interpretive dispute:

- **A debunking reading**: knowing that pity and humility were born of resentment should loosen their hold on us.
- **But Nietzsche knows the genetic fallacy**; he says himself that a thing's origin and its present value are different questions. So others read the genealogy as raising a **question of value**: do these values make for flourishing human life, or for its decline?
- **Nor does he simply side with the masters.** He calls slave morality's revaluation an extraordinarily **creative** and spiritual act, and says the priests made man an *interesting* animal.

**Objections:**

- **Bad history.** The historical story is speculative and often wrong; Nietzsche gives few sources. Defenders: the genealogy is a psychological hypothesis, not a history book.
- **The values he attacks may be true.** Showing that compassion grew from resentment does not show that compassion is not good. The question of what makes a value good is still to answer.
- **Who are the masters now?** His praise of the "blonde beast" (Samuel's rendering) and of noble cruelty reads, after the twentieth century, as dangerous. Readers like Walter Kaufmann argued Nietzsche's real ideal is **self-mastery**, not mastery of others; this is a contested reading.
Nietzsche: will to power, eternal recurr:
These three ideas are Nietzsche's most famous and least agreed upon.

**1. The will to power** (*der Wille zur Macht*). In *Zarathustra* ("On Self-Overcoming") and *Beyond Good and Evil* (sections 13 and 36), Nietzsche suggests that the basic drive of living things is not self-preservation, as Darwin's followers said, but **the will to grow, to expand, to overcome resistance**. Self-preservation is only one result of it. Section 36 extends the idea, hypothetically, to the whole world.

Two readings:

- **Metaphysical**: the will to power is Nietzsche's answer to "what is reality?", a revised version of Schopenhauer's will. **Heidegger** read him so, as the last metaphysician.
- **Psychological**: it is a hypothesis about human and animal motivation, explaining even asceticism and morality as expressions of power. **Walter Kaufmann** and **Maudemarie Clark** argue for this, noting that the metaphysical claims are mainly in his **unpublished notebooks**.

"Power" here is not mainly political domination. It includes the artist's mastery of his material and the philosopher's mastery of himself.

**2. The eternal recurrence.** Section 341 of *The Gay Science*, titled "The Heaviest Burden", in Thomas Common's translation (1910):

> What if a demon crept after thee into thy loneliest loneliness some day or night, and said to thee: "This life, as thou livest it at present, and hast lived it, thou must live it once more, and also innumerable times; and there will be nothing new in it, but every pain and every joy and every thought and every sigh, and all the unspeakably small and great in thy life must come to thee again, and all in the same series and sequence

Would you curse the demon, or call it divine?

Two readings again:

- **Cosmological**: time is infinite and the states of matter finite, so everything must repeat. Nietzsche sketched such an argument in his notebooks. **Georg Simmel** (1907) refuted it: three wheels turning at rates in irrational ratio will never return to the same arrangement, even in infinite time. There is broad agreement the cosmological proof fails.
- **Practical**: recurrence is a **test** of one's attitude to life. Could you will your life, unchanged, forever? To say yes is **amor fati**, love of one's fate. This is the reading most commentators now prefer, though it is unclear whether Nietzsche thought it was also literally true.

**3. The Übermensch** (overman; the older translation "Superman"). In *Zarathustra* (1883–85), the prophet comes down from his mountain and preaches, in Common's translation (1909):

> Lo, I teach you the Superman!
>
> The Superman is the meaning of the earth.

The overman is the type who could **create new values** after the death of God, affirming the earth and this life rather than another world, and who could say yes to the eternal recurrence. The contrast is the **last man**, who wants only comfort and safety, and blinks.

**Objections:**

- **Is it an ideal or a fantasy?** Nietzsche gives no clear picture of the overman; critics call it empty. Defenders say it is deliberately open, since new values cannot be described in advance.
- **Creating values** seems arbitrary: if values are made, why prefer Nietzsche's? He would answer that values that affirm life are healthier than those that deny it, which uses **health** as a standard he does not justify.
- **Biology.** Some early readers took the overman as a future species bred by evolution. Most scholars reject this; Nietzsche mocked Darwinists and the idea of progress.
Nietzsche: perspectivism, and how his si:
**Perspectivism** is the name for Nietzsche's view of knowledge. The clearest statement in his published work is in the third essay of the *Genealogy* (section 12), in Horace B. Samuel's translation:

> There is only a seeing from a perspective, only a "knowing" from a perspective, and the more emotions we express over a thing, the more eyes, different eyes, we train on the same thing, the more complete will be our "idea" of that thing, our "objectivity."

**What it says.** There is no "view from nowhere", no pure, will-less knowing (a dig at Schopenhauer). All knowing is from a point of view, shaped by interests and drives. But note the second half: **more perspectives give a more complete objectivity**. That is not "anything goes".

**The famous slogan**, in paraphrase, that there are no facts, only interpretations, comes from the **notebooks**, not his published books.

**The self-refutation objection.** If all claims are mere perspectives, then so is perspectivism, so why should we believe it? **Replies:** on the *Genealogy* reading, perspectivism denies only that there is a perspective-free knowing, not that some perspectives are better than others. Maudemarie Clark (*Nietzsche on Truth and Philosophy*, 1990) argued that the mature Nietzsche accepted ordinary truth and rejected only the metaphysical idea of a "true world" behind appearances. Others (often in French post-structuralist readings, Stage 13) read him as a radical sceptic about truth. **A live dispute.**

**The misuse.** Nietzsche's sister **Elisabeth Förster-Nietzsche** (1846–1935) married **Bernhard Förster**, a leading antisemitic agitator, in 1885. In 1887 they founded a colony, Nueva Germania, in Paraguay, meant to be free of Jews. It failed; Förster killed himself in 1889. Nietzsche had **broken with them over their antisemitism**, which he despised, writing to his sister angrily about it; his books contain many attacks on antisemites, and he broke with Wagner partly for the same reason.

**After his collapse**, Elisabeth took control of his papers. She founded the **Nietzsche Archive** (1894, moving to Weimar in 1897), controlled access, and shaped his image:

| What she did | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| Compiled ***The Will to Power*** from his notebooks (1901; enlarged 1906), arranging fragments he had set aside into a "main work" he never wrote | gave the impression of a systematic doctrine of power |
| Edited and in some cases **forged or altered letters** (shown by Karl Schlechta in the 1950s) | made herself his chief confidante and softened his hostility to her and her politics |
| Courted nationalist and then **Nazi** patrons; **Hitler visited the Archive** in the 1930s and attended her funeral in 1935 | the regime presented Nietzsche as a prophet of the master race |

Nazi readers, like **Alfred Baeumler**, quoted his praise of power and hardness and ignored his contempt for nationalism, the German Reich and antisemitism.

**The recovery.** **Walter Kaufmann**'s *Nietzsche: Philosopher, Psychologist, Antichrist* (1950) argued that the Nazi Nietzsche was a falsification. The critical edition of **Giorgio Colli and Mazzino Montinari** (from 1967) printed the notebooks as he left them, in order, ending the authority of *The Will to Power*.

**A fair conclusion.** There is broad scholarly agreement that the Nazi reading was a distortion, and that he was **no antisemite and no German nationalist**. But scholars still debate how far his **anti-egalitarianism**, his praise of hierarchy and his celebrations of cruelty lent themselves to abuse. Both can be true: he was misused, and his writing was misusable.
Peirce: the pragmatic maxim and fallibil:
**Charles Sanders Peirce** (pronounced "purse"; 1839–1914), of Cambridge, Massachusetts, son of a Harvard mathematician, was a scientist for thirty years at the US Coast and Geodetic Survey, a logician of genius, and the founder of **pragmatism**. He never held a permanent academic post: his lectureship at Johns Hopkins (1879–1884) ended amid scandal, and he died poor in Milford, Pennsylvania, leaving tens of thousands of manuscript pages.

**The setting.** In the early 1870s Peirce, William James, the future judge Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr. and others met in Cambridge as the **Metaphysical Club**. From those talks came two papers in *Popular Science Monthly*: **"The Fixation of Belief"** (1877) and **"How to Make Our Ideas Clear"** (1878).

**Belief and doubt.** Peirce (influenced by the psychologist Alexander Bain) treats a belief as a **habit of action**, and doubt as an uneasy state that drives **inquiry**, the struggle to reach belief again. There are four ways to settle belief:

| Method | How | Its failing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Tenacity** | cling to what you already believe | collides with other people's beliefs |
| **Authority** | let the state or church decide | cannot fix every question; breeds doubt in reflective minds |
| **A priori** | believe what seems agreeable to reason | makes belief a matter of taste and fashion |
| **Science** | let belief be fixed by something **independent of us**, real things, through experience | the only method that can correct itself |

**The pragmatic maxim.** How do we make an idea fully clear? Not only by definition (Descartes's clear and distinct ideas are not enough) but by its **practical consequences**. In the 1878 paper, from the text on Wikisource:

> Consider what effects, which might conceivably have practical bearings, we conceive the object of our conception to have. Then, our conception of these effects is the whole of our conception of the object.

**An example he gives:** to call a thing **hard** means that it will not be scratched by many other substances. If two hypotheses predict no conceivable difference in experience, they mean the same; a dispute between them is merely verbal.

**Truth and reality.** From the same paper:

> The opinion which is fated to be ultimately agreed to by all who investigate, is what we mean by the truth, and the object represented in this opinion is the real.

**Fallibilism.** Peirce's name for the view that **any of our beliefs may turn out to be wrong**. We never reach certainty; but inquiry, carried on long enough by a community, tends toward the truth. Hence his rule, in paraphrase: do not block the way of inquiry.

**Objections:**

- **Buried secrets.** Some truths, such as how many hairs were on Caesar's head when he crossed the Rubicon, will never be agreed on by any inquiry. Are they then not true? Peirce later reformulated the account in terms of what inquiry **would** reach if pushed far enough, a subjunctive. Critics say this either is not a definition of truth or quietly assumes one.
- **Is the maxim verificationism?** It looks like the logical positivists' verification principle (Stage 12). Peirce's maxim is more liberal: it speaks of **conceivable** effects and habits, not only observations.

**After James popularised "pragmatism"** in 1898 in a direction he disliked, Peirce renamed his own view **pragmaticism** (1905), a word, he said in paraphrase, ugly enough to be safe from kidnappers. He also did founding work in **semiotics** (the theory of signs: icon, index, symbol), logic of relations, and **abduction**, inference to an explanatory hypothesis.
William James: The Will to Believe and t:
**William James** (1842–1910), brother of the novelist Henry James, trained as a doctor, founded experimental psychology in America, and wrote ***The Principles of Psychology*** (1890), famous for its picture of thought as a continuous stream. He then turned to philosophy, and made pragmatism famous: *The Will to Believe* (lecture 1896, book 1897), *The Varieties of Religious Experience* (1902), ***Pragmatism*** (1907) and *The Meaning of Truth* (1909).

**1. The Will to Believe.** James is answering the mathematician **W. K. Clifford**'s essay "The Ethics of Belief" (1877), which James quotes:

> It is wrong always, everywhere, and for every one, to believe anything upon insufficient evidence.

(As quoted by James in the 1897 Gutenberg text.)

James defines an **option**, a choice between hypotheses, as:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Living or dead** | is each hypothesis a real possibility for you? |
| **Forced or avoidable** | is there no third way, no standing aside? |
| **Momentous or trivial** | is the stake great, the chance unique, the choice irreversible? |

A **genuine** option is living, forced and momentous. His thesis, in his words:

> Our passional nature not only lawfully may, but must, decide an option between propositions, whenever it is a genuine option that cannot by its nature be decided on intellectual grounds

**The argument, set out:**

1. Some genuine options cannot be settled by evidence.
2. In such cases, suspending judgement is itself a decision, with the same risk of losing the truth.
3. Clifford's rule says: better to risk loss of truth than chance of error. That is itself a preference, a passional choice.
4. Another rule is equally rational: better to risk error than lose the chance of truth.
5. So in genuine, evidence-undecidable options, we are entitled to believe.

**Some truths even need belief first**: whether someone likes me may depend on my believing they might. James applies the argument above all to religious belief, which for many is a genuine option.

**Objections:** it licenses **wishful thinking** (critics joked that it should have been called the will to make-believe); premise 1 is the weak point, since Clifford would deny that any option is truly undecidable and forced. **Reply:** James restricts the right strictly to genuine options that evidence cannot settle, and does not license belief against evidence. Pascal's wager (Stage 8) is a cousin, though James criticised it.

**2. Truth.** In *Pragmatism*, James applied Peirce's maxim to truth itself. What difference does it make if an idea is true? True ideas, he wrote (in capitals, in the Gutenberg text), are "those that we can assimilate, validate, corroborate and verify"; they work. The "cash-value" of truth is its role in experience. And, in the Gutenberg text of *Pragmatism*:

> 'The true,' to put it very briefly, is only the expedient in the way of our thinking, just as 'the right' is only the expedient in the way of our behaving.

**Objections, quickly made and still standard:**

- **Russell** (1908) and **Moore** (1907): "it is true that others exist" plainly does not **mean** "it is useful to believe that others exist". A belief can be useful and false, or true and useless.
- **Truth becomes relative and changing**: James wrote that "Truth HAPPENS to an idea": it becomes true. Critics say he confuses **truth** with **verification**.

**James's reply** (*The Meaning of Truth*) was that he never denied that true ideas **agree with reality**; he was explaining what that agreement consists in, and that "expedient" meant expedient **in the long run and on the whole**, as the sentence quoted above goes on to say. Peirce himself thought James too loose. Whether the theory survives, in revised forms like those of Dewey and later Richard Rorty, is open.
Solovyov and the Russian religious philo:
In nineteenth-century Russia, philosophy grew up late and in argument with the West: with German idealism, French positivism, and the question of whether Russia should follow Europe (the "Westernisers") or its own Orthodox and Slavic tradition (the "Slavophiles", such as Ivan Kireevsky and Alexei Khomiakov, active in the 1840s and 50s). Its greatest figure was **Vladimir Solovyov** (1853–1900).

**His life.** Son of the historian Sergei Solovyov, he passed through a youthful atheism and materialism and returned to Christianity. His master's thesis, ***The Crisis of Western Philosophy: Against the Positivists*** (1874), argued that Western thought, having passed through rationalism and empiricism, had reached a dead end in positivism. In 1878 he gave the ***Lectures on Godmanhood*** (or *Divine Humanity*) in St Petersburg; **Dostoevsky**, his friend, attended. In 1881, after the assassination of Alexander II, he publicly urged the new tsar to pardon the assassins, and was effectively barred from teaching. His later works include *The Justification of the Good* (1897) and *Three Conversations* (1900), which ends with a "short tale of the Antichrist".

**Total-unity** (Russian *vseedinstvo*). Solovyov's central idea: reality is an organic whole, in which God, the world and humanity are united without losing their differences. Western philosophy, he argued, had fallen into **abstract principles**: each school seizes one part of the truth (reason alone, experience alone, the individual alone, the state alone) and absolutises it. His *Critique of Abstract Principles* (1880) sets out to reunite them in **free theosophy** (an integral knowledge joining science, philosophy and faith), **free theocracy** (society) and **free theurgy** (art and creative life).

**Godmanhood.** History is the process by which humanity, in union with the divine, becomes what it is meant to be; Christ is the pattern. Linked to this is **Sophia**, divine Wisdom, which Solovyov said he had seen in visions (once in the British Museum reading room, once in the Egyptian desert, in 1875–76).

**The Justification of the Good** is his moral philosophy, read as philosophy. Morality, he argued, has three roots in primary feelings:

| Feeling | Relation |
| --- | --- |
| **Shame** | to what is below us: our animal nature, which we must not simply be |
| **Pity** | to our equals: other people and creatures |
| **Reverence** | to what is above us: the good, God |

These grow into a full ethics that, he argued, shows morality as **autonomous** (it can be known without first proving God), yet pointing beyond itself.

**Objections:** critics find his system speculative, closer to Schelling and Hegel than to argument, and his talk of Sophia mystical rather than philosophical. Defenders reply that his critique of "abstract principles" is a serious philosophical diagnosis, close to Hegel's, and his ethics of shame, pity and reverence stands on its own.

**His successors** in the early twentieth century, Nikolai Berdyaev, Sergei Bulgakov, Pavel Florensky, Semyon Frank and Nikolai Lossky, carried his ideas into theology and philosophy, many in exile after 1922. Their theology, and Solovyov's (Sophiology above all), belongs to the Theology curriculum.
Brentano: intentionality, the mark of th:
**Franz Brentano** (1838–1917) was a German Catholic priest, ordained in 1864, who taught at Würzburg. Troubled by the doctrine of papal infallibility declared in 1870, he **left the priesthood in 1873**. In 1874 he became professor in Vienna, and when he married in 1880 (Austrian law did not allow former priests to marry, so he gave up his citizenship and married in Saxony), he lost his chair but taught on as a lecturer until 1895.
